Trump announced a “massive” potash deal with Belarus—Lukashenka said the same day there is no spare potash to sell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:04:30 UTC
00:04:30 KST

US President Donald Trump announced a "massive deal" to buy Belarusian potash at prices far below what the US pays Canada, but Belarusian dictator Alyaksandr Lukashenka publicly contradicted him the same day, saying Belarus has no spare volumes to sell.
Washington has spent a year courting Lukashenka with sanctions relief and envoy visits in pursuit of both prisoner releases and trade openings—but the potash episode shows the limits of that courtship when the dictator's own supply chain cannot deliver what the US President has already promised his voters.
Trump promised cheaper potash for American farmers
Trump wrote on Truth Social on 21 September:
"The United States is working on a massive Deal with respect to the purchase of Potash from Belarus. The pricing would be for substantially less than we are currently paying to Canada, very good news for our Farmers and Ranchers."
Potash is a key ingredient in fertilizer. Canada is the world's largest supplier—the US takes 53% of Canadian potash exports, and 80% of the potash American farms use comes from Canada. Canadian potash remains exempt from US tariffs despite the ongoing trade war between the two countries.
The announcement came as Trump's trade dispute with Ottawa deepened—he recently called Canada a "terrible trade partner," and on 16 September European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate EU membership, which Trump said could be a "hostile act."
Lukashenka said all output is contracted
The same day, Lukashenka told officials Belarus cannot deliver. "Even if we wanted to supply potash to other, Western markets, we simply do not have those volumes—everything is contracted," he said during a meeting with the head of Belarus's State Customs Committee, Uladzimir Arlouski.
Arlouski reported that 85% of all Belarusian exports and imports now move eastward—primarily to China, other Asian countries, and Russia. Budget revenues grew almost 3.5% over eight months, and 5.2% so far this month.
A deal built on sanctions relief and prisoner swaps
The potash announcement followed a year-long US effort to engage Lukashenka. Washington lifted sanctions on Belarus's potash industry in exchange for the release of hundreds of political prisoners. US special envoy John Cole has played the central role, meeting Lukashenka last week and securing the release of 25 prisoners—far fewer than the 200 he had previously promised.
Over the course of Cole's effort, at least several hundred people have been freed, among them Nobel Peace Prize laureate Ales Bialiatski and Siarhei Tsikhanouski, husband of the internationally recognized winner of Belarus's 2020 presidential election. But human rights groups and freed prisoners say Lukashenka runs a "carousel"—arresting new political opponents to replace the ones he releases. Lukashenka denied this. "There are no political prisoners in Belarus," he claimed during last week's meeting with Cole.
With US midterms six weeks away on 3 November and the Republican Party struggling in the polls, Trump has been scrambling for wins on fuel and food prices. The same week, he urged Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian refineries, blaming Ukraine rather than his own war with Iran for record US diesel prices—a move a senior European official told Politico was a search for "scapegoats."

New rotation of US troops bound for Lithuania, Lithuanian president says

It comes despite repeated threats from US President Donald Trump to reduce the US' military presence in Europe.
Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda announced on Tuesday that a new group of American troops was heading to Lithuania.
"I have just received confirmation that the new rotation of U.S. troops is already on its way," Nausėda wrote in a post on social media, while also thanking the Trump administration for the decision.
"The U.S. military presence in Lithuania is an indispensable part of our deterrence and collective defence," he said, adding that the move was "important not only for Lithuania, but also for the security of the entire region."
It comes despite repeated threats from US President Donald Trump to reduce the US' military presence in Europe, as he increasingly shifts his focus to the Middle East and Latin America.
Lithuanian media reported in June that around 1,000 US troops had begun withdrawing from the Baltic state as their deployment came to an end.
Presidential adviser Deividas Matulionis told Lithuania's LRT Radio on Tuesday that the number of new US soldiers arriving in the country would not be lower than the last deployment.
Kęstutis Budrys, Lithuania's Foreign Minister, has hailed the move, saying the "decision on continued U.S. military presence in Lithuania is a powerful signal of Allied unity and resolve."
"Lithuania stands proud as committed Ally, leading by example with 5% defence spending, strengthening national capabilities, and providing the best training conditions for Allied forces," he wrote on X.
NATO's eastern flank
Lithuania sits in a crucial spot on NATO's eastern flank, bordering Russia's Kaliningrad region to the southwest as well as Russian ally Belarus to the east and south.
Its strategic location has seen the country, along with its Baltic neighbours Latvia and Estonia, increasingly impacted by Moscow's war in Ukraine, including a growing number of drone and airspace incidents in recent months.
Speaking to Euronews in May following a drone incursion over Vilnius, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas warned that the Baltics must be prepared for further such threats.
"This is the new reality of what the Baltic states face,” he told the Europe Today news programme.
“We need to adapt because the possibility of repeated similar scenarios is very high," he added.

Ukraine Has Pushed Russia’s Black Sea Fleet Into a Repair Trap
Ukraine’s repeated strikes on Russia’s Black Sea Fleet have created a growing maintenance problem for Moscow, leaving damaged warships with few safe places where they can undergo lengthy repairs without becoming stationary targets.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian Navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk on September 22, Russia is struggling to conduct full-scale maintenance at its Novorossiysk base, while its primary repair infrastructure in temporarily occupied Crimea has become increasingly difficult to use because of Ukrainian strikes.
For major repairs, Russian vessels need to enter dry dock and remain immobilized for extended periods—making them considerably more vulnerable to Ukrainian attacks.
“Therefore, there can currently be no talk of any prolonged repairs or maintenance,” Pletenchuk said.
The pressure comes as Russia’s naval missile capability in the Black Sea has also narrowed. Pletenchuk said Moscow currently retains two surface ships capable of carrying cruise missiles, as well as two submarines that have recently seen little operational use.
Russian surface vessels have also continued to suffer damage. Pletenchuk named the Admiral Essen and Admiral Makarov frigates, as well as a Buyan-M-class small missile ship, among vessels that have been struck.
Novorossiysk has become the main refuge for much of Russia’s Black Sea Fleet after Ukrainian attacks made operations from temporarily occupied Crimea increasingly dangerous.
However, concentrating ships there has created another vulnerability: vessels requiring serious maintenance must remain in predictable locations long enough to undergo repairs, potentially exposing them to further strikes.
Russia’s main Black Sea Fleet repair facilities remain in temporarily occupied Crimea, but Ukrainian operations against military infrastructure on the peninsula have significantly complicated Moscow’s ability to rely on those bases.
Despite the reduced activity of Russian warships, the threat from the Black Sea region remains. Pletenchuk said Russia continues to rely primarily on missiles, drones, and aircraft for attacks against Ukraine.
He added that Russian aviation remains active in the operational area, while Ukrainian strikes against military targets in temporarily occupied Crimea are aimed at further reducing Russia’s ability to launch attacks from the peninsula.
Earlier, on September 9, Ukraine struck Russia’s naval hub in Novorossiysk with missiles and drones, hitting at least three Black Sea Fleet vessels, including the Kalibr-capable frigate Admiral Essen. Separate imagery also indicated possible damage to the Admiral Makarov frigate and a Buyan-M-class missile ship.

Lithuania’s parliament votes to remove ban on hosting nuclear weapons in first of three votes
Lithuania’s parliament voted to remove from the Constitution the article banning the stationing of nuclear weapons on its territory, according to LRT. Ninety-nine lawmakers voted in favor, 13 voted against, and five abstained.
For the amendment to take permanent effect, parliament must approve it in two more votes held three months apart: the first on October 9, the second on January 12. At least 94 of the 141 lawmakers must support it for the amendment to pass.
In early June, the Financial Times reported that the United States was negotiating the stationing of nuclear weapons in Poland and the Baltic states, citing sources who said the talks involve American bombers capable of carrying nuclear weapons. Lithuanian authorities confirmed that they are holding these talks and are considering corresponding amendments to the Constitution.
In September, the Kremlin said that Lithuania would be “in the crosshairs” of Russian nuclear weapons if it stationed a nuclear arsenal on its territory.
American dual-capable aircraft able to carry nuclear weapons are currently stationed in six NATO countries: Belgium, the United Kingdom, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, and Turkey.
Russia stationed its nuclear weapons in Belarus after the start of the full-scale war with Ukraine.

Reform UK turns to YouTube to sidestep UK broadcast rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

Breadcrumb
Reform UK turns to YouTube to sidestep UK broadcast rules, reach voters
Reform UK's new YouTube venture could be "massively disruptive" to British political communications and news reporting, digital media consultant Matt Capon told The New Arab, as the party prepares to launch its own broadcasting platform following a string of controversies over racist and anti-Muslim rhetoric involving its representatives.
The far-right party, led by Nigel Farage, is planning to launch Reform TV on YouTube, with Reform sources telling The Times that the platform was chosen partly because it is not subject to the same Ofcom broadcasting rules governing traditional television channels.
Capon warned that the venture could find a significant audience and further blur the line between political campaigning and news-style broadcasting, allowing Reform to communicate directly with voters without many of the rules imposed on conventional broadcasters.
"I think they'll find an audience for it, I'm really sad to say," Capon told The New Arab.
The prospect of a Reform-controlled broadcasting operation is likely to attract particular scrutiny given repeated controversies surrounding figures associated with the party.
Reform representatives and candidates have faced a series of allegations over racist, antisemitic and anti-Muslim remarks, while some party figures have also faced scrutiny over links to far-right activists.
Earlier this month, Reform home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf was accused of "straightforward racism" by a government minister after questioning whether a Somali-born British politician who came to the UK as a child was "British".
Several Reform councillors have also been identified as members of a Facebook group linked to the far-right Patriot Platform, although some have denied links to the organisation or distanced themselves from it.
Farage himself has faced renewed scrutiny over his past rhetoric and associations, including allegations about racist and antisemitic comments dating back to his school years, which he has denied.
Online content accessible in Britain remains subject to legislation including the Online Safety Act, which Capon said "could help [curb the channel's use of discriminatory language] to an extent", but warned that "it won't deal with everything".
The venture would therefore give Reform a powerful platform from which to communicate directly with supporters while avoiding some of the regulatory requirements that apply to conventional television broadcasters.
Reform's links to GB News
Reform UK is already closely linked to GB News, where Farage currently hosts a prime-time programme three nights a week.
GB News presenter Matt Goodwin also unsuccessfully stood as a Reform candidate in February's Gorton and Denton parliamentary by-election.
The launch of Reform's own channel, however, could put the party in direct competition with a broadcaster that has provided considerable airtime to Farage and other figures associated with Reform.
GB News has recorded a higher average television audience than both Sky News and BBC News, but the prospect of Reform building its own digital platform appears to have prompted concern about whether some viewers could be drawn away.
On Friday night, GB News presenter and former Conservative MP Jacob Rees-Mogg made a direct appeal to his audience.
"I know you are wonderful, clever people and will remain loyal to GB News," he said.
The BBC has also repeatedly found itself in Farage's sights.
The Reform leader has said he would strip the broadcaster of the licence fee, one of its principal sources of funding.
He also accused the BBC of "double standards" after the corporation's Today programme questioned him over allegations that he made racist and antisemitic remarks while at school.
The emergence of a Reform-controlled channel would allow Farage and other party figures to reach viewers without relying on interviews or appearances on traditional broadcasters, where politicians can face independent questioning and editorial scrutiny.
£72 million funding boost
Reform's push into digital broadcasting comes shortly after the party received two donations totalling £72 million from cryptocurrency billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne.
The enormous injection of cash gives Reform considerable resources to professionalise and expand its political and communications operations, including its push into digital media.
Capon said the money would make it considerably easier for the party to establish its own broadcasting operation.
"I think that that piggy bank that's been thrown at Mr Farage and Mr Tice, that's definitely going to help with this," he told The New Arab.
The unprecedented donations have also intensified scrutiny of the influence extremely wealthy individuals can exercise over British politics and the country's political finance rules.
The planned channel could allow Reform to pour some of its new resources into producing and distributing its own political programming directly to voters, bypassing the editorial scrutiny that comes with appearing on independent broadcasters.
It would also give the party much greater control over how Farage and other Reform figures are presented, what issues they focus on and which voices are given a platform.
That prospect is particularly significant as political parties increasingly use social media and online video to circumvent traditional media organisations and communicate directly with voters.
For Reform, its own channel could become a permanent platform for its political messaging at a time when the party has acquired unprecedented financial resources and continues to face scrutiny over the rhetoric and conduct of some of its representatives.
Reform UK did not respond to The New Arab's request for comment.

Learning from Ukraine war, Chinese military doctors target injuries from drones
Head, face and neck injuries are becoming a big problem in armed conflicts dominated by uncrewed aerial vehicles
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Alcott Weiin Beijing
China’s military medical experts are making progress in finding cures for common injuries seen in drone warfare, drawing on lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, according to state broadcaster CCTV.
Chen Juxiang, a senior Chinese military doctor, told CCTV on Monday that cranio-maxillofacial injuries – damage to the hard and soft tissues of the head – had become a particularly big problem in conflicts dominated by drones.
Chen, director of neurosurgery at the First Affiliated Hospital of Naval Medical University, cited battlefield experience from Ukraine and the US-Iran conflict, saying that “in drone warfare, cranio-maxillofacial injuries account for more than 30 per cent of battlefield trauma”.
Chen said his team had been preparing for the shift for years and had made progress in treatment protocols and haemostatic materials for these kinds of head injuries.

Big tech says AI can find a cure for cancer. So where is it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:00:04 UTC
00:00:04 KST

Her name was June. June would be the last month she ever knew.
I remember the way her bed made her so small, swallowed her up in the middle of the room, turned as it was to face the window. With her liver failing, her skin was a ghostly apricot. June – I called her Nan – had been stalked by the king of terrors, the emperor of all maladies: cancer. That son of a bitch.
The cancer was in her pancreas. Odds of survival? “Not good” – putting it lightly. The maths, putting it darkly: it’s the 12th most common cancer worldwide, the sixth most common cause of cancer death. The World Health Organization says it is “one of the cancer types with the least favourable prognosis”. It was not favourable for my grandmother.
June died nine years ago. Lately I’ve been thinking about alternate futures – the ones in which my grandmother, and the many millions diagnosed with cancer each year, are still here. The thoughts creep in as we are bombarded by artificial intelligence chief executives making bold proclamations such as “AI will cure cancer in five to 10 years” or “AI will cure cancer in our lifetimes”. Those claims stand in contrast to apocalyptic scenarios, including AI being responsible for human extinction before 2030. AI, we hear, is both saviour and annihilator.
Park the world-ending scenarios and you’ll find there has been significant progress in using AI as a tool in the detection, prevention and treatment of cancer. If there is a future where a supposed AI apocalypse is averted, then it may be one in which cancer therapy has been completely redefined. But just how far can AI take us towards a cure?
Today AI is being turned toward drug development, treatment plans and, in some places, it’s being used clinically, studying imagery of lungs for early signs of malignancy and helping to remove brain tumours. Words like “efficiency” and “personalised care” are everywhere; the notion AI can free up time for doctors and medical professionals to get away from the busywork abound.
Cancer is not a single disease
Even with such positive advances, speak to clinicians, oncologists and researchers working at the coalface and you quickly find there is tension between the more grandiose claims of big tech and its race to “solve” disease, and the deliberate, considered progress of science.
“Until AI can actually think and do experiments itself at scale, I’m not sure that we’re going to find a cure for all cancer or medical illness in the next 10 years,” says Sherene Loi, a medical oncologist who specialises in breast cancer treatment at the Peter MacCallum Cancer Centre in Melbourne.
But Loi and other cancer experts the Guardian has spoken to believe there will be efficiencies for treatment, diagnostics and pathology services that will bear fruit, heralding more personalised and more equitable cancer care.
Cancer is not a single disease. It’s a catch-all term that describes the uncontrollable growth of abnormal cells. Typically, we describe cancers based on the location within the body that they are found: breast, prostate, lung, brain, blood, pancreas. These are complex, highly variable diseases, affecting a variety of different cells and underpinned by a host of genetic changes. In addition, cancer outcomes depend on many factors, including the biology of the disease and the treatments available. A single cure for cancer is not only unlikely but nigh on impossible.
Just take the brain. Though not all are cancerous, “there are more than 100 types of tumours in the brain, much more than in any other single organ”, says Felix Sahm, a neuropathologist at the University Hospital Heidelberg. “There are so many unresolved questions in brain tumour research and brain tumour care.”
We’ve made great leaps in cancer survival rates over the past century; chemotherapy and radiation have enabled solid tumours to be cured, monoclonal antibodies ushered in more direct targeting of abnormal cells, and emerging treatments are rewriting how we combat the disease. But, as Loi notes, “Human disease is very complex.” So where does AI fit in?
A shadow on a scan
“AI can improve several parts of that process by helping us identify risk, detect disease, characterise tumours, select treatments and monitor,” says Ajit Goenka, a radiologist and nuclear medicine specialist at the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota.
Medical imaging, in particular, stands to benefit from advances in AI and machine-learning models. Training models on huge amounts of patient data, such as CT scans, X-rays or tissue samples, enables those models to detect changes or patterns that may be imperceptible to the human eye.
Goenka has been exploring the early detection of pancreatic cancer with machine-learning tools since 2021, before the release of ChatGPT fully turned the public’s head toward generative AI. Since then, OpenAI and its rival Anthropic have pushed into new realms beyond chatbots: partnering with companies to accelerate access to treatment; striking deals with research centres; and working with pharmaceutical companies to incorporate large language models and AI into drug discovery.
Goenka noticed that some patients who developed pancreatic cancer had undergone CT scans months or years before diagnosis. Those scans were interpreted as normal but Goenka reasoned there could be microscopic, measurable changes invisible to a radiologist. “We began studying whether quantitative imaging and machine-learning methods could detect that signal,” he says.
In a proof-of-concept paper published in 2022, he confirmed that hunch. Machine-learning tools can detect pancreatic tumours, including in pancreases that appeared normal, before clinical diagnosis. Further studies by Goenka’s group have explored how robust and reproducible the method is and whether it is useful across institutions. The opportunity, he says, is to identify evidence of cancer earlier. My grandmother’s pancreatic cancer appeared as if out of nowhere, a shadow on a scan. Goenka’s models may have been able to see it sooner, which could have improved her outcome.
Reducing the duration of uncertainty
Sahm leads a European multi-disciplinary collaboration called EUcanAI, which is using agentic AI to improve the way brain tumours and central nervous system cancers are treated. The idea is that “every single chunk of this journey gets informed by the previous one and informs the next one in the sequence, so that it gets more efficient, quicker and less cumbersome for a patient”, he says.
He provides one example of a teenager who presented with a tumour in his brain stem. The expectation was that it was fatal, based on imaging and the patient’s age. The patient went in for surgery, his tumour was biopsied and rapidly sequenced to determine the mutations driving his disease.
Traditionally, these results go to a board of specialists to discuss the next steps in surgery and treatment. But today, these results can be delivered during a surgery, saving patients time and money. Sahm imagines a world where agentic AI accelerates this process even further – a surgeon could biopsy and image a tumour, then have an AI provide answers about the kind of mutation and potential drugs that may treat it. Sahm says this work is already happening in trials but stresses it is not yet routine.
The key for Sahm is a more tailored journey for each patient that “reduces the duration of uncertainty”. It’s about providing a wholly optimised approach to managing a patient’s cancer journey. He also notes it could provide more patients with better care.
This was a common thread in discussing AI tools for cancer diagnostics. “I think it will help with regards to equity of care, and access to care,” Loi says.
For instance, she says, in rural communities or locations that do not have cancer facilities or access to specialists or specialist diagnostic tools, access to machine-learning models could help medical professionals provide faster, more complete answers.
Can AI ‘solve’ disease?
The dream of curing cancer is one that big AI firms constantly seed. Dario Amodei, the head of Anthropic, has suggested that within a decade, cancer – and many other diseases – could be cured. The Google DeepMind spin-off, IsoLabs, has a bold mission statement to “solve” all disease.
Sam Altman, the head of OpenAI, has similar lofty goals, suggesting the ability to solve disease might just be a problem of how much computing power backs our AI systems. “Maybe with 10 gigawatts of compute, AI can figure out how to cure cancer,” he wrote. As AI firms experience growing backlash to the environmental cost of datacentres, the argument that just a little more compute could offer life-saving opportunities could be hard to sell.
But Emilia Javorsky, a physician and scientist at the Future of Life Institute, argues the opposite: “We cannot compute the fundamental truth of biology, we can only measure it.”
In her March essay on AI and cancer, she outlines the complicated process of developing and testing any new medication. “Thirteen years into the AI drug discovery movement, we still lack a single [Federal Drug Authority]-approved drug that cleared the full bar of regulatory approval, reimbursement, and clinical adoption,” she says.
Javorsky argues that curing cancer is a noble goal but the research community must be smart about where investment goes. It’s not intelligence that limits progress but the data, regulation and incentives that surround cancer research.
Even if all the data from research across the world was placed into these models, would that be enough to solve these diseases today? What about in five or 10 years? For Sahm, there are biological truths we are yet to uncover. In his work, he still encounters rare, unknown pathology that doesn’t “fit into a box”. While AI may be able to devise technology or tools to understand rare subtypes, it’s only as good as its training data.
The complexity of human physiology and biological processes comes up a lot in discussions with those working in cancer. Although AI may speed up the process of, for instance, hypothesising and creating new drugs that can treat specific forms of cancer, it is fundamentally limited in applying those learnings to the real world. “Someone actually has to go back and do the experiment, right?” Loi says.
An article published in The Australian newspaper in March revealed that a Sydney data scientist had been able to synthesise a bespoke cancer vaccine for his dog, Rosie, by uploading her genetic information to ChatGPT. And while some were astounded by the development, others noted that the hard work had still been done by humans in a lab.
Even if AI can determine the most effective targets for new drugs, it cannot cut through red tape. Sahm notes that the majority of AI-assisted or AI-led research being performed is experimental and remains in clinical trials. Even if AI tools were deemed safe for test patients, he says, the EU lacks a clear regulatory path to allow them to reach the market. “That ends up in a lot of AI research going on, a lot of surprising and promising things happening … but also surprisingly few of those really being applied,” he says.
The most vocal proponents of AI – those building the models – may make grand claims about cures but on the ground the reality is different. There’s a lack of understanding of cancer complexity, many researchers working in the space argue.
But it’s clear that AI does provide a sense of hope for clinicians and researchers. Alone it cannot dethrone the king of terrors; it cannot bring down the emperor of all maladies. Curing cancer will require more than extra-efficient computation.
“AI can come up with a million hypotheses,” Loi says – but we will still need humans to help understand which of them are true.
“Technology,” says Goenka, “is only one part of the answer.”

Meet the ‘fire amoeba,’ a record-breaking survivor of extreme heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

A single-celled blob living in a California hot spring has smashed a heat tolerance record for an entire domain of life.
The newly described “fire amoeba” can grow at 63° Celsius (145° Fahrenheit), a temperature that’s fatal to all other known eukaryotes, researchers report September 22 in Cell. Eukaryotes include all life-forms with nuclei and organelles, such as plants, fungi and animals.
Little was known about the genetic adaptations of microbial eukaryotes that live in extreme environments. From 2023 to 2025, microbiologist Beryl Rappaport and her colleagues brought water samples from geothermal hot springs in California’s Lassen Volcanic National Park into the lab. There, the team tried to grow any amoebas they found and study their DNA.
“We set up cultures at a few temperatures, with the hottest being 57° C because that is the highest temperature previously described for an amoeba,” says Rappaport, a member of microbial ecologist Angela Oliverio’s lab at Syracuse University in New York.
After seeing an amoeba growing at 57° C that looked different from the previous amoeba record holder Echinamoeba thermarum, the team cranked up the temperature. The mystery microbe continued to replicate and thrive at a blistering 63° C, above the eukaryote record of 60° C held by some algae and fungi. This resilient amoeba could even survive up to 70° C by entering a dormant state.
The researchers named the amoeba Incendiamoeba cascadensis, which means “fire amoeba from the Cascades,” after the volcanic mountains where it was discovered.
Some other, simpler microbes like bacteria and archaea can tolerate much higher temperatures. For instance, archaeon Methanopyrus kandleri holds the heat record for all life and can grow at 122° C.
The fire amoeba appears to share some adaptations with these kinds of organisms, like chemical features on the surface of its proteins that discourage the harmful clumping that happens at high temperatures.
The amoeba can also pivot between two body shapes, which might help it deal with rapidly fluctuating temperatures in its hot spring environment. “One slower [form] seems suited to foraging and one faster [one] seems useful for escaping if temperatures become suboptimal,” Rappaport says.
Even more heat-tolerant eukaryotes may yet to be discovered. “As far as we know, there is no reason why 63° is the hard limit,” Oliverio says. “We don’t really know what the upper temperature limits are.”

EU removes two Russian billionaires from sanctions list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:58:32 UTC
23:58:32 KST

Russian businessman, co-founder of Alfa-Group Mikhail Fridman attends a conference in Moscow on September 17, 2019. | Pool photo by Pavel Golovkin/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Two of Russia’s wealthiest men could soon be free to operate inside the EU after the bloc moved to remove restrictions on them and their empires as part of a high-stakes diplomatic play.
Capitals struck a deal on Tuesday to cut Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the sanctions list, five diplomats told POLITICO, granted anonymity to speak frankly.
For more than a week, France had been holding the EU’s entire framework of individual sanctions up as part of an unexpected standoff, risking the 3,000 or so listings expiring if they were not renewed. Earlier talks ended without a deal on Monday night, after Baltic nations initially refused to sign off the deal.
Advertisement
Paris launched a surprise campaign earlier this month calling for sanctions to be dropped on mining and telecommunications billionaire Usmanov and citing a “national security” issue at play. Luxembourg, meanwhile, had long been asking for the de-listing of banking magnate Fridman, who is suing the country for access to assets frozen by the Grand Duchy.
“It is done,” said one of the diplomats. “The question is what Baltic countries got in return.”
The agreement, reached in a meeting of ambassadors behind closed doors, will take effect if capitals submit their written consent by 6 p.m.
Three-year extension
A number of other countries — including Nordic and Baltic nations — had warned the move could jeopardize the entire sanctions list, leading to others lobbying for their specific interests. However, as part of the deal, the current selection of names will be kept in place for three years, effectively freezing any further debate until 2029.
France had riled other EU members by announcing its support for Usmanov at short notice, saying only that it was part of considerations around “a specific national security issue” and that Paris “wishes to respond positively to international partners who have approached us regarding Mr. Usmanov.”
The Financial Times reported that the delisting came as part of a deal that could see French nationals released from detention in Azerbaijan. Paris has significantly stepped up its role in the South Caucasus in support of Armenia, a pro-EU democracy that has spent decades locked in conflict with Azerbaijan.
However, some are concerned about the precedent that would set, if true. “If the reports are confirmed, Europe must not turn sanctions into a bargaining chip,” said Latvian MEP Rihards Kols, a member of the Parliament's foreign affairs committee. “France has every right and duty to seek the release of its citizens. But the price cannot be relief for a Russian oligarch sanctioned for his links to the Putin regime.”
Advertisement
At the same time, a handful of countries privately expressed frustration that further information had not been provided at Coreper, the meeting of ambassadors where sanctions rollover decisions are taken.
“Ambassadors were told that there are national security reasons. Coreper is not the right place to discuss those in detail,” said a senior French diplomat who was granted anonymity to speak frankly about the sensitive discussions last week. “Member states were told a week ago that if they needed more precision, they could get it through the appropriate channels.”
Usmanov has consistently denied supporting Russia’s war effort, rejected the idea he is an oligarch and campaigned for his removal from the sanctions list, while Fridman has likewise argued the seizure of his assets is unlawful.

Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:58:30 UTC
23:58:30 KST

Netherlands sets out route map to phase out fossil fuels
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
The Netherlands has become the second country in the world to publish detailed plans of how it intends to end its dependence on fossil fuels.
The Dutch government followed France in outlining a so-called “route map” to phasing out oil, gas and coal, in the run-up to the UN Climate Change Conference in Turkey in November.
The plan drew praise from international climate change experts for giving definition to the Netherlands’ ambitions, but there was also criticism for the failure to set a firm deadline.
The decision to draw up national route maps was an outcome of a smaller-scale summit organised by the Netherlands and Colombia in April to discuss moving away from fossil fuels, which 50 countries attended.
France was the first country to publish its plan, which was mostly a summary of existing policies and targets, such as ending the use of coal by 2030, oil by 2045 and gas by 2050.
The Dutch plan includes a reassertion of its commitment to stop using coal-fired power stations to produce electricity by 2030, but other targets have been delayed or downgraded.
Goals downgraded
The Netherlands has reduced the amount of wind energy it wants to produce at sea, abandoned its goal of making the electricity network CO2 free by 2035 and will not meet the EU’s target of reducing emissions by 90% by 2040.
Natalie Jones, of the International Institute for Sustainable Development, said the Dutch plan was a “good example for other countries”.
But climate campaigners were more critical. Maarten de Zeeuw of Greenpeace Nederland told Trouw: “The biggest problem is that unlike France, there is no clear end date. You can call it a route map, but you don’t know where the route is going.”
Joyeeta Gupta, professor of environment and development at the University of Amsterdam, said the plan did not go far enough, given that the limit for global warming of 1.5 degrees C, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, has almost been reached.
“Already 25 million people a year are fleeing because of the climate crisis, and that is just one of the many terrible consequences,” she said.
A spokesman for the Dutch environment ministry said the route map reflected the Netherlands’ ambition to lead the group of countries that wanted to take a pro-active role on climate change. “The fact that we have made our own route map helps our credibility,” the spokesman said.

Latvia gives in to France's demands to lift EU sanctions on two Russian oligarchs, diplomats say

Unknown Publisher

Latvia gives in to France's demands to lift EU sanctions on two Russian oligarchs, diplomats say
Editor's note: This is a developing story
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Latvia agreed to stop opposing a plan by Slovakia and France to remove two Russian oligarchs from EU sanctions on the afternoon of Sept. 22, three national diplomats told the Kyiv Independent.
The news comes as the Franco-Slovak push to delist Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman led to a weeks-long delay in renewing the European bloc's 3,000 sanctions on Russia.
"In maintaining the (sanctions) regime we have reached a difficult compromise," said a spokesperson for the European Council Presidency.
In exchange for the delisting, EU ambassadors have provisionally agreed to extend the sanctions for 36 months rather than the originally planned 12 months, the compromise that appeared to have been reached the previous day.
"What signal does this send? Frankly, astonishing and embarrassing," said Ukraine's sanctions chief Vladyslav Vlasiuk on social media.
All EU votes on sanctions policy require unanimity, which gave France and Slovakia leverage in securing the deal.
Initially, Latvia went public on the night of Sept. 21 to oppose the Franco-Slovak plan, with the country's Foreign Minister Baiba Braze writing on social media: "The Latvian government's stance has been unwavering. EU sanctions against Russia must be strengthened, not weakened."
That strong stance garnered the support of President Volodymyr Zelensky, who praised Latvia just two hours before Riga backed down.
Now, instead of voting against the compromise, Riga will abstain, which allows the measure to go ahead but without Latvia's blessing.
Three national diplomats said that they understand Belgium and Lithuania have also committed to abstaining, because they do not support the move, but equally cannot allow 3,000 listings to evaporate.
Latvia has yet to give a reason for its change of position, but national diplomats from three EU countries confirmed that Riga had signaled the shift in an ambassadors' meeting at 4 p.m. Brussels time.
Earlier that day, Latvia had demanded to postpone the decision for two weeks, so that the vote would be taken after an upcoming parliamentary election in the country, where delisting the two men would be a politically toxic move.
The two sanctioned individuals, Fridman and Usmanov, are both considered members of Russian leader Vladimir Putin's inner circle.
Fridman is a co-founder of the Russian conglomerate Alfa-Group, whose subsidiary provided insurance for vehicles used by Russian forces in Ukraine, and reportedly serviced the Main Office of Special Programs, which is responsible for guarding Putin.
The Ukrainian-born tycoon was also the owner of Sense Bank — formerly known as Alfa-Bank, one of Ukraine's largest banks — before its nationalization in 2023.
Usmanov made his fortune in metal and mining operations following the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was referred to as "one of Putin's favorite oligarchs" in the EU's original 2022 sanctions decision.
The ambassadors' agreement needs to be formally voted on in writing by national ministers. They have until 6 p.m. local time to do so.
Once passed, the sanctions renewal will last until Sept. 22, 2029.

“UEFA and FIFA should have suspended the Israel Football Association (IFA) over its refusal to exclude clubs based in illegal settlements in the Occupied Palestinian Territories,” Cockburn said.

Israel is set to play in League B's, Group B3 alongside Austria, the Republic of Ireland and Kosovo.

The Football Association of Ireland has also asked UEFA to consider suspending Israel, according to the rights group.
“Sport should never be used as a public relations spectacle for states committing atrocities,” Cockburn said.
“As the Israel team travels to Europe, Palestinian families are being displaced and dispossessed, their land stolen, their olive trees uprooted and their histories erased by settlers with the support of the Israeli military,” he said.
“The beautiful game should bring people together, not rubber-stamp apartheid,” Cockburn added.
Amnesty said it wrote to FIFA and UEFA in October 2025 to call for the IFA to be suspended unless clubs based in Israeli settlements were excluded from Israeli competitions.
FIFA announced in March 2026 that it would take no action against the IFA over the participation of settlement-based clubs, according to Amnesty.
The Palestinian Football Association subsequently appealed the decision to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

Amateur archaeologist finds 934 Roman silver denarii in German field
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:54:51 UTC
23:54:51 KST

An amateur archaeologist who discovered several Roman silver coins in a field in western Germany realised he had stumbled upon something much bigger when his metal detector kept beeping.
Oliver Riedl called the authorities for help and a group of experts who began digging immediately discovered a total of 934 Roman silver denarii. It is the biggest coin treasure ever found in Germany from the time of the Roman emperor Hadrian, the local office in charge of archaeological monuments said on Tuesday.
“It was clear to me that there was something bigger buried here,” Riedl said, describing how his metal detector continued signalling even after he had found several coins near Wesseling, south of Cologne, a year ago.
The hoard of coins, which weighs 3.1kg (6.8lb), went on display at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn on Tuesday.
The collection was probably buried deliberately in the second quarter of the second century AD, according to the LVR Office for the Preservation of Archaeological Monuments in the Rhineland.
“Of course, we can only speculate about the motives, but it’s very likely that someone wanted to keep this money safe. After all, banks didn’t exist back then,” said Erich Classen, a state archaeologist and the director of the office.
Classen said it was not clear why the treasure had not been recovered, adding that “perhaps the owner died before that could happen, without being able to pass on the knowledge about the coins”.
Treasure troves from ancient Roman times or other distant eras are not uncommon. However, few from the second century are as extensive as the one found in Wesseling, the archaeological office said.
It said it was difficult to estimate the coins’ value at the time of their burial, but the pay of Roman legionaries, which is well documented in written sources, provides a point of reference.
“At that time, an ordinary soldier in the legion earned 300 denarii a year,” said Rahel Otte, a research associate at the archaeological office. “However, about half of that was withheld for food and equipment.
“A legionary would therefore have had to save all of his disposable income for about six years to amass the Wesseling hoard,” Otte said. She added that it remained unclear exactly who ultimately amassed this considerable fortune.
The Cologne area was under Roman control roughly from 39BC to AD459. The Romans established a presence in the region under General Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa to secure their empire’s border along the Rhine River, setting up a military outpost which later became Colonia Agrippina – today’s Cologne.

====================================================================================================

Fertilizers: End the free pass for the merchants of death
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:53:49 UTC
23:53:49 KST

Fertilizers: End the free pass for the merchants of death
A worker operates a crane to lift sacks of Apaviva NPK(S) phosphate fertilizer at the PhosAgro-Cherepovets fertilizer plant, operated by PhosAgro PJSC, in Cherepovets, Russia, on Dec. 2, 2021. (Andrey Rudakov / Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Alan Riley
Visiting Professor at the College of Europe
Ever since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the Russian fertilizer industry has had a sanctions-free pass.
One can see why such a free pass was granted. When it came to Russian fertilizer exports, both the U.S. and the EU prioritized food security. They did not want to increase food prices and reduce food security by banning Russian fertilizer.
While that was an understandable reaction, it overlooked the role that fertilizer plays in munitions production.
Fertilizer production is inherently dual-use, and in wartime it is critical. As a result, that food security free pass has enabled and enriched the Russian fertilizer industry and Russia's financial capacity to wage war.
In addition, it has provided the Russian military with the explosives it needs to continue its attacks against Ukraine. The only truly significant sanctions that have fallen on the Russian fertilizer industry are those that fall from the sky in the shape of Ukrainian drones.
The EU has only belatedly begun to limit Russian fertilizer imports, and the U.S. has no tariff or sanction regime at all on the sector.
The most significant part of the fertilizer industry, and that which makes up approximately 75% of globally traded fertilizers, is a nitrogen-based one. The ultimate source of nitrogen fertilizer is a fossil fuel, usually natural gas, which is used to produce ammonia, the base product for all nitrogen fertilizers.
However, in addition to producing fertilizers to assist food production, the ammonia-based product can be used to produce downstream chemical precursor products vital for explosives, such as nitric acid and ammonium nitrate.
During the war, these downstream products vital for explosives production have been produced in large quantities by the Russian fertilizer industry.
The two principal producers are Eurochem and Uralchecm. We know, for instance, from Reuters and Bloomberg reports that Eurochem shipped 5000 tonnes of nitric acid from its Nevinnomyssk Azot plant to the Russian munitions industry between 2022 and 2024.
To give some sense of the impact of 5000 tonnes of nitric acid, it can provide the key explosive filling ingredient for 500,000 large caliber shells.
Uralchem provided 27,000 tonnes of ammonium nitrate and 6000 tonnes of nitric acid from its Bereznki plant in the same 2022-2024 period.
Toaz, which is also controlled by Uralchem, is one of the world's largest producers of ammonia, the base chemical for most explosives, and therefore, from the point of view of the Russian state, is a critical chokepoint in its explosives production supply chain.
The food security focus of European and U.S. policymakers has, until recently, led them to wholly ignore the security threat posed by the Russian fertilizer sector.
Even now, the EU has only imposed limited progressive tariffs on Russian fertilizers, which began to be imposed in mid-2025.
The U.S. situation is worse. There are still no tariffs or sanctions whatsoever on Russian fertilizers entering the U.S. While Brussels and Washington have taken a long time to recognize the security threat posed by the Russian fertilizer industry, this is not the case in Kyiv. Ukrainian drones have hit the Nevinnomyssk plant at least seven times, and the main Togliattiazot ammonia production facility controlled by Mazepin at least three times.
The sanctions regime on both Russian fertilizer executives and their companies remains fragmented to non-existent to being shot through with loopholes.
There are no corporate sanctions on the Russian fertilizer sector, and only a limited tariff regime for fertilizers entering the EU; personal sanctions remain fragmented.
It is true that various Russian actors sought to avoid sanctions. If we take the two principal owners of Eurochem and Uralchem at the onset of the war, like other owners in the sector, they had tried to reduce their nominal control of their companies to avoid sanctions.
Andrey Melnichenko at Eurochem handed his wife control of his companies via a trust, and Dmitry Mazepin at Uralchem nominally reduced his shareholding of Uralchem to 48% from 100%.
Western courts, however, have not been convinced by such mechanisms. For example, in North-West 2 v. Societe Generale, the English High Court was not particularly impressed by this "trust maneuver" and held that Melnichenko still owned and controlled Eurochem.
Still, their corporate entities have not been subject to sanctions.
It is true that both Mazepin and Melnichenko have been subject to personal sanctions. Nevertheless, those sanctions have been fragmented. So while Melnichenko is subject to U.S. and EU sanctions from a number of third states, Mazepin has been sanctioned by the EU, not the U.S.
Given their role and that of their companies in underpinning the Russian war effort, there is a compelling justification for comprehensive Western sanctions both on the individuals who ultimately control and run these companies and the companies themselves.
This argument is reinforced by their proximity to the Russian leadership. The de facto owners of Eurochem and Uralchem were at the meeting of business leaders at the Kremlin on the first day of the war, and have both been condemned by the EU courts as close to the Russian leadership.
That proximity in respect of Melnichenko is underlined by his recent article in the Economist, in which he pleaded for the West to understand Russia's legitimate concerns. An article that could not have been written and published without the highest level of clearance from within the Kremlin.
Equally, Mazepin, in his long-running ‘corporate raid’ to control and then sustain his control over the ammonia firm Togliattiazot, was only possible due to his proximity to power, which gave Mazepin his capacity to deploy state resources to carry out and sustain that raid.
It should be possible for the Western allies to ensure that comprehensive personal sanctions are imposed on the de facto owners, shareholders, board members, and managers of the Russian fertilizer sector. After all, they are collectively benefiting from the death and suffering being inflicted on Ukrainian civilians in this war.
It is admittedly more difficult to just cut off Russian fertilizer flows. However, it is possible for the West to develop alternatives both for itself and the wider world.
Critically, the key source feedstock, natural gas, exists in enormous quantities in the United States. Yet the U.S. remains a significant importer of fertilizer. The U.S. could transform fertilizer production rather like the way it went from being a net importer of liquid natural gas (LNG) to being the world's largest exporter of LNG; it has the resource base to become the world's largest fertilizer exporter.
In so doing, it would secure food supplies and push the merchants of death in the Russian fertilizer industry out of global markets.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

Navigating the Regulatory Framework for Anti-Wrinkle Injection Clinics Across the European Union  - The Baltic Times

14:51:13 UTC
23:51:13 KST

The aesthetic medicine industry has experienced remarkable growth throughout the European Union over the past decade, with anti-wrinkle injections becoming one of the most sought-after non-surgical cosmetic procedures. As millions of Europeans seek to maintain a youthful appearance through treatments such as botulinum toxin injections and dermal fillers, the regulatory landscape governing these procedures has evolved significantly. Understanding the complex framework of rules, standards, and guidelines that govern anti-wrinkle injection clinics across the EU is essential for both practitioners and patients seeking safe, effective treatments.
1. The EU Medical Device Regulation Framework
At the heart of anti-wrinkle injection regulation in the European Union lies the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) 2017/745, which came into full application in May 2021. This comprehensive regulatory framework classifies most injectable products used in aesthetic medicine, including dermal fillers, as medical devices. The regulation establishes stringent requirements for the safety, performance, and quality of these products before they can be marketed within the EU.
Under the MDR, manufacturers must demonstrate that their products meet essential safety and performance requirements through rigorous clinical evaluation and conformity assessment procedures. Products must bear the CE marking, indicating compliance with EU legislation, before they can be legally placed on the market. This harmonised approach across member states aims to ensure a consistently high level of patient safety whilst facilitating the free movement of medical devices throughout the single market.
Botulinum toxin products, however, fall under a different regulatory category. These are classified as prescription-only medicines and are governed by pharmaceutical legislation, including the centralised authorisation procedure overseen by the European Medicines Agency (EMA). This distinction is crucial, as it subjects these products to even more stringent pre-market approval processes, including extensive clinical trials and ongoing pharmacovigilance requirements.
2. Professional Qualifications and Training Standards
Whilst the EU has harmonised product regulations, the requirements for practitioners administering anti-wrinkle injections vary considerably across member states. Each country retains the authority to determine which healthcare professionals may perform these procedures and what level of training they must possess.
In most EU countries, medical doctors are permitted to administer anti-wrinkle injections, though some nations extend this privilege to dentists, nurses, and other healthcare professionals under specific conditions. The United Kingdom, before Brexit, required practitioners to be registered healthcare professionals, and many EU countries have adopted similar frameworks. Countries such as France and Germany maintain particularly strict requirements, generally limiting these procedures to qualified medical practitioners or those working under direct medical supervision.
The European Committee for Medical Laser Applications (ECMLA) and other professional bodies have advocated for standardised training programmes across the EU, recognising that the quality and safety of aesthetic procedures depend heavily on the skill and knowledge of practitioners. Many member states now require practitioners to complete specialised training in aesthetic medicine, covering topics such as facial anatomy, injection techniques, complication management, and patient assessment.
3. Clinic Licensing and Operational Standards
The establishment and operation of anti-wrinkle injection clinics within the EU are subject to national healthcare regulations, which can vary significantly between member states. Most countries require clinics offering injectable aesthetic treatments to register with relevant health authorities and comply with specific operational standards.
These standards typically encompass requirements for clinical premises, hygiene protocols, equipment standards, patient record-keeping, and emergency preparedness. Many jurisdictions mandate that clinics maintain appropriate resuscitation equipment and that staff receive training in managing potential complications such as allergic reactions or vascular occlusion.
In Ireland, for instance, clinics such as Facial Rejuve in Dublin must adhere to strict healthcare standards whilst operating within a regulatory environment that is continuously evolving to address the growth in aesthetic medicine. Several EU countries have implemented inspection regimes to ensure ongoing compliance with established standards, recognising that regular oversight is essential to maintaining patient safety.
4. Advertising and Marketing Regulations
The promotion of aesthetic medicine services is subject to stringent regulation across the European Union, with member states imposing various restrictions on how clinics may advertise anti-wrinkle injection treatments. These regulations aim to protect consumers from misleading claims and ensure that marketing communications are responsible and accurate.
The EU's Unfair Commercial Practices Directive provides a baseline framework prohibiting misleading and aggressive commercial practices, which applies to the advertising of aesthetic treatments. Additionally, many countries have specific rules governing healthcare advertising, often requiring that promotional materials be factual, balanced, and not exploit patients' anxieties about their appearance.
Several member states restrict the use of before-and-after photographs in advertising, recognising the potential for such images to create unrealistic expectations or fail to represent typical results. Others require that any marketing claims about treatment efficacy be substantiated by appropriate clinical evidence. Practitioners and clinics found to breach advertising regulations may face sanctions ranging from warnings to fines or restrictions on their ability to practise.
5. Patient Consent and Information Requirements
Informed consent has become a cornerstone of aesthetic medicine regulation throughout the EU, with increasing emphasis placed on ensuring patients understand the nature, risks, and limitations of anti-wrinkle injection treatments before proceeding. This aligns with broader principles of medical ethics and patients' rights enshrined in EU law.
Most member states require practitioners to provide patients with comprehensive written information about proposed treatments, including details of the products to be used, potential side effects, alternative options, and realistic expectations regarding outcomes. Patients must typically be given adequate time to consider this information before treatment, and their consent must be documented.
The General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) also significantly impacts how clinics handle patient information, requiring robust data protection measures and clear policies regarding the collection, storage, and use of personal health data. Clinics must ensure that patient records are maintained securely and that data processing complies with GDPR principles.
6. Emerging Regulatory Trends and Future Developments
The regulatory landscape for anti-wrinkle injection clinics in the EU continues to evolve in response to the sector's growth and emerging safety concerns. Several member states have recently strengthened their regulatory frameworks, introducing more rigorous requirements for practitioners, clinics, and product manufacturers.
There is growing momentum towards greater harmonisation of standards across the EU, particularly regarding practitioner qualifications and training requirements. Professional organisations and regulatory bodies increasingly recognise that the current patchwork of national regulations can create inconsistencies in patient safety standards and complicate cross-border practice.
The European Commission has signalled its commitment to enhancing consumer protection in aesthetic medicine, with discussions ongoing about potential EU-level initiatives to establish minimum standards for non-surgical cosmetic procedures. These developments may include requirements for practitioner registration, standardised training curricula, and enhanced reporting systems for adverse events.
Additionally, increased scrutiny of social media marketing and the influence of non-medical aesthetics providers has prompted calls for stronger enforcement of existing regulations and the development of new rules addressing the unique challenges posed by digital platforms and mobile treatment providers.
7. Conclusion
The regulatory framework governing anti-wrinkle injection clinics across the European Union represents a complex interplay of harmonised product regulations and diverse national requirements for practice standards, professional qualifications, and clinic operations. Whilst the EU's Medical Device Regulation provides a consistent foundation for product safety, significant variation persists in how member states regulate practitioners and clinics offering these increasingly popular treatments.
For patients, understanding this regulatory landscape is crucial to making informed decisions about where and from whom to seek treatment. Reputable clinics operating within robust regulatory frameworks offer the greatest assurance of safety and quality. As the aesthetic medicine sector continues to grow, ongoing regulatory development and enhanced enforcement will be essential to protecting patient welfare whilst supporting the legitimate practice of aesthetic medicine throughout the European Union.

Mandatory old-age retirement in Italy
will rise to 67 years and six months in 2029, the State General
Accounting Office (RGS) said Tuesday.
                                    
                                       
				In 2029, the age for old-age retirement will be 67 and a half,
while in 2031, it will rise to 67 years and 8 months, according
to estimates by RGS regarding "Medium- to long-term trends in
the pension and health/social care systems." To qualify for
early retirement—regardless of age—individuals will need 43
years and four months of pension contributions in 2029, and 43
years and six months in 2031 (one year less for women).
                                    
                                       
				In 2027, the old-age retirement age will be 67 years and one
month, rising to 67 years and three months in 2028. For early
retirement, 42 years and 11 months of contributions will be
required in 2027, and 43 years and one month in 2028.

Russia is holding Ukraine’s south with convicts: 69 percent have records. And they’re fighting where civilians live
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:49:20 UTC
23:49:20 KST

More than two-thirds of the Russian soldiers holding the Zaporizhzhia front carry criminal records. Ukraine's "South" grouping says a third of them enlisted to escape prosecution, most are over 30, and no fresh reinforcements are arriving, spokesperson Anastasia Shevchenko told Ukrinform.
The reasons they signed up track with that: 31 percent enlisted to dodge criminal liability, 24 percent for money, 26 percent on ordinary contracts, and 13 percent through mobilization. It is Russia's prison pipeline in a single snapshot, a model that has pulled well over 100,000 inmates into the war with pardons and suspended sentences and thrown many of them at Ukrainian lines in disposable assault waves.
"It is worth noting that 69 percent of the Russian personnel have a criminal record," Shevchenko said.
The model dates to Wagner's prison recruiting in 2022 and has run under the Defense Ministry since.
A middle-aged force holds the line
The men are not young. More than a third, 36 percent, are between 31 and 40; another 24 percent are 41 to 50; 31 percent are 21 to 30; and just 9 percent are 20 or under.
This is a force of grown men with records, not fresh conscripts, and it points to who Russia can still find willing to fight in the south: people with little to lose and a sentence to escape among Ukrainian civilians, women and children.
The prison pipeline runs dry
What Shevchenko did not report is any sign of that force being rebuilt. Russia has enough men and equipment to keep fighting on the Zaporizhzhia front, she says, but no substantial replenishment is coming.
That fits a wider problem for Russia: its supply of convict recruits is thinning as word of the front's lethality spreads through the prisons, with some inmates now signing military contracts only to bolt on the way to the front, in one case killing their escort to get away.
Russia's practice of replenishing its ranks from prisons is breaking down, and officials are resorting to ever more coercive measures to keep the flow going.

Irish athletes sign open letter urging national soccer team to boycott Israel matches
More than 160 Irish athletes have signed an open letter requesting the Republic of Ireland's men's soccer team to boycott their upcoming international match against Israel as a diplomatic furore between the two countries continues to grow.The Republic of Ireland is due to play Israel twice over the next few weeks in UEFA Nations League qualifying games — first in Hungary on Sept. 27 and then again in Serbia on Oct. 4. Both games are being played without fans in neutral countries after protests by both players and supporters in Ireland against the civilian death toll of Palestinians in Gaza.
The activist group Irish Sport for Palestine said Monday in a social media post that more than 160 Irish sportspeople had signed a letter to the Irish senior men's soccer team "urging them to act collectively with conscience & refuse to participate in their upcoming games against Israel."
This comes after the Israeli Football Association slammed Irish head coach Heimir Hallgrímsson for comments he made at a press conference last week.
Hallgrímsson was asked by reporters whether it would be difficult to keep his players focused on football during the upcoming games against Israel given the public outcry in Ireland.
"We are not playing with genocide, we are playing against genocide," he said. "We are playing against Israel; we are not playing with Israel."
Those remarks drew a strong rebuke by the Israeli football association in a social media post on Monday.
"We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way. Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by @IrelandFootball team coach," the post read. "We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, We're playing against the coach who embodies them."
The Irish government has been one of the most vocal critics of the Israeli government in recent years over its military action in Gaza and diplomatic tensions between the two countries have reached a boiling point over the past two years.
Israel shut down its embassy in Dublin in December 2024 over what Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said was the country's "extreme anti-Israel policies."
"The actions and antisemitic rhetoric used by Ireland against Israel are rooted in the de-legitimisation and demonisation of the Jewish state, along with double standards," Saar said in a statement at the time.
The announcement had followed Ireland's announcement of its support for South Africa's legal action against Israel in the International Court of Justice, which accused Israel of committing genocide against Palestinian civilians in Gaza. The Irish government would later formally join South Africa's legal case against Israel at the ICJ.
Members of the Irish football association also passed a vote last year requesting UEFA, European soccer's governing body, suspend Israel from its competitions.
But in a statement earlier this summer, members of the Football Association Ireland reiterated the Irish men's soccer team would fulfil its obligations to play Israel in UEFA qualifying games.
"While acknowledging the strength of feeling regarding support for Palestine and the upcoming UEFA Men's Nations League fixtures … the members recognise the profound impact that any non-fulfilment of UEFA fixtures would have on Irish football as a whole and on its future development, and accordingly endorses the Association fulfilling its obligations in respect of those fixtures," the statement said.

EU renews Russia sanctions but removes Usmanov at France's request
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:47:22 UTC
23:47:22 KST

France succeeded in its push to remove Alisher Usmanov from the EU sanctions list as part of a prisoner release with Azerbaijan. A second high-profile businessman, Mikhail Fridman, was also removed.
The European Union has agreed to remove Uzbek-Russian oligarch Alisher Usmanov from its sanctions list after fraught negotiations that saw France link his delisting to a prisoner release with Azerbaijan, unsettling Brussels.
A second Russian oligarch, Mikhail Fridman, was also removed after Slovakia vetoed his continued listing, several diplomats told Euronews.
Luxembourg had argued that if Usmanov was removed, Fridman should be too. Fridman has filed a $16 billion claim against Luxembourg over his frozen assets.
As a result of the changes, the asset freeze and the travel ban will be lifted.
Ambassadors sealed the compromise on Tuesday after two weeks of drawn-out talks that brought the bloc's sanctions regime to the brink of collapse.
Latvia held up the processon Monday, warning it was not the right time to ease pressure on Moscow. The Baltic country relented on Tuesday afternoon and opted for a constructive abstention, enabling the necessary unanimity.
As a way to offset the pain of delisting the two high-profile businessmen, the EU has extended its individual sanctions on Russia for an unprecedented 36 months.
Previously, the measures were renewed every six months, giving member states regular opportunities to seek concessions.
The sanctions list currently includes more than 2,600 people, organisations and entities accused of supporting Russia's war in Ukraine, including President Vladimir Putin.
"Today's decision to renew on a 36-month basis enhances the durability and predictability of the EU sanctions framework," said a spokesperson for the Irish presidency of the EU Council, which chaired the talks.
The spokesperson admitted the resolution was "difficult".
While the compromise keeps sanctions in place for much longer and shields them from unexpected vetoes in the future, the removal of two prominent Russian figures has enraged Kyiv, which vocally opposed the move.
As negotiations neared the final stage, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy publicly called on the bloc to keep Usmanov and Fridman on the blacklist.
His message thanked Latvia for its opposition.
"The world needs not a political delisting, but timely and unconditional rollover of individual sanctions, until Moscow engages in serious peace negotiations and takes concrete steps to end its war against Ukraine," Zelenskyy said.
"This is the shortest path to peace we all are striving for. Every Ukrainian family is counting on EU unity and solidarity."
The appeals, though, failed to swing the balance in the room. Member states quickly realised that France had invested too much political capital and would refuse to give up its demand on Usmanov, regardless of the controversy.
"No one is happy about this," a diplomat said. "But the consensus in the room was that it's better to maintain the rest of the listings under the regime and make sure we don't have to do this circus again any time soon."
Uzbek-French deal
The EU sanctioned Usmanov in the early days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, citing his "close ties" to Russian President Vladimir Putin and interests in "key sectors" of the Russian economy that provide "substantial" revenue to the state.
The 73-year-old businessman, whose fortune is estimated at $16.6 billion, has denied the allegations and challenged the sanctions.
Uzbekistan, alongside other Turkic states, has lobbied the EU institutions and several member states for two years to have Usmanov removed from the blacklist.
Euronews understands that Uzbek and French authorities reached a behind-the-scenes agreement under which Azerbaijan would release two French nationals from prison in return for Usmanov's delisting.
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev would issue a pardon as part of the deal.
France has not confirmed the arrangement. French officials have only cited a "national security" issue and declined to provide further details, adding to the uncertainty surrounding the negotiations.
Since September 2024, Paris has warned against travel to Azerbaijan over the "risk of arrest, arbitrary detention and unfair trial".
"In the event of arrest or detention, respect for fundamental rights is not guaranteed," the French foreign ministry says in a travel notice that remains in force.
Last year, an Azerbaijani court sentenced French water-management executive Anass Derraz to 12 years in prison for accepting a bribe in 2018 from an Azerbaijani-Russian businessman in connection with efforts to free an impounded yacht.
Earlier this year, French national Martin Ryan was sentenced to 10 years in prison in Azerbaijan for spying on the military and collecting secret information for the French government. Ryan and Paris strongly contested the charges.
France updated its travel advisory in April following Ryan's sentence.

Fake passport images claim Zelenskyy and family chose Israel as homeland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:47:10 UTC
23:47:10 KST

A photo amassing thousands of views on social media allegedly shows a scan of Zelenskyy's passport, with Israel as his homeland. Not only are the allegations false, but they've been doing the rounds since 2023.
A fake photo circulating online of two alleged Israeli passports belonging to Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his wife, Olena Zelenska, allegedly shows that the Ukrainian president and his family have chosen Israel as their homeland instead of Ukraine.
The Facebook post was published at the beginning of September alongside the caption: "You can twist it any way you like, but we always come back to the same point: Zelenskyy and his family have a homeland of choice that inspires, protects and supports him in everything he does, and that homeland is certainly not Ukraine. This is common knowledge, just as it is common knowledge who his backers are at the top of the Ukrainian establishment, but people prefer to turn a blind eye so as not to disturb those pulling the strings. Shalom."
There is no truth behind these claims. The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, contacted Ukrainian official sources who denied them.
Furthermore, Ukrainian public officials are not permitted to hold multiple citizenships, unlike members of the general public, under a recent law which officially came into effect in January of this year.
Additionally, the false passport belonging to Zelenska lists the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic as her place of birth. This is inaccurate, as official identity documents issued for individuals born in Ukraine before independence routinely list Ukraine rather than the defunct Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic, which was one of the constituent republics of the Soviet Union from 1922 until 1991.
The Cube, Euronews' fact-checking team, also ran it through the image detector Hive Moderation, which revealed it to be AI-generated.
The fake passport appears to have been created based on a sample template published on the Council of Europe website.
Fake Zelenskyy passports resurfaced
It's not the first time false passports attributed to Zelenskyy and Zelenska have circulated online.
In April 2026, an image of an alleged Israeli passport of Zelenskyy was shared on Instagram, X and Facebook, gathering thousands of views, likes and reshares.
These posts claimed that the Ukrainian president was an agent for Israel's intelligence agency, whose main mission was "to Ukrainianise Europe and lead it to its own self-destruction".
In addition to a significant portion of the passport being cropped in the image, there is a spelling error in Zelenskyy's name.
According to the president's official website, his last name is stylised as "Zelenskyy" in English, not "Zelensky", as the alleged passport shows.
In fact, stories about Zelenskyy and Zelenska's alleged passport have been doing the rounds since at least 2023.
For instance, a photo of the first lady was shared on pro-Russian channels and in several Facebook posts.
In one of these posts, the caption can read: "While Ukrainian President Zelensky travels the world begging for money and weapons for his war, his wife spent a lovely vacation in Israel and even obtained an Israeli passport. Interestingly, is Mrs Zelensky preparing for a possible escape from Ukraine?"
All of these posts follow the same playbook: use an AI-generated passport to invent a scandal with some real elements to target Ukraine and undermine support from its allies, as Russia's war against the country continues.
The posts about the alleged Israeli passports stand at odds with one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's supposed justifications for his full-scale invasion: when it began in February 2022, Putin pledged to oversee the "demilitarisation and de-Nazification" of Ukraine.
However, as the grandson of a Holocaust survivor, Zelenskyy has Jewish origins and has previously addressed the series of attacks on his religious background by the Kremlin.
"How can I be a Nazi?" Zelenskyy said in 2022, just before the full-scale invasion, in a video address directed at the Russian people in the Russian language. "Explain it to my grandfather, who went through the entire war in the infantry of the Soviet army, and died a colonel in an independent Ukraine."
