The divisive nature of the 2016 Brexit vote has proved tricky to shake off for many in the UK, and the debate has once more been thrust under the spotlight this year.
Following damaging local election results for Labour in May, senior party figures, including now-Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, pointed to the impact of Brexit on the UK as they positioned themselves ahead of what appeared an increasingly likely leadership contest.
Speaking at the time, Streeting called the decision to leave a "catastrophic mistake" and argued that it had left the country "less wealthy, less powerful and less in control than at any point before the industrial revolution."

The agreements extend a partnership Naftogaz has leaned on increasingly since Russian strikes crippled domestic gas production during the 2025 to 2026 heating season, pushing Ukraine to import record volumes of gas through a widening set of European corridors.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Under the LNG memorandum, the additional volumes are intended to help cover Ukraine’s needs during peak seasonal consumption, Naftogaz wrote in its press release.
“Amid ongoing Russian attacks on our domestic production facilities, it is particularly important for us to have reliable sources of gas supply and diversified delivery routes,” the press release quoted Serhii Fedorenko, Acting Chief Executive Officer of Naftogaz.

The second memorandum was signed separately by Ukrnafta, Naftogaz Group’s oil and gas production subsidiary, and provides for petroleum product supplies to the Ukrainian market worth up to $500 million, Naftogaz wrote. Ukrainian Drone Swarm Strikes Key Russian Oil Refinery in Samara
The document also opens the possibility of exporting Ukrainian crude oil for processing at refineries in Central Europe, Naftogaz wrote, adding that the companies are also exploring transferring used fuel tanker trucks from ORLEN to Ukrnafta to help transport petroleum products domestically.
Ukraine’s growing network of backup LNG supply corridors
Tuesday’s deal is the latest addition to a multi-corridor import system Naftogaz has assembled over roughly the past year, after Russian strikes on domestic gas extraction facilities forced Ukraine to ramp up imports well beyond initial estimates.
During the 2025 to 026 heating season, the actual imports of gas reached 6.47 billion cubic meters in 2025, according to an ExPro estimate cited by Kyiv Post in February.
The buildout began earlier in 2025, when Naftogaz opened a Trans-Balkan route to import Azerbaijani gas via Bulgaria, Romania, and Moldova under its first deal with SOCAR Energy Ukraine.
In November 2025, Naftogaz signed a letter of intent with Greece’s DEPA Commercial to open a southern corridor through the ATLANTIC-SEE joint venture, under which US LNG arrives in Greece and travels through Bulgaria, Romania, and Moldova before entering Ukraine as part of the so-called Vertical Corridor.
The Poland route ORLEN supplied four LNG shipments moved through the Świnoujście terminal from late 2025 to January 2026, with total Naftogaz-ORLEN supplies through Poland said to reach 1 billion cubic meters in 2026.
On Feb. 24, Naftogaz completed its first delivery of US LNG through Germany’s Deutsche ReGas terminal on Rügen Island in the Baltic Sea, arranged with France’s TotalEnergies and transported to Ukraine via Poland.
Also, Naftogaz secured 90 million cubic meters of US LNG for February to March delivery through Lithuania’s Klaipėda seaport terminal, arranged with Lithuania’s Ignitis Group — the first time that terminal was used as a direct transit point for Ukrainian supply.

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22

22:40:10 KST

ICIJ Africa coordinator and journalist Micah Reddy has been released from custody in Djibouti.
Reddy, who had been held secretly after being detained on Saturday, flew out of the country today following his release.
Reddy arrived in Djibouti on Sept. 17 and went silent around 1 p.m. local time on Sept. 19, along with his local assistant, Mohamed Willo Ismael (“Kooki Mahmoud”).
Ismael is understood to be free as well.
ICIJ raised the alarm within hours of the two men’s disappearance from the Escale International Hotel in Djibouti City, when messages to the pair went unanswered.
On Sept. 21, ICIJ confirmed unofficially through diplomatic and other channels that Reddy was in custody, understood to be held for failing to obtain proper media accreditation.
The South African, British and U.S. governments all assisted in reaching out to Djiboutian authorities for information.
Djibouti authorities did not publicly confirm his whereabouts or provide access to Reddy until today.
The many calls for press freedom and for the men’s swift release are an example of the solidarity that matters when a journalist’s safety is put at risk.
—ICIJ director Gerard Ryle
Reddy’s family expressed its relief at his and Ismael’s release but dismay over his treatment and the secrecy surrounding it.
They thanked helpers on the ground, the South African and UK governments, press freedom organizations, ICIJ and the many journalists who had assisted.
They also thanked Reddy’s legal team for its international efforts.
“Waiting for news of a loved one whose whereabouts and wellbeing are unknown is unimaginably painful,” the Reddy family statement said.
“We are profoundly grateful that, for our family, this story has had a happy ending.”
ICIJ echoed the Reddy family in expressing its gratitude to all whose vocal response helped both to discover that Reddy had been held secretly in custody and to secure his freedom.
“The many calls for press freedom and for the men’s swift release are an example of the solidarity that matters when a journalist’s safety is put at risk,” ICIJ director Gerard Ryle said.
Ryle thanked the staff of the U.S. Embassy in Djibouti for their assistance in securing the release of Reddy.
He added his thanks to South African diplomat Zane Dangor, to the U.K. Embassy in Washington DC and to its consular services in London.
Ryle added that four days in secretive custody is unacceptable treatment for any investigative journalist.
And he thanked Reddy’s wife Nicole and brother Niall for their immense efforts to secure Reddy’s release, and their stoic forbearance under extreme pressure.
The Committee to Protect Journalists, Human Rights Defenders, Reporters Without Borders, Gift of the Givers and Amnesty International were among the organizations that assisted in these efforts.
Many reporters also lent their aid, notably South African publisher and journalist Branko Brkic.
At this stage, all the details and circumstances of Reddy’s arrest are unknown. But he and his local guide are safe, healthy and free.

Ed Davey promises £17bn income tax cut if Lib Dems are elected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:40:01 UTC
22:40:01 KST

Ed Davey has unveiled a plan for a £17bn income tax cut in a speech aimed at shoring up the party’s support among former Conservative voters, but which risked disappointing some Liberal Democrat MPs who want a bolder vision for the party.
Addressing the party’s annual conference in Brighton, the Lib Dem leader said the proposal, which would eventually increase the threshold for paying income tax to £15,000 and raise the level at which people pay the 40p higher rate by about £6,000, would be paid for entirely by increased growth.
This growth, the Lib Dems argue, would be created through rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union.
As making a deal with the EU would take time, the actual tax cuts would only happen in the final year of a parliament, potentially as late as 2034, costing £17bn. In the interim years, thresholds would be raised by inflation, thus keeping levels effectively stable.
There would also be a smaller increase to the 45p additional rate of tax, currently payable above £125,000.
Setting out what he described as “trusting people to spend their own money, not telling them the state knows best”, Davey took aim at what he called “the post-Brexit stealth taxes” of frozen thresholds, notably on the higher 40p rate.
“Thirty years ago, just 2 million people paid it. Now it’s 9 million,” he said. “A tax band designed for stockbrokers is now holding back teachers and nurses. That’s not fair. It’s not right.”
The plans mark a distinct shift in the party’s fiscal approach. While it is eyecatching and could appeal to the many former Conservative voters who backed the Lib Dems in 2024, helping them take 60-plus Tory seats, it is likely to cause unease among some of the party’s MPs.
A number of them have called privately for a more ambitious and comprehensive vision of what the party stands for, amid polling that shows most voters do not have much of a sense of this.
Davey’s advisers, however, argue that the cost of living is the subject that most affects many voters, and that tax cuts – even up to eight years in the future – directly address this.
Other elements of the speech included previously-trailed new policies, including a proposal for a global nuclear-style non-proliferation treaty to halt the development of super-intelligent AI.
The tax-cutting plan is predicated entirely on the EU allowing a swift deal on single market access, which could become even more difficult if rightwing populists take power in more EU states, and on this then increasing growth.
The Lib Dems insist the numbers stand up, saying they are based on a report from an independent economics consultancy, which calculated that a deal with the EU could generate 0.5% growth in the first fiscal year alone.
Reform UK has already pledged to increase the personal tax allowance to £15,000, paid for in part by significant cuts to social security.
Davey noted this in the speech, saying: “Think about that. Reform say you can have a tax cut, but only if they get to punish disabled people at the same time. We say no. We can cut taxes and support the most vulnerable people in our country.”
Opening his speech with a warning that black-shirted, and balaclava-wearing far-right protesters who gathered in Dover and Portsmouth “would tear our country apart”, Davey compared groups such as Patriot Platform to Oswald Mosley’s fascists in the 1930s, the National Front in the 70s and to Nick Griffin and the BNP.
“Each time, they tried to turn neighbour against neighbour, tried to pit community against community, tried to turn our streets into battlegrounds,” he said. “But we didn’t let them. The British people said no.”
He said this time, far-right vigilantes were not acting in isolation, but were the most visible part of a far-right threat that was “extremely well funded” and promoted by figures such as Elon Musk and given credibility by “cynical politicians like Nigel Farage”.
Davey slammed Farage as a cynical politician who was “not just willing, but eager to fan the flames of hatred and intolerance to make himself richer”.
He said: “It is the worst of Trump’s America. We must not let it become Farage’s Britain.” Pointing to the £72m donations Reform had received from two crypto billionaires, Davey added: “If there was any doubt before, there can’t be now. We are in the fight of our lives. And it is a fight we must win.”

Unrealistic to fully protect airspace, says Lithuanian official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

It’s unrealistic to protect Lithuania’s airspace completely, Deividas Matulionis, chief national security adviser to the president, said on Tuesday, adding that it was necessary to focus on protecting key sites.
“Covering the entire territory is truly unrealistic. No country in the world – perhaps Israel has some capabilities – is able to fully protect its airspace,” he told the Žinių Radijas radio.
He said the goal was to protect “cities, critical infrastructure facilities, and our border”, saying the measures should include “anti-drone defences along the border”.
Among other things, the presidential adviser emphasised that while air defence is a priority, the development of ground forces is also very important.
“We shouldn’t go from one extreme to the other. The development of our ground forces is just as important a priority,” he said.
According to Matulionis, drone detection and drone destruction – kinetic measures – should go hand in hand and be integrated as early as next year.
“We said that if there really is a shortage of funds, the members of the State Defence Council will certainly agree to reallocate some funds in favour of air defence – if there isn’t enough, so that this becomes a priority and we can protect our airspace,” the adviser said.
“Detection is one thing; destroying them is another. That is why it should be combined with so-called kinetic systems – whether they are interceptor drones or some other systems that would instantly transmit information, allowing the operator to make the appropriate decision,” he added.
Last week, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that had flown into Lithuania’s airspace from Belarus. The unmanned aircraft was downed in Kaišiadorys District, central Lithuania, near the Kruonis Pumped-Storage Power Station.
As Russia’s invasion of Ukraine continues, potential air threat alerts have been issued repeatedly in Lithuania over the past few months. However, the incident last Tuesday marked the first time a drone had been shot down in the country’s airspace.
A NATO fighter shot down a Ukrainian drone over Estonia in May, in what was the first interception of a foreign drone. In June, French fighter jets participating in NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission downed a drone over Latvia.
Previously, Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said that a larger portion of next year’s defence budget should be allocated to air defence.
Lithuania spent 524 million euros this year on beefing up air defences.

What Could the ‘Super’ El Niño Bring to Russia?

UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned earlier this summer that “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes” and called on countries to end their dependency on planet-heating fossil fuels.
“The world must treat it as the urgent climate warning it is. El Niño conditions will pour fuel on the fire of a warming world. Impacts will hit even harder, travel even farther, and cross borders with devastating speed,” Guterres said.
But a very strong El Niño does not mean that every region will be hit with equal force. So how will Russia fare?
El Niño involves the heating of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean. It happens every few years and is part of a natural climate cycle that alternates between a warm phase — El Niño — and a cool phase, known as La Niña.
During El Niño, the warmer ocean water drives major changes in global weather patterns, including drought and heightened wildfire risk in Southeast Asia and Australia, as well as heavy rainfall in parts of South and North America.
Scientists classify El Niño as “super” when the ocean heating reaches or exceeds +2 degrees Celsius for a few months. The current El Niño reached +2.7 C by August, and some forecasts say it could top out at an astonishing 4 C when it peaks somewhere between November and December.
While scientists have not established that man-made climate change is increasing or intensifying El Niño, it is true that a warmer atmosphere and ocean can amplify its effects since burning fossil fuels increases the heat and moisture that power extreme weather.
Several super El Niño events have occurred in recent decades, including in 2014-16, 1997-98 and 1982-83. According to the World Meteorological Association, the current super El Niño is on track to become the strongest on record and is expected to continue through February 2027.
The strengthening El Niño is already being felt across the globe. India is experiencing its weakest monsoon in two decades, while meteorologists point to the phenomenon as a primary factor behind an unusually quiet Atlantic hurricane season.
Because Russia lies far from the tropical Pacific, the direct oceanic drivers of El Niño do not hit the country head-on, Anna Skrigan, a researcher at Climate Action Network, told The Moscow Times.
“Past super El Niños had no significant impact on Russia, so there is little cause for concern. Compared to other climate phenomena, a super El Niño is not particularly destructive for the region,” Skrigan said.
For example, the 1997-98 super El Niño brought subtle shifts in Russia rather than outright catastrophe, such as higher rainfall driving up Caspian Sea levels.
While noticeable, those effects paled in comparison to the devastation seen in other parts of the world, where drought destroyed crops across Indonesia and southern Africa, severe flooding hit Peru and Ecuador, and cholera and malaria outbreaks surged in Kenya and Somalia.
Forecast for sea surface temperature anomaly based on several climate models, September-November 2026
Models from the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts project above-average snowfall across much of European Russia this coming winter. This sets the region apart from the western part of the continent, where lower snowfall is expected.
“Winter predictions for Russia remain mixed. Some models forecast a snowy but mild winter, while others point to colder conditions, assuming the Siberian High will override El Niño’s influence,” Skrigan said.
Instead, she noted, Russia is far more vulnerable to ripple effects, specifically through global food and energy prices. Economic strain in other countries can trigger a domino effect that impacts the cost of living in Russia.
At its peak, the 1997-98 super El Niño, which reached 2.4 C, wiped out an estimated $5.7 trillion in global GDP — more than double the economic loss of the 2008 financial crisis. Much of the damage was due to a prolonged drag on economic activity that lingered for years after the event passed.
For Russia, Skrigan said, the impact of recent super El Niño events was “real, but indirect and non-destructive.”
“The global mechanism is much clearer. Indonesia is already distributing water pumps and restoring irrigation networks in preparation for a 1997-98 scale drought,” she said.
“For the Russian economy, these effects will most likely be felt indirectly through global food and energy prices rather than through direct weather on domestic farmland.”

High-mileage electric cars are more reliable than petrol ones, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:37:50 UTC
22:37:50 KST

Motorists buying a secondhand car with a lot of miles on the clock are likely to find an electric vehicle (EV) ultimately more reliable than a petrol vehicle, according to a study.
An analysis of 47.4m MOT tests found that after cars were driven 90,000 to 120,000 miles, EVs were about 25% less likely to fail than petrol models of the same age (based on a failure rate of 16.5% versus 22.1%).
Beyond 120,000 miles, 16% of EVs failed, compared with 23.5% of petrol cars. The study found relatively little difference between the two fuel types at lower mileages.
The study by the consultancy New AutoMotive on behalf of the industry group the British Vehicle Rental and Leasing Association (BVRLA) comes as a growing number of EVs change hands. Many used to belong to company and leasing fleets so have potentially racked up a lot of miles.
Toby Poston, the BVRLA chief executive, said that mileage is “one of the first things people look at when buying a used car, and passing 60,000 or 70,000 miles can have a big impact on how a vehicle is perceived”.
He added: “What this data shows is that mileage alone should not put consumers off. A well-maintained, higher-mileage electric car can be an extremely durable used vehicle.
“That matters because the used market is where the transition to electric becomes accessible to millions more motorists. Giving buyers confidence in these cars will be critical to creating a healthy and affordable secondhand EV market.”
Ben Nelmes, the chief executive of New AutoMotive, which carried out the research, said that high mileage “isn’t a proxy for poor condition in the way buyers have traditionally assumed. The data suggests the mechanical simplicity of an electric drivetrain starts to become increasingly valuable as cars accumulate miles.”
The study also identified areas where electric cars performed worse, particularly tyres. EVs recorded nearly twice as many tyre defects as petrol cars and older, low-mileage electric cars showed increased friction-brake defects. Researchers attributed the latter to corrosion associated with the brakes being used less frequently.
MOT tests examine statutory roadworthiness, including brakes, tyres, suspension, steering and lights, but do not measure battery health, degradation or charging performance. This information would therefore need to be considered alongside mechanical roadworthiness when assessing any used EV, the researchers said.
“This isn’t an argument for buying a used EV without doing your homework,” Poston said. “Buyers should look at its history, condition, tyres and battery health just as they would scrutinise the engine, gearbox and service history of a petrol or diesel car.
“What we can now challenge is the idea that an electric car with 80,000 or 100,000 miles on the clock should automatically be regarded as worn out.”

Security officers detained the woman near the sports complex while she was allegedly conducting reconnaissance and looking for a suitable firing position, the agency said.

Exports are expected to remain around 16 million tonnes in 2027, supporting Malaysia's role as a key global supplier, it added. ■

Living in the shadow of LA's hidden oil wells
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:34:00 UTC
22:34:00 KST

Living in the shadow of LA's hidden oil wells
September 22, 2026
For most, Los Angeles conjures images of a city of beaches, palm trees, and movie stars. Few realize LA County is also one of the largest oil-producing regions in the United States.
Oil wells are strewn everywhere across Los Angeles. Including on Pico Boulevard, next to the affluent neighborhood of Beverly Hills, where two fake buildings house and hide active oil wells. From the street, it's nearly impossible to tell what is inside.
Artificial islands off the coast of Long Beach disguise further drilling sites. And the disguise is so good that tourists who assume they are hotels often ask the city how they can book a night's stay there.
Other sites, such as the Inglewood Oil Field, are out in the open. The largest urban oil field in the US, it is right next to Kenneth Hahn State Park, where there is a fishing pond, hiking trails, and playgrounds. The pumpjacks are visible from inside the park.
Elsewhere there are yet more wells that have been built over, making them invisible to unknowing residents who pass them every day. A map created by CalGem, the state agency that manages oil and gas, shows them beneath neighborhoods, schools, and playgrounds.
And that is a big issue, as they are potential sources of pollution linked to respiratory disease, cancer, cardiovascular problems, reproductive harm, and other serious health issues.
For people living near oil wells, one of the most immediate concerns is air quality. Oil wells can release a range of pollutants, including volatile organic compounds such as benzene, as well as hydrogen sulfide and methane. Research has found that people living near oil and gas operations may experience reduced lung function and elevated rates of respiratory illness.
Residents who do live close to oil fields often describe odors and report physical impacts including headaches, nausea, eye irritation, coughing and breathing difficulties.
Community advocates in LA say such symptoms have impacted generations of families living close to oil and gas drilling infrastructure. Regina Martin, who grew up near the Inglewood Oil Field, recalls days when pollution was visibly present in the air.
"We used to be able to see the air that we were breathing," she says, adding that it was so bad that playing outside was not possible. "We had to stay in for recess. I used to deal with the nosebleeds, the headaches, the upset stomach, and the red eyes.”
Though the air has become clearer since Martin was a child, the oil field is still operational. She canvases with Black Women for Wellness to talk about issues affecting LA residents and says many local families do not know about the health impacts of living near oil extraction. She herself wasn't aware until she started doing community advocacy work.
"I always felt that everybody lived near an oil field,” she says. "So it was just really, really normalized for me.”
Impacts of proximity to drilling beyond breathing problems
Studies have linked proximity to oil and gas extraction with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease, adverse birth outcomes, certain cancers, as well as reproductive health complications. Some studies have also explored associations between exposure to oil field pollutants and autoimmune conditions.
For Rosalinda Morales and Brenda Valdivia, the connection between oil drilling and health issues is all too familiar. The two women grew up in Vista Hermosa, a neighborhood scattered with oil wells.
Some, as Morales explains, are located close to schools and early childhood education centers. "To the right of us there's another school," she says.
"And down the block is a county preschool,” adds Valdivia.
The two are standing on the sidewalk next to a non-descript fence, which is impossible to see through or over from street level. But the smell is a giveaway. And behind the fence is a tank for storing oil as well as moving pumpjacks.
"This is mild today," Morales says, adding that the smell gets very strong. "You know, this is what we've grown up with."
While she struggles with respiratory problems, Valdivia has lupus, an autoimmune disease that contributed to multiple strokes.
Although proving that any individual illness was directly caused by nearby drilling is difficult, both women believe years of exposure to pollution from oil extraction played a role.
Inequality around the wells that are plugged
The health burden of urban oil extraction is not spread evenly across Los Angeles. Many of the city's most heavily drilled areas are predominantly Black and Latino neighborhoods, in South and East LA. In West LA, the neighborhoods close to the ocean, most of the oil wells have been plugged and sealed for decades.
Tianna Wakeman, who also does canvassing work with Regina Martin, argues that these communities have historically been forced to live with environmental hazards that wealthier neighborhoods were able to remove.
"There are protections that communities in South Los Angeles have been fighting for for decades, that whiter wealthy communities in West LA, have already received," she says, adding that there is very clear environmental racism at play.
"Black and brown people saying, I want clean air, I want clean water, I want clean soil for my kids to play in, is not received in the same way as when white, wealthy folks say the same thing."
One frequently cited example is how residents successfully pushed for the closure and plugging of oil wells located on the grounds of one of LA's most affluent schools, Beverly Hills High. Morales and Valdivia, meanwhile, say they have been trying to find out the owner of oil wells in their neighborhood for years. So far, with no luck.
Morales, Valdivia, and others are advocating for the closure of LA's urban oil fields, and phasing out of drilling entirely in LA County.
Los Angeles is currently debating both banning oil extraction and how to manage thousands of aging wells.

IN BRIEF: What is known about Hungary’s refusal to join Carpathian Eight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:33:57 UTC
22:33:57 KST

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar used a village football team example to explain to Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga why Budapest rejected the Kiev-backed "Carpathian Eight" regional format. Magyar also stated that the Hungarian government would block the construction of any oil product storage facilities for Ukraine on its territory.
TASS has compiled the key details known so far.
Hungary’s refusal to participate in Carpathian Eight
Speaking in the Hungarian parliament, Magyar stated that the country did not join the "Carpathian Eight" format promoted by Kiev, which involves Ukraine and several Eastern and Central European nations. He noted that while Hungary had been invited, it did not participate in the initiative, citing "valid reasons" for the decision.
Commenting on Sibiga’s statement, Magyar remarked that "declaring a sovereign country a member of an international organization – the 'Carpathian Eight' – without prior consultation or that country's consent is completely unacceptable."
Magyar illustrated Budapest's refusal to join the Kiev-backed format using a village football team analogy: "Let me give you an example: 'Hello, we’ve formed a football team from the neighboring village. We don’t know each other, but you’re on the team--and you have to bring the ball, too.' "
Refusal to build a petroleum storage facility for Ukraine in Hungary
Magyar stated that the memorandum of understanding regarding the construction of a petroleum product storage facility for Ukraine on Hungarian territory – signed by Hungarian company MOL and Ukraine’s Naftogaz – will not be implemented. The memorandum "stated that this was merely a theoretical possibility," he noted.
Earlier, Naftogaz had posted a message on its Telegram channel regarding plans to build an oil storage facility in Hungary near the Ukrainian border. Magyar also reported that negotiations on this matter had been initiated by MOL with Ukraine and the US with the authorization of Hungary's previous government.
However, no progress was made beyond the signing of the memorandum of understanding, and no further agreements were reached. Magyar recounted that he had discussed the issue with MOL CEO Zsolt Hernadi on September 20. The Prime Minister made it clear that, going forward, he expects actions to be coordinated with the country's new government, given that the state still holds a 25% stake in the company.
Kiev's reaction
Kiev is surprised by Magyar's statements regarding Budapest's refusal to join the "Carpathian Eight" format promoted by Ukraine, Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga said. According to a statement by Sibiga cited by the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry, Kiev is surprised by the Hungarian Prime Minister's remarks concerning Ukraine.
Sibiga also described them as "unjustifiably confrontational," adding that the "reasons for such a categorical refusal by Hungary" remain unknown to Ukraine. He also called Magyar's statements regarding the prospects for cooperation between Ukrainian and Hungarian energy companies "strange."
Recent statements from Budapest have left Kiev confused, Sibiga said. According to him, "one gets the impression that, although Viktor Orban has left, his policies <…> continue to flourish."
Expert opinion
Relations between Budapest and Kiev have not become trouble-free following the change of government in Hungary, Ilya Grashchenkov, a political analyst and president of the Center for Regional Policy Development, told TASS. He noted that while relations between Hungary and Ukraine "might become less confrontational in form, this by no means implies the disappearance of serious underlying contradictions."
By refusing to build an oil storage facility for Ukraine, the Hungarian government sent a clear signal to the business community about the need to align the state's position, Grashchenkov observed.
About the format
On September 18, Vladimir Zelensky announced the creation of a new regional format, the "Carpathian Eight." According to him, the group comprises Austria, Hungary, Poland, Romania, Serbia, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, and Ukraine.
The inaugural meeting in this format was held that same day in the town of Bukovel (Ivano-Frankovsk region).

Feature: SW China wilderness grows wilder as gunshot memories fade

Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
21:33:54 CST
22:33:54 KST

LHASA, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Twenty-four years after her father was shot dead while chasing poachers, Tsewang Lhamo finally saw the place where he died.
It took a day and a half from Nyima County to reach the remote corner of the Changtang, a vast nature reserve in northern Xizang Autonomous Region in southwest China. There were no villages, power lines or clear roads at this spot, only rivers cutting through the grassland, distant mountains and wildlife roaming under a restless sky.
A cenotaph stood alone beside a few weather-beaten structures.
Tsewang Lhamo bent down before it and wept.
Her father, formerly a police officer named Norbu Yugyel, was killed there on June 1, 2002, after his patrol encountered suspected Tibetan antelope poachers. He was 40. The patrol vehicle, still marked by bullets, remains in the garage of Nyima County's forestry and grassland bureau.
His two daughters were waiting for him to come home for Children's Day back then. He never did.
"I was not yet 11," recalled his youngest daughter, Socho Lhamo. "I only knew that he had not come back as promised."
For years, she had struggled to understand why her father had spent so much time away protecting wildlife, until she saw piles of confiscated wildlife pelts in 2013 and began to see his work differently.
"You could no longer imagine what those animals had looked like when they were alive and running," Socho Lhamo said. "It was 11 years after his death that I came to understand my father."
She later entered a police academy. Today, she works primarily on household registration, while also serving as Nyima County's first police officer assigned specifically to ecological protection, taking part in patrols, public education and wildlife protection work.
A wildlife protection station named after her father stands opposite her workplace.
Karma Trinley joined a wildlife protection station in 2016 at the age of 17. When he first saw Tibetan antelopes on patrol, he wanted to get closer. Now he does the opposite.
He later learned that even a well-meaning approach could frighten a mother into running, potentially separating her from a newborn calf. Now, while on patrol, he watches the herd's direction, the wind and the distance, and keeps well away until the animals have passed.
The rangers still drive along the same rough tracks into the Changtang. What has changed is what happens when they encounter wildlife: often, the right response is simply to stop and wait.
Two decades ago, protecting wildlife here could mean moving toward armed poachers. Today, it can entail simply keeping a respectful distance from the animals themselves.
The Changtang reserve covers nearly 300,000 square kilometers, much of it above 5,000 meters. Since 2015, 73 wildlife protection stations have been built and more than 700 rangers deployed.
This growing network has also changed what protection looks like on the ground. Herders now often call protection stations when they find injured animals or young animals separated from their mothers. Rangers monitor wildlife, carry out rescues when needed and, as Karma Trinley's experience shows, increasingly know when to keep their distance.
China's law on ecological conservation of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in the west of the country, which took effect in September 2023, has also strengthened protection of the plateau's ecosystems and nature reserves.
The results are increasingly visible on the grassland. Tibetan antelopes in Xizang have increased from just more than 70,000 in the late 20th century to over 300,000 today, while the wild yak population has risen from several thousand to more than 20,000.
Tibetan antelopes now appear more often on the grassland, and wild yaks sometimes stop across a valley and look at patrol vehicles.
The rangers do not rush after them. They stop, lift their binoculars and watch the animals move deeper into the wilderness. Only then do they move on.
Twenty-four years ago, a gunshot echoed across this grassland. Today, the rangers hope to leave behind as little sound as possible.
"The best way to remember those who came before us, is to let the gunshots grow ever more distant, and let the sounds of life grow louder across the grassland," said Kalzang Lhundrup, head of the Norbu Yugyel wildlife conservation station. ■

Chinese premier stresses faster development of emerging, future industries

Chinese Premier Li Qiang, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, visits a pilot test base for artificial intelligence (AI) application in Shanghai, east China, Sept. 22, 2026. Li made an inspection tour in Shanghai on Tuesday. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen)
SHANGHAI, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Tuesday called for efforts to vigorously develop next-generation intelligent manufacturing, accelerate the cultivation of emerging and future industries, and continue to expand and strengthen advanced manufacturing.
Li, also a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee, made the remarks during an inspection tour in Shanghai.
Li called for implementing decisions made at a recent national conference on advanced manufacturing.
At a pilot test base for artificial intelligence (AI) application, Li inspected special-purpose and industrial robots, as well as their applications in complex scenarios, stressing that emerging industries such as AI are advancing rapidly, creating new space for technological innovation and brand upgrading in the manufacturing sector.
He called for combining China's strengths in manufacturing with digital and intelligent technologies, and further implementing the "AI plus manufacturing" to better empower the development of advanced manufacturing.
Li urged efforts to target common challenges in the manufacturing sector, focus on key links such as industrial design, pilot test and intelligent operation and maintenance, and build more manufacturing production and service platforms.
At a sci-tech innovation and incubation platform focused on future industries, Li inspected technological products in fields such as brain-computer interfaces and quantum computing, stressing that future industries are a potential blue ocean for advanced manufacturing.
He called for intensifying research on core technologies, consolidating support for basic research and building a first-class innovation ecosystem.
Given the long growth cycles and high market risks of future industries, Li urged vigorous development of venture capital and expansion of patient capital. ■

ISTANBUL, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Major Turkish airlines, including Turkish Airlines, AJet, and Pegasus, have suspended their flights to Iran following the imposition of new U.S. sanctions targeting the Iranian aviation sector, local media reported on Tuesday.
Turkish Airlines and budget carrier AJet have removed all scheduled flights to Iranian destinations from their booking systems through March 2027, while Pegasus Airlines has also removed Iranian destinations from its reservation platform, according to Ekonomim, an online financial news outlet.
A search on the Turkish Airlines website for flights to Iranian cities currently returns an automated message saying, "There are no flights on the date and route you selected, or all our flights are full."

Earlier this month, the U.S. Treasury Department announced new sanctions targeting Iran's aviation sector, suspending authorizations that allowed non-U.S. airlines to fly U.S.-origin or U.S.-controlled commercial aircraft into Iran. ■

China
Unknown Publisher

21:33:22 CST
22:33:22 KST

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Closer collaboration among the government, universities, industry and private investors is needed to bridge the missing middle in research commercialization and turn promising local technologies into global enterprises, Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Ahmad Zahid Hamidi said here on Tuesday.
While Malaysia has built a strong base in global supply chains, many locally developed technologies face challenges in securing industry partners or capital between research validation and commercialization, Ahmad Zahid said in his speech at the University Research and Innovation Investment Summit 2026 (URIIS 2026).
"The problem is not always the quality of the research. More often, it is the lack of the right partner, capital or pathway to scale. This is where government, universities, industry and investors must work more closely together," he said.
Ahmad Zahid said Malaysia must shift from heavy reliance on public grants to a broader capital ecosystem that involves private investors and industry partners to scale promising ideas into marketable products.
He also called for research to focus more on national challenges such as food security, healthcare, energy and productivity. ■

A former mayor of Russia’s Belgorod who joined the military after being sentenced to five years in prison for bribery has died from wounds sustained while fighting against Ukraine.
Konstantin Polezhayev, who headed the city from 2015-19, and later served as deputy governor of Russia’s Belgorod region, was reportedly killed while serving with Russian forces, according to Russian media.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The circumstances and location of his reported death were not immediately disclosed. Neither Russia’s defense ministry nor Belgorod regional authorities had publicly provided further details at the time of publication.
Polezhayev was convicted in August 2024 of accepting a particularly large bribe while serving as deputy governor.
Investigation said he received two foreign-made luxury vehicles worth about 18 million rubles ($213,400) from the head of a construction company. In exchange, he allegedly provided the company with favorable treatment, including assistance in securing contracts and obtaining payment for completed work.
A court sentenced Polezhayev to five years in a maximum-security penal colony.
Shortly before the verdict, however, Polezhayev announced that he had signed a contract with the Russian defense ministry and said he was prepared to “sacrifice his life.”
A Russian appeals court later suspended proceedings in his case at the request of a military unit commander. Polezhayev was released from custody in October 2024 to begin military service, Russian newspaper Kommersant reported.
Ukraine Hits Major Russian Drone Hub 175 Kilometers From Border, Damages 5 Launchers
Independent Russian outlet Meduza subsequently reported that Polezhayev had initially joined a mobilization reserve unit rather than being sent directly into combat. It remains unclear when he was deployed to the front in Ukraine.
Russia’s war has offered convicted officials and other prisoners a path out of detention through military service. Moscow has recruited extensively from prisons since the full-scale invasion began in February 2022, initially through the Wagner mercenary group, and later through contracts administered by the defense ministry.
Russian legislation allows criminal proceedings and sentences to be suspended when defendants or convicted prisoners sign military contracts. Those who receive state awards or complete their service may also become eligible to have their convictions cleared.

Ladin: Dolomites villages refuse to give up on ancient language
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:30:40 UTC
22:30:40 KST

Ladin: Dolomites villages refuse to give up on ancient language
Year after year, the mountains of the Dolomites become more popular with tourists. Amid millions of visitors, 30,000 inhabitants speak a language only they understand: Ladin, one of the oldest minority languages in Europe.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Tourists crammed onto a ridge, hikers stuck on the trails, long queues to reach a mountain hut... This past summer, hundreds of videos posted on social media showed the flip side of the Dolomites, a mountain range in northern Italy.
Long favoured by Italians themselves, the Dolomites have become a highly popular destination for foreign visitors in recent years. Today, the mountain range welcomes several million tourists every year, boosted by the 2026 Winter Olympics.
This growing influx of visitors worries people in the valleys as much as it contributes to their economy. "This tourism that's settling in almost everywhere in Val Badia scares us a bit, because it risks forcing young people like us to leave for financial reasons," explains Marco, a 29-year-old graphic designer.
Marco and his brother Samuel, a 32-year-old pharmacist, both grew up in the Badia Valley, in a small town of less than 4,000 inhabitants. The brothers have watched prices skyrocket, and locals forced to leave their land. "We need to preserve our community, otherwise it will become a bit like a box that’s beautiful, but empty."
'Why do you speak that language? Speak Italian, no?'
The community Samuel is talking about is the Ladin community: about 30,000 people, located in five valleys across the Italian regions of Trentino Alto-Adige and Veneto. Most of these Italians speak both German and Italian, but they also speak Ladin, one of the very last living alpine languages and one of the oldest in all of Europe.
At school, at home, at work, in the mouths of the locals, Ladin naturally comes first. "If you're with Ladins, you speak Ladin. If there's an Italian in the group, you try to speak Italian, or German. You manage about five minutes in Italian, then you go back to Ladin. And for the Italian... too bad, he has to learn it!" laughs Fabian, a cheesemaker and childhood friend of Samuel's.
Read moreGrecanico: Ancient Greek language still spoken in southern Italy
In these valleys, Ladin is the majority language, and hardly understandable to tourists, even Italian ones. "In some restaurants or hotels, they have menus in Ladin. So there are those who wonder what it is, people who have been coming here for years who sometimes aren't even aware that Ladin exists. And then there are people who get annoyed and say: 'Why do you speak that language? Speak Italian, no?'" Samuel recounts.
Rap to keep this 2,000-year-old language alive
If Ladin takes up such an important place in the daily life of South Tyroleans, it is thanks to the autonomous status granted to the region in 1972. In addition to guaranteeing the Italian/German bilingualism of South Tyrol, the decree places particular emphasis on the teaching of Ladin. "Ladin is used in nursery schools and is taught in the primary schools of Ladin-speaking areas," the text reads. In the Ladin valleys, there is therefore a system of trilingual schools, where classes are taught in Italian and German, and where Ladin is used as the everyday language.
"Everyone who was born with this language cares about it, and tries to keep it alive." Samuel is a fervent defender of his mother tongue. With a group of friends, he set up a rap group several years ago, Cooperaziun Planta. "Doing rap in Italian would have just been a passion project. But, since we're Ladins, doing it in Ladin is something a bit special."
Even if rhymes are harder to find in Ladin than in Italian, Samuel and his group make it a point of honor to sing only in Ladin. It’s a way, according to the young rapper, of contributing to its survival. "The best weapon to keeping a language alive is to enjoy it."

Iran delegation to present narrative of resilience, diplomacy at UNGA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:29:53 UTC
22:29:53 KST

Iran delegation to present narrative of resilience, diplomacy at UNGA
Iranians are divided on whether the UNGA will help end the war with the US.
Tehran, Iran – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and his team are heading to New York for the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), where they are expected to express grievances about the United States’ war on Iran, but also look at ways of resolving it.
Pezeshkian, who departed Tehran on Tuesday morning local time, is joined by Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and other officials, and is scheduled to address the 193-member assembly on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Russian strikes on Ukraine kill three as Zelenskyy arrives for UN summit
- list 2 of 4Why United Nations says US boat strikes may be ‘crimes against humanity’
- list 3 of 4Can the US ban Iranian airlines worldwide – and what would it mean?
- list 4 of 4Trump-GCC Summit in New York: What does each side want?
“The issues we will raise at the UN concern expressing the plight of the Iranian nation, the crimes that have been committed against it, and the distrust that has been created,” Pezeshkian told reporters before boarding a flight out of Tehran.
He also warned that the renewed use of force by Iran’s foes would be counterproductive.
“We will make the enemies disappointed,” he said.
Araghchi, who had arrived in New York earlier, said his main goals during meetings on the sidelines will be to “defend the rights and interest of the Iranian people”.
The war started by the US and Israel on Iran on February 28 continues, with disruptions to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz that have affected global energy prices.
In the backdrop, Araghchi slammed the UN’s lacklustre performance in establishing peace and security.
“Trust in this organisation has been lost, and this is unfortunately because of its ineffectiveness in establishing international peace and security,” he said.
He said the Minab school bombing by the US and the assassination of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei on the opening day of the war would be among the issues Iran will raise at the UN.
Sina Toosi, senior non-resident fellow at the Center for International Policy, told Al Jazeera that he believes the Iranian delegation will aim to send a message that it is “open to diplomacy”, but not willing to “de-escalate unilaterally”, as Tehran believes it did in June after the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the US.
“I expect Pezeshkian to present Iran’s current pressure campaign not as an alternative to diplomacy, but as leverage for achieving a more durable agreement,” Toosi said. “The immediate Iranian demands are … an end to the naval blockade, and respect for the Iran-Oman agreement governing transit through Hormuz. In many respects, this amounts to returning to the June understanding and actually implementing it.”
The Iranian delegation will be in New York for five days and is scheduled to return to Tehran on Saturday.
The US has denied visas to Pezeshkian’s accompanying media team and imposed tight restrictions on their movement in the country, according to the president’s office. Iranian delegates will also be barred from buying luxury goods during their stay.
Still, Pezeshkian plans to hold discussions with Iranian expatriates, intellectuals, think tanks and media in the coming days.
Regional tensions
The UNGA brings together representatives of nearly 130 countries at the body’s headquarters in New York.
This year’s assembly, which begins on Tuesday, comes as the US tightens economic pressure through sanctions and a naval blockade on southern Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz.
US President Donald Trump said earlier this week that he was considering a new major military assault on Iran, but wanted to hear from the Arab leaders of the region first. He is set to meet with representatives from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Kuwait and Bahrain in the coming days to discuss the war on Iran.
This and a military escalation in Yemen, where Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces are fighting the Iran-aligned Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, are other concerns for the assembly.
The Houthis have expanded control over the strait of Bab al-Mandeb in recent weeks after making rapid military advances in western Yemen and the Red Sea coast.
Mediation
Regional mediators – including Pakistan, Qatar, Oman and Turkiye – have pushed for a diplomatic end to the crisis amid prospects of escalated conflict.
As Iran demands a return to the memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, its diplomats are expected to sit down with mediators in New York as well.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, told Al Jazeera earlier this week that Tehran has communicated seven conditions to the US to reopen the strategic waterway.
These included an end to war on all fronts, the release of Iran’s frozen assets, the lifting of the blockade on Iranian ports, an end to military attacks on Iranian territory, and noninterference in the country’s internal affairs. But he also said Iran remains prepared for escalated fighting, and could potentially abandon the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) depending on future US actions.
Toosi told Al Jazeera that there was a “real opening” for diplomacy, but “no guarantee of a breakthrough”.
“The fundamental obstacle is credibility,” Toosi said. “Tehran’s conclusion from the June MoU was that de-escalating first left it dependent on US commitments that Washington could reverse or simply fail to implement. That helps explain why Iran is now trying to negotiate while maintaining coercive leverage, particularly over Hormuz.”
“The UN therefore presents a potentially important opportunity because both sides have reasons to explore an off-ramp,” Toosi added. The question is whether Trump is prepared to negotiate a genuinely reciprocal agreement, rather than treating diplomacy as a mechanism for Iran to surrender its leverage first.”
Meanwhile, in Iran, there are conflicting views about how to end the war with the US, with some parties open to a peaceful resolution and more hardline factions seeking to continue or intensify the war until all Tehran’s demands are met.
Hossein Mohebbi, the spokesman of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), told local media on Tuesday that Iran was prepared to use new weapons systems against the US if necessary, and pointed to its recent attacks on US warships.
But he added that the country was open to peace. “If our national interests call for it to conduct some negotiations alongside war, we must negotiate,” he said.
Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, had already said both options remain on the table, but said hardline factions have no end date for the war of attrition. Other factions underestimate Iran’s capabilities and believe it must surrender, he said.
“The first keeps the country in a state of perpetual crisis and the other offers national resources and dignity to the enemy on a platter,” Ghalibaf said. “Both approaches realise the enemy’s wish for disturbing the country’s cohesion and unity.”
Trump said on Sunday he would “probably be open” to meeting Pezeshkian in New York, although the Iranian government’s IRNA news service dismissed this as a “new propaganda game”.
The government’s daily Iran newspaper said New York could offer a “platform for the Iranian narrative”. The hardline Kayhan newspaper wanted Pezeshkian to turn the UN into “a courtroom for American crimes”.
Public expectations in Iran are sceptical that the UN meetings will produce any political breakthrough to end the war, which has deepened the average Iranian citizen’s economic woes.
“I think Pezeshkian going [to New York] is better than him not going, but there is no hope that anything comes of it,” one Iranian told Al Jazeera in western Tehran, on condition of anonymity due to security concerns.
Another resident of the capital also said she harboured no hopes of a diplomatic resolution.
“I think if [the politicians] want to, then yes, there can be an opening, but they don’t want to,” she said.

Lib Dems quietly commission review into religious inclusion amid case brought by dropped candidate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:28:49 UTC
22:28:49 KST

The Liberal Democrats have quietly commissioned a review into the treatment of figures within their ranks who hold religious views, weeks after the Guardian revealed a religious discrimination claim against the party by the former candidate David Campanale.
Campanale, a former BBC journalist, was selected in 2021 as the party’s candidate for Sutton and Cheam but was removed in August 2023. He has argued in a civil case against the party that discrimination against his Christianity cost him his political career.
Richard Newby, the former Lib Dem leader in the House of Lords, has been appointed to chair the party’s inclusion and faith review, which will examine how the party treats candidates and members of different faith and those without.
The inquiry, which has not been publicly announced, was set up in direct response to Campanale’s case, the Guardian understands, with figures at the top of the party understood to be keen to show they take the issue seriously.
The Guardian revealed last month that Campanale was seeking almost £790,000 in damages after the party admitted direct and indirect discrimination on the grounds of religion or belief, and failures in dealing with complaints about his treatment.
The case prompted the former Lib Dem leader Tim Farron and former deputy leader Simon Hughes to call for an independent inquiry into Campanale’s treatment by the party, as well as an apology.
The party cannot comment on court proceedings and will instead use Lord Newby’s review to seek to answer the general question of whether people of faith are being discriminated against, and to what extent any evidence shows this.
Hughes told the Guardian he would pursue a separate investigation once Campanale’s case was resolved.
“The Newby review is explicitly not about any past or present legal case and cannot be about David’s case, which is still before the courts and with one remaining possible internal party appeal,” he said. “The review however is greatly to be welcomed and I believe it will allow the party to meet one of the two big objectives which David, [the] Lib Dem Christian Forum, I and others were seeking.”
The Newby review was announced last week to party members via an email from the Lib Dem leader, Ed Davey, and president, Josh Babarinde, days before the start of the party’s conference in Brighton.
It will examine whether candidate approval, selection and deselection processes are inclusive of different faiths, whether candidates receive adequate support, the operation of complaints and disciplinary processes, and training for local party officers.
A Lib Dem source said: “This review offers no remorse, no apologies to members misled so badly nor contrition towards the victims of breaches including Campanale and other Christians who once formed a bedrock of activists among our party’s nonconformist tradition. All should have had an apology by now.
“As it stands, the review looks like a ploy to impress a court judge as the review of Campanale’s case is meant to be published right before damages are considered.”
Another source said: “The review doesn’t recognise the pain [Campanale’s case] brought on members, and it has to be asked why key individuals refused to act when they received complaints or requests to investigate complaints around Campanale’s deselection.”
Campanale submitted a schedule of loss that puts his claim at £788,740.75, including interest. It seeks compensation for injury to feelings, aggravated damages, past and future earnings, the loss of an MP’s pension, counselling costs and the “loss of a chance” or “loss of political capital”.
In his claim, Campanale said that at a meeting in January 2022 he was questioned about his Christianity by about 30 people and asked whether he was enjoying his “martyrdom just like Jesus did”.
Questions have emerged within the party about the remit of the review. A number of Lib Dem figures and activists have also privately criticised its lack of formal announcement. One figure questioned whether Newby would have access to complaints and candidate selection material, and whether the review would extend beyond religious faith to other protected beliefs.
There is a particular concern among some members about whether the review will examine the party’s treatment of people with gender-critical beliefs. In a motion passed at party conference on Monday, members rejected official guidance by the equalities watchdog on how organisations should implement the supreme court ruling on transgender people, calling it “discriminatory and unworkable”.
The party’s conference fringe programme over the weekend included discussions about Christian nationalism and political use of religion.
The Lib Dems previously said the party was “home to people of all faiths and none, including many Christians”, but have declined to comment.

Häkkänen faces no-confidence move over Israel visit
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:28:30 EEST
22:28:30 KST

Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen faces a no-confidence move in parliament after his visit to Israel and meeting with Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz prompted criticism from opposition parties. The Greens have questioned who approved the meeting and whether it reflected the government’s wider policy towards Israel.
Häkkänen visited Lebanon and Israel from 13 to 18 September. According to the Ministry of Defence, he met Katz, reviewed the David’s Sling air defence system purchased for the Finnish Defence Forces, examined Israeli civil defence arrangements and visited defence companies supplying Finland.
In Lebanon, Häkkänen met President Joseph Aoun, Defence Minister Michel Menassa, UNIFIL commanders and Finnish peacekeepers.
The Israel part of the trip has since become the focus of a dispute in parliament.
Greens chair Sofia Virta said she plans to submit a no-confidence motion against Häkkänen. She has demanded an explanation of whether the government approved the meeting with Katz or whether Häkkänen made the decision himself.
Häkkänen told Finnish news agency STT that the decision to make the visit was his.
Virta has argued that a ministerial meeting carries political significance because of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and Katz’s statements concerning Palestinians. She has also questioned whether the visit conflicts with Finland’s stated support for international law.
The Left Alliance has said it will support the Greens’ no-confidence initiative. Virta has called on the Social Democratic Party, which has been considering its position, to join the motion.
Left Alliance chair Minja Koskela has also submitted a written parliamentary question over the visit. Koskela said the government should explain whether it assessed the trip in relation to Finland’s campaign for a UN Security Council seat for 2029–30.
Greens MP Atte Harjanne has separately asked whether the meeting had the backing of the foreign minister, the government and the president. He said Finland’s existing defence purchases from Israel created practical ties but questioned the need for a ministerial meeting.
Prime Minister Petteri Orpo defended Häkkänen on Tuesday and described the criticism from the opposition as disproportionate.
Orpo said the trip involved a normal ministerial duty linked to Finnish defence and Häkkänen’s visit to Finnish personnel serving with UNIFIL.
He also pointed to David’s Sling, which Finland agreed to purchase from Israel during the previous government’s term. Häkkänen has said developments to the system following Iranian missile attacks were among the reasons for his visit.
“He was there ensuring the delivery to Finland of the air defence system ordered by the previous government, meaning the current opposition parties,” Orpo told reporters in parliament, according to Yle.
Häkkänen has also stressed Iran’s role in regional conflicts. In comments to Ilta-Sanomat, he said Hamas and Hezbollah operate in practice as extensions of Iran’s armed forces.
Middle East researcher Timo R. Stewart of the University of Helsinki disputed parts of that framing in comments to Helsingin Sanomat. Stewart said Iran has maintained close links with Hezbollah and has supported Hamas, but argued that placing the emphasis on Iran follows a narrative favourable to Israel and leaves out factors connected to Israel’s own policies.
Stewart also told HS that the ministerial visit sent a signal of closer cooperation with Israel, questioning the need for a political-level visit after the defence purchases had already been agreed.
The dispute also comes as Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen has backed a joint statement with other countries concerning restrictions on products originating from Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.
The controversy comes weeks after Finland’s defence cooperation with Israel drew criticism from opposition parties. Yle reported in August that the two countries had renewed a memorandum on defence materiel cooperation for 10 years, extending the arrangement until 2034, without a public announcement from the Ministry of Defence.
The Greens and Left Alliance criticised both the agreement and the way it was handled.

El Nino poses growing global health threat as temperatures rise: UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:28:24 UTC
22:28:24 KST

El Nino is strengthening rapidly and is expected to have health impacts worldwide, with the most severe consequences likely in countries already facing weak health systems and humanitarian crises, UN agencies have warned.
"We've just lived through the two hottest months on record. Sea surface temperatures are at record levels," Armel Castellan, extreme heat adviser at the joint WHO-WMO climate and health program, told reporters in Geneva on Tuesday.
Castellan said El Nino is expected to peak toward the end of 2026, but stressed that its impacts would continue beyond that point.
As the event peaks, much of the Southern Hemisphere, including southern Africa, South America and Australia, will move into its hottest season in early 2027, potentially increasing risks of drought, wildfires, smoke and air pollution, he said.
‘Public health threat, not just a climate phenomenon’
Teresa Zakaria, WHO's unit head for risk reduction, humanitarian operations and climate change, told reporters that El Nino is "a significant public health threat, not just a climate phenomenon."
She said malnutrition and cholera are assessed as "very high" risks in both drought- and flood-affected settings.
More than 150 million people are already facing acute food insecurity globally, with that figure expected to increase as climate shocks disrupt food production and livelihoods, she said.
Warmer temperatures and changing rainfall could also increase transmission of mosquito-borne diseases including malaria, dengue, chikungunya, yellow fever and Zika, potentially spreading them into areas where they have not traditionally occurred.
"We have a window of opportunity to act now before these risks become crises," Zakaria said.

Hundreds flee homes in Far North Cameroon after armed group raid kills 15

Hundreds of people have fled their homes after an armed group killed 15 people in the village of Madegoua near the town of Makary in the Far North region of Cameroon.

North Korea's Kim lauds test of apparent new hypersonic missile
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:28:05 UTC
22:28:05 KST

North Korea's Kim Jong Un lauds apparent hypersonic missile test, calls it "incurable headache" for foes
Hong Kong — With his teenage daughter and possible successor by his side, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un watched on Sunday as his country tested a purported new hypersonic weapon designed to evade missile defenses. North Korean state media said Kim had lauded the weapon as an "irresistible force" that would be an "incurable headache" for North Korea's adversaries.
The country's state-run KCNA news agency said the "new weapon" tested on Sunday was "of great significance."
The type of weapon was not specified by the reports, but photographs released by KCNA showed Kim, with his daughter Kim Ju Ae, inspecting a screen with a label reading, "Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory."
Analysts say the title suggests the test was of an upgraded version of an existing North Korean short-range ballistic missile that adds a retrofitted hypersonic glide vehicle. Hypersonic missiles can generally fly lower and faster than conventional rockets, making them more difficult to intercept. North Korea has tested various hypersonic weapons systems since 2021.
They are among the advanced weapons Kim has wanted his country to develop as he seeks to upgrade North Korea's nuclear capabilities.
The test launch on Sunday will come as a blow to South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who is expected to lay out plans to improve relations with Pyongyang at the U.N. General Assembly this week. The two Koreas have remained technically at war since fighting in the Korean War ended in 1953 with a ceasefire agreement rather than a full peace deal.
Lee has proposed dropping South Korea's longstanding demand for Pyongyang to give up its nuclear weapons as a precondition for talks, suggesting instead a freeze on further nuclear weapons testing or development by North Korea, at least initially.
President Trump has also repeatedly expressed interest in meeting with Kim, possibly around the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, in November. The White House has suggested that talks could be held "without any preconditions."
Mr. Trump met with Kim three times during his first term, but failed to make any progress on the issue of denuclearization. Since then, North Korea has continued to develop its nuclear and conventional weapons programs and is now believed to possess dozens of nuclear warheads.
South Korea's government claims Pyongyang has between 80 and 120 warheads. Mr. Trump recently said the North had 57 nuclear warheads.
The Kim regime has given no indication of interest in a new round of talks with Mr. Trump or with Lee, despite Mr. Trump's move last month to scale back annual military drills with South Korea, which he called "hostile" to Pyongyang.

Settlers storm Palestinian towns as Israeli forces raid W. Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:27:33 UTC
22:27:33 KST

Breadcrumb
Settlers storm Palestinian towns as Israeli forces raid West Bank
Israeli settlers backed by occupation forces attacked several Palestinian communities across the occupied West Bank in the early hours of Tuesday, as settler violence and military raids continue at unprecedented levels across the territory.
Dozens of settlers, accompanied by a large Israeli military force, stormed the town of Silwad, east of Ramallah, and seized dozens of livestock belonging to three Palestinian residents.
Property was damaged during the attack before local residents confronted the settlers and forced them to withdraw.
Silwad Mayor Raed Hamed told The New Arab that "hundreds of settlers entered the town of Silwad in the early hours of Tuesday via an unpaved agricultural road near the Ayoun al-Haramiyah area."
He said Israeli forces accompanied the settlers and provided them with protection, while other troops entered the town through its main entrances.
In nearby al-Mazraa al-Sharqiya, Mohammed Malash, a volunteer with the town's ambulance service, told The New Arab that settlers attacked the outskirts of the town at around 2 a.m. as the assault on Silwad was under way, prompting confrontations with Palestinian residents.
Malash said live ammunition was fired at young Palestinian men, although no injuries were reported. Residents quickly reached the area and prevented the settlers from breaking into one of the homes.
He added that settlers smashed Palestinian-owned vehicles and attempted to attack a house before residents confronted them and forced them to withdraw.
Israeli forces raid Palestinian towns
The settler attacks came alongside a series of Israeli military raids across the occupied West Bank.
In Nablus, Israeli forces stormed several areas of the northern West Bank city, searched homes and detained 68-year-old Samir al-Asta from his home.
Israeli forces also raided several areas of the Bethlehem governorate, including Beit Sahour and Beit Jala, as well as the towns of al-Ubeidiya, al-Shawawra and Zaatara. No arrests were reported there.
In Tammun, southeast of Tubas, Israeli forces detained 86-year-old Burhan Rashid Bani Odeh and his 57-year-old daughter, Rashida, on Tuesday morning.
Kamal Bani Odeh, director of the Prisoners' Club in Tubas, said the pair were detained in an attempt to pressure Rashida's son to turn himself in, adding that other members of the family had previously been arrested for the same reason.
In Ramallah and al-Bireh, Israeli forces tightened movement restrictions and erected a checkpoint at the entrance to Ain Sinya, north of Ramallah, disrupting hundreds of vehicles, particularly those leaving the city.
Another checkpoint was erected between Silwad and Yabrud, east of Ramallah, restricting residents' movement, while Israeli forces established a further checkpoint at the entrance to Aboud, west of Ramallah, where soldiers searched Palestinian vehicles and checked residents' identification documents.
Late on Monday, Israeli forces withdrew from the town of Biddu in the central West Bank following a day-long military operation involving raids, arrests, field interrogations and assaults on Palestinians.
Biddu Mayor Nazmi Mansour told The New Arab that "Israeli forces withdrew from the town overnight, and institutions, schools and shops resumed operations this morning."
He said five Palestinians remained in detention after others were released following the field interrogation of hundreds of residents. Dozens of injuries were also reported during the raid.
Settler violence reaches unprecedented levels
The attacks come amid an unprecedented surge in Israeli settler violence against Palestinians across the occupied West Bank.
Since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right coalition took office at the end of 2022, settler attacks have increased sharply alongside settlement expansion and increasingly severe restrictions on Palestinian movement.
The UN has said settler violence has reached unprecedented levels in 2026, documenting more than 1,430 incidents resulting in casualties or property damage by 10 August and affecting around 260 Palestinian communities.
UN officials have also documented Israeli settlers and security forces acting together in attacks on Palestinian communities, while UN experts have described the escalating violence as "settler terror" carried out with the support and acquiescence of the Israeli state.
Thousands of Palestinians have been displaced this year amid settler violence, demolitions and evictions, with entire communities forced from their land.
The violence has included killings and physical assaults, as well as attacks on Palestinian homes, livestock, farmland, vehicles, water infrastructure and other property.
The Israeli Institute for National Security Studies warned earlier this month that surging settler terrorism posed a threat to Israeli state institutions.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law. The UK and several other European governments have also imposed sanctions targeting settlers and entities linked to violence and settlement activity.
Israeli settlements and settlers have recently faced UK measures amid mounting international pressure over settlement expansion and attacks on Palestinians.

Malta attorney general appeals blogger murder trial verdict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:24:21 UTC
22:24:21 KST

Malta attorney general appeals blogger murder trial verdict
VALLETTA, Sept 22 - Malta’s attorney general has filed an appeal against a jury verdict finding a businessman not guilty of charges of complicity and criminal association in the murder of prominent journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia.
Caruana Galizia was killed when a bomb placed in her car blew up as she drove out of her home in 2017.
While the men who planted the bomb and those who produced it are serving long jail terms, the man suspected of masterminding it, Yorgen Fenech, was acquitted by an 8-1 verdict earlier in September after a two-month trial.
The verdict shocked the country and sparked protests.
No details were immediately available on the grounds of the appeal, but an appeal in jury trials is limited to points of law.
The Criminal Code allows the Court of Criminal Appeal to order a retrial if it considers that the interests of justice require it.
Malta police last week confirmed that three jurors, a reserve juror and the husband of a juror involved in the trial had been arrested and questioned on the basis of social media posts they are alleged to have authored, along with suspicions that one juror had access to a phone while sequestered for the trial.
All four were released on police bail and no charges have been filed.
The killing of Caruana Galizia nine years ago shocked Europe and set off a political firestorm in Malta as well as focusing international attention on its police and judiciary.
Prosecutors alleged that Fenech, the heir to a property empire that includes hotels and casinos, wanted Caruana Galizia dead because she was about to reveal information about his business dealings. He denied the accusations against him. REUTERS

Romanian court grants former presidential candidate conditional release in fraud case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:23:26 UTC
22:23:26 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
A Romanian court on Tuesday ordered the conditional release of former presidential candidate Calin Georgescu in a fraud case, broadcaster Digi24 reported.
The Bucharest Tribunal rejected prosecutors’ request to keep Georgescu and co-defendant Ionel Rusen in custody for 30 days, placing both under judicial control.
Georgescu cannot leave Romania and must report regularly to police.
Prosecutors from Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) detained him for 24 hours on Monday in an investigation into organized crime and an alleged €1.1 million ($1.3 million) fraud.
Prosecutors allege that three people formed an organized criminal group in September 2021 and operated mainly in Romania and the UK as part of a scheme involving promises of foreign financing, according to DIICOT.
The investigation concerns a businessman who allegedly lost about €1.1 million after being promised access to financing.
Georgescu was detained after investigators carried out searches at five locations in Bucharest and nearby areas, including his home in Mogosoaia.
He exercised his right to remain silent during questioning, according to judicial sources cited by Romanian news agency Agerpres.
Dozens of supporters gathered outside the courthouse during Tuesday’s closed-door hearing, chanting “We do not give up!” Digi24 reported.
Georgescu, running as an independent, unexpectedly won the first round of Romania’s 2024 presidential election with about 23% of the vote.
However, the Constitutional Court later annulled the election following intelligence reports alleging campaign irregularities and foreign interference. Georgescu was subsequently barred from running in the repeat election in 2025.
The latest fraud case remains under investigation.
