====================================================================================================

The Strugatsky brothers’ Soviet sci-fi classic ‘Hard to Be a God’ took aim at dictatorship. Russia’s new state-backed TV adaptation strips away the politics.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:11:06 UTC
22:11:06 KST

The Strugatsky brothers’ Soviet sci-fi classic ‘Hard to Be a God’ took aim at dictatorship. Russia’s new state-backed TV adaptation strips away the politics.
The streaming platform Wink is releasing a series called “Hard to Be a God,” based on the novel by the Strugatsky brothers. The creators have noticeably changed the book’s plot: now we follow Earth’s envoy, Don Rumata, from his very first days working in Arkanar. There are more characters and more adventures, but the most important thing has vanished: a coherent vision of a utopian future and the theme of science as the driving force of progress. Where Aleksei German argued with the Strugatskys’ novel in his famous film, the series’ creators simply prefer to ignore the inconvenient parts. Critic Anton Khitrov writes about the project.
The Internet Development Institute (IRI) funding an adaptation of Hard to Be a God is even funnier than Apple producing the anti-capitalist series Severance.
The Strugatskys’ now-classic novel was published in 1964, near the end of the Thaw, when the central subject in Soviet art — even permitted art — was the experience of living under dictatorship. Like other artists of their generation, the Strugatskys attacked totalitarianism from a leftist perspective: they “fought Stalin with Lenin’s help,” as Veniamin Smekhov, an actor at the Taganka Theater and another emblematic figure of Thaw-era culture, once put it.
Hard to Be a God, like other works in the Noon Universe cycle, is set in a future where communism has triumphed on Earth but has yet to be established on other inhabited planets. To gently nudge them in the right direction, Earth sends “observers”: historian-scientists who gather data about distant worlds and, where possible, support local progressive forces.
The novel’s protagonist, the observer Anton, works undercover in the feudal city-state of Arkanar under the pseudonym Don Rumata Estorsky. His main mission is to save the philosophers, scientists, and poets targeted by the all-powerful Don Reba, the closest adviser to Arkanar’s king. The parallels with the Great Terror are obvious, though Rumata himself — a product of Soviet literature, after all — draws a different historical parallel: German National Socialism.
Boris Strugatsky insisted that Hard to Be a God was political commentary, not just adventure science fiction. But on today’s Russian streaming platforms, political commentary is unthinkable, unless you count propaganda like the Z-themed melodrama Landyshi “Lilies of the Valley,” which airs on the same Wink platform as the Strugatsky adaptation and, naturally, is also backed by the IRI. Although a few lines of dialogue can, if you look for it, be read as timid dissent, the new adaptation is on the whole deeply apolitical: it has more characters and storylines but incomparably fewer difficult questions.
In the series’ opening scenes, an unnamed character played by Leonid Yarmolnik — an observer — is killed by an Arkanar arrow. “If only you knew who they replaced you with,” whispers his comrade Don Kondor (Sergei Bezrukov), who has just been assigned the newcomer Rumata (Serbian actor Aleksandar Radojičić) as his charge. The joke: in the full-length film adaptation of the same novel — Aleksei German’s famous farewell picture, shot from 1999 until his death in 2013 — Rumata was played by none other than Yarmolnik.
If this is meant as a claim to continuity, it’s unconvincing. German’s Hard to Be a God is a three-hour black-and-white film — slow, bleak, and utterly uncompromising. The Wink series is high-budget entertainment complete with spaceships, cool gadgets, and armored war horses. In the Strugatskys’ novel, the Earthling characters were, naturally, scientists (the favorite profession of 1960s writers); in the adaptation, they’re more like superagents, characters out of a spy thriller — security forces, in a word, not unlike Don Reba’s gray guardsmen, only good.
The textbook-masculine Radojičić is convincing with a sword and unbearably phony whenever the script requires him to say something smart. The protagonist is arguably the series’ weakest point: these days, a virtuous, square-jawed strongman doesn’t even cut it as the simplest action hero — something more complex is required. It’s no accident that the new Superman looks less like a demigod and more like an awkward intern.
Rumata busies himself with anything — court intrigues, rescuing pretty girls, fleeing from bandits — anything but his direct duties: helping the persecuted intellectuals, whom the series remembers only for the sake of appearances. Even the hero’s main motivation — finding the missing Doctor Budach — has nothing to do with his mission in Arkanar. In the book, Budach was a native of Arkanar, a scientific luminary who needed the Earthlings’ protection. In the series, Budach is an observer, Rumata’s father, and saving him isn’t about a better future but simply filial love. It’s a noble cause, certainly, but no longer selfless help for a gifted alien.
Far more interesting is Fyodor Lavrov’s Don Reba. The minister of the royal guard isn’t just insinuating, cunning, and cruel — he’s a fervent believer, convinced that his destiny is to become second only to God. A security officer who has seized power and has a messiah complex is the most topical figure in the whole show. This would work if the rest of the series weren’t so toothless.
Hard to Be a God showrunner Andrei Zolotarev has adapted Soviet science fiction before: he co-wrote the screenplay for the film Sto Let Tomu Vpered “One Hundred Years Ahead,” based on the novel by Kir Bulychev. Both projects ignore ideology: Zolotarev carefully avoids not only the word “communism” but any details about the social system of the future.
This isn’t a polemic with the source material — it’s an attempt to avoid dangerous territory, nothing more. The 22nd century in the series is clearly meant to be utopian, but the project carefully avoids saying what that utopia actually consists of, since imagining an ideal future in today’s Russia is apparently a hopeless task. The creators take refuge in clichés: biotech and minimalism, white suits and white uniforms. Instead of Zoom, there are holograms like in Star Wars; instead of pets, Boston Dynamics robot dogs (vintage items, in the series’ universe).
Every so often, though, we get hints about how things are going on Earth: some of the station’s staff are American, but the working language is Russian, and the equipment here and there bears the logo of Russia’s state nuclear energy corporation Rosatom. “In the 21st century, we were saved by pure chance,” Don Kondor, Rumata’s morally flexible mentor, remarks in the first episode. It’s unclear from the dialogue exactly what danger was avoided, but judging by the international space mission under Rosatom’s patronage, the Russian Federation apparently ended up as the world’s hegemon. Behold the happy future, according to the IRI.
Hi, I’m Katya.
I’ve been running Meduza’s crowdfunding since 2021. Today, supporting Meduza is a crime in Russia. You can be sent to prison just for donating. We’re still able to do our work thanks to thousands of our Russian readers who now live abroad. But even they’re no longer safe.
Imagine you’ve left Russia, but then your mom becomes seriously ill. It could be your last chance to see her, so of course you go home. At the border, you’re interrogated. Officers hack into your phone and search for any trace that you’ve donated to Meduza.
The Kremlin is counting on that fear, and it’s working. People are afraid to donate. I’m afraid for our supporters, because any one of them could end up in prison. And I’m afraid for Meduza. Without crowdfunding, we simply can’t continue. So if you live outside Russia and don’t have to worry that donating to Meduza could keep you from going home to your family, I’m asking for your help. Please support our work.
Meanwhile, communism in the Strugatskys’ work isn’t just a nod to mandatory ideology. The entire novel grows out of the conviction that humanity is, in principle, capable of building an ideal society — and building it by relying on universal laws of science: social, economic, historical, and so on.
That’s exactly why the Earthlings fuss over Arkanar’s scientists: they know for certain that sooner or later, these scientists will inevitably come up with not just the internal combustion engine but Marxism too. However bleak the novel’s resolution may be, the Strugatskys ultimately offer hope: no despotic power can wipe out science, progress is unstoppable, and it brings people happiness.
Actually, Hard to Be a God is ideal material for an adaptation: smart prose that practically begs to be argued with. More than 60 years after the novel’s publication, we’ve had plenty of reasons to conclude (or at least entertain the possibility) that intellectuals and autocrats sometimes form a fine symbiosis, that progress isn’t always a good thing, and that history doesn’t move in a single direction.
What’s more, a polemical take on this story already exists: German’s film. Yarmolnik’s Rumata was noticeably older and more cynical than the character in the book. Neither he nor the other observers still held out hope for change in Arkanar; they worked mostly out of inertia, rapidly degrading to the level of the locals — even raising their children according to Arkanar customs. In German’s version, progress capitulates to the onslaught of archaism, ideals fade, and the characters turn into villains without the slightest anguish.
Far from all Strugatsky fans embraced the film adaptation, probably because the director made no effort whatsoever to be engaging — an undeniable virtue of the original. If anything, he deliberately “drowned” the plot in repellent details of Arkanar daily life. Not every viewer will agree with the film’s misanthropy either, but whether or not you like German’s interpretation, it at the very least complicates our understanding of the novel rather than simplifying it.
This, ideally, is exactly what an interpreter should be doing: if a film adaptation doesn’t convince you that you were missing something important about the source material, it’s unclear why the adaptation was needed at all. You could also make Hamlet into a political thriller about medieval Denmark, or War and Peace into a patriotic blockbuster about defeating Napoleon, and there would surely be viewers satisfied with such a reading. But wouldn’t it be more honest just to do without the classics here?
The difference between the full-length adaptation and the series is especially clear in how each handles the same Strugatsky idea: Rumata’s hidden camera. In the novel, the observers wear special headbands so they can supply their fellow Earthlings with documentary material day and night. In German’s film, Rumata is a human movie camera, the viewer’s avatar in Arkanar: we follow him through narrow streets, breathe in sweat, and trudge through mud — in short, we’re immersed in real, unappealing life. The series’ Rumata, who wears high-tech contact lenses instead of a headband, is more like a first-person-shooter character: when we’re shown the world through his eyes, health indicators glow at the edge of the frame.
The Arkanar of the new adaptation really is a virtual reality with little connection to ours. An otherworldly sky with a giant planet, plasticky CGI architecture, immaculate costumes fresh from the wardrobe department, tedious battle scenes set to generic action music — everything suggests we’re not watching a Strugatsky adaptation but a Twitch stream.
Even so, all these complaints are aimed at the wrong target. It seems the creators’ real creative ambition wasn’t a dialogue with the Strugatskys but the notorious policy of import substitution. It’s telling that Fyodor Bondarchuk is involved: not only did he produce the series, he also played one of Arkanar’s courtiers. His last directing work in feature film was the two-part Prityazhenie “Attraction” and Vtorzhenie “Invasion,” a dubious attempt to play on Steven Spielberg’s turf and make a Hollywood-style blockbuster about contact with aliens. This same “import-substitution” logic is obvious in the Wink series too, which is straining hard to become a homegrown Game of Thrones made from homegrown material: violence, sex, and court intrigue, but without magic and, for some reason, without politics.

Turkey's Erdogan may push for FM Fidan to take over UN Sec.-Gen. role, causing concern in Israel

22:10:32 KST

Concern is growing in Israel over the possibility that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan could use his visit to New York for the UN General Assembly to promote Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan as a candidate to become the next UN secretary-general, potentially even announcing the move during his Tuesday UNGA address.
Sources familiar with the matter told The Jerusalem Post that the possibility of putting Fidan forward for the top UN post is on the table and has been considered more than once.
Turkish officials, however, strongly denied that any such move is planned.
The possibility carries particular significance as the race to succeed UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres enters a crucial stage without a consensus candidate.
Guterres's second term expires on December 31, with his successor due to take office on January 1. Under the UN Charter, the secretary-general is appointed by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council.
Erdogan arrived in New York on Sunday for the UNGA and has already begun a series of diplomatic meetings. Fidan is also in New York and has been holding meetings with foreign counterparts on the sidelines of the UNGA.
The timing is particularly sensitive because the succession race remains unsettled.
In the third secret straw poll held by the Security Council on Friday, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan emerged as the narrow front-runner, receiving nine "encourage" votes, five "discourage" votes and one "no opinion."
Guyana's UN Ambassador Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett followed with eight votes encouraging her candidacy, six discouraging it and one expressing no opinion.
At this stage, the ballots do not distinguish publicly between votes cast by the Security Council's five permanent members and those cast by its 10 elected members, meaning it is not yet known whether any of the leading candidates face opposition from a veto-wielding power.
The field became even more fluid over the weekend when former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet withdrew her candidacy following a weak showing in the latest poll.
New candidates can still enter the race, leaving open the possibility that Security Council members could ultimately coalesce around a late entrant if the current field fails to produce a consensus.
Fidan is Erdogan's longtime confidant
Fidan, 58, has for years been regarded as one of Erdogan's most trusted figures in Turkey's foreign policy and national security establishment.
Before becoming foreign minister in 2023, he spent 13 years as head of Turkey's National Intelligence Organization, known as the MIT. He previously held several senior government positions, including serving as a special representative to the prime minister and president and as a member of the International Atomic Energy Agency's Board of Governors.
The concern in Jerusalem comes against the backdrop of Fidan's sharply critical stance toward Israel since the October 7 massacre and the Israel-Hamas War.
Fidan has repeatedly accused Israel of committing "genocide" in Gaza and has described what he calls "Israeli expansionism" as a threat extending beyond the region. In April, he argued that such policies had become a global security concern and said the international community needed to act to stop them.
He has also maintained direct contacts with senior Hamas officials as part of Turkey's involvement in Gaza ceasefire diplomacy.
Fidan met members of Hamas's political leadership in Ankara in December for talks on implementation of the Gaza ceasefire, and Turkish officials have repeatedly argued that Hamas has shown willingness to advance ceasefire arrangements while accusing Israel of failing to fulfill parts of previous agreements.
Relations between Israel and Turkey have deteriorated dramatically in recent years. Ankara halted direct bilateral trade with Israel in May 2024, while Erdogan and Fidan have made the Gaza war a central focus of Turkish foreign policy and international diplomacy.
Race to become next UN secretary-general remains unresolved
The formal process to select the next UN secretary-general began in November 2025, when UN member states were invited to submit nominations.
Candidates are formally nominated by member states before being considered by the 15-member Security Council. Council members have been conducting confidential straw polls in which they mark candidates as "encourage," "discourage," or "no opinion."
Ultimately, a successful candidate needs at least nine votes in the Security Council and must avoid a veto from any of its five permanent members, the United States, Russia, China, Britain and France. The Security Council then recommends one candidate to the General Assembly for formal appointment.
There is a strong, though non-binding, expectation within the UN that the next secretary-general should come from the Latin American and Caribbean regional group, which has not held the post for decades. There has also been a significant push for the UN to appoint a woman as secretary-general for the first time in its history.
Neither convention is legally binding, however, and the eventual choice will depend above all on whether a candidate can secure agreement among the Security Council's major powers.
If Turkey does decide to nominate Fidan, he would therefore enter the contest relatively late and outside the regional expectation surrounding this year's race.
But he would also enter at a moment when three rounds of Security Council straw polls have yet to produce a candidate capable of commanding clear consensus, leaving the door open for the race to take an unexpected turn.

Austrian government agrees to extend mandatory military service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:09:48 UTC
22:09:48 KST

Timo Kirez
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
The Austrian governing coalition has agreed on a new model to extend military service, Yannick Shetty, leader of the New Austria and Liberal Forum (NEOS), announced on Tuesday.
Under the proposed reform, the current six-month basic training will be immediately followed by one month of active drills. Conscripts will then complete the remaining two months of reserve training at a later date.
Currently, military service in Austria is limited strictly to six months of basic training.
To pass the reform, the coalition requires a two-thirds majority in Parliament, meaning it must secure votes from the opposition.
The largest opposition party, the far-right Freedom Party of Austria (FPO), is calling for an even longer extension of both military and civilian service.
The Austrian Greens, on the other hand, remain opposed to the planned changes.
Austria is not the only country in Europe making changes to its conscription system in response to the war in Ukraine and perceived security threats from Russia.
Latvia reinstated mandatory military service in 2024 after a nearly two-decade hiatus. Croatia, following a 17-year hiatus, reintroduced mandatory two-month basic training for men starting in January 2026.
Denmark implemented a comprehensive reform starting in 2026. Military service will be drastically extended from four to eleven months.
Similarly, in Germany, which suspended a draft in 2011, a new model has emerged.
Under the new Military Service Act passed under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, conscription was not fully reinstated, but it was comprehensively reformed.
Starting in 2026, all 18-year-old men will be required to complete a digital questionnaire on physical fitness and military readiness.
Based on the responses, candidates will be invited to a physical examination in, with the goal of recruiting approximately 20,000 volunteers each year.

Border Crossing Stamp: Do Ukrainians Need It and What to Do If It Is Missing
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:06:13 EEST
22:06:13 KST

Border Crossing Stamp: Do Ukrainians Need It and What to Do If It Is Missing
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian border guards place a stamp only upon personal request. Missing data can be confirmed by submitting an application to the State Border Guard Service.
Have you crossed the Ukrainian border but have no stamp in your international passport? This is not necessarily a mistake: Ukrainian citizens receive one at their personal request, while data on departure or return is stored in the database of the State Border Guard Service. Rules may be different abroad.
When it is worth asking for a stamp in your passport and how to confirm your trip without one is explained by UNN.
Are Ukrainian border guards required to stamp passports?
The rules are set out in Article 12 of the Law of Ukraine "On Border Control." Under paragraph 1 of part three, marks confirming the crossing of the state border are not placed in the passport documents of Ukrainian citizens, except when a person personally requests this. Therefore, a border guard is not required to automatically stamp every Ukrainian citizen when they depart or return. If a person has passed the inspection and received permission to cross the border, the absence of a stamp in the passport does not in itself make the trip illegal. Nor does it indicate that the border guard forgot to record the crossing.
If a stamp is needed, it should be requested directly during the document check. After the passport is returned, it is advisable to check whether the stamp was added and whether the date was entered correctly. In the event of an error, one should immediately contact a border service officer.
What a stamp may be needed for
A stamp makes it possible to quickly confirm the entry or departure date indicated in it. This may be convenient when an institution requests documents confirming a person’s stay abroad or the circumstances of their trip. However, there is no universal rule requiring all institutions to demand a stamp specifically. Before preparing documents, it is worth clarifying what type of confirmation the relevant authority accepts: a passport page, an official response from the border guard service, or other documents.
It is also important to distinguish between departure from Ukraine and entry into another country. A Ukrainian stamp confirms that the Ukrainian border was crossed. It does not replace the registration of entry by a foreign border service and does not determine the permitted length of stay abroad.
What to do if there is no Ukrainian stamp
If the absence of a stamp is noticed during the inspection, you can ask the border guard to add one. If the trip has already taken place and the date of the crossing needs to be documented, a practical option is to obtain the relevant information from the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine. The Service maintains a database of persons who have crossed Ukraine’s state border. To obtain data on a border crossing, an application must be submitted to the agency.
It is worth remembering that this information is confidential, so it is not provided to third parties without a proper legal basis.
How to obtain information from the State Border Guard Service
The application must state the person’s surname, first name and patronymic, place of residence or stay, details of the identity document, and contact information. The period for which information about crossings is required should also be specified, and a copy of the passport document should be attached. A sample application is available on the State Border Guard Service website.
The request can be submitted in person to the public reception office of the Administration of the State Border Guard Service of Ukraine, sent by post, or emailed to [email protected].
It is worth noting that an electronic request must include a scan of a handwritten application bearing the applicant’s handwritten signature, or an electronic document certified with an electronic signature that can be verified. Therefore, simply sending a message requesting the data without a properly completed application is insufficient. In addition, before sending it, it is advisable to check the requirements and details against the current instructions of the State Border Guard Service.
Why there may also be no stamp at the Schengen Area border
The electronic Entry/Exit System (EES) applies to short-term trips to the Schengen Area. According to the European Commission, as of April 10, 2026, it is fully operational at the Schengen Area’s external border crossing points. For travelers covered by the system, stamps have been replaced with digital records of border crossings.
If there are doubts regarding the registration of a crossing of a foreign border, you should contact the competent authority of the respective country. For EES data, there is a right to request access to one’s own information, as well as its correction or supplementation. Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service does not correct records of foreign border services.
Reminder
Earlier, UNN reported that the official authorities in Warsaw plan to introduce paid electronic queue reservations for freight transport at certain road border-crossing points on the European Union’s external border. The fee will be 20 zlotys, or UAH 237.

Humpback whale mother may have mourned her dead calf for days
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:05:14 UTC
22:05:14 KST

Humpback whale mother may have mourned her dead calf for days
- Date:
- September 22, 2026
- Source:
- Griffith University
- Summary:
- Researchers observed a humpback whale mother staying beside her presumed stillborn calf for hours and possibly days off Australia’s Gold Coast. She maintained eye contact and remained close to the calf in behavior resembling caregiving and nurturing. Scientists say the rare observation may provide new insight into grief, maternal attachment, and emotional complexity in humpback whales.
- Share:
A rare observation of a humpback whale mother remaining beside her dead calf is offering researchers a closer look at how these animals may respond to loss.
The encounter, documented by researchers from Griffith University and Sea World Foundation, raises the possibility that humpback whale mothers may experience grief when a calf dies.
In 2025, a female humpback whale was observed off the southern Gold Coast with an escort whale after apparently giving birth to a deceased calf. The mother stayed near the calf for several hours and may have remained with it for days.
[See link to video below article.]
Rare Death-Related Behavior in Humpback Whales
Dr. Olaf Meynecke, from Griffith University's Whales and Climate Research Program, said attentive behavior toward dead individuals has been recorded mainly in toothed whales and delphinids (known as odontocetes). Similar observations remain far less common in published research involving baleen whales such as humpbacks.
"Unlike reports of toothed whales where mothers have been observed lifting their dead calves to the surface, this humpback whale mother showed prolonged post-mortem behavior and attention towards her deceased calf under the surface," Dr. Meynecke said.
"She remained close to the calf, maintaining eye contact and positioning herself next to her calf over several hours and maybe even days.
"These observed behaviors were consistent with care-giving or nurturing actions and post-mortem attentive responses documented in socially complex mammals, and indicated an inherent, strong maternal attachment to the calf."
Cetaceans are among the most widely recognized and closely watched marine animals, regularly attracting significant public attention.
An Unexpected Encounter at Sea
Sea World Foundation Rescue Boat Captain Andrew Mulville witnessed the unusual interaction firsthand.
"When I actually worked out what was happening, I was totally surprised."
"At first sight, I thought it was just two whales resting on the surface, but their behavior was unusual.
"It was definitely not what I was expecting to see out at sea that day."
The observation adds to the small number of documented cases involving deceased calves in baleen whales. According to Dr. Meynecke, these rare and deeply sad encounters could help scientists better understand how large whales process death and what their behavior may reveal about cognition and emotion.
What Whale Behavior May Reveal About Grief
Because such events are rarely witnessed, researchers say careful documentation is important for determining whether these behaviors reflect maternal attachment, grief-like responses, or other forms of social and emotional behavior.
"This case study highlights the need for continued systematic documentation of rare neonatal mortality events to better understand the cognitive, emotional, and evolutionary significance of post-mortem behavior in large whales," he said.
"Understanding how non-human animals responded to death provides insight into their emotional lives, social bonds, and cognitive capacities."
The study, 'First documentation of humpback whale (Megaptera novaeangliae) post-mortem attendance of a stillborn,' has been published in Discover Animals.

Poland’s drone defenses get a way to work without GPS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:04:34 UTC
22:04:34 KST

- Advanced Navigation signed an $18.5 million deal to supply inertial navigation systems for Kongsberg's PROTECTOR counter-drone platforms headed to Poland.
- The systems let PROTECTOR stations track position and orientation without GPS, part of Kongsberg's roughly $1.5 billion counter-drone contract with Poland.
Advanced Navigation, an Australian navigation technology company, has signed an $18.5 million deal to supply inertial navigation systems for Kongsberg’s PROTECTOR counter-drone platforms, the company said Sept. 22. The systems are bound for Poland, where Kongsberg is delivering 18 counter-drone batteries under a contract worth roughly NOK 16 billion, or about $1.5 billion, with Poland’s state-owned defense group Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa.
Under the deal, Advanced Navigation will supply hundreds of its Boreas fiber-optic gyroscope inertial navigation systems. The systems give Kongsberg’s PROTECTOR stations a way to track their own position, orientation, and heading without relying on GPS, which lets the platforms keep detecting and tracking aerial threats even when satellite navigation signals are jammed or spoofed.
PROTECTOR is Kongsberg’s remote weapon station family, used on vehicles, ships, and static installations. The Polish contract, signed in January and known as the SAN CUAS program, covers a mix of guns, missiles, and interceptor drones mounted on both PROTECTOR remote weapon stations and Kongsberg’s Medium Caliber Turret, a lightweight, unmanned 30mm turret already in full-rate production. Kongsberg has delivered more than 20,000 PROTECTOR systems to over 30 countries.
This is not Advanced Navigation’s first work with Kongsberg. The company previously supplied its Boreas D90 inertial navigation system for Kongsberg’s PROTECTOR RS4 platform under an earlier, smaller deal.
GPS jamming and spoofing have become routine in recent conflicts, and militaries have increasingly sought navigation systems that do not depend on satellite signals to function. Advanced Navigation’s inertial systems use onboard sensors, rather than GPS, to calculate a platform’s position and movement, which the company says lets its equipment keep operating accurately in electronically contested environments.
Advanced Navigation said its production is supported by Australia’s Department of Defence Global Supply Chain Program, and that its facilities allow for internal component sourcing and testing meant to speed delivery timelines.

Hurricane Polo grows into Category 5 storm off Mexico
Unknown

Hurricane Polo grows into Category 5 storm off Mexico, could produce life-threatening flooding
Hurricane Polo rapidly intensified off the coast of southwestern Mexico on Tuesday, growing into a powerful Category 5 storm that could bring life-threatening flooding to parts of the states of Guerrero and Michoacán, the National Hurricane Center said.
Polo reached Category 5 strength Tuesday morning after its maximum sustained winds had risen from 150 mph to 160 mph. It may continue to strengthen somewhat through Wednesday, according to the hurricane center.
At 6 a.m., Polo was about 220 miles south of Zihuatanejo, a coastal resort city in the state of Guerrero, and about 360 miles south-southeast of Manzanillo, another coastal city and resort destination in the state of Colima. It was traveling eastward near the Pacific Coast of Mexico at 6 mph, according to the hurricane center.
The hurricane center said that "rainfall may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain."
A tropical storm watch was in effect for a stretch of the Mexican coast, from Tecpan de Galeana, in Guerrero, to Manzanillo. The hurricane center issues tropical storm watches when meteorologists forecast possible tropical storm conditions within the watch area, usually at some point in the next 48 hours.
Forecasters said they expect Polo to continue on its current path before making a sharp turn toward the northwest Tuesday night and Wednesday, bringing the core of the hurricane near the southwestern Mexican coast in the coming days. As of early Tuesday, the storm was forecast to remain offshore, but it would likely bring heavy rainfall, in addition to what the hurricane center described as "life-threatening flooding and mudslides" to some coastal places, especially those located in steep terrain.
Parts of Guerrero and Michoacán may receive between 4 and 8 inches of rainfall as Polo barrels past, with up to 12 inches possible in certain spots, through Thursday. Between 3 and 6 inches of rain could also fall in coastal parts of the states of Oaxaca, Colima, and Jalisco through Thursday, forecasters said.

Boys' life expectancy in Finland reaches record 80 years
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
16:02:26 EEST
22:02:26 KST

The life expectancy of newborn boys in Finland reached 80 years of age in August, according to Statistics Finland.
The agency said that the difference between boys' and girls' life expectancy is now less than five years — the narrowest gender gap in more than a century.
Boys' life expectancy in Finland exceeded the 70-year mark in 1982 and the 75-year mark in 2003. Girls' life expectancy is already approaching the 85-year milestone.
According to preliminary statistics, life expectancy over the past 12 months was 84.7 years for girls. Girls reached the 70-year mark in the 1950s, the 75-year mark in 1973 and the 80-year milestone in 1994.
However, the life expectancy of Finnish boys is the shortest among Nordic countries, and only the 14th highest in the EU, according to statistics agency Eurostat's 2024 figures. Meanwhile, Finnish girls' life expectancy was the second highest in the Nordics and ninth longest in Eurostat's comparison.
In Sweden, Norway and Iceland, the gender gap in newborns' life expectancy is around three years, and in Denmark just under four years.
Life expectancy is a statistical measure showing how long a newborn can expect to live based on current death rates across all age groups. It provides a snapshot of mortality at a specific moment rather than a prediction of the future.
If health conditions continue to improve and death rates keep falling, as they have historically, today's newborns will likely live longer than current life expectancy figures suggest.

The Past Decade’s Emissions Are Already Driving Worse Heat Waves in Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:02:10 UTC
22:02:10 KST

The heat waves Europe has seen in recent years were made measurably more intense because of the greenhouse gasses emitted since the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, according to a new study published today in Geophysical Research Letters.
“We found that the emissions released since the signing of this Paris Agreement in 2015 have substantially and significantly increased the intensity of Europe's recent individual heat waves,” says lead author Jared Trok, a PhD student in Earth system science at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. The study also determined that that held true for Europe’s hottest week in every individual year since at least 2021.
Their findings come on the heels of this summer's back-to-back heat waves on the continent, which broke heat records and contributed to at least 35,000 excess deaths.
The Paris Agreement was a legally binding international treaty on climate change adopted by nearly 200 countries in December 2015, with the aim of limiting global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial temperatures. A decade later, the world is expected to blow past that 1.5°C target, with optimistic estimates finding that temperatures will peak at 1.8°C under current climate policies.
Beyond the 1.5°C threshold, every extra fraction of a degree matters. The world can expect to see intensified extreme weather, ecosystem loss, and flooding in coastal cities and island nations, along with far-reaching impacts to human health and food security.
Europe is particularly vulnerable in the face of a warming climate. The continent is heating up at more than twice the global average rate. The June and July 2025 heat waves broke records across the continent—only to be surpassed by 2026 heat waves. Surface air temperatures exceeded 40°C (104°F) in several countries, and up to 46°C (114.8°F) in Spain and Portugal.
The researchers created a generative AI model known as a diffusion model using simulated weather data from 10 global climate models to predict how extreme heat waves in Europe could have unfolded under different global emissions levels.
“This is a purpose built machine learning model that we trained on large amounts of climate model data…to make predictions about how individual heat waves might have unfolded differently if those same weather patterns had occurred under different levels of human emissions,” says Trok.
The team gave the model the observed weather conditions that caused Europe’s most intense annual heat waves from 2016 to 2025, which typically coincided with a persistent, high pressure system known as a heat dome. They had the model predict daily temperatures under emission levels at the time of each extreme heat event, and under the lower emissions levels of 2015.
They found that the emissions from the last decade increased the intensity of 2025 heat waves by roughly a third of a degree Celsius. “That third of a degree might seem very small, maybe imperceptible to us walking around, but there's a large body of scientific literature that suggests that even small increments of temperature on a hot day can have these disproportionate impacts on the damages caused by those heat waves,” says Trok.
Scientists have long known that the burning of fossil fuels trap greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, raising global temperatures. In recent decades, researchers have developed methods to study how historical emissions have affected heat waves, hurricanes, droughts, wildfires, and other extreme weather events. The researchers say that the methodology represents a step forward for climate modeling.
“This research shows that we can systematically and objectively ask questions about subsets of historical emissions, including individual heat waves,” says co-author Noah Diffenbaugh, professor at the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability. “A key part of what we've identified here is we've been able to say with high confidence that this subset of emissions has shifted the distribution of temperatures that could occur during this individual heat wave to such an extent that we can say we are very confident that this individual heat wave would have been cooler if the same weather patterns had occurred without this subset of emissions.”
It also serves as a warning, says Diffenbaugh, noting that the emissions that have already been released will impact our climate regardless of any mitigation efforts we take going forward. “Even in the context of the most optimistic, ambitious future for reducing emissions, there's still more intensification of extremes that is essentially committed.”

More than 170,000 respiratory cases were recorded in regions affected by haze in Indonesia, a health ministry official said on Tuesday, as the country continues its battle to control fires that caused the toxic smog.
Blazes in Borneo, Sumatra and Papua have blanketed parts of the vast archipelago of more than 280 million people with haze, as well as neighbouring Malaysia and Singapore, sending air quality indices plummeting.

“There were 174,694 cases of acute respiratory infections between August and September 21 in areas affected by forest and land fires,” she said.

At a moment when emerging technologies are driving both the global economy and the news cycle, business leaders must not only keep up with an industry moving at a breakneck pace—they must look around the corner at what’s next. At Paris-based Back Market, a global online marketplace for refurbished electronics, CTO Dawn Baker is applying an environmental mission to the company’s use of computing power. “We have to make sure we’re not using more than we need,” she says. “It’s about using AI smartly and not falling for the hype.”
These leaders and their fellow honorees are the catalysts of some of the most consequential transformations taking place across modern enterprise—translating innovation into meaning.

Although AI is fundamentally changing cybersecurity, Bartley Richardson thinks the hackneyed IT refrain still rings true: “The best security is the security you don’t have to think about.” Richardson, a former Nvidia engineer who joined cybersecurity company CrowdStrike in June as its chief AI and autonomous systems officer, says his title perfectly reflects his belief that once consumers trust AI, they’ll stop regarding it as “AI.” Instead, it will be just another autonomous tool making life better in the background, like a grammar check in word processing.
Richardson is shepherding that transition as leader of CrowdStrike’s new Cyber Superintelligence Lab. An AI research lab dedicated to building autonomous cybersecurity systems, its first release is SafeMind, an agentic system that combats AI attacks by pairing an offensive cybersecurity model with a defensive one, creating an autonomous loop of learning and remediation. “An attacker has to be right once, but the defender has to be right all the time,” Richardson says. “We’re giving the advantage back to the defender, and we’re doing that with ... better automation.”

Rethinking Waste: The journey towards a circular economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:38 UTC
22:00:38 KST

From advanced sorting in Sharjah to new waste infrastructure in Uzbekistan, efforts to recover materials and generate energy are changing what happens to rubbish.
Every year, the world produces more than 2 bn tonnes of municipal waste — much of it disappearing from view the moment it is thrown into a bin. But that is where the story of waste really begins.
A discarded plastic bottle might be recycled into something new. Food waste can become compost or biogas. Material that cannot be recycled may be burned to generate electricity. And what cannot be recovered may ultimately end up in landfill. The more materials that can be recovered and put back to use along the way, the less waste reaches the end of that journey.
That is the principle behind a circular economy: keeping resources in use for as long as possible, first by using less, then by reusing and recycling materials rather than simply throwing them away.
Separating what still has value
At BEEAH’s waste management complex in Sharjah, municipal waste moves through a sorting line. Machines separate plastics, metals, paper and cardboard, turning what arrived together as rubbish into materials that can potentially be used again.
Plastics can be processed into new packaging and consumer goods, while paper and cardboard can re-enter the manufacturing cycle.
But not everything can be recovered. In Sharjah, some residual waste goes to a waste-to-energy plant, where it is burned to generate electricity rather than being sent directly to landfill.
“Recycling preserves material. Waste-to-energy addresses what remains, ensuring residual waste still creates value,” says Alya Al Obeidli, Lead Engineer at Emirates Waste to Energy.
Recycling keeps materials in use; waste-to-energy comes later, recovering energy from material that cannot be recycled. Whatever cannot be recovered ultimately leaves the circle and ends up in landfill.
It is this entire journey that Uzbekistan is now trying to reshape.
Rethinking where Uzbekistan’s waste goes
Uzbekistan generates roughly 15 ml tonnes of household waste annually. Government figures suggest that only around 5% to 6% is currently recycled or processed by specialist companies.
For much of the rest, landfill remains the end of the journey.
A new 24-hectare landfill outside Tashkent receives roughly 1,500 to 2,500 tonnes of waste a day, depending on the period and season, according to Shahzod Safarov, Chief Specialist of the Agency for Waste Management of Uzbekistan.
For decades, the capital’s rubbish was deposited at an older landfill nearby. At the newer facility, waste is compacted and covered with soil, while protective layers underneath are intended to prevent contaminated liquid from seeping into the ground.
But buried waste can continue to have an environmental impact. As organic material decomposes without oxygen, it produces methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.
“There was a very large build-up of methane gas at the old landfill site,” says Rafael Bekmullin, Director of the Waste Recycling and Disposal Branch. “Now, there’s actually a project underway there to extract that gas and generate electricity from it.”
Officials say 47 landfills have been closed and rehabilitated over the past several years, while Uzbekistan aims to halve the number of landfills by 2030.
But closing landfills does not make the waste disappear. If less rubbish is buried, it needs somewhere else to go.
Turning waste into electricity
One part of the answer is taking shape outside Samarkand.
A new waste-to-energy plant is being built to process around 1,500 tonnes of household waste a day and is expected to generate around 240 ml kilowatt-hours of electricity annually once operational.
Aziza Nazarova, Head of the Investment Department at Uzbekistan’s Agency for Waste Management, says the longer-term aim is to separate waste into different streams: recyclable materials returning to production, organic waste going towards compost or biogas, and residual waste to waste-to-energy plants.
The order matters. Waste-to-energy can reduce the volume going to landfill, but recovering recyclable materials first keeps more of them in circulation.
And that brings the journey back to where it began: the bin.
The circle begins at home
In Angren, east of Tashkent, private waste company Zero Waste distributed 10,000 bags to residents in a pilot encouraging households to separate their rubbish.
According to Sobir Mashrabov, the company’s regional representative, only around 1% were returned with the waste separated.
“Without sorting the waste, nothing is achievable,” Mashrabov says.
For him, infrastructure alone cannot solve the problem. Separating waste, he argues, has to become an everyday habit, taught from kindergarten and school through to university.
The experiment brings the waste journey full circle. Once plastic, paper, food and everything else are thrown together, recovering useful materials becomes harder. Separating them earlier creates more opportunities for recyclable materials to return to production rather than move towards incineration or landfill.
Sharjah and Uzbekistan are tackling different stages of that journey, from sorting and recycling to landfill management and energy recovery.
But all this infrastructure deals with what society has already decided to throw away.
A circular economy begins earlier — by using fewer resources, keeping products in use for longer and recovering valuable materials before they become waste.

====================================================================================================

Parents with two daughters report the highest levels of happiness, Chinese study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:28 UTC
22:00:28 KST

A study in China found that parents tend to be happier than non-parents. Among parents, those with more children tend to be happier, but only among those aged 60 and above. Parents who only had daughters tended to be happier than those having only boys, particularly those who had exactly two daughters. The paper was published in Acta Psychologica.
Happiness is an important component of quality of life. It can depend on both personal circumstances and broader social conditions. Family structure can play an important role in how happy a person is, particularly through the number of children, their ages, and the kinds of support they provide. Parenthood can make a person happier by creating emotional meaning and companionship, but it can also increase financial demands, daily responsibilities, and work-family conflict. These costs and benefits may change across the life course as children grow older and parents’ needs shift.
Adult children can contribute to parents’ well-being through financial assistance, practical help, emotional support, and maintaining close family relationships. Sons and daughters can provide different forms of support because cultural expectations and gender roles shape how family responsibilities are distributed.
Daughters tend to be more involved in maintaining family contact and providing emotional support, whereas sons may be expected in some cultures to provide greater financial or practical assistance. The relationship between children and parental happiness can therefore depend strongly on cultural norms, economic resources, social security systems, and whether families live in urban or rural settings.
Study authors Zhong Fei and Wenqin Jin wanted to explore how a person’s happiness is associated with the number of children the person has and their gender. More specifically, they wanted to answer the following question: “what kind of offspring composition, in which ways, and for which parents, can improve their quality of life in Chinese society?”
These researchers analyzed data from the Chinese General Social Survey (CGSS). The CGSS is a large, multistage survey initiated by Renmin University of China in 2003. It covers all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities in China and targets the civilian population aged 18 years and above. Study participants were recruited from 100 counties and five metropolitan areas (Beijing, Shanghai, Tianjin, Guangzhou, and Shenzhen) across China. There were six data collection waves in the study between 2012 and 2021, each involving between 8,000 and 13,000 participants. The dataset used in this analysis included data from 49,752 individuals, 45,108 of whom had children.
From this dataset, the study authors used data about participants’ self-reported happiness (“Overall, do you feel happy in your life?”), the number of children, and their gender (“How many biological children do you have (including deceased children)? How many sons and daughters do you have (including deceased children)?”). They also used data on participants’ gender, age, ethnicity, and various other pieces of sociodemographic information.
Results showed that, on average, parents were happier than non-parents. Participants with a larger number of children tended to be happier than those with fewer children, but only when participants aged 60 and above were considered. Parents with all-female offspring tended to be happier than those with all-male offspring, and this association was strongest among middle-aged parents and those who had exactly two daughters. Parents with a mix of sons and daughters did not report a statistically significant difference in happiness compared to those with only sons.
Additionally, the positive association between the number of children and happiness was more pronounced among men, urban residents, and those with a pension, whereas the happiness advantage of having only daughters was more pronounced among rural residents, middle-aged parents, and those with a spouse.
“It is important to interpret these findings with appropriate caution. As our analyses are based on data from the CGSS, the observed associations – particularly the pronounced positive association of the ‘two daughters’ combination in two-child families – should be viewed as sample-specific evidence within the contemporary Chinese context. The generalizability of these patterns to other cultural settings or time periods remains to be established through future cross-cultural and cross-national research,” the study authors added.
The study contributes to the scientific knowledge about factors associated with psychological well-being. However, it should be noted that happiness was assessed using a single item, so the reliability and particularly the temporal stability of such ratings remain unknown. Additionally, the design of the study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results. Therefore, it remains unknown whether having children makes people happier, whether happier people are more likely to decide to have children, or whether this association is caused by some other factor.
The paper, “Who reports higher happiness? The association between number of children, gender composition of offspring and parental happiness,” was authored by Zhong Fei and Wenqin Jin.

2026-09-22
13:00:01 UTC
22:00:01 KST

The images from Nepal stopped Daniela Schmidt in her tracks. A geologist at the University of Buenos Aires in Argentina, she watched the deadly flash floods on 26 August tear through everything in their path, people running for their lives as the water and debris swept over the landscape.
“I had never seen anything like it,” she says. “This was one of the most catastrophic events on a global scale related to these glacial floods.”
The shock deepened as the first geological figures emerged: the volume of glacier ice and rock that had collapsed and the scale of the resulting flow. Schmidt began comparing them with the cases she had studied during her PhD. Very few glacial lake outburst floods, she realised, had reached anything close to this magnitude.
But Nepal also changed the way she saw her own work. Schmidt studies the glacial lake outburst flood (Glof) that could occur at Laguna Torre, in Argentina’s Santa Cruz province, and its potential impact on El Chaltén, a nearby town known as the country’s trekking capital.
The disaster already exists on her computer screen: data, models, flood simulations and maps. According to her studies, if the northern slope of Cerro Solo were to collapse into Laguna Torre, at the base of the Torre glacier, a massive volume of water could travel the 5 miles (8km) to El Chaltén in 20 minutes, sweeping along logs, rocks and sediment.
The discharge could reach 1,769 cubic metres (62,472 cubic feet) a second, rushing down the Fitz Roy River towards the town and inundating its only access bridge and other critical infrastructure. For anyone in the valley, those 20 minutes would be the window to reach safety. “It is the worst-case flood scenario,” says Schmidt, adding that, in the most conservative analysis, the flow would take between 45 minutes and an hour to reach the town.
“You can’t say it will happen on a specific day or at a specific time, but society needs to be prepared,” Schmidt warns. “It is going to happen.”
The threat was already changing how El Chaltén prepared for the future, but the disaster in Nepal has brought these risks to the forefront. Although the scale of that event and the El Chaltén scenario differ, Schmidt sees a similarity in the mechanism: a mass suddenly plunging into a body of water can trigger a flash flood with immense destructive power.
Authorities from Los Glaciares national park and the municipality of El Chaltén, along with local organisations and various scientific institutions, are working to develop the country’s first Glof early-warning system and draft evacuation protocols.
“We are preparing for the worst-case scenario,” says Enrique Rivero, El Chaltén’s secretary of government.
The silhouette of Cerro Solo is unmistakable. The vertical granite peak, rising to 2,121 metres (6,959ft) above sea level, is reflected in Laguna Torre amid floating icebergs. That is where the risk begins.
The Torre glacier is estimated to have lost 4 sq km (1.5 sq miles) of surface area, while its ice thinned by 60-70 metres between 1952 and 2023. As the ice retreats, the balance of the surrounding slopes also shifts – a process researchers describe as a “release of stress”.
This transformation is visible in landslides and rockfalls that leave scars across the mountainside. Between 2002 and 2023, the volume of displaced material increased, while the speed of movement doubled. “It moves slowly, but during heavy rainfall or high temperatures, it accelerates in pulses,” Schmidt says. “As the slopes become unstable, they can slide, dumping a large volume of material into the lake and causing it to overflow. It just needs a trigger.”
Her models contemplate landslides involving between 8m and 13m cubic metres of material. If a mass of that size were to collapse into Laguna Torre, it could generate a wave up to 5.8 metres high. The wave would travel across the lake at approximately 20 metres a second, reaching the Fitz Roy River in just one minute and 40 seconds.
Under the most conservative and the worst-case scenarios, a flood would eventually reach the bridge and render it unusable. The bridge is the only land access connecting El Chaltén to provincial route 41.
The municipality has already ordered the dredging of the river channel and the clearing of the riverbed beneath the bridge. “But now we are being told that the water level could rise by up to 5 metres, which suggests the bridge could be swept away,” Rivero says.
The flood could also affect critical infrastructure located just metres from the riverbanks, including gas and power plants, schools and homes. Discussions have already begun on a contingency plan that considers, among other measures, potential relocation.
“Gas supplies coming from Río Gallegos – the capital of Santa Cruz province – would be cut off, leaving us without heating,” says Paula Chaparro, a member of the El Chaltén Mountain Guides Association. “If the power grid fails, El Chaltén relies on generators running on fuel oil; if they run out of fuel, we lose electricity. It’s a problematic chain reaction.”
If the event were to occur in summer, peaking in December to February, the town would be cut off, with more than 27,000 people – locals and tourists alike – stranded in the town. At present, according to residents, there is no signage indicating evacuation routes or instructions, nor do hotels warn guests about the risk.
The risk has been known for years, but the available instruments could not precisely determine how quickly the slope was moving or, crucially, how much water could be displaced in a collapse. “We’ll have to wait and see if it happens” was a common reaction among locals, says Sofía Bonangelino, a member of Friends of Los Glaciares National Park, an association that manages three campsites.
Even Horacio Pelozo, the park superintendent, acknowledges this: “The initial studies really weren’t alarming, or anything of the sort.”
However, a key new piece of data emerged, Pelozo says, alongside the measurements of the slope’s movement: sustained melting had created a second body of water within Laguna Torre, the depth of which now exceeds 220 metres. Previous estimates had placed the depth at about 80 metres.
Then, in May 2025, an image from the Swiss Alps demonstrated the potential scale of a collapse involving ice and rock: the Birch glacier collapsed on to much of the village of Blatten, burying it in a matter of seconds.
Los Glaciares national park has taken steps to address the risk of a Glof, including relocating the De Agostini campsite, rerouting hiking trails, installing warning signs and establishing an evacuation protocol involving at least 25 personnel to manage potential floods during peak visitor seasons.
The response has expanded to include coordination with local and national agencies, such as the municipality of El Chaltén, in the Santa Cruz province, the Federal Emergency Agency and the Argentine Geological and Mining Service, though no formal contingency plan has been finalised yet.
The El Chaltén city council has passed a resolution to develop an evacuation plan, while a detection system with six monitoring stations – equipped with cameras, sensors and emergency buoys – is in development to trigger alerts via sirens, SMS and email. Yet funding cuts have delayed implementation, with the estimated cost of $220,000 (£163,000) exceeding the park’s current capacity, as noted by Eduardo Marino, a former secretary of government for El Chaltén.
“Let’s not talk about Glofs, because it will scare off tourists” – that concern is circulating around town. And it is not hard to understand why – a large part of the community relies on tourism for its livelihood.
Marino owns a hotel; Bonangelino runs a bookstore, rents out a cabin, and works as a ski instructor. For them, as for so many other residents, protecting tourism also means protecting their own livelihoods.
Marino was asked to drop the subject until the summer season was over. He refused. He knows a day of heavy rain or exceptionally high temperatures could be enough to trigger an event they are not yet prepared for.
For those who work in the mountains, information is key to risk management. “Closing down isn’t the solution,” says Chaparro. The idea, she says, is to offer alternatives: different trails, different activities. “It’s not about being afraid; it’s about staying alert.”
When her colleague Ariel Puntin speaks to local people about the threat he still encounters some who doubt the mountainside could collapse. The problem, he says, is that the gap between “it could happen today” and “it might never happen” is too wide to easily learn how to live with the risk.
For Schmidt, the events in Nepal should serve as a wake-up call, but also as an opportunity to improve the town’s preparedness. “The community and the tourists must be protected and kept safe in the face of this new reality of constantly changing glacial landscapes,” she says.
Bonangelino has noticed a positive shift in recent months. As the studies’ findings have been explained to the community, she says, acceptance has grown that the phenomenon is real and that preparation is necessary.
“We are a resilient, responsible community that cares deeply about its environment,” she says. “We rely on tourism, and we aren’t going to neglect it.”

Viture’s Vonder Glasses Are Meant to Map Your Mind
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

David Jiang, cofounder and CEO of smart glasses company Viture, tells me about how he used to yell at his kid.
His 10-year-old son played tennis. During tournaments, Jiang says he had a habit of shouting and criticizing his son’s mistakes as he played. He wanted to apply pressure to make him succeed—it was the way he’d been taught to raise kids, after all. It made sense.
But then, unprompted, his smart glasses sent him a message. The AI assistant in his company’s newest wearable had picked up on what he was doing, recognized that his behavior wasn’t helpful, and messaged him about what he should do differently. Stop shouting. Stop criticizing. Just be there, be present, and show that you support your son. That worked, Jiang says, and being called out like that has supposedly made him a better father and improved the relationship with his kid, all thanks to his yet-to-be-released Vonder AI glasses.
“I didn't know this until Vonder could find my pattern,” Jiang says. “This is not only a tool that can summarize your life, but also a tool that can help yourself to be a better person.”
Viture, a San Francisco-based company known for its plug-in virtual display glasses, announced its first pair of spectacles with no virtual display on Tuesday. The glasses instead look remarkably like normal glasses, but aim to map out your memories, ideas, and goals and plop them on a digital vision board, all without embedded cameras.
Now co-headquartered in California and Beijing, Viture has made glasses like the Viture One and the Viture Beast—wearable face computers that connect via USB-C cable to a device to project its screen right before your eyes. The company's products have primarily targeted gamers or anyone interested in big-screen entertainment. They work well for that purpose, but their chunky design means they fall short in comfort and fashion.
The new glasses are a bit of a pivot. They're called Vonder, you know, like “wonder” but with a V, and they don't have cameras. The glasses' arms feature mics and speakers that can play music, dictate map directions, and let the wearer make phone calls. Vonder also features a built-in AI assistant that combines the top large language models. It can trigger OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, or even DeepSeek. Based on the task’s complexity, Vonder AI will source the answer from whichever model is the quickest and most economical.
They cost $299, can be fitted with prescriptions, come in a variety of frame shapes and colors, and can have clear, transition, or shaded sunglass lenses. Preorders launch September 28, and they’ll ship in November.
The company, like other smart-glass brands Xreal and Even Realities, is trying to make it very clear that it is not Meta, distancing itself from the ire Meta’s Ray-Bans have generated for their privacy-encroaching features. Viture says above all else, it wants its smart glasses to be a good pair of glasses. Ones that operate privately—the kind of frames people will willingly wear without worrying about being labeled a creep.
A blue indicator light turns on when the glasses are recording audio. It’s a small dot on the arms of the glasses, less central and less immediately noticeable than the indicator light on the Ray-Ban Meta glasses.
But Viture stands apart because most of the time, the glasses can collect data only when the wearer is speaking. You can trigger a meeting mode, and it will use on-board microphones to record the environment around you, but the rest of the time, they use bone-conduction sensors in the frames that can passively pick up the audio vibrations of the person wearing them all day long. (The Vonder glasses get about 16 hours of battery life.)
Once it collects information about your day and what you talk about, the assistant generates a personal memory graph that tracks your memories—things like what coffee shops you’ve been to, what sports you play, or whatever else you choose to confide in the glasses. As long as you’re talking about something, the glasses will pick that up and try to interpret the context to make a broader picture of what you’re up to. In the app, it displays all those connections in a big web graphic.
In a demo of how the glasses work, Jiang showed that the Vonder glasses he's wearing have kept tabs on his life over the past three months. He can ask it where to find coffee shops based on his caffeine preferences or have it help figure out why he's felt so stressed lately. The tech is also preemptive, pulling up topics he's been thinking about, like help with hiring decisions he's been mulling over and a plan for announcing his new smart glasses a day before Meta Connect. It also pulled up a dossier on me that it presented to him the morning he came to visit. It clearly knew who I was, what I write about, and had suggested some topics for him to prepare for.
“We just want to mimic the way your brain works,” Jiang says. “This is not a transcript or a summary. This is just how your memory organizes in your brain, even better than your memory.”
The Vonder glasses raise a question of how self-indulgent the information you’re collecting across your day is. It only records one perspective, after all—yours. That means you have to be comfortable sharing your thoughts with the glasses if you want them stored in the memory graph or have conversations with others all day.
I ask Jiang about this: how you make sure the information in your mind web considers other factors than your own perspective. Jiang says if he wants something to stick, he tends to repeat what someone else said.
“In a conversation, a human tends to repeat because a conversation is turn by turn—if you have a question, I follow up your question and then AI knows what the question is,” Jiang says, “Even though there's a missing part, it's not 50 percent missing. It's maybe only 10 percent or 15 percent.”
I ask what he’d do if we were arguing right now. If I’d felt one way and he another, and then he went back to his mind web and tried to revisit the conversation. Would it bias him if his own voice was only the information it was given? This is what prompts him to talk about his kid playing tennis. That the glasses had outright told him he was wrong about something.
“The problem right now is that AI has really, really powerful somatic knowledge, but the missing part is the human episodic memory there,” Jiang says. “In the past three months I’ve used these glasses, I feel my life has been changed or improved.”

Debunking Bucha false-flag operation, UN’s confusing reports: top diplomat’s statements
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. The Bucha false-flag operation is nothing but "the most cynical farce," and the UN Secretariat is unlikely to investigate these 2022 events constructively, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said at the Dialogue about Fakes 4.0 international forum, of which TASS is a strategic partner.
The top diplomat noted that the West has nurtured a generation that believes the wildest anti-Russian cliches.
TASS has compiled the foreign minister’s key statements.
UN position on probing into Bucha incident
It is difficult "to expect the UN Secretariat to provide constructive assistance in the Bucha false-flag operation."
UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres is making clearly confusing statements over the Bucha events: "The departing chief of the UN Secretariat is frankly confused in his statements. He stated at some point that there was information at hand about the victims and their real names, but it was confidential and subject to certain internal rules of the Secretariat – no one has ever shown us these rules. He later said that they had no such information and then at another point he claimed that the relatives of the deceased were against disclosing this information, while no one knows the names of the relatives either. This is a truly striking fact."
Debunking Bucha false-flag operation
The false flag operation in Bucha can be considered as the most cynical farce: "I consider the faked footage of civilians allegedly killed in Bucha to be the most cynical farce."
"It turns out that back in 2023, the Kiev regime erected a special memorial dedicated to this so-called 'Bucha massacre' and organized regular 'pilgrimages' to the site for their sponsors from NATO and the European Union. They lay flowers in front of the cameras and deliver speeches full of accusations. Incidentally, UN Secretary-General [Antonio Guterres] was also taken there. Yet, this did not help him grasp the essence of the issues that are obvious to normal people. A list of names has appeared on the memorial itself – and is periodically updated – names that, according to Mr. Guterres, supposedly could not be shared with us. Yet, they were inscribed on the memorial as civilians, as was claimed."
In its first report on the first results of the Bucha incident investigation, the International Public Tribunal on the Crimes of Ukrainian Neo-Nazis "analyzed these surnames immortalized on the memorial." "According to repeated statements by a representative of [Vladimir] Zelensky’s office, all the deceased were exclusively civilians with no connection whatsoever to the military. This is an outright lie. Even a preliminary analysis of the surnames inscribed on the memorial yields a very interesting result."
The Kiev regime is blatantly lying by listing the names of Ukrainian servicemen as those civilians killed in Bucha on the memorial: "Based solely on open-source data, it has been established that the memorial lists the names of dozens of individuals – including Ukraine servicemen, Ukrainian Security Service officers, members of so-called defense units, police, and the National Guard, as well as fighters from the nationalist 'Azov' force (designated a terrorist organization and banned in Russia – TASS)."
"More than 70 names refute the myth about the alleged killing of hundreds of civilians in Bucha."
Independent investigations
"While I was in New York amid the impasse in relations with UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres, I openly called on UN pool reporters and representatives from the world's leading media outlets during my press conferences. I know most of them very well. I asked them to remember their professional pride and conduct an honest journalistic investigation. There was no reaction. It seems the reporters have been told something."
Despite the lack of response from UN pool reporters and leading global media outlets, several public organizations are now analyzing materials related to the Bucha false-flag operation: "Apart from reporters, there are also public figures and organizations that seek truth in today's complicated world. Several groups of specialists are now analyzing publicly available materials on the Bucha incident."
Western information aggression against Russia
The West has successfully prepared a significant part of society to believe the wildest anti-Russian cliches: "The Western information space and industry, including entertainment, have long and consistently prepared their populations to believe any anti-Russian cliche and fantasy. This continues until now. But we have to give them their due; they did manage to nurture part of society in this atmosphere. So, to speak, their efforts did not die in vain."
The information war against Russia began a long time ago, well before the special military operation: "Right after the beginning of the 2000s, when President [Vladimir] Putin came to power, Russia started ridding itself of neo-colonial forms of cooperation with our Western colleagues and engaging in independent policies, returning to its traditions, foundations, and roots. That's when they started containing us. This process led to the current situation in which over 30,000 sanctions have been imposed on us, a record compared to other countries in the world."
The Western media are absolutely groundlessly "blaming" Russia for the appearance of certain drones in Europe: "The topic of Russian drones – allegedly appearing here and there across European countries and attacking various facilities – has become fashionable in Western media lately. Yet every time, it turns out that it was either not a drone at all, a Ukrainian drone, or a drone that could not be positively identified as belonging to Russia."
The details behind such accusations "no longer interest anyone," the issue has instead become a matter of "playing information games."
It is evident that "Moscow’s assessment is repeatedly confirmed: the main thrust of Western information policy is to quickly concoct a fake, blow it up into a global catastrophe within a few days, and simultaneously block access to alternative information regarding the specific incident being sensationalized."
"One or two or three days pass, and then the news is pushed to the back pages of newspapers or into the obscure corners of other media outlets."
War on Russian culture
The West is launching a "frenzied onslaught" against Russian centers of science and culture: "This, too, is a struggle. The cancellation of cultural events reflects the fact that, like most countries, Russia upholds traditional values in culture and all spheres of life. Meanwhile, the West considers these values incompatible with its so-called liberal ideals."
The German authorities closed the Russian cultural center in Berlin, which was "enormously popular" among German citizens, and the Consulate General in Bonn, "simply because someone thought it was possible to portray the discovery of certain debris as the crash of a Russian drone, and that Russia should be punished for it."
Skripal case
The UK authorities never provided Moscow with any response regarding the Skripal case; in effect, London took Russian citizens hostage: "If we’re talking about specific provocations involving the information sphere, eight years ago, in the English town of Salisbury, it was claimed that Sergey Skripal and his daughter had been poisoned by Russian intelligence. To this day, we have been unable to obtain a response to the numerous official requests sent by our Investigative Committee and the Prosecutor General’s Office to their UK counterparts. These requests cite our legal obligations under various conventions to provide information on the whereabouts of these Russian citizens. In other words, we have received no response. To put it simply, London has taken our citizens hostage."
