New rare diseases identified in Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:57:53 UTC
20:57:53 KST

New rare diseases identified in Iran
TEHRAN – Eighteen more rare diseases have been identified in the country, bringing the total number of rare diseases to 531, according to the Rare Disease Foundation.
Idiopathic camptocormia, Intellectual disability, eye abnormalities, microcephaly, peripheral spasticity syndrome, Riboflavin transporter deficiency (Brown-Vialetto-van Laere syndrome (BVVL)), Mantle cell lymphoma, Chronic eosinophilic leukemia, combined immunodeficiency due to IL21R deficiency, Isolated tibial hemimelia, Phyllodes tumor of the breast, and 3MC syndrome are among rare diseases that have been identified in the country, Mehr news agency reported.
According to WHO, rare diseases are often serious, chronic, and life-threatening. The European Union (EU) definition of a rare disease affects fewer than 5 in 10,000 people. Around 80 percent of rare diseases are genetic disorders, and half of them occur during childhood.
Rare diseases affect millions of people globally and are often complex, involving multiple organ groups and resulting in disabilities and premature death. Many people living with a rare disease frequently experience diagnostic delays, fragmented care, limited access to effective interventions, financial hardship, stigma and social exclusion.
The incidence of rare diseases is very low to the extent that maybe one or two people with a certain rare disease are present in the country. Some rare diseases such as ‘butterfly skin or EB’, ‘Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)’, ‘Metabolic diseases’, ‘Autism’, and ‘Dystrophies’ are among the most common cases in the country.
Among rare diseases, cancers are the most expensive ones covered by the Rare Disease Foundation so that 70 percent of the funds is allocated to cancer-related medicines. The rise in cancers highlights the need for the development of preventive programs, early detection, targeted screening, and fair access to health services.
The budget allocated to rare and hard-to-treat diseases has increased over the past few years, rising from 50 trillion rials (about 21.7 million dollars) in the first year to 120 trillion rials (about 52.17 million dollars) this year.
Health insurance provided for some 2m patients
In May, Sajjad Razavi, an official with the health ministry stated that about two million patients with rare and hard-to-treat diseases are covered by the Health Insurance Organization.
The Rare Disease Foundation also covers the patients, IRNA quoted Razavi as saying.
The official made the remarks on the occasion of the national day of rare and hard-to-treat diseases observed annually on the 18th of Ordibehesht, the second Iranian calendar month, which falls on May 8.
 
 The day is a good opportunity to rethink the health system’s responsibilities toward patients who need ongoing, multidimensional care and comprehensive support because of the complex, chronic, and mainly hard-to-treat nature of their diseases.  
To safeguard the patients’ health and lower financial burden on households, tens of specialized healthcare service packages have been defined for them, with some more being continuously developed.
The packages include diagnostic, therapeutic, pharmaceutical, rehabilitation, and dental services, whether in the form of outpatient or inpatient services, which are provided with minimal deductibles or free of charge.
Despite lower prevalence, rare and hard-to-treat diseases are among the top health priorities due to difficulties in their diagnosis and treatment.
There are no cures for rare diseases, and patients with rare diseases need supportive care and rehabilitation services throughout their lives. Hence, the day highlights the need for coherent planning, the development of recurrent specialized services, genetic counselling, the expansion of insurance coverage, and social support.
Promoting health literacy, strengthening the referral system, and expanding preventive services are key factors to lower mortality among patients.

Former Pussy Riot member says FSB recruited her to spy on Russian activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:57:46 UTC
20:57:46 KST

Rita Flores, a Russian activist, artist, and former member of Pussy Riot, told The Guardian that she was forced to work with Russia’s FSB to spy on others in her left-wing circle
Flores, whose real name is Margarita Konovalova, said the FSB recruited and handled her for at least three years. In a recent video with her lawyer, Dmitry Zakhvatov, she admitted to providing the Russian security service with personal information about her fellow artists and activists. She said the wanted to go public with her story so others in a similar predicament would feel bold enough to break their ties with the FSB.
“For the first time in years, I feel calm. All this time I was dreaming about getting out and being able to talk about it all,” she told The Guardian.
The Guardian noted that its reporters could not corroborate her claims, but that there have been numerous cases over the years in which the FSB has recruited activists and artists to spy on opposition groups.
Pussy Riot is a Russian feminist punk artist collective that protests against the Kremlin with guerrilla art performances in public spaces. Many of its members have been exiled from Russia or imprisoned.
How did the FSB recruit a Pussy Riot member?
Flores was recruited in 2023 when police searched her house, which had become a semi-routine occurrence, after she made an Instagram post criticizing the war in Ukraine.
Two police officers introduced themselves as FSB agents, threatened to open a criminal case against her for the Instagram post, and insinuated that they would kill her mother if she did not agree to work with them.
“I believed them. I believed they could do everything they said they would … My fear was too great. I was so worried for my family and also for myself,” she told The Guardian.
She claimed that, as a reward for signing cooperation papers, she received a cash payment of around 40,000 roubles.
Her first task was to collect information on other opposition activists in the same circles as her.
She was not supposed to tell anyone about her arrangement, but she told “about 20 people” anyways, claiming that it was because she enjoyed gossiping. However, she neglected to inform many of the people she was meant to report on. She claimed she established contact with them using pre-planned pretexts designed to keep them away from her and from sharing personal information.
She noted that because of the war in Ukraine, many opposition-minded artists had fled the country, and those who remained understood the threats they faced for speaking out.
“Moscow is booming; restaurants, bars and clubs are opening, and there are a huge number of events. But those people who understand things have empty eyes and speak empty words.
“People who have stayed in Russia have accepted the rules of a game. You go to a gallery, and every artwork may as well come with a sign saying ‘we were forbidden from saying anything’ … there are artists who used to make strong statements, and in 2026 they are drawing flowers in a vase.”
The officers who recruited her in the 2023 raid became her regular handlers. Flores said that they tended to play up a good-cop, bad-cop act, and identified one as “the Jacket” and the other as Ivan. She told The Guardian that Ivan seemed friendlier and more helpful on the surface, and that he would let the Jacket make any direct threats.
“Whenever I met with Ivan and the Jacket together, Ivan was silent. The Jacket would be rude, threatening; he’d insult me as a woman. He was the devil incarnate. Then just me and Ivan would meet, and Ivan would be nice, friendly,” she told The Guardian.
“He liked to say, ‘The FSB will re-educate you, I will re-educate you, you’ll have a nice and calm life, and you’ll love Russia, have children and be an obedient wife.’”
In late Spring, Ivan and the Jacket began asking her questions about Pyotr Verzilov, an artist and activist associated with Pussy Riot who later moved to Ukraine to serve in the Ukrainian Army. He had been considered an enemy of the Kremlin for a long while, and reportedly faced an assassination attempt in 2018.
FSB's plot to kill Russian artist Verzilov
Flores’s handlers asked her to get more information from Verzilov, including his address in Ukraine, and then to arrange a meeting with him in Serbia. FSB operatives would then travel there to kidnap and kill Verzilov. Her handlers promised her an additional 50,000 roubles a month to help with the case.
In the meantime, Flores married her partner later that summer, and told the FSB agents that he would never allow her to take a trip to go to a private meeting with another man.
She noted that before that, her handlers had banned her from leaving the country. When she met her lawyer, Zakhvatov, she realized escape would be easier than she had realized.
She claims that, to her knowledge, no one was killed or arrested because of the work she did with the FSB.
Flores left Russia last month to live in exile.
Notably, her escape was not as dramatic as some other Pussy Riot members who were forced to leave Russia in disguise or in the back of a delivery truck, but she and Zakhvatov did not disclose the details.
Since Flores’s escape, Zakhvatov has opened a secure line to others in a similar predicament. Flores said she wants to work to help others in similar situations to hers, and added that she is certain FSB's recruitment of activists and artists is a “mass phenomenon.”
Flores claimed in a video last month that she called those whom she informed on to explain herself, as well as other old friends in Russia.
She claimed that everyone has been supportive of these conversations.

Global water reserves decline as river discharge falls to 35-year low in 2025, WMO report shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:57:34 UTC
20:57:34 KST

Rivers around the world in 2025 had one of the driest years in more than three decades, according to a new report from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).
The report provides a comprehensive analysis of the Earth’s water cycle, including river discharge, groundwater, evapotranspiration, land water storage, and snow and ice.
Some parts of the cycle are fast, such as precipitation and river flow, which can respond to weather within days or weeks. Other parts of the cycle, like glaciers and seasonal snowpack, are much slower and can take up to decades
“Traditionally these slow reserves have acted as the planet's savings account: a buffer that absorbs bad years so that a single drought or a single dry season does not translate directly into a water crisis,” said WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo. “We are depleting that savings account.”
“Global terrestrial water storage has shown a declining trend since 2014–2016, a persistent, decade-long signal. For the fourth consecutive year, every major glaciated region on Earth lost ice mass.”
“Groundwater tells a similar story,” she said. “Nearly two-thirds of monitored wells worldwide showed conditions outside the historical norm in 2025, and the balance shifted further toward deficit compared with 2024, not toward recovery.”
“At the same time, we are seeing more water-related disasters. The strengthening El Niño will increase the risk of drought in some areas, and flooding in others.”
River discharge in 2025 lowest in 35 years
According to the WMO State of Global Water Resources Report, the water cycle has become “erratic and unpredictable” over the past few years.
River discharge in 2025 was the lowest in 35 years, with below-normal flows across over 36% of the global basin area, the WMO report showed, based on data from 13 global hydrological models.
Additionally, the report showed that for the seventh consecutive year, the share of river basins in “normal” condition ranged from 34% to 38%, compared with an average of 46% between 1991 and 2020.
The report noted that the total amount of water stored in groundwater, lakes and rivers, soil moisture, vegetation, and ice and snow has been steadily declining since the mid-2010s.
It also found that 2025 marked the fourth consecutive year with widespread glacier loss, leading to mass flooding and long-term water insecurity.
Between 2023 and 2025, glaciers lost a cumulative 1,400 gigatonnes of water, roughly equivalent to the amount needed to fill about 560 million Olympic-sized swimming pools.
Numerous record-breaking natural disasters in past few years
WMO added that international National Meteorological and Hydrological Services (NMHSs) reported numerous record-breaking floods and droughts over the past few years.
The WMO report showed that Asia and Africa together accounted for at least half of all recorded water-related extreme events and more than 80% of reported associated deaths over the past five years.
“Water respects no borders. A river basin's water balance depends on what happens in another country,” said Saulo. “A glacier's retreat in one country reshapes water availability for populations hundreds of kilometers downstream.”
“This is precisely why we need shared data, shared standards, and shared early warning, the exact function WMO exists to perform.”
The Environment and Climate Change portal is produced in cooperation with the Goldman Sonnenfeldt School of Sustainability and Climate Change at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev. The Jerusalem Post maintains all editorial decisions related to the content.

Explainer: How China's Global Development Initiative serves as a public good
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:52:06 CST
20:52:06 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Five years after its debut, the Global Development Initiative (GDI) has evolved from a Chinese proposal into broad international consensus, translating vision into action and delivering concrete progress across the world.
First proposed during the general debate of the 76th UN General Assembly in September 2021, the GDI anchors six core principles: development as a priority, a people-centered approach, benefits for all, innovation-driven development, harmony between humanity and nature, and results-oriented actions. The framework fully aligns with the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development.
Amid a widening global development deficit and stalled progress of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development for many developing nations, China has positioned the GDI as a global public good. Upholding mutual benefit and shared growth, the country has served as a reliable partner for the Global South, delivering a result-oriented platform for pragmatic development cooperation.
Since its launch, China has established more than 30 cooperation mechanisms and platforms, mobilized over 23 billion U.S. dollars through vehicles such as the China-UN Peace and Development Fund and the Global Development and South-South Cooperation Fund, carried out over 1,800 "small yet smart" livelihood projects, and trained upwards of 200,000 professionals.
DELIVERING TANGIBLE BENEFITS
Across the Global South, China's commitment to common development aligned with the GDI has been translated into projects that improve people's lives.
Skills training programs exemplify the initiative's on-the-ground impact. This September, 34 Indonesian students enrolled in a three-year industrial mechatronics program at Wuhu Vocational Technical University in east China's Anhui Province.
The cohort joins a customized international order-tailored training program run in partnership with Anhui Conch Group Co., Ltd., a leading domestic cement manufacturer.
Launched in 2019, the program adopts a "Chinese language plus vocational skills" model, with courses covering automation, industrial robots and artificial intelligence.
"I will not only gain practical skills, but also understand the logic behind it," said Indonesian student Nilam Insirah, noting that the training allows her to pursue management-related career paths.
"I hope to bring the professional knowledge, management know-how and life experience I gained in China back to Indonesia," program graduate Brayen Difan Makatiwo told Xinhua. "I look forward to becoming a bridge connecting Indonesia with China and the wider world," he said.
Infrastructure connectivity is a key part of these efforts. The China-Laos Railway has turned landlocked Laos into a land transport hub. In Brazil, a "power highway" transmits clean electricity generated in the Amazon rainforest to urban clusters more than 2,000 kilometers away.
The initiative has also taken root in regional cooperation. Within the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) framework, China's trade with other member states has exceeded 2.3 trillion U.S. dollars. The China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, now under construction, will further boost regional connectivity. More than two-thirds of the 100 "small yet smart" livelihood projects, outlined at the 2025 SCO Tianjin summit, have now been approved for implementation.
In Guinea, Chinese hybrid rice has raised production efficiency, and "brought hope to the country's young people," said Guinean Prime Minister Amadou Oury Bah.
China's Juncao technology, which turns grass into mushrooms and animal feed, has been introduced in more than 100 countries, including Fiji and other Pacific island countries.
China has further extended cooperation in poverty reduction and agricultural technology, including hybrid rapeseed cultivation in Pakistan and a desertification control center with Mongolia.
Market access is expanding too. Since May 2026, China has granted zero-tariff treatment to all 53 African countries with diplomatic relations with China.
Innovation and green development feature prominently. China has put MAZU, its homegrown AI-powered meteorological early warning system, into service in some 30 countries.
Chinese technologies such as the BeiDou navigation system are also being applied in Egyptian industrial parks.
GROWING GLOBAL CONSENSUS
"With the 'six commitments' as its core philosophy, the GDI has grown from a Chinese proposal into a widely accepted international consensus and from China's cooperation concept into tangible joint action by China and the international community," said Dong Xiangrong, a researcher at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.
The initiative's practical results are matched by expanding international support. More than 130 countries and international organizations have endorsed it. Nearly 100 countries and international and regional organizations have signed cooperation documents with China, and the Group of Friends of GDI has grown to 88 members.
Key multilateral milestones have sustained GDI momentum, including the 2022 High-level Dialogue on Global Development, the 2023 "BRICS Plus" leaders' dialogue, and the 2026 SCO Summit.
"The Group of Friends of GDI has become an important platform for countries to coordinate development positions and match development resources under the UN framework, and a model of South-South cooperation that carries weight in global governance, climate change and development financing," said Dong. ■

NOUAKCHOTT, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese naval hospital ship Auspicious Ark on Tuesday wrapped up a seven-day friendly visit to Mauritania, marking the first stop of Mission Harmony-2026.
On the first day of its medical services, the ship welcomed the first baby born aboard during its current mission, whom the medical crew affectionately called the "Auspicious Baby."
His mother Aissata Ba had been receiving prenatal care locally, hoping for a natural delivery. As her due date approached, however, her obstetrician found that the baby was in a breech position and advised her to seek further treatment aboard the Chinese hospital ship then docked at the port.
Doctors on the ship also diagnosed Ba with gestational hypertension and recommended a cesarean section. After the doctors explained the risks and she consulted her family and friends, Ba agreed to the operation.
That day, Ba gave birth to a boy weighing about 3.4 kg in the first surgery performed during the ship's current mission. He was her fifth child and her first son.
"Both mother and baby are doing well, and the baby is in good health," an interpreter told Ba after the operation. Xue Juan, head of the ship's nursing department, recalled that Ba said "Thank you" again and again.
Xue then carried the newborn to the ward for a thorough examination, where a blanket bearing the words "Auspicious Baby" and a traditional red bellyband awaited him -- gifts specially prepared by the medical team. Wrapped in the blanket beside his mother, the newborn became a memorable part of the ship's seven-day visit to Mauritania.
For some members of the medical team, the visit marked a return to Mauritania.
Launched in 2010, the Mission Harmony series is carrying out its 12th mission this year. Zhu Gang, chief medical officer of the hospital ship, previously visited Mauritania in 2024 with the Peace Ark.
According to Zhu, the ship recorded approximately 900 patient visits on the opening day, 1,200 the next day and 1,400 on Sept. 18. Daily patient visits increased as clinical and diagnostic departments coordinated more smoothly, patient guidance and flow-control measures improved, and staff became more familiar with the working procedures.
Zhu noted that the mission went beyond consultations and examinations aboard the ship. It also included medical services in local communities, academic exchanges and study visits, technical training, health activities and cultural exchanges.
Meng Xiaohui, a nurse in the central sterile supply department, was also making her second visit to Mauritania aboard a Chinese naval hospital ship.
Recalling her first visit to Mauritania in 2024, Meng said communication was sometimes difficult because many local residents primarily spoke Arabic. What stayed with her most, however, was how readily the local people cooperated during treatment and how warm and friendly they were toward the Chinese medical staff.
For many patients, it was their first time aboard a hospital ship, and they were unfamiliar with its layout and procedures. Language barriers added to the challenge, but medical staff spared no effort to provide assistance.
"Even when our staff cannot resolve a problem immediately, they make sure the patient knows what to do next. Everyone works extra hours, trying to meet all the patients who come that day," Meng said.
The Chinese nurse recalled that many patients thanked the Chinese medical workers after receiving treatment. Two elderly patients even invited her to visit them at home as a gesture of appreciation.
Traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) was among the services that drew particular interest from local patients. Zhu Xu, a TCM doctor on his first overseas mission, saw many patients come to the ship specifically seeking such treatment.
One of his patients was Savia Zein. She received acupuncture aboard the Peace Ark in 2024 for pain in both knees and found that the treatment had brought significant relief. When the Auspicious Ark arrived, she came aboard for another acupuncture treatment and brought members of her family with her to receive care.
Another TCM doctor aboard the ship, Huang Nian, said TCM could help treat a range of common ailments in Africa.
During the visit, he treated many patients with back and leg pain and other musculoskeletal problems frequently seen locally. Many TCM techniques are relatively inexpensive and require little equipment, making them practical in areas with limited medical resources.
According to Huang, many local patients had never tried acupuncture or cupping therapy before, but readily accepted the treatments after they were explained.
"Some patients recommended the therapies to relatives or friends, who came to the ship the following day seeking treatment themselves," he added.
In his view, such acceptance reflected trust built over time. "Local patients' trust in Chinese doctors comes from more than 60 years of work by Chinese medical teams in Africa," Huang said.
The 36th Chinese medical team to Mauritania is currently serving in the country. During the ship's stay, its members conducted joint consultations with doctors aboard the Auspicious Ark in ophthalmology, orthopedics and other specialties.
Wang Yu, head of the Chinese medical team, noted that the team's local clinical experience complemented the ship's team of specialists and advanced equipment, allowing the two sides to provide more accurate diagnoses and efficient treatment. ■

China delivers customized MAZU early warning solution to Nepal
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
19:51:28 CST
20:51:28 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- China has delivered a customized version of its homegrown AI-powered meteorological early warning system to Nepal to help the country improve early warning and disaster response, China's meteorological authority said Tuesday.
The move came after the China Meteorological Administration (CMA) gave Nepal's meteorological department a version of MAZU for cloud-based trial use on Aug. 29, following a deadly mudslide at the Gyirong-Rasuwa border crossing on the China-Nepal border.
MAZU, short for multi-hazard, alert, zero-gap and universal, is an AI-driven meteorological early warning platform named after the Chinese guardian goddess of the sea.
The CMA announced the delivery at the Second China-Central Asia Meteorological Cooperation Forum, held in Urumqi, capital of northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region.
After the mudslide, China provided meteorological forecast and early warning support to Nepal, including high-resolution and rapidly updated forecasting and early warning products to support Nepal's disaster relief, the CMA noted.
The Nepal-customized version of MAZU was developed by taking full account of local geographical conditions, disaster characteristics, infrastructure and data conditions, the CMA said.
At the same event, the CMA unveiled a plan for implementing the MAZU system in Central Asian countries for 2026-2027, aiming to deepen meteorological cooperation between China and Central Asian countries, jointly enhance regional disaster prevention and mitigation capacity, and better serve regional economic and social development.
MAZU has been applied in seven countries and is currently being trialed on the cloud in more than 50 countries, according to Chen Zhenlin, head of the CMA. The CMA will work to accelerate the global application of the MAZU system, Chen added. ■

Over 200,000 foreign nationals enrolled in Iranian schools
TEHRAN – More than 200,000 foreign national students, including boys and girls, have been enrolled in schools in Iran and will benefit from educational services in the current academic year, which starts on September 23.
The schools have even enrolled students who faced residency status issues, preserving their right to education, IRNA quoted Ali Farhadi, an official with the Ministry of Education, as saying.
In July 2025, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), Filippo Grandi, lauded the efforts of the Education Ministry in supporting and providing services to foreign students.
“The main reason why I am visiting Iran is to appreciate the country’s valuable services provided to refugees. I have repeatedly talked about this issue in international forums, and urged them to follow Iran as a role model,” Mehr news agency quoted Grandi as saying.
The official made the remarks in a meeting with Education Minister Alireza Kazemi on July 23.
During the meeting, Grandi referred to Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei’s statement in 2015, according to which all Afghan refugees, including undocumented ones, were allowed to be enrolled in schools. The official called it a valuable historical measure that surprised everyone, including rich countries.
For his part, Kazemi expounded on the country’s measures and challenges in assisting refugees.
Iran spends 100 million dollars annually on providing services to foreign nationals, while UNHCR's contribution has been less than a percent over the past two years
The presence of refugee students at schools has made classes overcrowded, which has consequently affected Iranian students’ academic performance, the official added.
Referring to the lack of educational space and the substantial financial burden of providing it, Kazemi said it is socially and economically costly; people expect these expenditures to be spent on Iranians, which is a logical demand.
The education minister went on to highlight the economic and social challenges caused by foreign nationals, saying that due to economic problems, Afghan refugees involve their children in helping generate income, which leads to severe social impacts in the country.
“Despite all these problems, Iran has never reduced the services provided to refugees. The country continues to provide the best services to legally permitted refugee students, ensuring none of them is deprived of education,” Kazemi noted.
Now that Afghanistan has attained stability, Afghan nationals are better able to return, with dignity, and serve their home country, he said.
Even to support (deported) refugees to continue education and learning, Iran is ready to educate all Afghan students using the local education platforms, within the framework of the tripartite cooperation agreement, and provide them with a valid educational certificate based on the statutes of virtual schools approved by the Supreme Council of Education, the official added.
Grandi lauded the proposal and voiced the UNHCR’s support of the program, calling it an invaluable measure for the young generation.
“I am aware of low contributions, and I admit more funds have to be assigned to your services, but due to the current situation and sanctions, it is not possible. We are not a rich partner, but we would be happy to remain your partner,” the official said.

This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:46:55 UTC
20:46:55 KST

This new concrete is stronger and pulls CO2 from the air
- Date:
- September 22, 2026
- Source:
- Shenyang Agricultural University
- Summary:
- Researchers have created a concrete mixture that is both stronger and capable of absorbing carbon dioxide. The best formula, combining zeolite with bamboo biochar, boosted compressive strength by 7.48% and tensile strength by 15% compared with conventional concrete. It also captured about 1.2 grams of CO₂ per day in laboratory testing.
- Share:
Engineers have created a new type of concrete that is stronger than conventional concrete while also capturing carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The findings, reported in Carbon Research, suggest that adding carefully selected natural materials could give concrete a second role beyond construction by helping remove CO2 from the surrounding air.
Researchers at Mepco Schlenk Engineering College in India developed the mixture as a possible way to make construction materials more sustainable. Their approach targets a major environmental challenge: rising atmospheric CO2 levels driven in large part by fossil fuel use and cement production.
The team, led by Srinivasan Revathi, focused on two natural additives. One was zeolite, a highly porous mineral, and the other was bamboo biochar, a carbon-rich material. Both have large pore volumes and high specific surface areas, properties that make them well suited for trapping gas molecules.
Testing a Stronger Concrete Mix
The researchers tested several versions of M35 grade concrete, which is commonly used in infrastructure designed for moderate traffic. They replaced fine aggregate with zeolite at levels of 25% and 50%. They also substituted bamboo biochar for cement at concentrations of 0.5%, 1%, and 1.5%.
Each formulation was tested for several important properties, including compressive strength, split tensile strength, water absorption, and impact resistance. The researchers were looking for a mix that could absorb more CO2 without weakening the concrete. Ideally, they wanted the material to become stronger at the same time.
One combination stood out from the rest. The mix containing 50% zeolite and 1% bamboo biochar (dubbed ZB5) delivered the best overall performance.
Its compressive strength reached 38.49 MPa, about 7.48% higher than conventional concrete. Its split tensile strength reached 4.39 MPa, representing a 15% improvement over the standard mixture.
The researchers attribute the added strength to the interaction between zeolite's alumina-silicate structure and the hardness of bamboo biochar. Together, these materials appear to produce a denser and more durable cement-based matrix.
Concrete That Captures CO2
Strength was only part of the result. The ZB5 mixture also demonstrated an ability to absorb carbon dioxide.
When the concrete was placed inside a carbonation chamber, it captured 1.2 grams of CO2 per day. Over seven days, the gas penetrated 15 mm into the material.
The researchers linked this carbon uptake to the microporous structure of zeolite and the high carbon content of bamboo biochar. By combining these properties, the concrete can serve both as a structural material and as a medium for capturing atmospheric CO2.
Srinivasan Revathi, the corresponding author from the Department of Civil Engineering, provided her perspective on the findings. "Our work demonstrates a dual-benefit approach. We are not just creating a stronger concrete, but we are transforming a common building material into an active tool for environmental remediation. By integrating zeolite and bamboo biochar, we can build structures that not only stand strong but also actively cleanse the air of excess carbon dioxide, paving the way for truly sustainable infrastructure in high-emission areas like urban roadways and industrial zones."
Potential for Carbon-Neutral Construction
The findings point toward a possible new approach to developing carbon-neutral construction materials. Concrete made with the ZB5 formulation could be especially useful in locations where CO2 concentrations are relatively high.
Potential applications include concrete pavements, highway parapet walls, and sewer pipelines. These structures could continue serving their traditional engineering functions while also capturing some carbon dioxide from their surroundings.
The researchers caution, however, that the work is still a proof of concept and that additional testing will be necessary before the material can be widely adopted.
Next Steps for Carbon-Capturing Concrete
Future studies will examine how the concrete performs over longer periods, including whether it maintains its durability and ability to absorb CO2.
The researchers also plan to test other forms of biochar, evaluate the mixture in different grades of concrete and mortar, and study whether pre-soaked biochar can further improve its performance.
Those experiments will help determine whether the technology can be scaled for broader commercial and industrial use. If successful, the approach could provide the construction industry with a way to produce stronger infrastructure while also reducing some of the environmental impact associated with the built environment.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Shenyang Agricultural University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Srinivasan Revathi, Dobson Alice Elizabeth Tania, Sutharson Ancy Shadin, Jegatheesan Keerthana. Effect of zeolite and bamboo biochar as CO2 absorbant in concrete. Carbon Research, 2024; 3 (1) DOI: 10.1007/s44246-024-00116-1

What follows is the text of his speech:
Today, I wish to speak on behalf of a nation that, over the past year, has endured profound consequences arising from a blatant and brutal aggression perpetrated by the United States and the Israeli regime.
Most of the crises that we suffered from war to economic hardship, were shaped, fueled, and, externally instigated by the United States, with serious consequences for our national sovereignty, social stability and regional security.

The acts of aggression by the United States and Israel, following multiple documented violations of international humanitarian law (IHL) and human rights, marked one of the darkest pages in human history. Our people found themselves standing before some of the most criminal and reckless Foreign States, who showed utter disregard for international law and demonstrated no restraint in their brutality.

British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
12:44:34 BST
20:44:34 KST

British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager
- Published
Italian authorities are searching for a British man who went missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue a teenager.
The local coastguard said the man, in his late thirties, had been attempting to rescue two people - a father and his 16-year-old son - who were in distress in the water near the lake's western shore on Monday afternoon, local officials said.
The man, who was friends with the family, had been on a boating trip with them at the time, the coastguard said. The father and son were later rescued by a passing boat, but the man has not been seen again.
The UK Foreign Office said: "We are supporting the family of a British national missing in Italy and are in contact with the local authorities."
A helicopter, divers and boat units from the fire department, coastguard and state police have been drafted into the search.
As the lake's depth can reach more than 250m in the search area, rescuers were also preparing to deploy two underwater robots to scan the lake bed where the lake becomes too deep for divers, the Italian Coast Guard said in a statement.
The alarm was first raised around 13:30 local time (12:30 BST) on Monday, when the man noticed his friend and the boy experiencing difficulty swimming and jumped in to help them.
The teenager's mother, who had remained on the boat with her younger son, called the emergency services when she saw the man sinking beneath the surface.
The father and son were transferred to a coastguard boat that had responded to the call and were given medical treatment after suffering from the onset of hypothermia, officials said.
The mother and younger son, who were at this point adrift around 600m from shore, were then brought back to land.
The coastguard earlier said that it had been the father who had jumped in to save the boy and the 37-year-old man, before revising its statement of events.
Lake Como, around 30 miles north of Milan, is a popular tourist hotspot, with more than 78,000 foreign visitors in 2024, local chamber of commerce research shows.
However, water temperatures there can start to fall from September onward.

During a special operation in Kyiv, an alleged Russian agent was detained after receiving instructions to assassinate a Russian opposition activist who currently heads one of Ukraine’s nationwide public organizations.
According to the investigation, the woman was supposed to shoot the activist from an ambush near a Kyiv gym where he works as a kickboxing coach. In this way, Russia sought to kill the Russian opposition figure, who had fought for Ukraine since 2022, first in the Kyiv region and later on the eastern front.
SBU officers acted preemptively and detained the suspect near the sports complex while she was conducting further reconnaissance of the area to select a firing position for the planned attack.
According to the case materials, the Federal Security Service recruited the unemployed woman, a resident of temporarily occupied Melitopol, to carry out the assignment.
The investigation established that Russian intelligence services recruited the woman in exchange for dropping a criminal case against her for illegal drug possession. The recruited agent underwent training at a local “FSB branch,” where she was taught operational security, terrain navigation and firearms handling.
After completing her training, the agent was sent to Zhytomyr via Belarus and then traveled to Kyiv.
In the capital, the suspect regularly changed hotel addresses. Whenever she left her room, she left a mark on the door to check whether anyone had entered.
Later, the agent received coordinates from her Russian handler for a weapons cache in a forested area of the capital, where she retrieved a pistol and ammunition.
SBU counterintelligence officers found the weapon during a search of the suspect’s hotel room. They also seized a smartphone she had used to communicate with her FSB handler, whose identity has already been established by the SBU.
SBU investigators notified the agent that she was suspected under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law).
The suspect is being held in custody without the right to bail. She faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. European bureaucrats fear that without seizing Russian assets they will not be able to indefinitely fund the corrupt Kiev regime, Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) said in a press release on Tuesday.

TASS has compiled key statements from the SVR.
Operation to steal Russian assets
European officials fear that without seizing Russian assets, they "will not be able to endlessly fund the corrupt Kiev regime, which constitutes the expenditure side of NATO’s conflict with Russia," the SVR argued.
EU leaders are rushing to carry out the operation to confiscate Russian assets before next year’s elections in a number of European countries: "EU leaders have a vital interest in completing the operation to steal Russian assets before the elections in a number of European countries in 2027."
EU’s plan to seize Russian assets
According to information made available to the SVR, minds in Brussels are "still all hyped up over plans to misappropriate the Bank of Russia’s assets frozen in the EU."
The EU is discussing proposals at the expert level to remove Russian assets from the Euroclear depositary: "This time around, they are discussing proposals at the expert level on creating a new supranational entity where Russian assets could be ‘hidden’ after being removed from the Euroclear depositary."
Potential impact for EU
The SVR warned the EU that attempts to confiscate sovereign Russian assets may erode global confidence in pan-European institutions: "The current ruling elite in the EU should come to understand that its attempts to steal sovereign Russian assets will undermine the credibility of pan-European institutions." "Countries in the Global South will no longer consider European jurisdictions as a safe haven," the SVR said. "For Europe will not be able to maintain the stability of its own financial system without relying on large foreign holders of European securities, such as China, India, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Singapore. So, the thief will be punished in any case," the SVR argued.
EU’s attempts to remove Russian assets from Euroclear depositary
On September 2, Euractiv reported that the EU is considering an option to remove the frozen Russian assets from the Belgian jurisdiction and transfer them away from the Brussels-based clearing house Euroclear into a "completely new legal vehicle."
According to the website, the proposal was presented to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen as a creative effort to override Belgian resistance to using the funds held at Euroclear.
On August 29, Belgium blocked the latest attempt by four EU member states to revive discussions on the possible expropriation of frozen Russian assets, Belgian Defense and Foreign Trade Minister Theo Francken told VRT television.
The kingdom declared the plan to expropriate and use €200 billion in sovereign Russian assets immobilized at Euroclear in Belgium to support Ukraine’s military operations "non-negotiatible," he said.
Belgium blocked the European Commission’s initial attempt to appropriate the funds in December 2025.
Russian assets freeze
The EU and the Group of Seven (G7) nations have frozen approximately €300 billion in Russian assets, with about €185 billion held at the Belgian depository Euroclear.
The EU is looking for ways to utilize these funds for Ukraine’s needs. It acknowledges a lack of legal mechanisms for such operations, which threaten to erode international investor confidence.
In December 2025, the Bank of Russia filed an 18.2-trillion-ruble ($216 bln) lawsuit against Euroclear with the Moscow Arbitration Court, seeking the return of frozen funds, the value of blocked securities, and lost profits. On May 15, the court ruled in favor of the Russian regulator.
By May 29, court bailiffs initiated almost 60 enforcement proceedings against Euroclear Bank to recover nearly 28 billion rubles ($332 mln), according to court and other materials seen by TASS.

Court bars solitary confinement for Agam Tsarafi, rebukes IPS over prison video
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:41:06 UTC
20:41:06 KST

The Tel Aviv District Court barred the Israel Prison Service (IPS) from holding 19-year-old Agam Tsarafi, a defendant in the Benyahu Razi murder case, in solitary confinement, and it limited her current arrangement to an additional six days. The court also sharply criticized her treatment in a related video circulated from detention.
Tsarafi is charged with intentional murder and aggravated injury in the July killing of Razi, 19, in a Jerusalem apartment. Prosecutors assert that she and alleged accomplice Shilat Huta helped organize an attack carried out by four minors. All six are charged in the killing, and the criminal case remains pending.
Friday’s ruling concerns Tsarafi’s detention conditions rather than the charges against her, easing some of the restrictions imposed by the IPS, but does not restore her general access to telephone calls or determine who recorded or distributed the footage.
Judge Gilad Hess wrote that the actions taken against Tsarafi appeared excessive, harmed her dignity, and lacked justification. The video displayed her handcuffed with her hands behind her back, bent forward while masked officers led her through the facility.
Hess added that such handling of a female detainee should, where possible, not be carried out by male officers. However, he also said that this was a general assessment of the footage rather than a final ruling on all of the defense’s allegations about the situation, which were not fully before the court in the prison petition.
The immediate impact is that Tsarafi may not be held alone. The IPS may continue separating her from the general prison population, but she must be housed with at least one other detainee. Hess limited that arrangement to six additional days, through Thursday, rather than the 30 days sought by the service.
The court said the need for continued separation must then be reassessed if no new intelligence emerges. Tsarafi may petition again if the IPS extends the measure.
Court largely sides with IPS on telephone access
On telephone access, however, the court largely sided with the IPS. After reviewing classified material from the service and Israel Police, Hess said the restriction was based on reliable, corroborated intelligence and that even monitored calls could undermine its purpose.
The general phone restriction remains in place. Tsarafi’s lawyers may submit a specific request for a call, including with her parents, for the IPS to consider.
Public defender Daniel Mirsky filed the petition on September 14, challenging Tsarafi’s separation and restrictions on calls and visits. The dispute became urgent after the escort video circulated while the IPS still had several days to respond.
The defense argued that the footage humiliated a detainee who has not been convicted and risked prejudicing her criminal trial. It also asked the court to identify who authorized its release and prevent further publication of material about her from inside IPS facilities.
The IPS responded by telling the court that it had not published the video and that no authorized official had approved its release. It said the matter was being examined. Hess did not determine who filmed or distributed the footage, saying those questions would require a separate, properly filed proceeding.
The service also argued that intelligence material justified the restrictions because of the risk Tsarafi allegedly posed to prison order and public safety. The court found the material sufficient to support the telephone ban and temporary separation but not solitary confinement or a 30-day period.
Ben-Gvir defends IPS, says Tsarafi disrupted order, mistreated prisoners, staff
“Prison officers are expected to respect themselves, the law, and Agam’s presumption of innocence,” the defense said after the ruling. It added that the question of Tsarafi’s responsibility for Razi’s death should be determined in court and criticized the professional standards displayed in the video as well as its distribution.
National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir had defended the IPS after the footage emerged, alleging that Tsarafi disrupted order and mistreated prisoners and staff and that her detention transfer was justified.
The murder proceedings are continuing separately in the Jerusalem District Court.

Rwandan man charged in UK with genocide offenses appears in court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:41:03 UTC
20:41:03 KST

A former Rwandan official appeared in a London court on Tuesday charged with encouraging the massacre of Tutsis and ordering six killings in the first week of the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
Vincent Brown, formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, is the first person to be charged in Britain over the genocide, in which more than 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in 100 days in massacres orchestrated by the Hutu ruling majority.
He is charged with one offense of conduct ancillary to genocide in Rwanda's capital, Kigali, between April 6 and 13, 1994 – the first week of the genocide, after Rwanda's president Juvenal Habyarimana was killed alongside Burundi's president Cyprien Ntaryamira in a rocket attack on their plane.
Brown also faces six offenses of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity, alleging he ordered six killings in four days, including a young mother and her baby son.
Prosecutor: Brown was Rwanda's Family Health Department chief when genocide began
The 65-year-old appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court, where prosecutor Jane Stansfield said Brown was head of the Department of Family Health within Rwanda's National Office of Population when the genocide began.
Stansfield said Brown was alleged by witnesses, including his neighbors, to have been "the leader and supervisor of physical acts of violence which were carried out by others."
Brown, who has lived in Britain for more than two decades, denies involvement in the genocide and says he left Kigali in mid-April 1994, with his family leaving Rwanda that July.
His lawyer, Sam Blom-Cooper, said Brown welcomed being charged as an opportunity to clear his name.
"These are appalling crimes, terrible murders that were committed back in 1994," he said. "But this, finally, does represent the beginning of the end for Dr Brown."
Judge Paul Goldspring said he would grant Brown bail ahead of his next court appearance at the Old Bailey on October 9, subject to him providing sufficient funds as a security.
Prosecutors, however, said they wanted to appeal against that decision, meaning Brown remains in custody until a hearing later this week.
British police's War Crimes Team said on Monday that six others remain under investigation, including two men arrested on suspicion of genocide and crimes against humanity.

Alibaba unveiled a new AI chip and plans for a vastly larger artificial intelligence model on Tuesday, highlighting China’s drive for greater technological self-reliance just days before President Xi Jinping is due to meet US President Donald Trump in Washington.
At its annual Apsara conference in Hangzhou, Alibaba CEO Eddie Wu said the company’s new Zhenwu V900 chip is the most powerful AI processor in China and delivers three times the performance of its predecessor.
The chip is designed to support both AI training and inference, the computing used to generate responses from trained models.
Alibaba also said it plans to train a new AI model with between 5 trillion and 10 trillion parameters — potentially more than four times the size of its current Qwen 3.8 Max model, which has 2.4 trillion parameters.
AI race moves to chips and computing power
The announcements underscore Alibaba’s effort to build a full AI ecosystem spanning chips, models and cloud infrastructure as Chinese companies face restrictions on access to some advanced US technologies.
The company said it expects Alibaba Cloud’s global data-centre capacity to exceed 20 gigawatts by 2032, reflecting what Wu described as rapidly rising demand for AI computing. The V900 is expected to enter mass production and commercial release in early 2027.
Alibaba’s push comes as other Chinese technology companies, including Huawei, are also developing domestic alternatives to advanced AI hardware amid US export restrictions.
Chinese developers have also gained international attention with open AI models that can be cheaper and more accessible than some proprietary US systems, adding another dimension to the competition.
New backdrop for Trump-Xi talks
The timing of Alibaba’s announcement is notable as Xi prepares to meet Trump in Washington on Thursday, with AI expected to be among the issues shaping discussions between the world’s two largest economies.
The two countries remain deeply competitive over advanced technology, while Washington has restricted China’s access to some high-end AI chips and semiconductor equipment.
Beijing, meanwhile, has pushed to strengthen domestic capabilities and reduce its dependence on foreign technology.
US and Chinese officials have also discussed creating mechanisms for greater transparency around AI-related incidents, even as broader disagreements over technology controls remain unresolved.
Wu compared the rapid development of AI to the Industrial Revolution and said Alibaba was mobilising its resources to meet growing demand.
The latest announcements show how quickly the AI competition is expanding beyond individual models to the chips, data centres and computing infrastructure needed to power the next generation of systems.

US National Archives recovers over 120 previously unknown American POW statements from WWII
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:40:44 UTC
20:40:44 KST

Approximately 300 pages of World War II American Prisoner of War (POW) interrogation reports and ancillary reports were recovered by the US’s National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) earlier this summer.
The documents were discovered by Waterloo resident Jason Hurdle inside a cardboard box hidden in a previously unknown crawlspace in his garage, The Washington Post reported last week.
Marked with a “SECRET” stamp on the first page, the files are made up of mostly handwritten, first-person accounts of over 120 American POWs held by the Germans during World War II.
After finding the documents, Hurdle brought them to a nearby museum where he was recommended to contact NARA. In January, NARA sent two representatives to Hurdle’s home, and in July, it announced that its Archival Recovery Team (ART) had safely recovered the documents.
“I’m in podunk little Waterloo, New York, and this went all the way to the National Archives,” Hurdle told The Washington Post. “We’re kind of in shock here.”
The documents appear to be part of a larger American initiative investigating whether or not Germany was upholding its end of the international treaty regarding the dignified treatment of future POWs, signed in Geneva in 1929.
Handwritten accounts detail inhumane conditions
Pictures of the documents, shared by The Washington Post, show soldiers recounting being held in inhumane conditions by the Germans after being captured during the Battle of the Bulge.
Over 23,000 American soldiers were taken as POWs from the Battle of the Bulge.
“During an air raid near 7A, an unteroffizier [NCO] shot at and wounded an American from our barracks. I did not know his name,” wrote Private First Class Waldon Joseph Green, adding that he had been witness to a bombing that killed three Americans and left 28 missing.
Private First Class Henry Daly, in his account, wrote that when he had been first captured, “we were marched for days at times without food and water, at times we were crammed into boxcars as many as 80 men to a car, and we were not even allowed to get off and relieve ourselves.”
Second lieutenant Robert Warren Bieber shared that Nuremberg had very little medical supplies and food, and that he had seen “one boy die of malnutrition, name unknown.”
“A prisoner [stopped] to adjust his pack and a guard shot him. I do not know the boy’s name,” wrote First Sergeant Eugene William Eidschun.
According to The Washington Post, the files did not appear on NARA’s list of missing federal documents.
No one has yet figured out how they ended up in Hurdle’s garage, though The Washington Post said Hurdle suggested they may have come from a former neighbor.
Documents now displayed at archives
Kimberly Guise, the National World War II Museum’s associate vice president of curatorial affairs, told The Washington Post that the documents found by Hurdle are significant for the large number of firsthand accounts they contain.
“It’s really lucky that this material was discovered, that the gentleman looked inside the box, and that he got it to a safe place,” Guise said. “It’s pretty great in terms of POW research.”
The documents are now displayed inside a gray box with a typed label marking them “declassified,” according to The Washington Post, in the same order they were found in.
The Washington Post noted that at least one page, which had been partially ripped, has been preserved in a clear plastic sleeve, and that NARA archivists are the only ones allowed to handle the fragile files.
NARA spokeswoman Grace McCaffrey explained to The Washington Post that the archives is planning to digitize the records and make them available to the public.
“This stuff was stuff that you don’t learn in history books,” Hurdle told The Washington Post. “You actually see this and read this; that to me is very, very special. I was like, I got to find a place these can go."

====================================================================================================

The weak have one weapon the strong often lack - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:40:44 UTC
20:40:44 KST

How can the Houthis in Yemen, Hamas in Gaza, or Hezbollah in Lebanon continue fighting enemies with vastly greater military power?
The answer is not that these movements are secretly stronger than the armies confronting them; it is that military strength and strategic endurance are not the same thing.
The weaker side often has several advantages.
First, there is a large pool of young people with too few opportunities.
Where economies cannot provide jobs, dignity, or a plausible future, an armed movement can provide money, status, comradeship, protection, and purpose.
This does not mean that poor young men inevitably become fighters – the majority do not. But it gives an organization a large potential recruiting pool.
Second, there is ideology.
Religion is often the vehicle, but it need not be. Nationalism, Marxism, ethnic identity, or revolutionary ideology can perform the same function.
Ideology transforms a military struggle into a moral one. The fighter is no longer simply fighting an enemy; he is defending his people, his faith, or his historical mission.
Third, there is institutional weakness.
When the state cannot reliably provide security, justice, electricity, water, employment, or education, an armed movement becomes a parallel society. The organization supplies services, distributes money, settles disputes, and creates a sense of belonging.
Fourth, there is outside sponsorship.
A local movement that could otherwise be contained can become a formidable strategic problem when an external power supplies money, weapons, training, intelligence, and technology.
Iran’s support for regional armed groups is a particularly important example of how a relatively poor movement can acquire capabilities far beyond what its local economy could produce.
And then comes the fifth advantage: time.
This is where the arithmetic becomes particularly cruel.
A powerful democratic country generally wants wars to be short. Its citizens will tolerate casualties for a compelling objective, but tolerance for an open-ended war tends to decline as the years pass.
Soldiers have families. Reservists have jobs. Businesses suffer. Governments face elections. The public begins asking the most dangerous question a government can hear during wartime: When does this end?
The weaker side often faces a very different calculation.
It may not need to win; it may only need to survive.
If it can survive long enough, the stronger enemy may eventually begin fighting its own domestic clock.
This creates a great strategic asymmetry: the stronger side has something to lose every day; the weaker side often turns survival itself into victory.
The longer the war continues, the more the stronger side’s military superiority is offset by political exhaustion.
This dynamic has appeared repeatedly in modern warfare. Vietnam demonstrated the enormous difficulty of translating overwhelming American military power into a political settlement.
Afghanistan demonstrated the difficulty of defeating an insurgency whose organizational and social foundations survived successive military campaigns.
And Gaza has again demonstrated how military superiority does not automatically determine the political end-state.
The lesson is not that democracies are weak. It is almost the opposite.
The most important strategic lesson
Democratic societies possess enormous military and economic resources. But those societies also place constraints on the use of those resources. They debate, protest, hold elections, count casualties, and eventually demand results.
Their enemies understand this and use strategic patience as a weapon.
But there is another recurring advantage enjoyed by the weaker side: the hubris of the stronger side.
Military superiority creates a dangerous psychological trap. Leaders with enormous capabilities can begin to believe that they possess enormous understanding.
More often than not, they do not.
Before major conflicts, powerful states repeatedly underestimated the adversary’s willingness to fight, its ability to absorb punishment, and the depth of its social support.
Israel’s October 7, 2023 experience – the Hamas-led massacre and subsequent war – provides a contemporary warning.
Whatever the eventual findings about individual decisions and intelligence failures, the central lesson is unmistakable: a technologically sophisticated intelligence system does not necessarily guarantee correct understanding of the enemy.
And this is where hubris becomes particularly dangerous.
When an enemy appears weak, intelligence can seem like an unnecessary expense. Why devote enormous resources to understanding a movement that appears incapable of defeating you?
Because the enemy does not have to defeat you.
It only has to surprise you, then survive and wait.
The combination of demographic pressure, ideology, institutional weakness, external sponsorship, strategic patience, and the stronger side’s own political constraints creates a remarkably powerful formula.
It explains why the history of modern warfare is filled with apparently irrational confrontations in which the weaker side refuses to surrender despite overwhelming odds.
The weaker side understands something the stronger side sometimes forgets: You do not have to win the war today. You only have to make sure the other side eventually wants it to end more than you do.
That may be the most important strategic lesson of all.
The writer is a Senior Research Fellow at the Neaman Institute and an Emeritus Professor at the Technion, Israel Institute of Technology, where he has served in various leadership positions. He also serves as a member of the Board and as a strategic consultant to some companies and organizations.

Qatar attempting to distance itself from Hamas, looking to West, expert tells ‘Post’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:40:40 UTC
20:40:40 KST

Doha is attempting to publicly distance itself from Hamas, denying that it knowingly funded the group, as attacks on its oil infrastructure have pushed Qatar to pursue financial relationships with Western groups that are less willing to engage with a country associated with the Palestinian terrorist organization, Dr. Ariel Admoni, a researcher of Qatari policy at Ariel University and the Jerusalem Institute for Strategy and Security (JISS), told The Jerusalem Post on Tuesday.
Admoni spoke with the Post after Qatar’s International Media Office issued multiple statements rejecting accusations that Doha had directly funded Hamas. The office claimed that the allegations originated from a “sustained campaign involving pro-Israel media, lobbyists, lawyers, think tanks, and so-called research organizations.”
The office further argued that any Qatari funds that reached Hamas did so as a result of Israeli failures, while maintaining that Qatar had coordinated with international partners to ensure humanitarian aid reached Palestinian civilians in Gaza.
Admoni said the statements represented a noticeable change in tone for a country that hosts Hamas’s leadership, whose state-funded media reportedly operates under a directive to portray Hamas sympathetically and which has allegedly spent years financing the terrorist group, according to Hamas’s own documentation.
According to Hamas documents seized by Israel and obtained by The New Yorker, Hamas officials directly thanked Qatari leaders for financial support, describing Qatari grants as “the main artery of the Hamas movement.” Qatar has rejected the documents as “falsified and fabricated information.”
Doha had also rejected accusations that it supported Hamas financially in the past, notably denying US House Oversight Committee Chairman Rep. James Comer’s 2024 claim that Qatar had paid Hamas $30 million per month since 2018.
Though Qatar has long denied the allegations, Admoni noted that the seriousness of its response, including threats of legal action and countering with allegations that Israel’s far right is using Doha to “deflect attention from domestic political failure,” was a sign that Qatar wanted to “rebrand itself.”
Admoni: Qatar relying on American financial systems
“This is a delicate time for Qatar, because right now, they rely on American financial systems,” he explained, highlighting recent meetings Qatar has held with potential investors in recent days.
Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al-Thani met with President and Chief Investment Officer of Alphabet and Google, Ruth Porat, and with Microsoft Co-Founder Bill Gates on Monday, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Doha’s Foreign Ministry confirmed.
It was also announced on Monday that the Qatar Investment Authority and J.P. Morgan Asset Management agreed to a $20 billion strategic partnership spanning public equities and private credit, which would expand the fund’s investment ties with the US.
With Qatar’s energy-based economy still suffering as a result of Iranian attacks, “they need the American financial system by their side,” Admoni reasoned, adding that Doha was particularly aware of the “importance of narrative” and image when engaging with American industry giants.
Iran’s attacks knocked out 17% of Qatari LNG in March alone
The hydrocarbon sector contributed around 60% of Qatar’s GDP in 2024, making it a significant resource for the Qatari economy, and Iran’s attacks in March alone knocked out 17% of Qatar’s liquefied natural gas (LNG) export capacity, causing an estimated $20 billion in lost annual revenue, according to statements made by QatarEnergy’s CEO and Energy Affairs Minister Saad al-Kaabi to Reuters.
Though Admoni said that Qatar’s “vulnerability is showing” as a result of the war, and “Qatari money seems less persuasive than before,” he maintained that he had not witnessed a drastic change in attitude from the West, which still seems willing to accept Qatar’s peacemaker image.
Still, he insisted that the excuse Qatar has so far used to maintain ties with Hamas would continue to be threatened as international media probes deeper into the “terror kingpin” funding the Islamist groups.

Israeli defense companies head to Marrakesh Air Show
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:40:23 UTC
20:40:23 KST

Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI), Elbit Systems, and other Israeli defense companies are heading to Morocco’s Marrakesh Air Show next month with a broad portfolio of air-defense, precision-strike, unmanned, and space technologies, as the Jewish state seeks to deepen its position in a market long served by French and US defense companies.
Defense & Tech by The Jerusalem Post has confirmed that IAI, Elbit Systems, Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, Xtend, Shilat, Uvision, and Orbit Technologies will be officially participating for the first time in the Moroccan exhibition, which will take place October 7-10 at the Royal Moroccan Air Force base in Marrakesh.
At the airshow, IAI will showcase its Barak air-defense solution, LORA precision-strike system, Heron MK II unmanned aircraft, OPAL collaborative-combat technology, and communications satellites. The company will also promote its aircraft conversion and maintenance capabilities. IAI said it will also use the exhibition to pursue local cooperation, industrial collaboration, knowledge sharing and technology transfer with Moroccan and regional partners.
Elbit Systems will exhibit its PULS multiple rocket launcher, Lizard modular precision guidance kits, SPECTRO advanced, multi-spectral electro-optical (EO) payload system, and several families of drones including the Hermes 900 unmanned aerial system, TerminaTHOR tactical airdrop munition system, the THOR tactical multi-purpose UAS, and others.
It has not been shared what the other defense companies will exhibit.
Rapid expansion
Morocco has had close economic, diplomatic, and military ties with Israel for years, and in 2020, Jerusalem and Rabat reestablished ties under the Abraham Accords.
A year later, the two countries signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) surrounding arms deals, intelligence cooperation, and joint military projects. The North African kingdom has since signed several deals with Israeli defense companies as it has significantly increased its defense budget over the past year. This increase is part of the country’s effort to modernize its military and build a domestic military industry to reduce its reliance on foreign imports.
In January, the two countries signed a joint military work plan for 2026 and agreed to upgrade diplomatic ties last week.
For IAI, Morocco is already a major customer. The company signed a $500 million deal with Morocco for the Barak MX air-defense system, adding a major Israeli layer to the kingdom’s air-defense architecture. The system was jointly developed in close collaboration between India’s Defense Research and Development Organization (DRDO) and IAI’s RAFAEL ELTA Systems.
The versatile system can fire three types of missiles from the same vertical launcher, including the Barak MRAD for short-to-medium range of up to 35 kilometers, the Barak LRAD of up to 70 km., and the Barak ER, which can reach targets up to 150 km.
IAI has also been linked to a much larger space deal. In 2024, the company disclosed a $1 billion contract with an unnamed customer to be executed over five years. While neither IAI nor Marrakesh commented on the report, Reuters said at the time that Moroccan media had identified Morocco as the customer for an Ofek 13 reconnaissance satellite, which would replace Morocco’s existing satellites supplied by France’s Airbus and Thales.
IAI’s Moroccan footprint has also expanded through BlueBird Aero Systems, its unmanned-systems subsidiary. In 2025, the company opened a factory to produce SpyX loitering munitions, the first time advanced Israeli drone technology will be produced locally in North Africa.
The plant in Benslimane, Morocco, will focus on producing SpyX drones, which are lightweight, portable loitering munitions designed for precision strikes. With an endurance of two hours and a range of 50 km., these drones can carry a variety of warheads of up to 2.5 kilograms and enable tactical teams to detect, confirm, and strike targets.
Rabat has also purchased Elbit Systems’ ATMOS Howitzer and Elbit’s EXTRA rockets (cost-effective, precise, and with a range of up to 150 km. and an accuracy of 10 meters CEP), among others.
In addition to IAI’s Barak system, Rafael’s Spyder surface-to-air missile system has been deployed to the Sidi Yahia El Gharb military base outside of the capital.
The French connection
The deals between Israel and Morocco - as well as the strong Israeli presence at the Marrakesh Air Show - illustrate the scale of the competition now emerging between Israeli and French defense industries.
France remains deeply embedded in Morocco’s aerospace and defense ecosystem, with French companies, including Airbus, Thales, Safran, and Dassault, having long supplied the kingdom. But Israeli companies are now moving into the market as Morocco expands its requirements.
The companies set to display in Marrakesh also reflect where Morocco’s defense requirements are moving. Alongside traditional aerospace products, the Israeli companies are showcasing integrated air defense, long-range precision strike, unmanned systems, collaborative combat, and space-based capabilities.
The Israeli push in Morocco comes against a complicated backdrop in relations between the Israeli defense industry and France. French authorities excluded Israeli defense companies from the 2024 Eurosatory exhibition and 2025 Paris Airshow. The French Defence Ministry publicly said that conditions were not appropriate for their participation due to the war in Gaza and Lebanon, though Israeli officials criticized the move and blamed it on competition.
The same Israeli companies blocked from exhibiting their systems in France are now preparing to display many of the same categories of capabilities at the Marrakesh airshow, this time geared toward a market where French companies remain major players and where Israeli companies will not be blocked by large black walls like in Paris.

Turkish Cypriot leader heads to New York with call for results-oriented talks

Turkish Cypriot President Tufan Erhürman (IHA Photo)
Turkish Cypriot President Tufan Erhürman said on Sept. 22 that any new round of negotiations on the Cyprus dispute should be aimed at achieving a settlement rather than simply restarting talks, ahead of meetings with senior U.N. officials in New York.
Erhürman is scheduled to travel to New York on Sept. 23 to meet separately with U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and his Personal Envoy for Cyprus, Maria Angela Holguin.
The meetings are expected to address efforts to revive negotiations on the decades-old division of the island.
“We do not believe in holding a 5+1 meeting simply for the sake of holding one, nor negotiations simply for the sake of negotiations,” Erhürman said.
He stressed that the Turkish Cypriot side wants a 5+1 meeting to be preceded by progress in Nicosia that would improve its chances of producing concrete results, adding that any renewed negotiations
should ultimately lead to a settlement in line with the Turkish Cypriot community’s desire for a solution.
The 5+1 format includes the Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot sides, the three guarantor countries, Türkiye, Greece and Britain, and the United Nations.
Erhürman said progress should first be made in three areas highlighted by Guterres: Confidence-building measures, the methodology of negotiations and substantive issues.
Measures currently under consideration include opening additional crossing points between the two sides, carrying out demining efforts, cooperating on disaster response and irregular migration, and creating joint mechanisms involving sports and civil society.
