Iran, US diplomatic signals raise hopes for renewed peace talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:38:00 UTC
20:38:00 KST

Senior Iran and United States officials made diplomatic overtures Tuesday, raising hopes for a renewed talks to the Middle East conflict.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz to Gulf shipping within days if the U.S. lifts its blockade, describing a gathering at the U.N. as a "golden opportunity" to renew diplomacy with Washington.
U.S. President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian are both due to attend the U.N. General Assembly in New York, the first time they will be at the same event since Trump launched "Operation Epic Fury" against Iran in February.
The Iranian official said Iran's delegation had full authority to revive talks, although no direct meetings between the two presidents were planned.
No face-to-face meetings between Iran and the United States are known to have taken place since July, when an agreement on an interim deal to end the war collapsed just weeks after it was signed by Trump and Pezeshkian.
"The U.S. needs to announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official and then agree on a timeline for how the process will move forward," the Iranian official said.
"The U.N. General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the U.S. to return to diplomacy," the official said. He said Iran had sent its latest proposal to Washington via mediators on Sept. 16.
Meanwhile, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told NBC's "Today" show the U.S. was open to speaking with the Iranians at the General Assembly.
"We're open to that. I don't think anything is scheduled at this point, but we're certainly open to something like that, especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about," Rubio said.
"And that is the fact that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. They just simply can't."
Trump is due to meet Tuesday with the leaders of the six Gulf Arab states: Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.
The Gulf countries are keen to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz but wary of giving their longstanding rival Iran too much power.
All apart from Oman host huge U.S. military bases that have come under repeated Iranian attack throughout the war, which has strained their decades-old security partnerships with Washington.
The biggest of them, Saudi Arabia, has been drawn deeper into the war this month, with Iran-backed Houthi rebels advancing in Yemen, routing forces of a Saudi-backed government there and threatening Saudi oil exports through the Red Sea.
There was some relief on oil markets Tuesday, after sources told Reuters that Saudi Arabia had restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline and could resume exports within hours, albeit at reduced volume, from the Red Sea port of Yanbu.
The pipeline, Saudi Arabia's main alternative route for exports to bypass wartime disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, was shut down after attacks on Sept. 10 that Riyadh blamed on Iranian allies in Iraq.
The Houthis have pushed back Saudi-supported government forces with the aim of controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the southern mouth of the Red Sea and have attacked Saudi Arabia directly with missiles and drones.
The U.S., which bombed the Houthis for two months last year, has so far rebuffed repeated pleas from Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to rejoin the fight against the group.
The New York Times reported that Trump called off U.S. strikes against the Houthis Sunday at the last minute, after troops had already begun loading bombs onto planes.
On the table at the Gulf states' meeting with Trump is a Qatari proposal for a framework to bring Iran and the Arab Gulf states into a common security architecture, regional sources said.
Speaking at a Qatar Economic Forum in New York on Sunday, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani said any such arrangement would need to provide security guarantees for the Gulf states and expand economic interdependence with Iran.
"Lasting security cannot be built through repeated cycles of escalations and retaliation, or arrangements that leave any state permanently exposed to insecurity," Sheikh Mohammed said.
Another source in the region told Reuters Iran was reviewing the proposal.
Houthi fighters in Yemen are pushing to seize the strategic heights of the Kahboub Mountains to cut off the Red Sea coast from remaining areas held by Saudi-backed forces.
The area of Kahboub overlooks the western coastline and Bab el-Mandeb, and would provide a commanding position from which the Houthis could seek to exert greater control over both.
Its rugged landscape also makes it easier for Houthi fighters to remain concealed from drones and air strikes than on the coastal plain.
The fighting has already displaced more than 130,000 people this month and the U.N. refugee agency said Tuesday that tens of thousands more people could be driven from their homes.

Rosneft Launches Commercial Crude Deliveries From Massive Arctic Vostok Oil Cluster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

20:35:53 KST

- Category
- World
Rosneft Launches Commercial Crude Deliveries From Massive Arctic Vostok Oil Cluster
Russia has commenced commercial crude exports from its “Vostok Oil” development in the Arctic, marking the launch of the country’s largest new oil project since the collapse of the Soviet Union, The Moscow Times reported on September 21.
State-owned oil giant Rosneft began loading four specialized ice-class tankers at the newly built Sever Bay terminal on the Taymyr Peninsula. Overseen directly by Rosneft CEO Igor Sechin, the Vostok Oil cluster unites more than 13 fields across Eastern Siberia and Taymyr, holding an estimated 51 billion barrels of oil reserves—accounting for roughly one-fifth of Russia’s total explored deposits.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Through a campaign of deep-strike drone attacks against Russian energy infrastructure, Ukraine had knocked out roughly a quarter of Russia’s refining capacity, forcing Moscow to enact internal export bans and rely on state subsidies to shield domestic drivers from mounting fuel shortages.
Initial export volumes at “Vostok Oil” development are launching at a modest 150,000 barrels per day (bpd), a figure significantly below Rosneft’s initial ambitions, The Moscow Times wrote. The project faced years of delays after major international backers—including BP, Trafigura, and Vitol—exited the venture following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine and the imposition of Western sanctions.
To keep the project moving independently, Rosneft secured 2.6 trillion rubles ($30 billion) in state tax relief. Rosneft now aims to expand export capacity to 600,000 bpd (30 million metric tons annually) in the second half of 2027, with a long-term goal of reaching 1 million bpd by 2030.
Following a formal launch announcement by Russian leader Vladimir Putin on September 5, vessel-tracking records confirmed that the Aframax tanker Akademik Gubkin and Panamax tanker Valentin Pikul loaded initial cargoes at Sever Bay, with two additional Aframax vessels—Vladimir Monomakh and Vladimir Vinogradov—scheduled for loading.
While the extreme geography of the High Arctic originally presented severe logistical hurdles, the project’s remote location has evolved into a key strategic asset, The Moscow Times noted.
Positioned thousands of kilometers away from Ukrainian deep-strike operations, the Sever Bay terminal provides Moscow with a secure maritime corridor to export crude directly to Asian markets via the Northern Sea Route, bypassing increasingly vulnerable processing facilities and ports in the Black and Baltic Seas, according to The Moscow Times.
A recent retaliatory long-range Ukrainian drone strike forced Moscow’s primary oil processing facility into a complete operational shutdown. The attack targeted the Gazprom Neft-owned plant, striking its AVT-6 distillation unit and EURO+ combined processing unit, which together account for 100% of the facility’s 230,000-barrel-per-day refining capacity.

Trump-GCC Summit in New York: What does each side want?
Trump will meet with leaders from Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait and Oman on the sidelines of UNGA.
Leaders of the six Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) states are set to meet United States President Donald Trump in New York on Tuesday, as the US-Israel war on Iran nears seven months.
The meeting, to be held on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), brings together countries that have borne much of the fallout from a war they did not start.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Mapping Iran war’s strikes on Gulf energy and its impact on future of oil
- list 2 of 4Iran says US bombed a wedding party in Sirik, killing at least four people
- list 3 of 4What is Jordan’s Al-Azraq base and why is Iran targeting it?
- list 4 of 4Iran and Gulf states to discuss Strait of Hormuz in Oman on Monday
Since the war began on February 28, Iran has repeatedly struck US bases across the Middle East as well as airports, energy facilities and hotels. The war has particularly hit the Gulf nations hard, as their oil and gas exports – the mainstay of their economies – have been disrupted, causing a global energy crisis.
A June memorandum of understanding (MoU) briefly raised hopes of an end to the war, but it collapsed last month amid disputes over navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, which remains effectively closed.
These talks come as Trump says he faces a “big decision” on the war, and as Iran’s president and foreign minister are also in New York for the UNGA.
So what is on the table and what might come out of the talks? Here is all you need to know:
What do we know about the GCC-Trump meeting?
Trump is set to meet the leaders from Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, which form the GCC, on the sidelines of the UNGA.
Trump told US media outlet Axios on Thursday that he wanted to meet the GCC leaders as he faced a “big decision” on the war and wanted to speak with them directly.
Experts say there are two interconnected issues – the US-Israel war on Iran and the conflict between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government forces in Yemen.
What do the GCC countries want from the meeting?
Broadly, experts say, the GCC nations share a common goal for the meeting.
The GCC has “shared positions on the main principles of regional security and de-escalation”, Luciano Zaccara, a researcher with the New Ground Research think tank in Doha, Qatar, told Al Jazeera.
“With Trump recently threatening to ‘wipe out’ Iran, I expect the six GCC states, or at least most of them, to convey to the US president their grave concerns about the likely consequences of another round of intense US military strikes on Iran,” Giorgio Cafiero, CEO of Gulf State Analytics, told Al Jazeera.
“They will probably seek to underscore their own vulnerabilities to a renewed cycle of all-out fighting between the United States and Iran,” he said, adding that they will try to persuade Trump into making certain concessions to Tehran.
Cafiero said they will look to develop an arrangement that builds on the MoU and which “offers the most viable path toward winding down the crisis”.
Chief among their common concerns is freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, according to Ahmed Helal, managing director for the Gulf region at The Asia Group.
‘Divergent’ goals
Despite common goals, the Gulf states have still experienced “divergent” outcomes from the war and will also look to persuade Trump to address their particular predicaments, Helal said.
The UAE, he explained, has been able to keep exporting oil by pipeline to its port of Fujairah, which bypasses the Strait of Hormuz, although not at the volumes it would like.
But fellow GCC member Qatar, whose gas exports depend on the strait, has seen its LNG shipments severely curtailed and wants to avoid any renewed escalation that could see its energy infrastructure targeted again, Helal said.
Speaking at an event in New York, US, on Sunday, Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani described the economic fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran as an “earthquake”.
Saudi Arabia has another problem, as it is now under “enormous pressure” as the Houthis gain ground in Yemen, and has been “intensifying their lobbying” for US strikes on the group, he said.
What does Trump want from the meeting?
Predicting what the US president plans has been difficult since the outbreak of the US-Israel war on Iran, experts say.
“It could be possible that the US is expecting a more direct GCC engagement against Iran in exchange for a direct US intervention to stop the Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, but without the GCC leaving the main role in defending themselves”, Zaccara told Al Jazeera.
“Regarding Iran, Trump has not ruled out another major military escalation. At the same time, the administration seems to be open to exploring diplomatic options,” he said, adding there are rumours of a possible indirect US-Iran meeting on the sidelines before Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s speech on Wednesday.
Helal said the administration’s focus is domestic, with the midterm elections weeks away and Trump’s approval ratings at a record low; there is “immense pressure” to lower petrol prices.
While Trump has threatened further military action, he remains politically sensitive to an “escalatory ladder” that could spike oil prices, Helal said.
The talks are unlikely to produce a breakthrough, he added, with the best-case scenario an agreement to return to negotiations potentially brokered by Qatar or Pakistan.

Settlement sanctions are a start. Ending EU complicity is key
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:32:31 UTC
20:32:31 KST

Breadcrumb
Settlement sanctions are a start. Ending EU complicity is key
The UK and eleven other countries issued a joint statement expressing their intention to sanction Israel’s expanding illegal settlements in the West Bank. But before we celebrate too loudly, it's worth asking what this statement actually changes on the ground and what it conveniently leaves out.
After decades of near‑total Western silence, accompanied by political, economic, and military support that enabled settlement expansion, a joint statement from 12 European and Western governments is significant. It recognises years of public pressure, institutional mobilisation, and BDS work. But “overdue” is the operative word here.
For years, the international community watched settlements metastasise across the West Bank while issuing calls for “restraint” or expressing “concern.”
Between 2023 and 2025, the Israeli government advanced plans for 50,785 new settlement housing units, according to Peace Now. In 2025 alone, the Higher Planning Council approved 27,941 units, the highest annual figure on record.
By the end of April 2026, Israeli settlers had established 363 outposts in the occupied West Bank; more than 58% were created under the 37th government. This construction surge has coincided with widespread Palestinian home demolitions and severe restrictions on Palestinian building
The value of intentions?
The governments’ statement confirms only an “intention” to introduce national measures and/or back European trade restrictions on goods. However, intention is not action; it means whatever follows will also not be immediate.
Bulldozers do not wait for diplomatic intentions to be enforced on the ground. Each day of deliberation buys another month for outposts to become settlements, and for settlements to become permanent facts on the ground, at the expense of Palestinian land and lives.
Belgium, Ireland, and a handful of other states have passed national measures restricting trade with the settlements. That sounds like progress, but it isn't.
Take Ireland's Occupied Territories Bill. It bans goods from Israeli settlements, but says nothing about services. Belgium's ban follows the same pattern: it restricts goods, not services, and leaves exports entirely alone.
Compare that to what the law actually requires. The ICJ's July 2024 advisory opinion is clear: all trade in settlement goods and services - every import, every export - must end. Not be curtailed. Not be managed. Not be rebranded. The settlements themselves must be dismantled, and their inhabitants evacuated, not administered more gently.
What’s really illegal
Article 49(6) of the Fourth Geneva Convention exists for one reason: to stop an occupying power from re-engineering the demographics of the territory it occupies. Israel's presence in the territories under its control has violated that principle for decades.
The throughline is visible across over 78 years. The 1948 Nakba, which displaced more than 700,000 Palestinians; the 1976 Naksa that displaced over 300.000 Palestinians, the ongoing expansion of settlements in the West Bank and East Jerusalem; the 1981 annexation of the Golan Heights; the continued military presence in southern Lebanon; and now the genocide in Gaza, which has killed over 73,000 Palestinians, brought roughly 70% of the territory under Israeli military control, and displaced more than 1.9 million people.
These are not isolated violations. They reflect a consistent pattern grounded in a logic of elimination and a sustained effort to replace an indigenous population, not merely to govern or extract from it.
This isn't a matter of opinion. It's the same legal framework that Western governments themselves created, just applied selectively when convenient.
If international law is the standard, it must apply consistently. Not only to the violations that are politically easy to name, and not only where naming them carries no economic cost.
Most of the diplomatic energy poured into this issue goes toward preserving the viability of a two-state solution. But that's not the international community's call to make. Its actual obligation is to end complicity in the occupation and let the occupied population in Palestine determine its own political future, on its own terms.
Outsiders don't get to design the outcome. They must stop standing in its way by ending their complicity, and respect colonised people’s right to self-determination.
An infrastructure of complicity
Settlements are often discussed as though they're the work of a rogue fringe acting outside state policy, but this is evidently not the case. Settlers operate with the economic, financial, and military backing of the Israeli state.
Framing settlement expansion as a private, grassroots phenomenon rather than a matter of state policy is itself a political strategy. A settler-colonial project cannot run on individual initiative alone; it depends on infrastructure, funding, and armed protection.
In 2023, the Israeli government allocated $1.1 billion to the Ministry of Transport to upgrade and develop roads that settlers use in the West Bank. In December 2025, the government approved the plan to strengthen and develop settlements and related infrastructure, with a budget of around $919 million.
The government has also directly funded and equipped unauthorised outposts. In 2023, it provided roughly $8 million to 68 settler herding outposts and 33 additional outposts.
In response to the governments’ statement, the EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, welcomed the step and highlighted the EU's role as the largest humanitarian donor to Gaza and the West Bank, a territory now increasingly referred to, diplomatically, as "the State of Palestine".
That funding is real, but it doesn't cancel out complicity. The EU remains Israel's largest trading partner, a relationship underwritten by the EU-Israel Association Agreement.
Several European states, including the UK and Belgium, continue to host arms manufacturing tied to Israel's military industry. And dual EU-Israeli citizens who are members of the Israeli army implicated in war crimes and crimes against humanity can travel in and out of the EU freely, facing no consequences there.
None of this is a radical demand from Palestinians and the solidarity movement in Europe. The European Citizens' Initiative Justice for Palestine, signed by over a million Europeans, calls on the European Commission and member states to invoke Article 2 of the EU-Israel Association Agreement — the clause that makes the relationship conditional on respect for human rights and democratic values.
The clause already exists. The violations are already documented, including by the EU's own investigations. What's missing is enforcement of EU and international law.
Settlement sanctions cannot be allowed to serve as a symbolic gesture that condemns the settlements while leaving intact the very agreement that enables business as usual, including continued political cooperation, trade, energy links, and research partnerships.
As world leaders continue to force us to watch a genocide unfold before our eyes, it matters that we acknowledge and celebrate victories. But those victories also remind us that organised, strategic work can't be let off the hook just because its influence looks small or slow to arrive.
These bans didn't happen on their own; they happened because people organised, showed up, and refused to let their governments look away. Even when they were exhausted, worn down, and felt like nothing was moving, they have kept going.
Tamam Abusalama is a Palestinian-Belgian communications professional, born and raised in the Jabalia Refugee Camp. She is currently leading the strategy for the European Citizens’ Initiative Justice for Palestine, which calls for the full suspension of the EU-Israel Association Agreement.

Only 22% of Russian gold consumed domestically

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. Domestic consumption of gold produced in Russia accounts for 22% of the country’s total annual gold output, according to a presentation by Sergey Kashuba, Chairman of the Russian Union of Gold Producers.
The presentation also noted that 78% of gold produced in Russia is exported, making exports the industry’s main sales channel. At the same time, the geography of exports is narrowing: Turkey has sharply reduced purchases, shipments to the UAE have declined following the military conflict in the Persian Gulf, India has reinstated duties on gold bullion, and European Union countries continue to impose sanctions on gold mining companies.
The presentation also said that gold production has increased by 87.8% over the past 15 years, while domestic demand for gold has risen by only 9%.

EU in showdown over Russian oligarch sanctions as deadline nears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:32:28 UTC
20:32:28 KST

Uzbek-born Russian businessman Alisher Usmanov attends the Congress of the Russian Union of Industrialists and Entrepreneurs in Moscow on March 26, 2026 (AFP Photo)
EU countries on Sept. 22 resumed their scramble for an agreement on prolonging sanctions on Russia, after Latvia held up a deal to take two oligarchs off the blacklist.
The 27-nation bloc had looked set to remove asset freezes and visa bans from Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman after demands from France, Luxembourg and Slovakia.
The move — slammed by Kiev — was part of a compromise to extend sanctions on almost 3,000 other individuals and companies over the Ukraine war for three more years, before a deadline that could see them lapse at 2200 GMT on Sept. 22.
But that agreement hit an obstacle at the finishing line when Latvia lodged a last-ditch objection late on Sept. 21.
"The Latvian government's stance has been unwavering. EU sanctions against Russia must be strengthened, not weakened," Foreign Minister Baiba Braze wrote online.
EU diplomats said after an early morning meeting that the deal involving the oligarchs remained on the table and that ambassadors could reconvene after 1200 GMT if it was rejected again.
Diplomats have been haggling for days over a way forward after France joined Slovakia in demanding Russian-Uzbek billionaire Usmanov to be removed from the blacklist.
Luxembourg then seized upon the demand by Paris to insist that if sanctions were lifted on Usmanov, then they should be lifted for Fridman as well.
Officials in Paris have cited "national security" concerns for their request on Usmanov, but refused publicly to give details.
A senior diplomat in Brussels told AFP that Paris explained the demand was linked to a potential prisoner release deal involving French nationals held in Azerbaijan.
Luxembourg has pushed for Fridman to be removed. Diplomats said the move comes as he is suing the country for 15 billion euros ($17 billion) for freezing his assets under EU sanctions.
The demand from France in particular has riled other EU member states who argue that removing people for political reasons sets a dangerous precedent.
"It really sends the signal that you can blackmail your way to delisting," said one EU diplomat talking on condition of anonymity.
"It's shocking that France is the one blocking it all."
EU diplomats insist there is widespread agreement that the bloc's sanctions should not be allowed to lapse — and a temporary extension could be agreed if no deal is reached on Sept. 22.
But the Kremlin seized on the EU's standoff to demand that the EU lift sanctions on "all Russian businessmen".
Ukraine has reacted furiously to the prospect of the EU removing sanctions on the two prominent Russian businessmen seen as close to the Kremlin.
"Delisting is unacceptable and would send the wrong signal to Moscow at a time when pressure needs to increase," Ukraine's foreign minister Andriy Sybiga wrote online.
EU top diplomat Kaja Kallas urged the bloc's member states on Sept. 21 to maintain the sanctions imposed on Moscow.
"Sanctions are a core pillar of our response to Russia's war", she told reporters in New York after a meeting of EU foreign ministers.
"We need to have this stability," with sanctions remaining in place for a longer time, Kallas added.
As an offering to those opposed to the delisting move, the compromise deal on offer in Brussels would see the sanctions remain in place for the next three years — as opposed to the previous extensions of six months each.
The EU's sanctions blacklist includes key figures such as Russian President Vladimir Putin and Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov.
Metals tycoon Usmanov and banking magnate Fridman are among dozens of Russian businessmen suing the EU over the sanctions.
Both were added to the sanctions list shortly after Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022 over allegations that their businesses provided significant revenues to the Kremlin.

People living in Chad’s Lake Province are bearing the brunt of climate change. The region and the communities that have developed there have historically depended on this vast body of water. Autonomous trucking company Aurora looks to accelerate toward profitability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:30:01 UTC
20:30:01 KST

Take a drive in Texas on Interstate 45 between Houston and Dallas or I-20 between Fort Worth and El Paso, and you will see dozens and dozens of tractor trailers. They are two of the busiest highways in the country for trucks — and two routes where Aurora Innovation is operating completely autonomous semis.
"It's using lasers, radar, and cameras to look all around it and see the other cars, see the other trucks on the road, and figure out how to drive safely," said Chris Urmson, Aurora founder and CEO. He talked with CNBC's Phil LeBeau for more than three hours as they rode in the cab of an autonomous Aurora truck.
With 20 driverless trucks currently on the road and plans to grow the autonomous fleet to 200 trucks by the end of this year, Aurora is targeting major growth over the next several years. The company's selling point is that it says an autonomous truck can operate more efficiently and at a lower cost than a semi with a driver behind the wheel.
"We can help them [truck operators] save on fuel economy," Urmson said. "We can move goods more quickly and then we can fill the need when they can't hire amazing drivers for their teams."
Ravi Shanker, transportation analyst with Morgan Stanley, estimates that "an autonomous fleet should be nearly 7.5X as profitable as a human-driven fleet today."
Bank of America, meanwhile, estimates "Aurora services will cost ~$0.85 per mile versus approximately $1.30 per mile for human driver wages and benefits, before considering indirect labour costs."
With its next generation of driverless trucks to hit the road, Aurora believes its "driver as a service" business model, where customers pay by the mile driven, will be attractive to shipping and freight customers looking to lower costs.
A shortage of truck drivers in the U.S. has freight firms looking for reliable service at a lower cost. Autonomous trucks have the potential to roll for up to 20 hours a day, while a truck driver's hours are limited by federal laws that require drivers to take breaks.
Sean Wu, CEO of the online shipping marketplace uShip, said he understands the appeal of a driverless truck when it comes to lowering costs, but he questions how many shipping firms will want to ditch their drivers.
"The drivers do more than just move the rig. There is judgement. There is customer service. There is protection," Wu told CNBC. "There is just a lot more to think about than 'Hey they are moving a truck from point A to point B.'"
The Department of Transportation estimates there are approximately 3.5 million Class 8 semitrucks on the road in the U.S. Only a fraction are autonomous, but the market is growing, and Wall Street sees huge potential. Kodiak AI, Gatik and Tesla are also developing autonomous vehicles.
Aurora CEO Urmson said he knows there are plenty of skeptics, including those who will continue to question the safety of a driverless truck rolling down the highway at 65 or 70 mph.
"We've got millions of miles of experience," he said. "We put this through 15 million tests before we put it out on the road."
As we completed our freight run in Palmer, Texas, what stood out was the fact the ride was uneventful with no disruptions. The truck pulled off the highway once for less than a minute to reset the hazard lights which had come on for some unknown reason. Otherwise, over the course of three hours on I-45, we saw more than a few double takes from truck drivers passing by who looked twice when they saw nobody behind the wheel.
For Urmson, it is another 200 miles where Aurora's autonomous driving technology has delivered a shipment. Since it began testing its AV technology on public roads in 2022, Aurora has logged more than 440,000 miles. Most of those included a human safety operator behind the wheel in case the technology failed.
After losing more than $800 million in 2025, Aurora is targeting positive free cash flow by 2028, driven by a substantial increase in the number autonomous trucks on the road.
"We've been able to put out timelines and we've basically hit those timelines," he said.

GoPro Mission 1 Pro ILS Review (2026): Cinema-Quality Action Cam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

For example, GoPro sent a Laowa 7.5-mm lens for me to test with. When HyperSmooth is on, that's the equivalent of shooting with a 23-mm lens on a full-frame camera. With HyperSmooth off, it becomes a 20-mm lens. I bring this up mainly because if you want to go really wide on the ILS, you'll need a very, very wide lens (fisheye lenses are probably your best bet).
Now for the downside to the ILS: There are no electrical contacts, which means lenses that rely on electronic focus or aperture control probably won't work. For example, my all-time favorite MFT lens, Panasonic's original 20-mm pancake, won't work on the ILS because there's no manual aperture ring.
Your best bet is to stick with fully manual lenses that have a mechanical aperture ring. There aren't many, but there are enough with quality glass to cover a good range of focal lengths. GoPro's Abe Kislevitz put together a nice collection of lenses that he has tested with the Mission 1 Pro ILS, along with his recommendations for various shooting scenarios. Be aware that the camera is sold body-only, and so far, we haven't seen any bundles from GoPro or resellers that include a lens.
And yes, you have to manually focus. I could drop some jokes here about kids today not knowing how to do it, but the truth is, I shoot vintage manual-focus lenses all the time on my Sony A7R II. While I've shot sports and wildlife with these lenses and had a pretty high success rate, I struggled to focus on the ILS.
The problem with focusing on the ILS is the small screen. It's hard to see, not just in bright daylight. It's just really small. There is focus peaking, which uses color banding to indicate what's in focus, but it can be hard to see exactly where it ends, and I've learned from my Sony not to fully rely on peaking.
You can zoom in to get very precise focus, which is what I do on the Sony, but again the small screen makes it hard to see. Worse, for filmmakers especially, you have to have the camera at eye level to focus it well, which limits your shooting ability (or you get to contort into all sorts of weird poses). I would love to see the next Mission 1 Pro ILS get a tilting screen; it's not waterproof anyway, so it doesn't seem like there would be a need to reengineer. GoPro no doubt would suggest using the app on my phone, as it does make it considerably easier to focus, but then you need a cage, and then a handle, and at that point most of the Mission 1 Pro ILS' size advantage is gone; you might as well get a Panasonic GH7, which has an even larger sensor.
Ultimately, while focusing on the small screen is challenging, using a phone or other external monitor sidesteps that issue (and is what pro filmmakers do anyway), but the inability to control the lens iris electronically feels like a bigger limitation since it eliminates a significant number of lenses. It would be nice to see a future Mission 1 Pro ILS support at least electronic connectors for aperture and manual focusing on lenses that require it.
Shooting With the Mission 1 Pro ILS
Once you get past the hurdle of manual focusing, there's a lot to love about the ILS footage. Testing it reminded me more than anything of the Blackmagic Pocket Cinema Camera from several years ago. I can't believe this tiny little thing can match the quality of those early Blackmagic cameras.

The leaders of Denmark, Greenland and the United States are expected to sign a security and defense agreement concerning Greenland on Tuesday.
The ceremony is scheduled for 10:30 a.m. local time, or 4:30 p.m. Danish time, at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office described it as “a joint agreement that strengthens security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic region.”
The agreement will be signed by Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Jens-Frederik Nielsen, head of Naalakkersuisut, Greenland’s government.
Few details about the agreement have been released since it was announced Friday.
Trump said on Truth Social that the agreement gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen has said the agreement recognizes the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom of Denmark, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We are not ceding sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I never will as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told Danish broadcasters DR and TV 2 on Monday.
She said sovereignty could be maintained alongside closer defense cooperation with other countries.
The USA plans to reopen a former military base in Narsarsuaq in southern Greenland and establish a military presence on Greenland’s east coast, Reuters reported Monday.
The eastern site is currently used by the Sirius Dog Sled Patrol, a Danish military unit operating in Greenland.
Reuters attributed the information to three unnamed sources familiar with a defense agreement involving Greenland, Denmark and the USA. Danish public broadcaster DR also reported that the USA plans two new bases.
The agreement’s text has not been published, and its details may change before it is signed, Reuters reported.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, US President Donald Trump and Greenlandic head of government Jens-Frederik Nielsen are expected to sign the agreement Tuesday at the United Nations headquarters in New York.
The Danish Prime Minister’s Office said the agreement would strengthen security in the Arctic and North Atlantic.
Trump has said it gives the USA “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Frederiksen of the Social Democrats said the agreement recognizes the Kingdom of Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as Greenlanders’ right to self-determination.
“We do not surrender sovereignty, and I can give a guarantee that I will never do that as Danish prime minister,” Frederiksen told DR and Danish broadcaster TV 2.
More than 20 percent of Nordic teenagers drink energy drinks at least once a day, according to a survey of 4,916 people ages 15 to 19.
The study covered Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden. Six in 10 respondents drank energy drinks at least weekly.
Almost half said they could not get through the day without an energy drink or sometimes felt that way.
The report found that 46 percent began drinking energy drinks at age 14 or younger. One in 10 started before age 12.
Among those who consumed the drinks, 30 percent reported feeling unwell or experiencing other negative health effects. Heart palpitations and sleep problems were among the most common complaints.
“When a habit begins to affect sleep, well-being, or everyday life, there is reason to act,” said Sabina Litens Karlsson, a toxicologist at Livsmedelsverket, Sweden’s national food authority, which conducted the study.
Taste was cited by 73 percent of consumers, while 51 percent wanted more energy and 34 percent wanted to stay awake.
Weekly consumption was highest in Sweden at 75 percent and lowest in Denmark at 43 percent.
Norway has banned sales to people under 16. Denmark has no legal age limit, but its food authority advises children under 15 not to consume energy drinks.
Denmark now expects to complete the final compensation cases for the mink industry in the third quarter of 2028, at least six months later than previously planned.
The Danish Civil Aviation and Railway Authority disclosed the delay in a briefing shared with the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“The decisions on compensation have unfortunately proven to be more time-consuming than assumed,” said Transport and Rural Affairs Minister Signe Munk of the Socialist People’s Party.
The authority previously expected the final cases to be completed during 2027.
The delay is linked to European Commission approval for state aid, which expires on April 1 and cannot be extended.
Officials must prioritize partial decisions determining whether applicants qualify for compensation before that deadline. Two teams have been reassigned to the Mink Secretariat unit preparing those decisions, leaving fewer employees to complete final compensation awards.
The delay could add about 40 million DKK in costs, the authority estimated.
At the beginning of 2026, the total expected cost of compensation, farm demolitions and administration was 29.1 billion DKK.
Denmark ordered all 15 million farmed mink killed in November 2020 over concerns about a mutated coronavirus.
When lawmakers agreed on compensation in 2021, the total bill was expected to be between 15.6 billion DKK and 18.8 billion DKK.
Shares in several companies operating in Greenland rose sharply after reports that Denmark, Greenland and the United States are close to an agreement concerning the Arctic territory, TV 2 reports.
Greenland Energy, which extracts oil and gas, rose 135 percent in US trading. Greenland Mines gained 148 percent.
Both companies had lost more than 80 percent of their market value before Monday’s increases.
Critical Metals Corp., which extracts rare earth minerals in Greenland, rose 34 percent.
The increases followed indications that Greenland, Denmark and the United States had reached or were close to reaching an agreement. Its details have not been made public.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats and Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates have traveled to the United States.
They are expected to take part in the signing of an agreement involving Denmark, Greenland and the United States during the week.
The three governments have said the planned agreement is intended to strengthen security cooperation in Greenland, the Arctic and the North Atlantic.
Seven emergency medical vehicles in Denmark’s Central Denmark Region will begin using direct blood pressure monitoring during cardiopulmonary resuscitation, or CPR.
The regional prehospital emergency service said the method could help staff adjust chest compressions and improve survival after cardiac arrests outside hospitals.
“With blood pressure measurements, we get a better idea of whether the cardiopulmonary resuscitation sufficiently drives the blood around the body, or whether we need to adjust and adapt the chest compressions,” emergency doctor Jesper Fjølner said.
Fjølner, who developed the project, said the method had already contributed to successful resuscitation in several cases.
The procedure, called invasive blood pressure measurement, involves placing a catheter with a monitor into an artery. Hospitals already use it to monitor patients in operating rooms and intensive care units.
Using the method outside a hospital is more complex and requires training, equipment and experience.
Chief physician Allan Bach said the service expects the procedure to help resuscitate more people without reducing patient safety or the quality of CPR.
The European Resuscitation Council, which prepares European guidelines for cardiac arrest treatment, recently recommended the method. The Central Denmark service said it is among the first in the world to introduce it.
About 5,000 people experience cardiac arrest outside hospitals in Denmark each year. Around 15 percent survive.
Diabetes patients taking a low dose of Novo’s experimental drug Cagrisema lost more weight than those taking a low dose of Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide in a new study.
Patients receiving 1 milligram of Cagrisema lost an average of 12.4 percent of their weight over 60 weeks, Danish pharmaceutical company Novo said.
Those receiving 5 milligrams of tirzepatide lost 9.1 percent during the same period. Tirzepatide is the active ingredient in Eli Lilly’s approved weight-loss drug Zepbound.
Cagrisema has not been approved. Novo expects the US Food and Drug Administration to decide on its application near the end of 2026.
The treatment combines semaglutide, the active ingredient in Novo’s Wegovy, with a newer substance called cagrilintide. Novo hopes the combination can produce greater weight loss than semaglutide alone.
Results from another study released in February favored tirzepatide. Participants taking tirzepatide lost 25.5 percent of their weight over 84 weeks, compared with 23 percent for those receiving Cagrisema.
Novo shares fell more than 16 percent after those earlier results.
The company released the new findings during its capital markets day. Novo shares were down more than five percent around 1:15 p.m. Monday, and the announcement did not significantly change the share price.
Drivers using Denmark’s Vejlefjord Bridge should expect daily queues and longer travel times while two expansion joints are replaced, the Danish Road Directorate said.
Preparation work will take place during the final two weeks of September. The main repairs will run from early October until early November, with work continuing seven days a week.
Two of the bridge’s five expansion joints in the southbound lanes will be replaced.
Expansion joints are movable sections that allow a bridge to expand and contract as temperatures change. The joints have repeatedly caused problems in recent years, leading to emergency repairs, delays and traffic queues.
The Road Directorate, the Danish government agency responsible for national roads, expects the work to reduce the need for emergency repairs in the near future.
Almost 100,000 vehicles cross the nearly 50-year-old bridge each day.
“When we take lanes for a work area, and road users only have one lane in each direction, queues will occur,” project manager Allan Højgaard Madsen said.
Queues are expected in both directions from about 7 p.m. and for several hours afterward throughout the repair period.
Morning and afternoon rush-hour traffic is expected to face delays only in the southbound direction.

Most Danes want the government to temporarily cut taxes on gasoline and diesel as fuel prices reach unusually high levels, a Voxmeter poll for the Danish news agency Ritzau shows.
In September, diesel reached a record 19.19 DKK per liter at gas stations.
The poll found that 53.8 percent supported temporary tax cuts, while 33.3 percent opposed them. Another 12.9 percent did not know.
Torben Kudsk, policy chief at FDM, Denmark’s main car owners’ organization, said rising prices were creating serious problems for motorists.
“Fuel is historically expensive. As far as we can see, prices have not been higher in recent times,” Kudsk said.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats said the government was monitoring the situation.
“If energy prices continue to rise, and the situation develops further, we are of course ready to do more,” he wrote on Facebook. He did not describe possible measures.
The poll also asked what should guide decisions on fuel taxes. A total of 39.2 percent said reducing motorists’ costs should come first.
Another 27.2 percent said taxes should remain because of climate and environmental concerns, while 25.9 percent gave both issues equal weight. The remaining 7.7 percent did not know.
The price increases have been linked to wars and conflicts causing a global fuel shortage.

US President Donald Trump described the agreement differently, saying it gives the United States “permanent control over security and all other necessities in Greenland.”
Denmark registered 502 suicides in 2025, the lowest annual number recorded from 2015 through 2025, according to the Centre for Suicide Research.
The total included 370 men and 132 women older than 15. It was 91 lower than in 2024.
Denmark’s suicide rate fell to 9.9 deaths per 100,000 people, an 18 percent decline from 2015. The rate dropped 30 percent among women and 12 percent among men.
Erik Christiansen, research head at the center, linked the decline partly to a national action plan introduced in 2024 and greater willingness to discuss suicide.
“At one time it was believed that it was dangerous to talk about suicide because it could inspire doing it. Today we know that this assumption is incorrect,” Christiansen said.
Doctors asking people directly about suicide risk can help them receive support earlier, he added.
Merete Nordentoft, a professor, chief physician and member of Denmark’s Council for Suicide Prevention, said help had become more accessible.
Suicide prevention clinics in Denmark’s five regions received additional funding to offer consultations to more people with suicidal thoughts or previous suicide attempts.
Livslinien, Denmark’s national suicide prevention helpline, received about 28,000 inquiries in 2025, up from fewer than 16,000 in 2019. Current funding allows it to answer about half of them.
Danish chef Jimmy Holm of Aarhus was among 12 finalists competing Sunday to be named the world’s best paella chef in Valencia, Spain.
Mexican chef Froilán Mújica won the World Paella Day Cup 2026, according to a live blog from organizer Visit València Foundation. Japanese chef Keisuke Mutsuura finished second.
Holm has worked at the Spanish restaurants El Bulli and El Celler de Can Roca. He also owned the tapas restaurant Los Socios in Aarhus.
He qualified for the final by winning the Nordic-Baltic semifinal in Denmark on June 11. That competition included chefs from Denmark, Sweden, Finland, Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
The Valencia final brought together chefs from Europe, Asia and North and South America. Seven judges assessed the dishes based on taste and presentation.
Each finalist prepared an individual version of paella and selected the type of rice to use. The competition was held in tents at Valencia’s harbor.
World Paella Day is held annually on September 20 to celebrate the dish and its origins in Valencia.
Paella is a traditional Spanish rice dish originating from Albufera, south of Valencia. Farmers originally cooked it over an open fire using local rice and available vegetables.
The dish takes its name from the large, flat pan used to prepare it. The pan allows the rice to form a thin, crisp layer.

Denmark’s plan to send foreign prisoners sentenced to deportation to a prison in Kosovo has been delayed again.
The 300 prison places are now expected to become available at the end of 2027 at the earliest and possibly not until the beginning of 2028, Justice Minister Nicolai Wammen informed the parties behind the agreement Friday.
“I have been informed by the Danish Prison Agency that the construction of the prison in Kosovo is delayed, so the prison places can at the earliest be put into use at the end of 2027 and possibly not until the beginning of 2028,” Wammen said in a written statement to Ritzau.
Denmark reached a political agreement in 2021 to lease 300 prison places in Kosovo to reduce pressure on Danish prisons.
When the agreement with Kosovo was finalized, the first foreign nationals sentenced to deportation were expected to begin serving their sentences there in early 2023.
The latest delay means the prison could open about five years later than originally planned.
Wammen said the project remains an important priority for the government so “we can relieve pressure on the Danish prisons and get criminal foreign nationals sentenced to deportation out of the country.”
“It must happen as quickly as possible, and I naturally would have very much liked for us to have long since begun sending inmates there. Therefore, I am of course far from satisfied that the project is further delayed,” he said.
According to the Ministry of Justice, authorities in Kosovo have now emptied the prison of inmates.
An agreement with a contractor was signed in July, and the renovation work is expected to take about a year.
The project has previously been delayed by the approval process in Kosovo’s parliament, where opposition parties did not support international agreements.
Danish prisons have faced overcrowding for years, adding pressure to make the Kosovo prison places available.
The number of people injured in traffic accidents in Denmark increased in 2025, while the number of deaths fell slightly, according to new figures from Statistics Denmark.
Police recorded 2,832 people as injured or killed in traffic accidents during the year, an increase of 313 compared with 2024.
The number of traffic deaths fell from 145 in 2024 to 143 in 2025.
Denmark has now recorded fewer than 200 traffic deaths a year for 10 consecutive years. This is well below levels seen between 1965 and 1973, when more than 1,000 people were killed in traffic each year.
Of those recorded in 2025, 1,732 were seriously injured and 957 suffered minor injuries.
The number of injured road users increased across almost all forms of transport, with mopeds the exception.
Injuries among people riding electric bicycles increased from 173 in 2024 to 211 in 2025. Nearly three-quarters of those injured in this group were aged 45 or older.
The police figures do not show the full number of people injured on Danish roads because they only cover accidents reported to police.
Hospital emergency departments keep separate records of traffic injuries. In 2024, they registered 29,589 injured people, more than 1,000 above the previous year’s figure.
Denmark will bring forward and increase a military aid package for Ukraine to DKK 1.8 billion, days after a Russian frigate fired two flares toward a Danish military helicopter.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen of the Moderates and Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats announced the decision Friday after a meeting of the Danish Parliament’s Foreign Policy Committee.
Most of the money will go toward air defense systems produced in Ukraine. The support had been requested by Ukraine.
Løkke described the incident involving the Danish helicopter as a “severe Russian provocation.”
“If they think they can provoke us into being restrained with our support for Ukraine, then they are mistaken,” he said.
Ukraine has faced difficulties defending itself against Russian ballistic missile attacks because of shortages of suitable air defense missiles, including Patriot missiles produced by the United States.
The decision follows an incident Monday involving a Danish Air Force Fennec helicopter and a Russian frigate in international waters off Gedser in southern Denmark.
The Danish Defence said the helicopter was carrying out routine photographic surveillance of the Russian vessel when the frigate fired two flares toward it. One passed close to the helicopter.
According to Bruus, the Russian ship did not establish radio contact with the helicopter before firing the flares.
NATO has described the incident as an “irresponsible Russian act.”
“This fits into a pattern we are seeing around Europe, where Russia is escalating and constantly testing boundaries. It serves the purpose of shaking our unity and our support for Ukraine, and that must not work,” Løkke said.
Denmark summoned the Russian ambassador following the incident. Russia has said the Danish helicopter acted “provocatively.”
“If the Russians think that they can rattle us by doing this kind of thing, then our counter-response is that we will step up our support for Ukraine faster than we had intended,” Bruus said.
The captain of the Russian frigate has since received an award from Russia for his actions, according to the Danish report.
Denmark has been a major supporter of Ukraine since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. However, since December, Denmark has announced only one other major aid package in addition to Friday’s package.
The Danish Ukraine Fund, which has financed much of the country’s support, has almost run out of available money. Further support would therefore require politicians to find funding elsewhere.
So far, much of Denmark’s support has been financed through the government’s projected future fiscal surplus.

Denmark plans to raise the fine for repeated violations of residency requirements to 100,000 DKK, Housing Minister Jacob Mark of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, told Jyllands-Posten.
The current maximum fine for a second violation is 20,000 DKK, meaning the proposed penalty would be five times higher.
“Cheating on the residency requirement is destructive to smaller towns and small island communities,” Mark said.
“When a citizen buys a house, but chooses not to live there, the consequence is that lovely towns in beautiful surroundings turn into ghost towns, the local grocery store closes, and community life and neighborhood spirit die,” he said.
Owners of homes intended for year-round use must ensure that the property is inhabited for at least 180 days a year. If they do not live there themselves, they can rent it out for permanent residence.
Under current rules, a first violation can lead to a fine of up to 10,000 DKK, rising to 20,000 DKK for a second offense.
Municipalities set the detailed rules for different types of housing. Holiday homes are generally exempt, while some properties can be designated as flexbolig, allowing a year-round home to be used as a holiday home.
Several island municipalities, including Samsø, Ærø, Fanø, Bornholm, Læsø and Langeland, have previously called for stronger monitoring powers. They want to be able to check water and electricity use weekly when they suspect violations, rather than monthly.
Mark said he has invited the island municipalities and Landdistrikternes Fællesråd, an organization representing rural areas in Denmark, to discuss possible additional measures.
Bus and light rail tickets in Aarhus will cost 15 DKK from 2027 under a new municipal budget agreement approved Thursday evening.
Aarhus Municipality will allocate 35 million DKK a year from 2027 to lower ticket prices, TV 2 Østjylland reported.
A consultancy firm had estimated that introducing 15 DKK tickets across the municipality could cost 122 million DKK, although the figure was uncertain.
Mayor Anders Winnerskjold of Socialdemokratiet, Denmark’s Social Democratic Party, argued that the actual cost would be lower, and the City Council agreed.
The budget agreement also notes that the national government plans to introduce free public transport for people under 22. Aarhus expects that measure to cover part of the cost of the cheaper local tickets.
Since March, residents have already been able to buy 15 DKK tickets on three bus routes as part of a trial.
The municipality has said the trial is intended to show how cheaper fares affect passenger numbers and what changes may be needed if more people choose public transport.
The experience will also be used in planning for a permanent price reduction and for making sure buses and the light rail can handle more passengers.
Frie Grønne leader Sikandar Siddique has been removed from Copenhagen City Council after authorities ruled that he does not meet the requirement of living in the municipality.
The City Council approved the decision Thursday, following a long dispute over Siddique’s residence.
Siddique has called the case a “miscarriage of justice” by “the system” and said it had been influenced by Zionists, meaning supporters of the Jewish national movement and political ideology. Several parties rejected those claims during Thursday’s meeting.
“I believe that it is quite damaging when an election is called into question by Sikandar Siddique’s statements, but also so-called experts,” Lord Mayor Sisse Marie Welling of SF, the Socialist People’s Party, said before the decision was approved.
Before the November 2025 municipal election, Siddique registered a move from Herlev to Copenhagen so he could run in the capital.
Copenhagen Municipality later cancelled his residence registration, citing, among other things, an unusually low electricity bill and a lack of documentation showing purchases near his registered Copenhagen address.
Siddique appealed, but the Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization upheld the municipality’s decision on September 8.
His seat will now go to Frie Grønne’s first alternate, Asham Agha Nadeem, meaning the party keeps its mandate.
Frie Grønne received nearly 7,000 votes in the election, including more than 3,000 personal votes for Siddique. Nadeem received 612 personal votes.
Denmark’s oldest living person, Kirsten Schwalbe, has entered the list of Europe’s 10 oldest living people, TV Midtvest reported Thursday.
Schwalbe turned 112 in March. She was born in Salling in 1914, a few months before the outbreak of World War I, and grew up with nine siblings.
She married her first husband in 1938 and had three children. Today, she lives in her own home in Struer.
Schwalbe has previously said that genetics may partly explain her long life. Four of her nine siblings also lived past the age of 100, she told Berlingske in 2024.
She has also said that mood plays an important role in living a long life.
Europe’s oldest living person is British woman Ethel Caterham, who is 117 and is also the world’s oldest living person.
Schwalbe is not yet among the world’s 20 oldest living people, according to TV Midtvest.
Meanwhile, a man in Costa Rica, Jose Flores, claims to be 119 years old. His age has not yet been confirmed, and specialists are reviewing documents to determine his date of birth.

Three Danish government ministers from Moderaterne, the Moderates, want schools to stop using Aula, the digital platform used for communication between schools, daycare facilities and families.
Ministers Monika Rubin, Christina Egelund and Jakob Engel-Schmidt made the proposal in a joint interview with Berlingske. They have not proposed an alternative to Aula.
“An IT system has been created that sucks so much oxygen out of the school and the classroom that it is harmful to our children’s well-being and learning,” Engel-Schmidt said.
Aula was introduced in 2019 to replace Skoleintra. Danish public schools and public and self-governing daycare facilities have access to the platform, where students, parents and employees can receive and share information.
Rubin told DR that the amount of communication on the platform had become excessive.
“More communication is not always better communication. 10,000 messages are sent on Aula per minute between half past seven and nine in the morning. It has gotten out of hand,” she said.
According to Berlingske, Egelund said answering parents’ questions is not a core task of Denmark’s public schools.
The proposal follows the latest PISA study, an international assessment of 15-year-old students’ performance in reading, mathematics and science, which showed a decline among Danish students.
Other government parties have expressed skepticism about removing Aula.
Nanna Bonde, education spokesperson for SF, the Socialist People’s Party, one of Denmark’s governing parties, suggested guidelines for the platform could be introduced instead, according to DR.
Apartment sales in Copenhagen fell sharply in August, while several other parts of Denmark saw more houses change hands than a year earlier, new figures from Boligsiden show.
A total of 390 owner-occupied apartments were sold in Copenhagen Municipality in August, 36 percent fewer than in the same month last year.
It was also the third-lowest number of apartment sales recorded in Copenhagen for an August since Boligsiden began collecting the data in 2011.
“Significantly fewer owner-occupied apartments are being traded in Copenhagen, and there has been a clear shift in the otherwise hectic pace that we have seen for a long time in Copenhagen,” said Birgit Daetz, communications director and housing economist at Boligsiden.
Across Denmark, apartment sales were 20 percent lower than in August 2025.
Overall housing sales also fell slightly during the first eight months of the year compared with the same period last year, after seasonal changes are taken into account.
Brian Friis Helmer, personal economist at AL Sydbank, said the apartment market was largely responsible for the decline, while sales of houses and holiday homes remained strong.
Boligsiden recorded more sales of detached and terraced houses than a year earlier in South Jutland, West and South Zealand, North Jutland and Funen.
House sales fell in Copenhagen, the Copenhagen suburbs and North Zealand.
“Now, we see the activity spreading to other parts of the country to a greater extent,” Daetz said.
A Lego model of the Danish royal yacht Dannebrog has been sold at auction for 60,000 DKK after spending 28 years at Legoland in Billund.
The model was sold Wednesday by auction house Bruun Rasmussen for twice its estimated price of between 20,000 and 30,000 DKK.
Legoland said the proceeds will be donated to the Mary Foundation, which works to combat social isolation.
“We think it could be nice to donate the money to the Mary Foundation, now that it is the royal yacht ‘Dannebrog’ that we have had up for auction,” said Jan Mouritzen, head of Legoland’s model department.
Bruun Rasmussen specialist Line Hjorth Langkjær said the model’s history at Legoland and the royal yacht’s place in Danish history had helped increase interest.
It is the first time Legoland has auctioned an original model from Miniland, where landmarks are recreated in miniature using Lego bricks.
The original Dannebrog model contains about 25,000 bricks. It was replaced after a new Copenhagen Harbour area opened in Miniland in July with an updated version made from 225,000 bricks.
The real Dannebrog serves as the official and private residence of the Danish royal couple and other members of the royal family during summer cruises and official visits overseas.
The Mary Foundation was established by then-Crown Princess Mary in 2007. The foundation said the donation will support efforts to combat bullying among children and loneliness among young people.
A patient at Landssygehuset in Tórshavn underwent surgery for an inguinal hernia on Wednesday while the surgeon performing the procedure was in Aabenraa, southern Denmark.
The operation used robot-assisted telesurgery, with the surgeon controlling a robot in the Faroe Islands from an office in Aabenraa.
It was the first time the technology had been used for an operation in Denmark and between two public hospitals in the Nordic region, Sygehus Sønderjylland, the Southern Jutland hospital, said in a press release.
Chief physician Jan Krzak said the operation had a “highly satisfactory result.”
“We have started out with a few selected patients with an uncomplicated inguinal hernia. The first step was to document whether the technology, safety, communication, and cooperation functioned stably in practice,” Krzak said.
The operation is part of a project examining whether telesurgery could eventually provide treatment to patients who live far from major medical facilities.
Elinborg Mortensen, chief physician at Landssygehuset in Tórshavn, said the technology could be particularly useful in the Faroe Islands, where many patients currently have to travel long distances for hospital treatment.
“Therefore, it is interesting for us to investigate whether new technology can bring some of the expertise closer to the patients in a safe and controlled manner,” Mortensen said.
A full surgical and anesthesia team was present with the patient in Tórshavn throughout Wednesday’s operation. The team was ready to take over if the technology or connection failed.
Robot-assisted telesurgery has previously been used internationally, including for operations performed remotely between London and Gibraltar.

Trump admin's hardline deportation policy an 'attempt to break the global refugee and asylum system'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Trump admin's hardline deportation policy an 'attempt to break the global refugee and asylum system'
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
François Picard is pleased to welcome Washington Post national security reporter Adam Taylor. The Forbidden Stories consortium, involving France 24 and 25 other media outlets, has spent six months investigating the thousands of people abruptly deported from the United States to third countries, amid concerns over due process and their ability to challenge their removal. The investigation examines how the Trump administration has made deportation a major focus of both US immigration and foreign policy.
It raises fundamental questions about due process and non-refoulement: the principle that people should not be returned to places where they face persecution or torture - as deportees can be sent to countries with which they have no connection and, in some cases, where they may face persecution, torture or prolonged detention.
"The real impetus comes from Stephen Miller"
Taylor attributes the broader shift to Stephen Miller and a small group of allies within the Trump administration. His description is that officials have redirected parts of the State Department’s refugee-related machinery toward negotiating deportation arrangements with third countries that rely heavily on US humanitarian aid.
The State Department’s changing role
According to Adam Taylor, the investigation found that third-country deportation arrangements have become a major "diplomatic" priority for the State Department. A relatively small new office, described as the The Office of Remigration, is involved in this work, parts of the State Department’s refugee machinery have been redirected toward negotiating these arrangements.
"Flooding the zone”
Taylor describes the sheer volume of deportation arrangements and cases as making it difficult for journalists, lawyers, legislators and advocacy groups to scrutinize and challenge each development. Stephen Miller as a deterrent message, a test of legal protections, and part of a volume of cases that risks overwhelming scrutiny and desensitizing the public.
As Taylor explains, this goes far beyond an expansion of immigration enforcement. He points to an institutional transformation in which the machinery of American diplomacy itself has been dramatically redirected toward deportation whereby agreements with foreign governments become a central instrument of migration policy.
Taylor also identifies a less visible consequence: normalization through scale. As deportations multiply, he suggests, individual cases risk losing their ability to command public attention. The investigation therefore shifts the lens from isolated stories of removal to the diplomatic and bureaucratic infrastructure making those removals possible - revealing how immigration policy can reshape not only borders, but the priorities and purposes of the institutions charged with conducting American foreign policy.
The legal dimension Taylor emphasizes is especially timely: on September 18, 2026, the First Circuit upheld a ruling that the administration's third-country deportation policy was unlawful because migrants had not been given sufficient notice and opportunity to raise fear-based objections. The administration, meanwhile, insists that third-country removals are necessary for people subject to final removal orders who cannot be returned to their countries of origin.
The Trump administration will most likely fight the ruling, so it may end up going back to the Supreme Court. While the High Court has not yet issued a final ruling on the policy's ultimate legality they have already intervened twice to allow third-country deportations to continue while litigation continues.

Iran ready to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days if US eases military pressure and lifts blockade
Iran can reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States eases military pressure and lifts its blockade on Iranian ports, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Tuesday.
On Sunday, Iran's military central command said it was informed the US was preparing to restart military operations with the support of regional countries, and warned this would lead to Tehran's retaliation "without limitations and considerations".
"The US needs to announce that it wants to resolve the issue diplomatically, make that official, and then agree on a timeline for how the process will move forward", the senior Iranian official said, adding the Iranian delegation to the United Nations General Assembly is in New York and has full authority to revive diplomacy with the United States.
Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who left Tehran for New York on Tuesday morning, will not meet US President Donald Trump at the UN headquarters in New York, the official told Reuters.
The Iranian official said details on an agreement to end hostilities with Washington can be discussed in New York via mediators, explaining that Tehran's proposal was delivered to the US via mediators on 16 September.
"The UN General Assembly is a golden opportunity for the US to return to diplomacy", the official said, adding that Tehran would welcome a revival of diplomacy if Washington takes tangible steps.
Meanwhile, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday the US is open to speaking with Iranians at the UN General Assembly, but no meeting is currently scheduled.
"We're open to that. I don't think anything is scheduled at this point, but we're certainly open to something like that, especially if it has the prospects of leading to something positive and ultimately achieving the goal of what this is all about," Rubio said in an interview with NBC's "Today" show.
"And that is the fact that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon. They just simply can't," he insisted.
Both the United States and Israel—who jointly launched a war on Iran at the end of February—possess nuclear weapons.

Investment appeal of Kyiv-area recreational property shaped by security factor - ABH
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
14:27:33 EEST
20:27:33 KST

Development of recreational real estate in the Kyiv region is being shaped by "security belts," according to an analytical report by ArtBuild Hospitality (ABH).
"Within a 100-kilometer radius of Kyiv, a distinct resort segment has already taken clear shape, with its own geography, unique formats, pricing and specific demand patterns. Its further development is being shaped not only by traditional factors (water, forest, transport accessibility) but also by a specific one: security distance from Kyiv," said ArtBuild Hospitality managing partner Oleksiy Yevchenko.
In his view, the security factor is key for future projects: it creates its own logic, layered on top of market logic, for distributing investment appeal across three belts.
The suburban zone (belt 0-15 km), closest to Kyiv, is also the riskiest: the area is regularly affected by air raid alerts and shelling. "This doesn't mean properties here don't function, but the operator is forced to build in constant operational risk and additional spending on shelters and guest safety into the business model," the expert explained.
The 25-50 km belt (the "overnight stay" buffer zone) is a place Kyiv residents head to primarily not for recreation but for relative calm, to wait out a few days during intense shelling of the capital. Demand here is stable and even grows during periods of escalation. But it's also this belt where the bulk of existing market players are concentrated (the Vyshhorod and Obukhiv directions), meaning there is objectively less available land for new development, and competition for it is higher.
The 50-80+ km belt offers the best balance of safety for recreation and development opportunities: security risk here is significantly lower than in the closer belts, while there is much more available, still-undeveloped land. Experts consider this belt the most promising for new development projects even during wartime.
"The security logic directly strengthens the case for developing less obvious directions, such as the Zhytomyr direction and the deeper southern cluster along the Ros River - both lie precisely within the safest 50-100 km belt. In other words, what previously looked like a purely market-driven shortfall (limited development due to weaker natural resources or worse logistics) has taken on additional investment weight during the war. These directions are objectively safer for long-term capital investment, which is exactly the factor missing in the 25-50 km belt, despite its higher short-term demand," he said.
The analysis of Kyiv's recreational belt covered 30 recreational projects across three categories: upper upscale, upscale and midscale. The economy segment is absent from this sample, since all the properties analyzed have a notable service and recreational component that goes beyond basic accommodation. The combined room stock of the analyzed projects totals approximately 1,500 units: about 1,000 are classic units, and 500-550 are houses, according to the report.
Five properties represent the upper upscale category: premium complexes with the highest service standards, signature dining and expanded, sometimes niche, infrastructure (Equides Club 5*, Riviera Zoloche, WISH Aqua & Spa Resort, Selfish Club, City Holiday Resort & SPA). Upscale, with 10 properties, represents the "gold standard" of recreation: hotel rooms plus cottages plus spa centers (Shelest, Sobi Club, Koncha Zaspa Park & Resort, Dom, Shambhala, and others).
The largest group in the study, with 15 properties, is midscale, covering everything from renovated classic recreation centers and family park complexes to concept cottage projects (Glibivka Family Park, Ulis, Pushcha Lisova, Congress Hotel Pushcha, KIDEV, and others).
Geographically, the recreational projects fall into four distinct clusters: the most expensive Obukhiv/Novoobukhiv cluster (Koncha-Zaspa, Kozyn, Pidhirtsi, Khodosivka); the Vyshhorod cluster (Kyiv Sea, Hlibivka), oriented toward family and water tourism; the historic resorts of the Zhytomyr/Western cluster, which also has the highest concentration of MICE venues; and the Boryspil/left-bank cluster of modern clubs with water park areas (Vyshenky, Boryspil district).
ArtBuild Hospitality (ABH) is a Ukrainian company with 20 years of international experience in hotel development and consulting. It has completed more than 100 projects (from audits to fee development) and operates in 15 countries, including Ukraine, Italy, Portugal, Hungary, Austria and Germany.

In Lithuania, parliament moved toward lifting the constitutional ban on nuclear weapons
