Three in four Americans say AI firms not doing enough to prevent disaster, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:08:00 UTC
20:08:00 KST

Three in four Americans say AI firms not doing enough to prevent disaster, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
- Three-quarters of Americans worry AI companies are not doing enough to prevent serious harm from AI, with 73% prioritising safe and responsible development over global competition.
- 39% believe AI negatively impacts society, the highest since March, while 55% support slowing AI development for better oversight and safety.
- Concerns include AI's cybersecurity risks and potential existential threats, highlighted by experts quitting and calls for stronger federal regulation amid political delays.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – Three-quarters of Americans, some 73 per cent, worry that AI companies have not gone far enough to prevent AI from causing serious harm to society, as concerns grow about where the technology may lead, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.
The four-day poll, which concluded on Sept 20, found that 39 per cent of respondents think that artificial intelligence is having a negative impact on society, up from 36 per cent in August and the highest share since Reuters/Ipsos began asking the question in March. Only 11 per cent said the new technology was a positive thing. The rest were not sure or did not answer the question.
The poll found many Americans lacked confidence in AI companies’ ability to regulate themselves, with most respondents saying federal officials should play a major role in setting safety standards.
While high-profile leaders ranging from US Senator Bernie Sanders – a progressive independent who caucuses with Democrats – to Steve Bannon – a close ally of US President Donald Trump – have called for federal action, little has come so far. Trump himself backs fast development of the technology and the Republican-led House of Representatives is on recess until November, leaving little chance for quick action.
The technology is upending how computer programmers work but it remains to be seen how much disruption it will cause in labour markets. The technology appears to pose significant risks to cybersecurity, with OpenAI revealing over the summer that its AI agents escaped a controlled test and hacked into another company’s systems without either company’s initial knowledge.
AI researchers quit over fears
Earlier in September, a researcher at Anthropic, another leading AI company, publicly quit his job over concerns that AI could be on a path to wipe out humanity. Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger echoed the warning, saying there was a more than 10 per cent chance of such an event within the next decade.
Most Americans – some 69 per cent of respondents – said they had followed the news that major AI companies were calling for a slowdown in AI development as well as greater oversight and safety standards.
Some 55 per cent of people in the Reuters/Ipsos poll said it would be a good thing to slow down AI development, compared with 13 per cent who said it would be a bad thing. The rest were not sure or did not answer the question.
Artificial intelligence burst onto the national stage in 2022 when OpenAI launched ChatGPT, a consumer-facing product that could answer user questions much as a human might and offered a new way to search the internet.
Supporters of the technology say AI has the potential to boost productivity, accelerate scientific discovery and transform industries ranging from healthcare to finance.
Heavy investment in the construction of data centres – vast collections of computers that power the technology – is boosting the economy but also creating enough noise to anger neighbours and put pressure on politicians ahead of the Nov 3 midterm elections.
Some 73 per cent of respondents in the poll said it was more important for the US to ensure AI is developed safely and responsibly, compared to 23 per cent who said it was more important for the US to stay ahead of the rest of the world on AI development.
The poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,277 US adults nationwide. Its results had a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction. REUTERS

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. The potential signing of documents concerning Greenland by the island’s leadership, the United States, and Denmark is a matter for the parties involved to decide, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
Media reports had previously indicated that an agreement concerning Greenland could be signed on September 22 in New York, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly.
"As for the possible signing of any documents regarding Greenland, that is a matter for the parties concerned," Peskov said when asked about the Kremlin’s reaction to the reports.

Denmark’s Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, whose country retains sovereignty over Greenland, had previously rejected Trump’s stated intention to gain control of the territory.
Trump has repeatedly argued that bringing Greenland under US control is necessary for national security. During his first presidential term, he proposed purchasing the island. In March 2025, he said he was confident that Greenland could ultimately become part of the United States and threatened Copenhagen with tariffs if Denmark refused.
Following a visit to Washington in January by Greenland’s Foreign Minister Vivian Motzfeldt and Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen, a working group involving representatives of all three parties was established to discuss issues related to Greenland.

The board called on all parties to uphold their commitments and avoid actions that could undermine the ceasefire, while urging international partners to translate political support into practical commitments.
"UNGA provides an opportunity to consolidate the international community behind one agreed framework," the statement said, emphasizing diplomacy as a means toward lasting peace and security in Gaza.
On the ground in Gaza Tuesday, the Israeli army injured a Palestinian woman and bombed a house, a medical source said, in fresh violations of the cease-fire in effect since last October
The source said the woman sustained moderate injuries after Israeli forces opened fire in the Ma'an area southeast of Khan Younis in southern Gaza.
Israeli military vehicles also opened heavy fire toward homes and tents sheltering displaced civilians near the Qizan Rashwan, Bir Zannoun and al-Shaer areas south of the city, local sources said.
In Gaza City, an Israeli fighter jet struck an empty home inside areas where the army is deployed east of the Tuffah neighborhood, according to local sources and eyewitnesses. No injuries were reported.
Israeli quadcopter drones also dropped several explosive devices on homes and streets near areas where Israeli forces are deployed east of the neighborhood, witnesses said.
According to the latest figures from Gaza's Health Ministry, Israeli violations of the Oct. 10, 2025 cease-fire agreement have killed nearly 1,400 Palestinians and injured over 4,800 others.
Since Oct. 7, 2023, Israel has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 others in its war on Gaza, while around 90% of the enclave’s infrastructure has been damaged or destroyed.

The human brain clears fluid directly into the skull, and poor sleep slows the process down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:00:21 UTC
20:00:21 KST

Brain fluid drains directly into the spongy marrow of the human skull, establishing a physical connection between the nervous system and the immune system. A recent imaging study reveals that this drainage process is slower in older individuals and those experiencing poor sleep or cognitive decline. The research was published in the journal eLife.
Historically, biologists thought the central nervous system was entirely isolated from the rest of the body. A specialized cellular boundary called the blood-brain barrier supposedly prevented immune cells and other substances from entering or leaving the brain. This isolation was thought to protect delicate neural tissue from damaging inflammation. Recent discoveries have challenged this view of the nervous system, revealing that the brain communicates directly with the surrounding bone.
Studies in mice and human tissue have identified tiny physical channels connecting the brain’s outer protective layers directly to the bone marrow inside the skull. The bone marrow is a spongy tissue inside bones that produces blood cells and immune cells. These microscopic channels allow cerebrospinal fluid to exit the brain and interact with the immune cells residing in the skull. Cerebrospinal fluid is the colorless liquid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord, acting as a waste removal system for the nervous system.
To better understand how this fluid moves in living humans, researchers at Zhejiang University in China organized an imaging study. The research team, led by Ying Zhou, Haidi Jin, and Min Lou, wanted to map exactly where and how fast the fluid travels into the skull. They also wanted to see if medical conditions, sleep quality, and memory might relate to how well this fluid system functions.
The researchers enrolled 87 patients who were already scheduled to receive a spinal tap for various neurological conditions. The medical team injected a contrast agent called gadolinium into the cerebrospinal fluid in the lower back of each patient. Gadolinium shows up brightly on magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, allowing researchers to track the fluid as it travels up the spine and into the head.
The patients underwent MRI scans before the injection and at three later time points. These follow-up scans occurred at 4.5 hours, 15 hours, and 39 hours after the initial injection. The research team focused their analysis on the bone marrow in three specific areas of the skull. They looked at the top of the head near a major vein called the superior sagittal sinus, the sides of the skull near the lateral fissure, and the base of the skull near the cisterna magna.
To measure the concentration of the contrast agent, the researchers compared the signal in the skull marrow against a reference point in the eyeball. The fluid inside the eye does not absorb the contrast agent, providing a stable baseline. By calculating the ratio between the skull signal and the eye signal, the team could track how much fluid had reached the bone marrow at each time point.
To evaluate health and lifestyle factors, the researchers also administered questionnaires to the participants. They used a standard survey to assess sleep quality over the previous month, looking at factors like sleep duration and nighttime disturbances. One month after the patients left the hospital, researchers evaluated their cognitive performance using a telephone-based test that measures attention, language, memory, and orientation.
The MRI scans showed the contrast agent moving from the cerebrospinal fluid directly into the skull bone marrow. The speed of this fluid movement varied depending on the anatomical region. Fluid reached the bone marrow at the top of the head the fastest. For a majority of the patients, the contrast agent peaked in this top region at the 4.5-hour mark.
Fluid movement into the bone marrow at the base of the skull was much slower. In half of the patients, the contrast agent did not peak in this lower region until 15 hours after the injection. The researchers hypothesize that fluid might travel through alternative pathways between the skull and the brain, speeding up delivery to the top of the head while bypassing other areas.
The researchers then analyzed what biological factors might influence the speed of fluid drainage near the top of the head. They found that older age, high blood pressure, and diabetes all correlated with slower fluid movement into the skull bone marrow. Female patients also showed slower drainage compared to male patients.
The drainage patterns were also linked to signs of systemic inflammation. Patients with slower fluid drainage had higher percentages of neutrophils, but lower percentages of monocytes and lymphocytes, in their blood. Neutrophils and monocytes are types of white blood cells that respond to infections and injuries. This suggests that higher levels of inflammation in the body might restrict the flow of cerebrospinal fluid into the skull marrow.
The patient questionnaires revealed a link between fluid drainage, sleep, and memory. Patients who reported worse sleep quality had slower drainage into the skull bone marrow at the top of the head. Slower drainage also correlated with lower scores on the cognitive telephone test.
Through statistical analysis, the researchers explored whether this drainage system might bridge the known gap between poor sleep and memory problems. Their calculations showed that the speed of fluid drainage accounted for roughly 38 percent of the statistical association between poor sleep and lower cognitive scores. The research team proposed that sleep disturbances might worsen inflammation, which in turn slows down fluid drainage and contributes to cognitive decline.
The study relies on observational data, meaning it cannot prove that slow fluid drainage causes cognitive decline or sleep problems. The statistical links only show that these variables change in tandem. Additionally, the patients in the study all had existing neurological conditions, such as peripheral neuropathy or encephalitis. Without a comparison group of healthy individuals, it remains unknown if these fluid dynamics operate the same way in the general public.
The methods used to measure sleep and cognition also present limitations. The researchers relied on self-reported questionnaires and telephone interviews rather than objective physiological measurements. A clinical sleep study measuring brain waves would provide a more accurate picture of how specific sleep stages relate to fluid movement.
The interpretation of the imaging timeline requires caution. The researchers classified the highest MRI signal at 4.5 hours as an indicator of drainage efficiency. This early time frame might just represent the fluid entering the bone marrow, while the later scans might better reflect the fluid actually washing out of the tissue. Future imaging studies with more frequent scanning intervals will be required to map the exact timeline of fluid entering and exiting the skull.
The study, “Skull Bone Marrow Drainage and Its Associations with Inflammation, Sleep Quality, and Cognitive Performance,” was authored by Ying Zhou, Haidi Jin, Xiao Zhu, Yifei Li, Ziyu Zhou, Xin Huang, Huihong Ke, Mengmeng Fang, Jianzhong Sun, and Min Lou.

McDonald's is hosting an investor day as its U.S. business struggles. Here are 4 things to expect
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:00:01 UTC
20:00:01 KST

McDonald's is expected to share more details about its new strategy to win back diners at its investor day on Wednesday in Chicago.
The company unveiled its new global growth plan, called McDonald's > NEXT, in June at its biennial worldwide convention for franchisees. Pillars of the strategy include a new restaurant design, better-tasting food and drinks and consumer-led innovation. But executives have otherwise offered few details, holding back until Wednesday's event.
Nearly three years after McDonald's previous investor day, the presentation comes after McDonald's U.S. business disappointed in its most recent quarter. The chain's same-store sales increased just 0.8%, and traffic to its restaurants fell.
CEO Chris Kempczinski said that the problems were due to shortcomings in execution, like a mixed implementation of its value offerings, rather than issues with the chain's overall strategy. Skye Anderson, who was tapped as president of McDonald's U.S. business in the wake of the weak quarter, will likely speak on Wednesday.
Kempczinski, Anderson and the rest of the McDonald's executive team will have to win over investors, who are increasingly skeptical that the fast-food giant can win over diners in the near term.
Over the past 12 months, the stock has fallen 18%, dragging McDonald's market value down to about $175 billion. The S&P 500 has climbed 16% in the same period, as optimism about artificial intelligence has offset concerns about the financial health of consumers.
Loading chart...
Here's what McDonald's presentation is expected to cover:
1) Value strategy
Over the past two years, value has become all-important to restaurants, which are competing over a smaller pool of customers who care about both price and experience. While chains like Taco Bell and Chili's have thrived, McDonald's has struggled recently as its value offerings got lost among its other promotional messages.
Plus, its franchisees have pushed back against discounts, which grow sales but eat into operators' profits, especially as high beef prices raise expenses. Only about two-thirds of McDonald's U.S. franchisees implemented its recent "under $3 menu," executives said in August. For its part, McDonald's lets franchisees set their own prices, but the company assesses how operators' menu prices help deliver value.
Analysts expect that McDonald's will continue to emphasize value, and franchisees' cooperation will be key to its success.
"We expect MCD to use this event to make it clear to franchisees that adherence to pricing recommendations will be a key factor in evaluating agreement renewals," Citi Research analyst Jon Tower wrote in a note to clients with his investor day predictions.
Tower also cut his price target for the company to $310 per share from $345 a share, citing investor concerns about franchisees' buy-in for the company's overall strategy.
2) Menu updates
Besides value, McDonald's is also looking to attract diners through menu offerings with elevated taste and quality.
In recent years, McDonald's has shifted its menu to include more chicken options, as beef prices have risen and rivals like Chick-fil-A threaten its sales. At the franchisee convention, executives shared that the next evolution of its chicken offerings will be hand-breaded. Chick-fil-A, Raising Cane's and Popeyes all hand bread or batter their chicken rather than using a machine. The technique usually results in a crispier exterior, but it takes more time and labor.
In addition to chicken, McDonald's has also leaned into expanded beverage options recently. After winding down CosMc's, its drink-focused spinoff, McDonald's has rolled out a variety of beverage options in the U.S., including crafted sodas, refreshers and energy drinks. A handful of international markets, like Germany, have also been rolling out more drink offerings.
"What's important — we'll talk a lot more about this at investor day — is beverages," Chief Financial Officer Ian Borden said on the company's earnings conference call in August.
3) Restaurant remodels
Roughly every decade, McDonald's mandates that franchisees remodel their restaurants to fit new aesthetic guidelines and improve their technology and equipment.
And it looks like another round of restaurant renovations is coming as part of the growth strategy. At the convention, franchisees got the first look at the new restaurant design.
Typically, McDonald's chips in some support for franchisees who are remodeling their restaurants. While upgraded locations usually generate higher sales, operators have to fund the remodels at a time when borrowing costs are elevated. And thanks to tariffs and high energy prices, construction costs are increasing, too.
As a result of the remodel program, McDonald's capital expenditures could increase by $600 million to $900 million in 2027 and 2028 from its projected spending in 2026, according to a research note from BMO Capital Markets analyst Andrew Strelzik. But executives are expected to share the company's own projected costs for the remodel program at investor day.
4) Cost cuts
While McDonald's will likely spend more on capital expenditures over the next two years, the company will likely try to cut costs elsewhere.
McDonald's will share its outlook for general and administrative spending during investor day, Borden said in August.
McDonald's could target G&A spending to be less than 2% of its systemwide sales, down from its current goal of 2.2%, Bernstein analyst Danilo Gargiulo wrote in a note to clients. In recent years, the company's workforce has shrunk as part of a reorganization effort.
Indirectly, McDonald's will also cut costs by refranchising some of its company-owned restaurants.
Selling locations to franchisees means that McDonald's will not be responsible for the operational costs or capital expenditures required to run a restaurant successfully. The company will also share more details about those plans at the investor day, according to Borden.

Everything You Know About Political Violence Is Probably Wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

It could have been a scene from Cape Fear: a quiet evening, an ordinary home, a sudden intrusion by a stranger convinced that the law has betrayed him.
In early July 2022, Democratic representative Pramila Jayapal of Washington and her husband were watching television at their Seattle home when men drove past their house screaming threats: vile, racialized, and unmistakably political. They called the police. The men left. Thirty minutes later, one returned, blasting music and approaching the porch. When officers arrived, they found him armed with a loaded handgun, a round already chambered. A neighbor heard him shout, “Go back to India. I am going to kill you.”
Jayapal later described the episode not as an aberration but as evidence of a broader transformation in American politics—a climate in which grievance increasingly functions as permission and intimidation is framed as justified political expression. The threats did not stop. Nor is Jayapal alone. For years, Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia lived under constant threat as one of Donald Trump’s most aggressive defenders in Congress. She reported hundreds of death threats, largely from ideological opponents.
But when Greene publicly broke with Trump—over the Epstein files, Gaza, and what “America first” had come to mean—the direction of the threats shifted. After Trump labeled her “Marjorie Traitor Greene,” messages arrived threatening her son by name. One threatened her assassination. Another claimed that a plane ticket had already been purchased. In November 2025, Greene announced her resignation from Congress, citing threats to her family. “I think that comes to a point,” she said, “where any American can look at that and say that’s a high bar and way too much to ask.”
What Jayapal and Greene have in common is not ideology, temperament, or policy; it is exposure. Both became targets in an era in which political violence is no longer confined to the fringe, no longer clearly condemned by leaders, no longer monopolized by either the right or the left—and increasingly treated as a legitimate instrument of political pressure.
What happened to Jayapal and Greene is no longer exceptional; it is revealing. Their experiences point to a deeper transformation: Political violence has moved closer to the center of American political life, touching elected officials across parties and becoming a recurring feature of contemporary conflict rather than a rare deviation.
Since 2016, Americans have argued fiercely not only about whether political violence is rising but about who is responsible. One dominant narrative attributes the problem primarily to the radical right: white nationalism, militias, election denial. A competing narrative insists that violence emanates just as strongly from the radical left, manifested in riots, assaults on police, and organized disruption in cities and on campuses. These claims are not merely rhetorical; they shape public trust, elite behavior, law enforcement priorities, and—most dangerously—the willingness of partisans to condemn violence committed by those they regard as allies. But what does the evidence actually show?
America’s political violence problem is neither one-sided nor symmetrical. Taken together, the evidence from federal threat assessments, terrorism databases, protest incident data, and congressional security records points toward the same conclusion. Political violence in the United States declined for nearly two decades after the 1990s and then rose sharply beginning around 2016. For decades prior to that year, politically motivated violence was concentrated overwhelmingly on the far right. Today, violence associated with the right and left is closer to balance, even as it takes very different forms. Right-wing violence has been substantially more frequent and far deadlier than left-wing violence since 2016—aimed at elections, federal institutions, and public officials—while left-wing violence has been more common in mass protest settings, from the 2020 George Floyd unrest to clashes over immigration enforcement, typically involving property destruction and confrontations with police.
Although uncertainty remains at the margins, the evidence strongly suggests that since roughly 2016, political violence on both the right and the left has reached levels unseen in the United States since the upheavals of the 1960s. These patterns reflect not a single ideology but the deeper forces of violent populism: hardened identities, perceived existential threats, collapsing institutional trust, and elite rhetoric that frames politics as a struggle between enemies rather than fellow citizens.
Much of the public disagreement about whether political violence is rising and who is responsible for it stems not from ideology alone but from competing definitions about what should be counted.
In scholarly literature, political violence is generally defined as the use or credible threat of physical force for political ends. Those ends may include coercion, intimidation, punishment, or symbolic signaling intended to influence public behavior, political outcomes, or institutional authority. Under this definition fall assassination attempts, armed assaults on public officials, bombings, arson attacks, violent intimidation, riots against buildings with explicit political aims, and organized plots to use force against political targets.
Just as important are the exclusions. Political violence does not include ordinary criminal activity lacking political motivation, interpersonal violence driven by private disputes, or lawful protest—even when protests are disruptive, angry, or unlawful. Nor does it include harsh rhetoric alone, however inflammatory, unless it is paired with a credible threat of force. These boundaries matter, because collapsing political violence into crime or protest obscures its distinct causes and consequences.
The hardest problem is determining intent. Political violence is defined not only by what happens but by why it happens—and intent is often ambiguous. When a crowd burns a police precinct, is the act political rebellion, criminal opportunism, or both? When a gunman attacks a synagogue, is the motive ideological antisemitism, personal grievance, or mental illness layered atop political belief? When an individual sends a death threat to a lawmaker, is it expressive rage, partisan trolling, or preparation for real-world violence?
Reasonable scholars answer these questions differently, often using dissimilar evidentiary thresholds. Some datasets require explicit ideological statements; others infer political intent from targets, symbols, or timing. Some classify riots as political violence only when their organizers articulate political goals; others focus on behavior rather than rhetoric. None of these choices is neutral, and each shapes the resulting picture.
These definitional choices explain why prominent datasets sometimes appear to disagree. Federal law enforcement datasets emphasize lethality, capability, and threats to national institutions. Protest-oriented datasets capture frequency and geographic spread. Terrorism databases prioritize ideological framing and tactical similarity to global movements. Each captures something real—and each misses something important.
For this reason, no single dataset can settle the debate. Accordingly, my work triangulates across several sources, combining federal threat assessments, incident-level databases, congressional security data, and survey research. The goal is not to produce a definitive body count but to identify patterns that recur across independent measures: who is targeted, how violence is carried out, how lethal it is, and how those patterns have changed since 2016.
This approach does not eliminate uncertainty. But it does attempt to move beyond partisan narratives and toward a more accurate understanding of how political violence in America has evolved—and why arguments over its meaning have become almost as intense as the violence itself.
The most authoritative window into political violence in the United States comes not from media tallies or advocacy groups but from the federal agencies charged with tracking national security threats—above all, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Yet even here, readers encounter a fundamental problem: There is no single, formal US government definition of “political violence.” Instead, federal agencies operate with overlapping categories—domestic terrorism, domestic violent extremism, hate crimes, threats against officials, and antigovernment violence—each shaped by legal constraints, investigative mandates, and statutory language rather than a unified conceptual framework.
This definitional fragmentation matters. Unlike many countries, the United States does not criminalize “domestic terrorism” as a stand-alone offense; the relevant statute (18 U.S.C., § 2331) defines “international terrorism” and “domestic terrorism” descriptively but does not by itself create a prosecutable offense. As a result, the FBI does not report a simple annual count of domestic terrorism incidents. Instead, the statistics reflect investigations, disrupted plots, arrests, and threat assessments organized around ideological motivation, such as racially and ethnically motivated violent extremism, antigovernment or antiauthority extremism, and hostile acts against government structures. The absence of a single metric has fueled public confusion and partisan cherry-picking, with critics on all sides accusing the FBI of either exaggerating or minimizing particular threats.
Despite these constraints, a consistent picture emerges from FBI testimony, annual threat assessments, and congressional reporting since 2016. Across political administrations, FBI directors have warned that domestic violent extremism is a persistent and elevated threat, with particular emphasis on right-wing ideologies—especially white supremacist and ethno-nationalist violence—as the most lethal category among domestic violent threats. This assessment is grounded not in ideology per se but in outcomes: The majority of fatal attacks tied to political or ideological motives in recent years have originated in right-wing ecosystems, often carried out by lone actors inspired by online propaganda rather than formal organizations.
At the same time, federal reporting makes clear that political violence is not monopolized by the right. The FBI and DHS have also documented significant spikes in violence associated with mass protest movements, assaults on law enforcement, arson, and attacks on government facilities during periods of intense unrest—most notably in 2020, when protests following the killing of George Floyd were accompanied by substantial violent confrontations in many cities. These events are more commonly linked to left-wing or anti-authority contexts, tend to cluster geographically, and are far less likely to result in mass casualties. The distinction federal agencies draw is therefore not between “violent” and “nonviolent” sides but between forms of violence that differ in frequency, lethality, and strategic orientation.
A further frustration is temporal. Much of the FBI’s publicly accessible data lags behind current events. Detailed breakdowns often stop several years short of the present, while ongoing investigations limit transparency about more recent trends. As a result, scholars and policymakers must rely on testimony, qualitative assessments, and partial datasets to infer patterns after 2021—a gap that has widened in the wake of intensified threats against public officials and institutions. This delay has created a disconnect between the lived experience of escalating threats—particularly against elected officials—and the statistical record available to the public.
These limitations should not be mistaken for insignificance. On the contrary, the persistence of the same core warnings across multiple administrations, political contexts, and leadership teams suggests institutional continuity rather than partisan distortion. While the FBI cannot provide a clean annual count of “political violence,” its threat assessments provide something arguably more important: a comparative judgment about which forms of violence are most likely to kill, destabilize institutions, and undermine democratic governance.
When federal threat assessments are read alongside terrorism databases, incident-level coding, congressional security data, and survey research, the contours of political violence since 2016 come into focus—even if the exact numbers remain contested. The challenge is not the absence of evidence but the difficulty of integrating imperfect sources into an honest and comprehensive account.
Excerpted from Our Own Worst Enemies: America in the Age of Violent Populism. Copyright © 2026 by Robert A. Pape. Used with permission of the publisher, The New Press. All rights reserved.

Top TV networks – including Fox – revolt in solidarity with media banned by Trump

Top TV networks – including Fox – revolt in solidarity with media banned by Trump
The top five US television networks staged a revolt on Monday when they effectively boycotted coverage of President Donald Trump to protest his decision to ban three news outlets from the White House. "No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a joint statement.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters said on Monday that they were halting "pool" coverage of the White House – where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day – in solidarity with CNN.
As a result of the row, the opening of Trump's cherished new White House helipad and his trip to the United Nations General Assembly proceeded without live television coverage.
CNN had been scheduled to serve Monday as the White House TV pool.
"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a statement.
CNN, MS NOW and Politico also sued Trump on Monday after he barred them from covering the White House last week.
The result is an unprecedented test of wills between the Trump administration and the press in a critical week during which Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting the White House.
White House launches 'Trump TV'
There may be no live TV of Trump's meetings with foreign leaders at the UN in New York, an annual forum that is closely watched around the world.
Meanwhile, the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the giant granite helipad on the South Lawn was only streamed on the White House's website – and Trump's comments were completely inaudible.
Several photo news organizations working at the White House, including AFP, decided to delay the release of photographs of Trump at the helipad in solidarity with the three banned media organisations.
Trump was unrepentant, branding the media a "cancer" and a threat to national security.
"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
"It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America."
On Monday evening, the White House launched a streaming channel, "Trump TV", which it said would show "top videos, major remarks, and must-see highlights streaming 24/7 and updated in real time".
When it went online it was showing archive footage of Trump delivering a speech on July 3 at Mount Rushmore.
Vice President JD Vance – a former CNN commentator before his move into politics – accused the news outlets of disseminating "left-wing propaganda".
"They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They're just not going to get an office in the White House anymore," he told reporters.
Trump's ban, however, went further than simply revoking office space from the outlets.
Press pass confiscated
Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied any access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated.
In their lawsuit, the three organizations asked for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.
"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the organizations said in a court filing.
A US district judge set a hearing on the complaint for Wednesday.
Trump's sudden announcement of the ban on Friday stunned the media – and reportedly many in his own administration.
The president has not detailed what prompted the ban, but said in response to a question from an AFP reporter in the Oval Office on Friday that it was "really just cumulative stories over the last two years".
Trump warned Friday that other outlets could face a similar fate.
The billionaire former reality TV star has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people".
The ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections, and the Iran war drags on with no end in sight.
In a lawsuit filed in a Washington, DC, federal court on Monday, CNN, MS NOW and Politico said the ban was unlawful retaliation for legally protected speech under the First Amendment and violated their rights to due process.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” the outlets said.
The president’s justification for the ban could be its undoing in a legal challenge because US courts have long held that the government cannot condition press access on favourable coverage once it has opened a space to the media, according to legal experts.
"They don’t have to allow anyone in, but once they do they cannot decide who gets in based on viewpoint or content,” said University of Maryland journalism professor Lucy Dalglish.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP and Reuters)

BEIJING, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, has extended festive greetings and sincere regards on behalf of the CPC Central Committee to farmers and people working on agricultural and rural fronts ahead of the ninth Chinese farmers' harvest festival.
Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, stressed the importance of solid efforts to advance all-around rural revitalization and ensure that farmers live happier and better lives.
Xi noted that this year, China's summer grain output hit a new record and early rice output remained stable, while a bumper autumn harvest is within sight.
Party committees and governments at all levels should work to ensure that policies aimed at strengthening agriculture, benefiting farmers and enriching rural areas deliver greater outcomes and enhance the overall production capacity, quality and performance of agriculture, he said.
Efforts should be made to expand channels for rural residents to increase incomes and build a beautiful and harmonious countryside for people to live and work in, based on local conditions, Xi said.
The Chinese farmers' harvest festival is the first national festival created specifically for the country's farmers. This year's festival falls on Wednesday.
Launched in 2018, the festival coincides with the Autumnal Equinox each year, which is one of the 24 solar terms of the Chinese lunisolar calendar and usually falls between Sept. 22 and 24 during the country's agricultural harvest season. ■

JAKARTA, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- At least one person was killed and four others were injured after a flash flood struck Solok district in Indonesia's West Sumatra province, local authorities said Tuesday.
The flood hit around 8 p.m. Monday, carrying sand, rocks and mud that blocked the main road linking Padang and Solok and disrupted traffic, West Sumatra police chief Djati Wiyoto Abadhy said.
The agency also said 11 government offices, 21 cars and seven motorcycles were affected by the flood.
About 300 additional police personnel were deployed to assist evacuation, search and clean-up operations, while the military, the search and rescue agency and local disaster management authorities also joined the response.
The meteorological agency BMKG said heavy rain triggered the flood. Authorities continued clearing debris and assessing damage in the affected areas. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Xi's upcoming U.S. visit to chart course for bilateral ties
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:55:38 CST
19:55:38 KST

BEIJING, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- At the invitation of U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping will pay a state visit to the United States from Sept. 23 to 25, marking an exchange of visits between the two leaders within six months.
As changes unseen in a century are accelerating and uncertainties continue to grow around the world, the visit is expected to bring greater stability and predictability to China-U.S. relations and beyond.
CONSTRUCTIVE STRATEGIC STABILITY
China-U.S. ties have been widely regarded as the world's most important bilateral relationship. More than 50 years ago, leaders from both countries, with remarkable courage and political vision, took the historic step of breaking the ice.
Since then, the relationship has repeatedly found a way forward despite tensions and setbacks, with head-of-state diplomacy consistently providing strategic guidance.
In recent years, China-U.S. relations have weathered ups and downs. How the world's two major countries manage their relationship matters far beyond their own borders.
Hosting Trump in Beijing in May, Xi underscored the responsibilities shouldered by both countries in these changing times.
"Can China and the United States overcome the Thucydides Trap and create a new paradigm of major-country relations? Can we meet global challenges together and provide greater stability for the world? Can we build a bright future together for our bilateral relations in the interest of the well-being of the two peoples and the future of humanity? These are the questions vital to history, to the world and to the people," said Xi.
Xi has repeatedly said that the broad Pacific Ocean is vast enough to embrace both China and the United States. He has also urged the two sides to be partners and friends, and work together to accomplish more great and concrete things for the good of the two countries and the whole world.
Since Trump's return to the White House in 2025, the two leaders have stayed in close contact, speaking by phone many times, exchanging letters on several occasions and meeting face to face twice since late last year.
"I look forward to working together with you to set the course and steer the giant ship of China-U.S. relations, so as to make 2026 a historic, landmark year that opens up a new chapter in China-U.S. relations," Xi said in his meeting with Trump in May.
It was during their Beijing meeting that the two leaders agreed on a new vision of building a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability, providing strategic guidance for bilateral ties over the next three years and beyond.
"The building of a constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability should not be a mere slogan, but concrete action taken by both sides toward the same goal," Xi said.
He outlined the "constructive strategic stability" as a positive stability with cooperation as the mainstay, a sound stability with moderate competition, a constant stability with manageable differences, and an enduring stability with promises of peace.
"The most important thing that comes out of leader-level meetings is that when the two leaders meet, they're able to build trust, and when they build trust, then everything else becomes easier," said Sean Stein, president of the U.S.-China Business Council.
"So for us, that's the most important thing we're looking for when President Xi travels to Washington to meet President Trump," he added.
WIN-WIN COOPERATION
As China and the United States share broad common interests and vast potential for cooperation, Xi has emphasized the need to expand mutually beneficial cooperation, strengthen dialogue and consultation, and turn shared interests into concrete outcomes.
China-U.S. economic ties are mutually beneficial and win-win in nature, Xi said in his meeting with Trump in May.
During his state visit to China, Trump was accompanied by top U.S. executives, including Apple's Tim Cook, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Tesla's Elon Musk, whom he called outstanding representatives from the U.S. business community.
"China will only open its door wider," Xi said during the meeting with Trump. American companies are deeply involved in China's reform and opening up, and the U.S. side is welcome to enhance mutually beneficial cooperation, he added.
"As the world's two largest, most dynamic and most technologically advanced economies, it's just impossible for the U.S. and Chinese economies to function as well without a strong and viable relationship with the other, so it's absolutely essential," said Stein.
Despite frictions and challenges, China-U.S. trade has demonstrated strong resilience. In the second quarter of this year, bilateral trade in goods grew 13.7 percent year on year. As of July this year, U.S. companies had established more than 84,000 enterprises in China.
"What has happened demonstrates yet again that the description of China-U.S. cooperation benefiting both sides and confrontation hurting both sides reflects a common sense that has been repeatedly proven by experience, and the vision of China and the United States helping each other succeed and prosper together is a tangible prospect within reach," Xi said in a phone conversation with Trump in 2025.
This year marks the launch of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) for economic and social development, and the 250th founding anniversary of the United States. As both countries enter pivotal stages of their respective development, new opportunities for cooperation are emerging.
In July, a delegation of Chinese business leaders traveled to Salt Lake City, Chicago and Washington, D.C., where they met with representatives of more than 120 U.S. companies and organizations. Their discussions underscored that the appetite for cooperation remains strong.
Across the U.S. business community, there is growing recognition of the vast potential for Chinese and U.S. companies to work together in cutting-edge fields, from green energy and the digital economy to artificial intelligence and biomedicine.
Kate Sullivan, executive director of the Greater Columbus Chinese Chamber of Commerce, pointed to Illuminate USA, a joint-venture solar panel manufacturer in Columbus, Ohio, as a success story of China-U.S. cooperation.
"It is the epitome of advanced manufacturing in the state of Ohio, drawing on multiple strengths of Chinese manufacturing and supply chains," she said. "It makes sense for the United States and China to be in business together. It's not an emotional decision there. It's business. Supply and demand."
Looking ahead, business representatives also voiced expectations for a more stable environment for bilateral cooperation.
"We hope the two heads of state will maintain strategic communication, bringing greater stability, stronger confidence and a longer-term outlook to markets and businesses in both countries," said Wang Qi, chairman of the U.S.-China Green Energy Council.
PEOPLE-TO-PEOPLE EXCHANGES
Xi has consistently emphasized that the foundation and future of China-U.S. relations ultimately lie in the connections between the two peoples.
"Though geographically far apart, our peoples boast a long history of friendly exchanges," Xi said in a speech at a welcoming dinner hosted by local governments and friendly organizations in Seattle in 2015.
Over the years, Xi has maintained close personal ties with people from all walks of life in the United States. In 2015, Xi visited Lincoln High School in the U.S. port city of Tacoma. Without a tie, he presented gifts to the students, including books on China, a ping-pong table, and his personal invitation for the students to visit China.
In 2023, before the Welcome Dinner by Friendly Organizations in San Francisco, Xi met with veterans of the Flying Tigers and descendants of late General Joseph Stilwell, whose stories have become an important part of the history of China-U.S. friendship.
In 2024, in his reply to a letter from Lamont Repollet, president of Kean University in the United States, Xi encouraged universities in China and the United States to strengthen exchanges and cooperation and contribute to China-U.S. friendship.
During this year's Spring Festival, Xi replied to friends in the U.S. state of Iowa and sent them a Chinese New Year card with festive greetings, continuing their warm exchange of New Year wishes for the third consecutive year.
In 2023, during his visit to San Francisco, Xi announced that China was ready to invite 50,000 young Americans to China on exchange and study programs in the next five years. "We hope that our two peoples will make more visits, contacts and exchanges and write new stories of friendship in the new era," he said.
The invitation was warmly received by young people in the United States. In just over two and a half years, more than 50,000 young Americans from all 50 states have traveled to China.
Their trips have taken them to different parts of the country. They have toured smart factories, visited rural communities and experienced everyday life in places far from home. For many, the journeys have also led to new friendships with Chinese peers.
"I am particularly grateful to President Xi for his initiative of 50,000 in five years. I think that is possibly one of the most consequential initiatives in the last 20 years," said Luca Berrone, a four-decade-long friend of Xi in Iowa.
"I believe that people-to-people exchanges, particularly between China and the United States, are fundamental in continuing to strengthen the relationship, to improve understanding and acceptance," he said. ■

Türkiye aims to turn climate targets into action through COP31
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:54:01 UTC
19:54:01 KST

Environment, Urbanization, and Climate Change Minister and COP31 President-Designate Murat Kurum (R), delivered a speech at the “Launch of the COP31 Action Agenda, High-Level Event” event held in the ECOSOC Chamber at the United Nations Headquarters in New York. (AA Photo)
Turkish Environment, Urbanization and Climate Change Minister Murat Kurum said on Sept. 21 that Türkiye aims to turn climate targets into measurable and actionable steps through the U.N. Climate Change Conference COP31, to be held in Antalya in November.
Kurum launched COP31 during his visit to New York for the 81st session of the U.N. General Assembly.
Speaking at the “Launch of the COP31 Action Agenda, High-Level Event” held at the U.N. Economic and Social Council Chamber, Kurum, in his capacity as COP31 president, said: “We are here today not only to introduce the COP31 Action Agenda, but also to discuss together how we can accelerate the transition from targets to implementation in climate action.”
There is now a strong common understanding of the urgency of the climate crisis, he said, noting that common targets have been set and that workable solutions are available in many parts of the world.
He stressed that the key issue was how these solutions could be put into practice.
Pointing to challenges, including access to finance, capacity gaps, and matching technology and investment with needs, Kurum said these questions would be addressed at the COP31 conference in Antalya in November.
“Our approach in this process is based on three fundamental principles: Dialogue. Consensus. Action. Through dialogue, we listen to different needs and priorities. Through consensus, we identify areas for joint action. Through action, we want to turn this partnership into concrete results,” he said.
Kurum stressed that their work was not simply about announcing more commitments, but about turning existing commitments into measurable results on the ground.
“Our Action Agenda brings common priorities together with measurable targets, concrete initiatives and implementation tools,” he said.
Kurum briefed representatives of countries party to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change on the 10 priority themes, six global targets, 11 initiatives, and 13 supporting outputs of the COP31 Action Agenda, which is built around the principles of “Dialogue, Consensus, Action.”

====================================================================================================

optician’s shop turned art installation satirizes bio-tracking tech at uncanny shifts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:50:52 UTC
19:50:52 KST

At Uncanny Shifts, an exhibition by Urbane Künste Ruhr set in reused spaces around Dortmund Train Station in Germany, Ellinor Aurora Aasgaard and Zayne Armstrong’s installation, The Factory, occupies a former optician’s shop. Walking down a street with a jazz bar, a hunting store, and a smattering of restaurants, it’s almost easy to miss the installation if it weren’t for a pile of inflatable figures pressing up against a glass case that would have formerly housed optical advertisements or product offerings. Within, a mise-en-scène emerges of a strangely ornate historic building-turned gym, bejeweled with ziplocked phones and embedded screens that lead the way into a short animated film bearing the name Charli & The Factory (2024).
In this immersive space, the duo create a hybrid video, painting, and sculptural environment that tells the story of a journalist, Charli, who is pursuing what could be a career-defining reportage on a FitWatch—a kind of bio-tracking smartwatch—that gets its users to achieve their goals no matter the cost. Aasgaard and Armstrong take us into The Factory, the gym in which the tale takes place, to consider ideas of labor, the body, and how we operate within contemporary capitalist dynamics. The artists most effectively introduce the project on their site themselves by saying: ‘Welcome to The Factory, where scandals sweat, and every step on the treadmill takes you closer to the edge.’
Upon entering the former optician’s shop in Dortmund, it’s difficult to quite make out what has been set in motion, as there are a whirl of figures and characters abound. Most noticeable within this scene are the painted figures of Transformers, the robots from the massively successful franchise, rendered in primary colors and luxe chromes, taking selfies with actual smartphones that are zipped up in clear baggies and embedded in cutouts within the paintings. It’s unfit, though, to call these paintings. They are more akin to the backdrops or scenics found setting the scene of a play than something found on a gallery wall. When looking closely at each panel—angled and arranged to create the artists’ medieval-gym-turned-surveillance center—one can see that the paintings are created over photos of a fairly mundane Berlin during the day.
The inside of this ‘gym’ was derived from a hodgepodge of temporally disparate paintings that range from Scenes from the Life of Saint Bertin and the Annunciation to Mary with prophets and evangelists (Simon Marmion, 1459), The Annunciation (Piero del Pollaiuolo, 1480), to Woman at a Window (Caspar David Friedrich, 1822). In this way, they evoke a kind of aesthetic and temporal weirdness that points to the strange temporal setting of contemporary Europe, with its trains and metros that zip underneath 16th-century castles and start ups that occupy offices in galleria buildings. In all these atemporal elements, the duo begin to nudge at the strangeness of contemporary life and the dredges of the past that remain visible.
the inside of this ‘gym’ was derived from a hodgepodge of temporally disparate paintings referenced by the artists
Inflatable Bodies vs. Chrome Transformers
Just as they greeted visitors into the space, more of the inflatable sculptures whip around the interior of the installation. The duo have referenced Henry Moore’s works as the core inspiration behind their vaguely human forms. Positioned above large, very visible fans, their bodies expand and contract – they are ‘working out’ in a way not so dissimilar to how one’s muscles would tense and relax while doing reps at a gym. With these creatures, so flaccid and flexible in front of the rigid, shining Transformers, they call into question the idea of the body. What does it mean to occupy a humanoid form? And what are the responsibilities that one has to take care of it, track it, and conceive of something that’s always in flux?
just as they greeted visitors into the space, more of the inflatable sculptures whip around the interior of the installation
The work that unites all the figures and forms of Aasgaard and Armstrong’s gym-turned-factory is the 30-minute animated film that follows Charli as she bumbles her way through the mystery surrounding a gory FitWatch ‘malfunction,’ her character complete with purple hair and bright orange The Fifth Element-style suspenders. As she journalistically investigates what happens, she unearths the closed-lip, hypocritical nature of the makers, users, and promoters of this explosive invention.
As Charli interviews the gym manager, the maker, and her sexy hook-up/trainer who witnessed the event, she attempts to piece together why and how the FitWatch is causing bodily harm to people. In creating her exposé, which eventually gets cut up into a puff piece, she discovers that this smart technology, made to push people to perfection, is perhaps not helping the human race, but hurting it. Ultimately, the installation leaves the viewer feeling fraught—if even the means by which we improve ourselves are turned against us, let’s say for capital, vanity, or another contemporary malaise, what remains as a path toward betterment? If one were to even exist.
trailer for Charli & The Factory (2024) written by Ellinor Aurora Aasgaard, Zayne Armstrong
Aasgaard and Armstrong’s installation is just one in the Uncanny Shifts program. In conversation with designboom, artistic director Britta Peters discusses how the duo fit snugly into the curatorial vision of the event with their strange techno-not-so-futuristic view of the now. After seeing previous iterations of the work, her and co-curator Alisha Raissa Danscher, invited them to create an expanded site-specific work for the program. ‘The focus on self-optimization and egocentric body culture fits perfectly with Uncanny Shifts because it brings in the themes of Neoliberalism and withdrawal of solidarity: People are turning into machines, like in the film serial Transformers. The film Charli & The Factory is a scathingly satirical work commenting on the social and economic dynamics of our times.’ The exhibition subtly snakes through the city, occupying timetables at the station, a pedestrian zone, and a church. Talking about how the artists’ faux gym occupies the former optician’s space, Peters hints at its uncanny timeliness, ‘there is already a big gym on the other side of the street.’

Russian Troops Again Use Gas Pipeline to Sneak Into Ukraine, ISW Says
Russian forces have resumed attempts to infiltrate Ukraine’s northern Sumy region through a major gas pipeline running across the border from Russia’s Kursk region, carrying out at least two such missions over the past week without securing an advance.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) on September 21, Russian troops have returned to using the Urengoy-Pomary-Uzhhorod gas pipeline connecting Ukraine’s Sumy region with the Russian city of Sudzha as a concealed route for infantry movements.
A spokesperson for Ukraine’s 8th Airborne Corps reported that Russian forces had attempted two infiltration missions through the pipeline during the previous week. ISW said it had observed at least two such operations in the Sumy region since September 13, including one involving a platoon-sized group.
One of the earlier attempts was reported on September 12, when Ukrainian forces struck roughly 10 Russian soldiers after they emerged from a pipeline leading from Russia’s Kursk region into Ukrainian territory.
A subsequent operation involved a larger Russian group attempting to reach Mala Korchakivka, north of Sumy. Ukrainian forces killed 29 Russian soldiers and wounded three during that assault, according to a Ukrainian brigade cited by ISW.
The renewed pipeline infiltrations come as Russian forces continue offensive operations along the northern Sumy front. ISW assessed that Russian troops conducted attacks in the area on September 20 and 21 but made no confirmed advances.
Russian forces have previously used underground infrastructure to bypass Ukrainian defenses. ISW noted that Russian troops employed pipelines during operations in Avdiivka in January 2024, Russia’s Kursk region in March 2025, and Kupiansk in September 2025.
Elsewhere along the northeastern front, ISW reported a recent Russian advance in Vovchansk in the Kharkiv region, based on geolocated footage showing Ukrainian strikes against Russian positions in the southern part of the city.
At the same time, the institute said available evidence did not support Russian Defense Ministry claims that Russian forces had captured Pilna and Novooleksandrivka. ISW assessed Russian positions to be as far as roughly 10 kilometers from Pilna and 25 kilometers from Novooleksandrivka.
In a separate operation in the Donetsk region, Ukraine’s Third Army Corps reported recapturing 125 square kilometers during the first two phases of Operation Vivaldi, including the liberation of Shandryholove and Derylove and full control of Drobysheve.
The corps said Ukrainian forces increasingly use drones and unmanned ground vehicles ahead of infantry during assaults, including deploying ground robotic systems by heavy drones more than 10 kilometers behind Russian lines.

Ukraine and France Sign Contract for Air Defense Radars and Interceptor Missiles

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We are strengthening its [Ukraine’s] air defense by signing a contract for the supply of radars, as well as the supply of interceptors,” Macron wrote on X.
The French president did not specify the types or number of radars and interceptor missiles covered by the agreement, nor did he provide a timeline for their delivery.
The agreement was announced following talks between Macron and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which focused primarily on security and a winter support package for Ukraine.

The air defense cooperation comes as France and Ukraine also deepen ties in combat aviation. France is preparing to begin initial training for Ukrainian pilots expected to transition to Rafale fighter jets as Kyiv moves toward integrating the French-made aircraft into its fleet.

CNG is a cost-effective alternative to other fuels amid global price surge - former GTSOU head
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:49:37 EEST
19:49:37 KST

Amid a price surge on global hydrocarbon markets, the price of Ukrainian-produced compressed natural gas (CNG) at filling stations is half that of other fuel types, making a switch to methane economically viable, at least for municipal transport.
That's according to former Gas Transmission System Operator of Ukraine (GTSOU) head Serhii Makogon, who wrote about it on Facebook Tuesday.
"Of course, you can't switch all transport to methane overnight. But right now is exactly the right moment to start, at least with municipal transport - buses, utility vehicles. This would immediately lower transport costs for cities and communities," he wrote.
According to Makogon, methane at car gas-filling compressor stations (CGFCS) currently costs UAH 49 per cubic meter, unlike regular auto gas, making it nearly half the price of diesel or gasoline.
"Ukraine is currently fully self-sufficient in methane. Industrial gas consumption has fallen sharply - the metals industry is effectively at a standstill (...) When you buy methane at a CGFCS, you're paying Ukrainian gas producers, not oil product importers," Makogon said.
He explained that another argument in favor of methane is that it doesn't need to be transported by fuel trucks. Methane is delivered to CGFCS via underground gas pipelines, providing an additional guarantee of safety and uninterrupted fuel supply, even in frontline cities.
According to Ukravtogaz, a subsidiary of NJSC Naftogaz of Ukraine, the price of compressed natural gas sold through Ukravtogaz's CGFCS network has stood at UAH 48.60 per cubic meter since April 9, 2026.
Ukravtogaz operates 90 CGFCS facilities across Ukraine with a combined capacity of 687.5 million cubic meters. The company currently has all the necessary technical capacity and personnel to convert vehicles to CNG use and to service vehicles already running on CNG.

Ukraine has exhausted resources to continue war, expert says

Unknown Publisher

10:48:20 UTC
19:48:20 KST

MOSCOW, September 22. /TASS/. Ukraine’s potential to continue military operations has been exhausted, and the authorities should have a "self-preservation instinct" to begin looking for ways out of the conflict, Ukrainian economist Alexey Kushch said.
"We see systemic damage accumulating, which is reflected in a whole range of factors, including economic and foreign policy ones. It is therefore clear that the resources needed to wage war are being depleted across the entire range of capabilities. In principle, the potential to wage war is not limited to money or financial resources. It also includes the resilience of infrastructure, demographic potential, as well as mental and, certainly, foreign policy potential," he said in a broadcast, a video excerpt of which was published by Strana. According to him, "if the situation approaches the risk of a systemic collapse <...>, the people who make decisions <...> should understand that either they will take certain steps to find a way out of the war, or simply the debris of this structure, which may begin to collapse, <...> could bury everyone beneath it." "In other words, everyone could be buried under this debris, including the political elites," Kushch said.
The expert said the authorities see destructive processes in the country, so they "should have a self-preservation instinct" to avoid these risks. "It is obvious that we are now at such a point -- the depletion of demographic, infrastructure and economic potential," the expert said. "The economy is on the verge of a recession, that is, a decline lasting more than two consecutive quarters. We see a reduction in foreign aid, so there is a whole combination of factors that come together into a single picture."
Kushch stressed that Ukraine has been in a fiscal crisis since 2022, but it was offset by "unlimited foreign aid." However, the "philosophy" of providing support to Kiev has been radically revised, with direct Western budget assistance falling by about threefold. The expert noted that under these conditions, Kiev’s financial problems had been obvious since the beginning of the year, so he does not understand why Ukrainian politicians are surprised by the current crisis.
Ukraine has been facing record budget deficits for several years. Kiev acknowledges that the country has fully exhausted its own resources and that securing funding is becoming increasingly difficult. On August 20, Vladimir Zelensky acknowledged that a lack of funds had become a major challenge, with the deficit in the defense budget alone reaching $27 billion. According to the latest government data, Ukraine’s budget gap stands at about $57.4 billion.

The Revisit: 125 shells, 10 minutes and a German attack on Madras - when WWI reached India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:47:13 UTC
19:47:13 KST

German cruiser SMS Emden that bombarded the city during the WWI on September 22.
When World War I broke out in Europe in July 1914, Madras was thousands of kilometres away from the battlefields. Yet there was little certainty among British authorities that the war would remain confined to Europe. The city's strategic importance as a major port made it vulnerable, and within weeks, residents were being advised to move towards safer places in the hinterland.By September, the anxiety had become real enough for some families to leave.Among them were the grandparents of PD Balaji, professor and head of the department of ancient history and archaeology at the University of Madras. Speaking to The Times of India in 2017, Balaji recalled that his grandparents lived in Royapettah and moved to Salem briefly, taking some valuables with them because they feared Madras could come under attack.Their fears were realised on the night of September 22, 1914, when the German cruiser SMS Emden appeared off the Madras coast and opened fire.The attack lasted only a short time, but it became one of the most remarkable episodes of India's experience of World War I.
The warship that did not look German
The Emden had already been operating in the waters around the Indian subcontinent, attacking shipping before turning towards Madras. But the cruiser had an unusual advantage: it did not necessarily look like an enemy vessel from a distance.
Historian Venkatesh Ramakrishnan told TOI that the Emden had a dummy fourth funnel, which made the German cruiser appear like a British ship.That deception was particularly useful in the busy waters of the region."Some enemy ships even saluted it during navigation," Ramakrishnan told TOI.The disguise allowed the cruiser to move through waters where a genuine German warship might otherwise have attracted immediate attention. By the time it approached Madras, the British authorities were facing a vessel that had managed to exploit both surprise and confusion.
130 shells in one night
At around 9.30 pm, the attack began.The precise nature of the German target remains one of the interesting questions surrounding the bombardment. Some accounts have suggested that Fort St George was the intended target, while historian Venkatesh Ramakrishnan offered a different explanation.According to Ramakrishnan, Captain Karl von Müller did not necessarily direct his guns at one particular building."The Emden's captain Karl von Muller did not aim at any particular target. The shells were fired on any structure that was illuminated by the lighthouse," he told TOI.Around 130 shells were fired that night, according to Ramakrishnan.One struck a storage tank belonging to the Burmah Oil Company near the harbour. The tank caught fire, and the blaze continued for three days, turning the attack into a highly visible spectacle for the city.A separate 2014 TOI report, quoting historian V Dhivakar, put the number of shells at at least 125, fired within around 10 minutes. Dhivakar said the shells hit oil tanks containing approximately 350,000 gallons of oil.Whatever the precise count, the scale of the bombardment was remarkable for an attack that lasted only a short period.The German cruiser had sailed close enough to Madras to fire into the city and then withdrew before the British could mount an effective response.
From harbour to high court
The attack was not confined to the waterfront.According to Ramakrishnan, shrapnel struck several parts of Madras, including the High Court, General Hospital, Vepery, Haddows Road, Poonamallee High Road, the gun battery at Royapuram, Casa Major Road and George Town.The geography of the damage is significant because it demonstrated how a naval attack on the harbour could quickly become a city-wide shock.For residents, the source of the explosions was initially not something they could easily understand. The war had until then existed largely in newspapers and official announcements. Suddenly, its sound could be heard across Madras.And the sight of the oil tank burning for days provided a lasting reminder that the British Empire's war had reached the Indian coast.
A city already preparing to flee
The Emden attack did not come completely out of the blue.Anxiety had spread through Madras in the weeks following the outbreak of World War I. British authorities had advised residents to move to safer locations in the hinterland because of fears that enemy forces could attack the city.The exodus had already begun when the German cruiser struck.For families who had left, the decision suddenly appeared prescient. For those who remained, the bombardment reinforced fears that the Emden might return or that other German vessels could attack the city.The account of Balaji's grandparents provides a glimpse into what that uncertainty meant at an individual level. They left their Royapettah home for Salem and carried valuables with them, not knowing how long they would have to stay away.This was not merely a military episode. It had begun affecting ordinary civilian decisions.
Why did Emden leave?
The attack also produced a question that historians continue to debate: Why did the Emden withdraw so quickly?The cruiser had managed to reach Madras, fire more than a hundred shells and hit important infrastructure. Yet it did not remain to inflict prolonged damage.Historian V Dhivakar challenged the later British explanation that Emden withdrew because of the British response.“After Emden reached a safe distance, the British started responding towards what for them was an unknown object in the dark far out at sea,” Dhivakar told TOI.He argued that the German cruiser could potentially have inflicted considerably more damage had it remained longer.The question becomes more intriguing when the Emden's capabilities are considered. Dhivakar described the cruiser as a formidable warship for its time, armed with ten 10.5cm guns and two torpedo tubes.Why Muller chose to stop when he did remains one of the enduring mysteries of the Madras raid.The Emden story also acquired an Indian revolutionary dimension through Chempakaraman Pillai, an Indian-born political activist and revolutionary who was living in Germany.A persistent claim has suggested that Pillai helped the Germans plan the Madras attack or was aboard the Emden.But the evidence cited by Dhivakar does not establish that.He told TOI that Pillai was not aboard the Emden during its wartime operations. Dhivakar referred to a book by Hellmuth von Mucke, the ship's vice-commander, which recorded several incidents aboard the cruiser without mentioning Pillai.Mucke did, however, refer to an Indian passenger who provided information.That detail has helped keep the Indian connection alive, but it does not prove that Pillai himself was involved in the attack.
The word 'Emden' survives
The most curious legacy of the raid may have been linguistic.The name Emden became part of popular usage in southern India, particularly in Tamil, where it came to be associated with someone formidable, daring or intimidating.The German cruiser therefore outlived its own military career in an unexpected way.The ship was eventually cornered and destroyed later in 1914, but its name had already acquired a place in Indian memory.For Madras, meanwhile, the physical reminders of the bombardment became part of the city's history. The High Court was among the places struck by shrapnel, while accounts of the attack have continued to document the damage caused across the harbour and surrounding neighbourhoods.
The night war came home
The Emden attack did not change the outcome of World War I. It did not result in the capture of Madras, nor did it lead to a prolonged German campaign on the Indian coast.Its significance was different.It showed that a war that seemed distant and European could reach an Indian city with little warning. It exposed the vulnerability of a major colonial port, sent residents fleeing towards the interior and forced the British to confront the possibility that India's coastline could become part of the global conflict.
For the people of Madras, September 22, 1914, was therefore not simply another date in the history of World War I.It was the night when the distant war suddenly became local: when a German cruiser appeared off the coast, 130 shells tore into the city, a Burmah Oil tank burned for three days, shrapnel reached the High Court and other parts of Madras, and a word that once belonged to a German warship entered the vocabulary of southern India.
