An FSB hitwoman who was preparing an assassination attempt on a Russian opposition figure was detained in Kyiv
Kyiv • UNN
The SBU detained in Kyiv a resident of the occupied city of Melitopol who, on the FSB’s orders, was preparing an assassination attempt on a Russian opposition figure. She faces life imprisonment.
In Kyiv, the FSB hitwoman who was preparing an assassination attempt on the leader of one of Ukraine’s civil society organizations—a Russian opposition figure—was detained. The SBU reported this on September 22, UNN writes.
The counterintelligence officers of the Security Service of Ukraine prevented another high-profile murder that was to take place in Ukraine on the orders of the FSB of the Russian Federation. As a result of a special operation, an agent of the Russian Federation was detained in Kyiv. She had been tasked with eliminating a Russian opposition figure who currently heads one of the nationwide Ukrainian civil society organizations
Details
According to the investigation, the SBU stated that "the hitwoman was supposed to shoot the activist with a combat pistol from ambush near one of the capital’s gyms, where he works as a kickboxing coach."
"In this way, the Russian Federation hoped to kill the Russian opposition figure, who had been fighting for Ukraine since 2022—first in the Kyiv region and then on the Eastern Front," the special service noted.
The SBU officers, as reported, acted proactively and detained the suspect near the sports complex while she was conducting additional reconnaissance of the area in order to choose a firing position for the assassination attempt.
According to the case materials, the FSB’s assignment was carried out by an unemployed resident of temporarily occupied Melitopol who had been recruited by the enemy.
It was established that Russian intelligence officers recruited the woman to cooperate in exchange for "closing" a case concerning illegal possession of drugs.
"The recruited agent underwent training at a local FSB "branch," where she was taught counter-surveillance measures, navigation in the area, and firearms handling. After completing her training, the hitwoman was sent to Zhytomyr in transit through the territory of Belarus, and then arrived in Kyiv. In the capital, the suspect regularly changed hotel addresses," the SBU said.
Also, when leaving her room, the suspect, according to the SBU, left a mark on the door to detect whether unauthorized persons might be present inside.
"Later, the agent received coordinates from her handler in the Russian Federation for a cache in a forested park area of the capital, where she picked up a pistol and ammunition. SBU counterintelligence officers discovered the weapon during a search of the detainee’s hotel room," the statement said.
The special service also noted that a smartphone was seized from the suspect, which she used to contact her FSB handler. The Security Service has already established his identity.
SBU investigators notified the agent that she was suspected under Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (high treason committed under martial law). The offender is being held in custody without the right to bail. She faces life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

World could warm 3.25C by 2100 under current policies, Swiss-German study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:46:44 UTC
19:46:44 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
22 September 2026•Update: 22 September 2026
Global temperatures could rise by around 3.25C (5.85F) by the end of the century under current policies, making Switzerland's most severe official climate scenario increasingly likely, according to research from Switzerland and Germany.
The study, conducted by researchers at ETH Zurich and Leipzig University suggests that previous climate projections may have underestimated future warming, Swissinfo reported Tuesday.
"For any emission trajectory without immediate and drastic emission cuts, we expect warming to be 25% higher," said Gergana Gyuleva, a doctoral researcher at ETH Zurich and lead author of the study.
"What happens in a 3C (5.4F) world isn't changed by our results. Our results only change how soon or how likely this 3C world becomes," she said.
The findings have particular implications for Switzerland, which is warming faster than the global average. A world that is 3C warmer than pre-industrial levels would translate into roughly 4.9C (8.82F) of warming in Switzerland.
The country's hottest summer on record offered a glimpse of such conditions. Basel recorded 58 days above 30C (86.5F), compared with 41 in 2003; Bern had 46 compared with 29, while Zurich had 38 compared with 27.
The scenarios published by MeteoSwiss and ETH Zurich last November project about 30 days with temperatures above 30C for the Zurich area in a typical summer under a 3C warming scenario.
Researchers revised their projections by accounting for natural climate variability and satellite measurements of Earth's energy imbalance — the difference between incoming solar energy and heat radiated back into space.
The study also estimates that the remaining global carbon budget is around one-fifth smaller than previous models suggested.
"Our results point to the need for faster mitigation for a given temperature target," Gyuleva said.
Researchers stressed that the higher warming scenario is not inevitable, saying that severe emissions reductions could substantially limit future warming.

Remains of 127 Polish and German soldiers exhumed at Holoskivskyi Cemetery in Lviv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:46:00 UTC
19:46:00 KST

Remains of 127 Polish and German soldiers exhumed at Holoskivskyi Cemetery in Lviv
Lubomyr Horbach, head of the “Pamiat” Society for the Search for War Victims, told Ukrinform in an exclusive interview.
“We are completing the work of locating and exhuming the remains buried in the first row. The work is already 90% complete. As of today, we have exhumed the remains of 110 Polish Army soldiers and 11 servicemen of the 1st Mountain Division of the German Wehrmacht,” Horbach said.
According to the searcher, the remains of six more German servicemen were discovered over the past few days. Two identification tags were found with them, which will help with their identification.
“The burial pits where we found the remains of the German soldiers had been partially destroyed because, during the Soviet era, water pipes were laid in this area and the site was dug up. As a result, the human skeletons were damaged. But generally speaking, the condition of the burials at Holoskivskyi Cemetery is good. Because the soil in this area has low acidity, even the smallest details, such as finger phalanges, have been preserved. When soil acidity is high, as I have encountered in the Carpathians, a significant portion of the remains can be lost,” Horbach added.
Search and exhumation work at Holoskivskyi Cemetery is proceeding according to schedule.
“In the middle of the first row, a memorial cross was installed. Since there are also burials beneath it—approximately five or six graves—we are removing the concrete slab and the cross today in order to exhume the remains. After that, we will put the site in order. At the same time, the anthropologists will continue their work: they are cleaning the bones, collecting samples for DNA testing, and examining associated items,” Horbach said.
Over the past several days, the searchers also surveyed the cemetery grounds to determine whether there was a fourth row of graves.
“We dug five exploratory trenches parallel to the third row, but we did not find anything,” Horbach added.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, about 30 specialists from Ukraine and Poland, on August 25, began search and exhumation work at Holoskivskyi Cemetery in Lviv. The work will continue until October 2. The exhumation research is being conducted pursuant to agreements reached following the work of the Ukrainian-Polish Working Group on National Remembrance.
On the Ukrainian side, the search and exhumation work is being carried out by a team from the “Pamiat” Society for the Search for War Victims; on the Polish side, by employees of the Institute of National Remembrance of the Republic of Poland and Wroclaw Medical University.
According to the results of searches conducted in 2010 and 2019, 110–120 individual graves of Polish Army soldiers were found in the cemetery. They were killed in battles against German military formations that surrounded Lviv from the west and south in September 1939.

====================================================================================================

Greece’s Israeli defence shield could be its very own Achilles’ heel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:45:50 UTC
19:45:50 KST

Last month, Greece signed an air and missile defence agreement with Israel in Tel Aviv worth more than €3 billion, placing one of the largest defence bets in its history.
Named the ‘Shield of Achilles’, the project aims to turn the air defence architecture of the Aegean and the Eastern Mediterranean into a single digital network woven together by the David's Sling, Barak MX, Spyder and MMR systems.
According to the government, it will reach full operational readiness within 35 months.
Yet by entrusting the nerve centre of its national security to a foreign state, Athens has chosen to disregard both the sharp objections rising from its own public and a murky network of actors entangled in a spyware scandal.
Borrowed from Homer's epics, the name may evoke the image of a powerful shield.
What has actually emerged, however, tells a more fragile story: a system whose money is Greek, whose name is Greek, but whose brain is entirely Israeli.
Who holds control?
The most striking feature of the agreement is that Greek industry's share of the project remains at around a meagre 25 percent.
A substantial portion of the radars, the command-and-control software, the missiles and the sensor systems will be supplied by Israeli companies; the new national command-and-control system will be developed under Rafael's lead.
Israel's Ministry of Defence has officially said that the system will be built on "Israeli architecture", laying that dependence bare.
For a country to tie the software backbone of its air defence so tightly to another state's supply chain raises the question of how far Athens can preserve its own say over its systems in a moment of crisis.
That question has been raised from within Greek domestic politics.
In a statement released on the day of the signing, the opposition SYRIZA argued that the New Democracy government was deepening Greece's military dependence on the administration of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is the subject of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant.
It also stressed that signing the agreement through a direct intergovernmental procurement had removed it from public scrutiny, and that the bill had been passed to Greek taxpayers.
The Communist Party of Greece (KKE) called the agreement "dangerous", warning that preparations for war were accelerating.
According to Nea Aristera's calculation, once the €650 million allocated to the Israeli-made PULS rocket system is added, the total bill reaches €3.75 billion.
The same statement noted that the missiles, the radars and the software of the system are Israeli, while only the money and the name are Greek, adding that it would be more accurate to call the project "Netanyahu's Shield".
The opposition's shared emphasis converges on one point: in a period of fiscal strain, billions of euros in spending were approved with transparency mechanisms switched off.
The transparency problem is not confined to the opposition's general rhetoric. It rests on a concrete contradiction.
In a formal parliamentary question and request for documents submitted to Defence Minister Nikos Dendias, PASOK MP Mihalis Katrinis asked the government to explain the cost of the Shield of Achilles, the role of Greek companies in the project and the national control of the central command and control system.
The questions went unanswered.
Lost source code
Before long, the source code question moved from theory to a concrete contradiction.
In an interview with the newspaper Kathimerini, Moshe Patel, head of the Israel Missile Defence Organisation, was asked whether Greece would have access to the source code associated with command and control capabilities.
His answer was plain: "No. Because the source code was not part of the usage licence agreement."
The sentence he added immediately afterwards revealed the nature of the dependence: they were there to provide support and maintenance, and they would provide whatever support and maintenance might be needed in the future.
Soon the interview itself became the subject of a transparency dispute. In the newspaper's online version, the question and answer on the source code were absent from the initial publication, although they appeared in the print edition.
The online version was later updated following backlash on social media, with the question and answer added alongside updated information from Israel's Ministry of Defence.
Patel's statement directly contradicted the assurance Dendias gave on July 23, when he said that, apart from very specific exceptions, the Greek Armed Forces would not purchase any system without its source code. Dendias had repeated that pledge openly on August 30, just a day before the signing.
Four MPs from Nea Aristera also demanded that the text of the contract, including the terms of access, intervention and oversight for the command and control system, be submitted to parliament.
Main opposition leader Nikos Androulakis addressed Prime Minister Mitsotakis directly in the middle of the dispute: "In the end, are we held hostage or not? Do we have access to the source code or not? The Prime Minister himself must answer this question today."
As public pressure mounted, Israel's Ministry of Defence issued a different statement on September 8, arguing that Greek companies would develop their own "Greek source code" and that it would remain entirely under Greek control.
That statement, however, only sharpened the attacks, as it became apparent that Greece would receive only the code for the interconnection software that links the Israeli-made systems.
The source code of the systems themselves, such as SPYDER, BARAK MX and David's Sling, remains out of its reach.
This is precisely where the critical distinction lies. Owning a system's source code and owning the code of the central software that links different weapons systems together do not amount to the same authority.
Athens will control the code of the layer that binds them, while remaining without access to the internal software of the weapons systems that make up the shield. Who will hold the system's cryptographic keys and control its network connections in a moment of crisis remains unclear.
The nature of the statement is also notable. The text in question was not a communiqué published on the official website of Israel's Ministry of Defence, but merely a note conveyed to the media by the press office.
The only official announcement still posted on the ministry's website remains the one dated August 31, which makes no mention of transferring any source code to Greece.
Another detail Patel gave in the same interview further narrows the limits of autonomy: David's Sling's ability to connect with other systems is subject to Washington's approval, owing to the American stake in the programme.
Nor did the debate end there. The government's silence in response to Nea Aristera's demand was partially broken.
Yet the contradiction deepened: Deputy Defence Minister Athanasios Davakis and the parliamentary rapporteur, New Democracy MP Yorgos Amyras, stated in successive announcements that the source code would be "Greek" and would remain "under full Greek control".
These statements do not clarify the scope of Dendias's pledge. The distance remains between the interconnection code described by the Israeli side and the system source code Dendias pointed to, and Dendias has so far made no new statement explaining that difference.
Indeed, on September 18, the KKE posed a fresh parliamentary question to Dendias, stating that it still remained unanswered who holds operational and technical control of the command and control system, and that even if a "Greek code" is produced for the central layer, this alone does not resolve the question of autonomy over the system as a whole.
It asked for the contract to be brought before the plenary of parliament with all its annexes.
This uncertainty over the scope of the source code shows that Athens cannot give its own people a clear and definite answer on the most critical element of the system it is paying for.
Names left in the shadows
Another uncomfortable shadow falls over the debate on dependence and transparency: allegations of a link between the Israeli defence network behind the Shield of Achilles and the Predator spyware scandal that has shaken Greece for years.
Predator is spyware developed by the North Macedonia-based Cytrox and later marketed under Intellexa.
A court ruling established that the phones of at least 87 people in Greece were surveilled with this software, including ministers, senior military officers, journalists, and civil society figures.
In February 2026, an Athens court found Israeli citizen Tal Dilian, who marketed the software, and three others guilty of violating the privacy of telephone communications, sentencing each of them to 126 years and eight months in prison. Under Greek law, the term actually to be served for these offences is capped at eight years, and the ruling is pending appeal.
Moreover, the Predator surveillance scandal is a separate controversy in its own right, given the Mitsotakis government's political responsibility and the surveillance of individuals, including members of the opposition.
The truly contentious claim is that there are points of intersection between the figures in this scandal and the names negotiating the Shield of Achilles agreement.
According to an investigation published by the Greek outlet Pronews, Stavros Komnopoulos, founder of Kestrel SA and the Greek representative of Israel's Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and Aeronautics Defense Systems, is alleged to have provided housing in Athens in 2020 to Rotem Farkash, the developer of Predator, with the rental guarantee provided through a company belonging to his nephew.
The same report notes that Komnopoulos's name does not appear anywhere in the final report of the prosecutorial investigation, which has been interpreted as an attempt at a cover-up.
This uncertainty alone constitutes a serious problem. That suspicions this grave can circulate in public around the intermediaries and representatives of a €3 billion national security agreement indicates how poorly the government has performed on transparency.
If Athens considers these allegations baseless, it must clarify why the prosecutor's report makes no reference to these names at all. Otherwise, the suspicion will continue to leave a more lasting mark than the shield itself.
The threat pretext
The Greek government is ignoring these striking allegations as it tries to shift public focus elsewhere, repeating the same sentence each time: the need for deterrence against regional threats, and above all against Türkiye.
Through this rhetoric, the Mitsotakis government is both seeking votes in next year's elections and showing its domestic audience only the part it wants them to see, while the root of the problem lies in Athens's unilateral and maximalist claims.
Greece has long maintained maximalist claims in the Aegean and the Eastern Mediterranean that are incompatible with international law, and it has not refrained from building hostile alliances directed against Türkiye.
These include the extension of territorial waters in the Aegean to 12 nautical miles, the claim to 10 nautical miles of national airspace, the approach that FIR responsibility confers sovereign authority on Greece, the militarisation of islands with demilitarised status, claims of sovereignty over islands, islets and rocks whose sovereignty was never ceded to Greece and which Türkiye designates as EGAYDAAK, and search and rescue activities.
Athens also ties the Aegean disputes to European security language. On his most recent visit to Meis (Kastellorizo), whose demilitarised status Greece violates, Mitsotakis emphasised that the island's soil is "European soil", which shows a desire to pull bilateral problems with Türkiye onto the Türkiye-EU axis.
The "Turkish threat" narrative is turning into a convenient armour that conceals this aggressive foreign policy line and constructs an image of victimhood before international opinion. Athens presents the tension it itself builds as grounds to take shelter behind a shield.
Seen through this lens, the Shield of Achilles serves as a justification that lends legitimacy to an armament and alliance strategy already in force.
In the end, what lies before Greece is an example of layered fragility. In trying to protect itself against imagined external threats through this project it calls the ‘Shield of Achilles’, Athens appears to have produced a new security vulnerability by sacrificing domestic political oversight and institutional transparency.
Homer's hero Achilles lost his strength through the single weak point in his heel. Only time will tell whether Greece's modern shield has a similar weakness, and perhaps at the most critical moment.

China tightens control on more fentanyl precursors ahead of Xi-Trump meeting
Two more chemicals added to export control list days after US president calls for ‘more aggressive action’
China tightened its controls on the export of fentanyl precursors to the United States, Canada and Mexico, adding two new chemicals to its list requiring export licences on Tuesday, one day ahead of President Xi Jinping’s announced visit to the US.
China’s Ministry of Commerce, together with four other government agencies, added two N-phenethyl piperidine esters to part one of China’s Catalogue for the Administration of Exports of Precursor Chemicals to Specific Countries (Regions), according to a statement from the ministry.
The list now includes 18 chemicals, all of which could be used in fentanyl production. The licensing requirement for these substances applies only to North America, with a separate section covering 41 chemicals bound for Myanmar, Laos and Afghanistan.
The news came on the day before Xi is set to depart for the US on his highly anticipated state visit. Fentanyl has been a core issue in US-China trade negotiations since the Trump administration returned to power last year.

Ukrainian defence forces units have destroyed more than 350,000 Russian drones since the beginning of 2026.
Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Defence
Details: The ministry said all the strikes were recorded on video in the DELTA battlefield situational awareness system. and verified by the Brave1 defence innovation cluster.

A strange circle on satellite maps turned out to be a 390-million-year-old impact crater
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:43:31 UTC
19:43:31 KST

A strange circle on satellite maps turned out to be a 390-million-year-old impact crater
- Date:
- September 22, 2026
- Source:
- NASA Earth Observatory
- Summary:
- An amateur astronomer searching satellite maps for a Quebec camping spot accidentally discovered a massive ancient impact crater. Scientists later found shatter cones that confirmed the 25-kilometer-wide structure was blasted into Earth roughly 390 million years ago.
- Share:
An amateur astronomer searching satellite maps for possible camping locations in Quebec ended up spotting something far more unusual: evidence of a previously unrecognized impact crater.
Earth has only about 200 confirmed impact structures, although geologists believe hundreds more have yet to be identified. One of those hidden structures now appears to have been found, and it is a substantial one. The newly confirmed site was first noticed by an amateur astronomer who was planning a camping trip in Quebec.
A Strange Circle on Satellite Maps
In 2024, Joël Lapointe was preparing for a trip to the remote Côte-Nord region when a circular feature near Lake Marsal caught his attention on online satellite imagery. He wondered whether the depression could have been formed by an impact and reached out to specialists in Europe and North America.
Lapointe's inquiry helped prompt a group of French researchers to identify the lake area as the center of a potential 11th known impact structure in Quebec at a 2024 meeting of the Meteoritical Society. The possibility eventually drew the attention of Gordon Osinski, a planetary geologist at Western University who also directs the Impact Earth database.
Osinski was skeptical at first, but the possibility was intriguing enough that he organized an expedition to the isolated location in October 2025.
A Difficult Journey Into the Quebec Wilderness
Reaching the site proved challenging almost immediately. Osinski and his colleagues flew in by floatplane, but the aircraft could not make it all the way to shore. Carrying their equipment, the team had to wade through 50 meters (165 feet) of water before reaching land.
Conditions did not improve once they arrived. The landscape was rugged and swampy, filled with insects and dense vegetation that Osinski described as "deep, twisty, gnarly vegetation." Despite years of fieldwork across six continents, he said the area ranked among the most difficult environments he had ever worked in.
Earlier geological surveys had interpreted the local breccia rocks as evidence of a funnel-shaped volcanic structure called a diatreme, which forms when explosive magma eruptions create a pipe filled with shattered rock.
By the expedition's second day, however, the team began finding something far more decisive.
Shatter Cones Reveal an Ancient Impact
Researchers discovered shatter cones in numerous rock outcrops. These distinctive structures form under the intense pressures produced during an impact and provided compelling evidence that the feature was not volcanic after all.
"It's the only unequivocal evidence of an impact event that you can see in the field with the naked eye," Osinski said.
The object responsible for the collision was powerful enough to produce a complex crater structure measuring about 25 kilometers (16 miles) across. The site includes a central uplift as well as high cliffs displaying columnar jointing.
A comparable impact in modern Quebec would have enormous consequences. Osinski said it would cause "regional devastation on a scale that would wipe out major cities and have global climate impacts."
A Crater About 390 Million Years Old
Analysis of rock samples suggests the crater formed roughly 390 million years ago. That places the impact around 100 million years before a major increase in cratering on Earth that researchers have suggested may be connected to collisions within the asteroid belt.
Following discussions with the Innu Council of Ekuanitshit, the researchers are referring to the crater as Uhackatik.
The team considers the impact origin essentially confirmed, although a Meteoritical Society committee is expected to provide formal recognition when it next meets.
Uhackatik is the largest impact crater discovered since the 31-kilometer Hiawatha structure was found in 2018.
Too Remote for Astronaut Training
Osinski is part of NASA's first Artemis Geology Team and helps train astronauts in geology. Even so, he does not expect Uhackatik to become an astronaut training site because reaching it is so difficult.
A younger and much more accessible impact crater in Labrador, Kameshtashtan (also called Mistastin Lake), has already hosted astronauts for geology training in the past, he said.
An Amateur Observation Leads to a Major Discovery
For Lapointe, alerting scientists to the crater has become an unforgettable experience. He told CityNews that he was "over the Moon" when researchers confirmed that the feature really was an impact crater.
"I encourage everyone to not ignore intuition or an observation, even if it isn't part of your field of expertise," he told another outlet.
Citizen Scientists Can Join the Search
People interested in contributing to scientific discoveries have many opportunities through NASA citizen science programs.
The Daily Minor Planet project allows volunteers to help search for asteroids and comets that could potentially pose a threat to Earth. Through Impact Flash, participants can examine dark regions of the Moon for flashes produced by meteoroid strikes. The Exoasteroids project gives citizen scientists the chance to look for evidence of asteroids beyond our Solar System.
Story Source:
Materials provided by NASA Earth Observatory. Original written by Adam Voiland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Could 1948 Palestinian political parties shape Israel elections?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:43:30 UTC
19:43:30 KST

Breadcrumb
Could 1948 Palestinian political parties shape Israel's upcoming elections?
As the Israeli election approaches, the importance of political parties and voters from the 1948 Palestinian community is increasing ahead of the election scheduled for 27 October, particularly amid a close race between the current far-right governing coalition and the opposition, as neither side has secured a majority to form a government.
Historically, Palestinian political parties have remained outside the circle of Israeli coalition and government formation.
This is partly because Zionist parties have excluded them from the political legitimacy framework for participating in government.
It is also because these Palestinian parties have not viewed themselves as partners in governments responsible for policies of occupation and killing against Palestinians, discriminatory policies towards 1948 Palestinian citizens, and operating within the self-declared definition of Israel as a "Jewish and democratic" state.
Another factor has been the ability of Israeli parties, over decades, to form governing coalitions without needing the support of Palestinian parties.
The emergence of Palestinian parties
One of the most prominent cases in which parliamentary support from Palestinian parties became decisive to a government's survival came in 1993.
After Shas withdrew from the government of Yitzhak Rabin, it lost its parliamentary majority; the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality and the Arab Democratic Party provided what became known as a "safety net" for the government from outside the coalition.
This came in exchange for understandings that included increased budgets allocated to the 1948 Palestinian community, reducing some aspects of discrimination in government policies, and addressing several civic demands from Palestinians holding Israeli citizenship.
However, this began to change over the last decade and became apparent during the 2019 election, amid shifts in the Israeli party landscape and patterns of Palestinian party representation that increased the weight of Palestinian voters and the role of Palestinian parties.
First, this shift followed the formation of a joint list by Palestinian parties in 2015 to contest the Knesset election, after the electoral threshold for entering the Knesset was raised from 2% to 3.25%.
This raised concerns at the time that these lists, if they contested the election separately, would be unable to cross the threshold.
The Joint List won 13 seats in that election, the highest representation achieved by Arab parties in the Knesset up to that point.
Second, the shift resulted from the sharp division that emerged in the Israeli political map from the 2019 election between the camp led by Benjamin Netanyahu, which included right-wing, religious and far-right parties, and the camp opposing him.
Both camps failed in more than one election to secure a parliamentary majority by relying solely on parties from their own camp, increasing the political weight of seats.
Parties in successive elections
This political crisis led to five elections between 2019 and 2022, most of which failed to produce a political resolution.
During this period, the Joint List underwent repeated changes.
It broke apart shortly before the April 2019 election, with Palestinian parties contesting the election in two separate lists.
It was then reconstituted ahead of the September election that year, winning 13 seats.
In the March 2020 election, the list achieved an unprecedented result by winning 15 seats, the highest parliamentary representation achieved by a list in the history of Knesset elections.
However, this achievement did not prevent renewed internal disputes.
The United Arab List (the Southern Islamic Movement), led by Mansour Abbas, withdrew from the Joint List shortly before the March 2021 election.
The split came against the backdrop of a political and strategic dispute over the role of these parties in the Israeli political system.
Abbas adopted an approach based on a willingness to negotiate and cooperate with either of the two Israeli camps, including the Benjamin Netanyahu camp, in exchange for, what he describes, as achieving civic and economic demands for the community.
The United Arab List believes that the most important aspect of parliamentary work is exercising influence and achieving gains and everyday livelihood demands for the community.
The other components of the Joint List, however, rejected this approach at the time, viewing it as crossing the political boundaries that should govern relations with the Israeli right, particularly the far right.
Indeed, the 2021 election resulted in the formation of a government led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, which included the United Arab List, in a first-of-its-kind precedent for an independent party to formally participate in an Israeli governing coalition.
The government became known as the "change government" but lasted only about a year before collapsing, the Knesset was dissolved, and a new election was held.
In the 2022 election, competing Arab parties contested the election in three lists: the United Arab List (the Southern Islamic Movement), an alliance between the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality and the Arab Movement for Renewal; and the National Democratic Assembly, which contested the election separately.
This came after the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality and the Arab Movement for Renewal withdrew, on the night the lists were submitted, from a partnership agreement signed with the National Democratic Assembly to contest the election on a joint list.
The Assembly was consequently forced to contest the election alone but failed to cross the electoral threshold.
The election, meanwhile, resulted in Netanyahu returning to power after his camp secured a clear majority and formed a right-wing religious coalition with 64 Knesset members.
The 2022 election therefore once again showed that the way 1948 Palestinian parties contest elections, particularly the risk of votes being lost because of failure to cross the electoral threshold, can directly affect the balance of power between Israeli camps.
These parties failed to overcome their differences and reconstitute a joint list including all their components for the 2026 election. Instead, they are contesting the current election on two main lists.
Three parties, the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, the National Democratic Assembly, and the Arab Movement for Renewal, have united under the "Joint List", while the United Arab List is contesting the election independently.
In an unprecedented move in its history, the United Arab List has included a Jewish candidate in a prominent position on its list: Yoav Segalovich, who served as deputy minister of internal security in the "change government" and was a Knesset member for the Yesh Atid party.
The move has been interpreted as an attempt by the United Arab List to broaden its acceptance within the opposition camp and strengthen prospects for cooperation with it in the post-election period, particularly if the opposition manages to form the next government and needs the list's support or participation in the coalition.
The existence of two lists does not simply reflect an organisational disagreement or competition over the ordering of seats.
It reflects two significantly different views of the role of Palestinian and Arab representation in Israeli politics.
The United Arab List adheres to an approach based on seeking to exercise influence from within the Israeli political camp system, using its parliamentary strength to negotiate over government formation or participate in government in exchange for budgets, decisions and civic gains for the community.
In the current election, following the experience of participating in the governing coalition in 2021, Mansour Abbas, head of the United Arab List, has announced his alignment with the opposition camp, setting two stated goals: bringing down the Netanyahu government and contributing to the formation of an alternative government.
The Joint List, meanwhile, does not rule out influencing the identity of the next government.
It has explicitly stated that one of its goals is to bring down the right-wing government and contribute, as far as possible, to preventing its return and forming an alternative government.
Some components of the Joint List also do not rule out, in principle, providing a "safety net" for a government led by opposition parties from outside the coalition if specific political conditions are met and understandings are reached that include political and civic demands related to the community and the Palestinian cause.
In this respect, the Joint List position differs from that of the United Arab List in that the former does not make participation in the governing coalition a goal in itself.
Instead, it raises the possibility of conditional influence from outside while maintaining greater political independence from the Zionist camps.
Increasing turnout by the community
The two lists also place increasing turnout in the community at the top of their objectives, after turnout remained at around 60% in the last election, compared with a higher rate across Israeli society.
They argue that increased participation would directly increase the size of Arab representation in the Knesset and could automatically reduce the chances of the Netanyahu camp and the right reaching the majority needed to form a new government.
Given the current balance of power, the close projected share between the current governing coalition led by Netanyahu and the opposition camp, and the absence of a clear majority for either side, the scenario of Palestinian parties becoming a decisive factor in determining the identity of the next government is no longer merely hypothetical.
The United Arab List's support for the opposition camp alone may not be enough to form an alternative government.
Some components of the "Joint List" abstaining from voting against the new government could become necessary to enable it to win the Knesset confidence vote.
The question therefore shifts from the position of these parties alone to that of the opposition parties themselves.
If they do not have an independent parliamentary majority, would they be prepared to form a government relying on support from Palestinian parties, even if that support were limited to abstaining from voting against it in the confidence vote?
Or could they move towards reaching an understanding or political agreement with the United Arab List that guarantees its support for the new government?
This scenario is particularly important because winning confidence for a government does not necessarily require an absolute majority of 61 Knesset members.
It can instead be achieved by a majority in the parliamentary vote, giving abstention political importance that could become decisive if the camps are closely balanced.
The opposition parties could therefore face a practical test over the extent to which they are prepared to accept an actual Arab role in forming the government.
Eisenkot's options
The issue of the position and role of these parties is therefore no longer linked only to their own decision over whether to support or oppose a government.
It also extends to the candidate tasked with forming the government and the extent to which his camp is prepared to recognise the legitimacy of the Arab political role in the equation of power formation.
Gadi Eisenkot, the most prominent opposition candidate to form the next government, had announced that he would not approach Palestinian parties after the election to seek their support for forming a governing coalition.
Instead, the decision would be in the hands of these parties themselves: either abstaining from voting against a government he leads in the confidence vote, supporting it from outside without joining the coalition, or opposing it, which could prevent the formation of an alternative government and allow Benjamin Netanyahu to remain in power.
At this stage, the position reflects Eisenkot's desire to avoid giving the Netanyahu camp additional campaign material to accuse him of seeking to form a government dependent on Palestinian parties.
However, Netanyahu has already begun attacking him on this issue, claiming that Eisenkot is seeking to establish a government based on Palestinian parties that he describes as "supporters of terrorism".
Through this rhetoric, Netanyahu is seeking two parallel goals: to pre-emptively delegitimise any alternative government Eisenkot might form with direct or indirect Arab support and raise concerns among some Jewish voters about Palestinian parties becoming a decisive factor in determining the identity of the next government.
Therefore, relying on Arab parties has become a central tool in the election campaign, not merely as a debate over the nature of political partnership, but also as a means of mobilising right-wing voters against the opposition camp. The upcoming Knesset election will not only be decisive over the identity of the governing camp but also over the question of the legitimacy and possibility of 1948 Palestinian parties exercising influence.
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

In Ukraine, the harvesting of wheat, barley, peas and rapeseed has been completed — how much was harvested

In Ukraine, the harvesting of wheat, barley, peas and rapeseed has been completed — how much was harvested
Kyiv • UNN
Ukrainian farmers harvested 33 million tonnes of grain crops and 6 million tonnes of oilseeds. The largest grain harvests were recorded in Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk and Kirovohrad regions.
Ukrainian farmers have threshed 33 million tonnes of grain and leguminous crops and more than 6 million tonnes of oilseeds; the harvesting of wheat, barley, peas and rapeseed has been completed. This was reported by the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food, UNN writes.
As of September 22, farmers had harvested 7.01 million hectares, or 61% of the projected area. The gross harvest of grain and leguminous crops amounts to 33 million tonnes, with an average yield of 4.7 tonnes per hectare", the statement said
By major crop, the following has been harvested:
-  wheat – harvesting has been completed, with 25.31 million tonnes harvested from an area of 5.11 million hectares at an average yield of 4.95 tonnes per hectare; 
-  barley – harvesting has been completed, with 6.39 million tonnes harvested from an area of 1.48 million hectares at a yield of 4.33 tonnes per hectare; 
-  peas – harvesting has been completed, with 812,200 tonnes harvested from an area of 301,900 hectares at a yield of 2.69 tonnes per hectare; 
-  millet – 62,200 tonnes from an area of 26,900 hectares at a yield of 2.32 tonnes per hectare; 
-  buckwheat – 37,100 tonnes from an area of 26,600 hectares at a yield of 1.39 tonnes per hectare; 
-  corn – 339,800 tonnes from an area of 67,900 hectares at a yield of 5 tonnes per hectare. 
Farmers in the southern and central regions harvested the largest volumes of grain
Odesa region – 4.83 million tonnes of grain were harvested from an area of 1.19 million hectares. In particular, wheat – 3.22 million tonnes from 773,200 hectares, barley – 1.31 million tonnes from 308,700 hectares, peas – 294,000 tonnes from 106,900 hectares.
Dnipropetrovsk region – 2.72 million tonnes of grain were threshed from 663,300 hectares. In particular, wheat – 2.04 million tonnes from 462,900 hectares, barley – 574,600 tonnes from 159,100 hectares, peas – 37,000 tonnes from 16,200 hectares.
Kirovohrad region – the gross harvest amounts to 2.43 million tonnes from an area of 561,000 hectares. A total of 1.92 million tonnes of wheat was threshed from 426,400 hectares, barley – 412,500 tonnes from 98,000 hectares, peas – 82,000 tonnes from 31,300 hectares.
The highest average grain yield was recorded at farms in Khmelnytskyi region (7.06 tonnes per hectare), Sumy region (6.06 tonnes per hectare) and Kyiv region (5.58 tonnes per hectare).
Farmers are also continuing to harvest late-season and industrial crops:
-  rapeseed – harvesting has been completed, with 3.857 million tonnes threshed from an area of 1.33 million hectares at a yield of 2.9 tonnes per hectare;  
-  sunflower – 1.5 million tonnes threshed from an area of 756,200 hectares, or 14% of the projected area, at a yield of 1.98 tonnes per hectare; 
-  soybeans – 655,400 tonnes harvested from an area of 327,600 hectares, or 21% of the projected area, at a yield of 2 tonnes per hectare; 
-  sugar beets – 19,300 tonnes harvested from an area of 450 hectares at a yield of 42.89 tonnes per hectare.

Kremlin says UN Security Council should add new permanent members, keep veto power that Erdogan urged scrapping
MOSCOW, Sept 22 - Russia believes the UN Security Council should expand its number of permanent members beyond the current five, and that the existing veto system should remain, the Kremlin said on Tuesday.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was responding to a question from reporters about Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan's call to abolish both permanent membership and the veto.

Is a Home Security System Subscription Worth It? (2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:36:00 UTC
19:36:00 KST

No one wants to worry about a break-in. But no one wants to end up paying fees every month just to check their video doorbell feed or find out their window was broken, and most smart security systems (even the original ones that weren't touted as smart!) rely on your fear to have you paying month after month for the promise of catching burglars and stopping intruders for you.
These systems do work, and they can give you a lot of peace of mind. This comes with a hefty price tag, though, and plenty of people would be more than happy with a system they build themselves sans monthly fees. If you're not interested in a system that will call the police or fire department if you don't respond fast enough to something that turns out to be minor, or don't want to have strangers looking through your security cameras at your property, I'm here to help with that.
This guide collects a handful of our favorite smart home security accessories that won't paywall you left and right, and will give you local storage options for video so you aren't locked into the cloud. This way you can build the system that works for you. Here's everything I recommend if you want smart home security without the subscriptions.
What Exactly Is a Smart Home Security System?
Smart security systems can look like whatever you want, in my opinion, but there are a lot of starter kits you've probably seen. Smart-home brands like Abode and SimpliSafe have starter packs you've likely seen before with motion sensors, door sensors, and security hubs that sound an alarm when one of those sensors is triggered.
But smart home security can go way beyond that. Most systems let you add on cameras and even video doorbells to monitor movement around your home and catch people at your door who shouldn't be there. (This is also a handy way to know when it’s a package delivery or another random salesperson.) These systems are usually modular and customizable, whether you DIY or go with a brand. Overall, the goal is to protect and monitor your home through motion sensors and video feeds.
Home security brands usually have various subscription options and some kind of self-monitored, subscription-free tier, but you usually lose out on a variety of features to encourage you to subscribe.
What Do Smart Home Security Systems and a Subscription Get You?
I remember running into the issue of paywalled features for the first time a few years ago when I was testing Abode's smart lock. I liked the lock, but I woke up to unclear notifications that happened in the dead of night. Had the lock been hacked? Had it sensed itself being manually opened when we were asleep? There was no way to tell because Abode’s base level would only tell me the lock was interacted with without explaining how. I signed up for the Abode membership that day to be able to review the events, and luckily it was just a loss of Wi-Fi connection and reestablishment that happened within a minute of each other. Crisis averted.
The main thing that subscription services paywall is video storage, which allows you to review past events at your home. Sometimes it can also be notifications, whether that's the type of notification or the ability to review notification history. What is or is not paywalled largely depends on the brand and its offerings. Professional live monitoring, however, is almost always paywalled, whether that's an agent calling police when an alarm has been triggered or an agent reviewing flagged footage (e.g., motion alerts) to either notify you of a situation or call emergency services on your behalf. That’s one thing you can't DIY—if you’re on vacation or otherwise not able to call police if there's an issue, you're out of luck.
Base stations from home security companies like ADT, SimpliSafe, and Vivint will act as a smart-home hub to connect and control sensors and other devices, and be able to sound an alarm. It might have a keypad that you can use to arm and disarm the system too.
A lot of subscription services also have a higher tier that gives you an on-staff specialist who will review live footage if a camera is triggered, or even use the microphone to speak to an intruder. It's a useful feature if it's something you're worried about, but those subscriptions can cost as much as a casual grocery trip each month.
Do You Need a Smart Home Security System Starter Kit?
You don't need a formal, branded home security kit to protect your home, but if you're interested in window and motion sensors that will trigger and sound an alarm, you might want one. You can buy a kit and even have a brand representative come and install the devices for you. (But as someone who's seen the bill for those, I'd recommend installing everything yourself, since it has to be connected to your phone and personal accounts anyway.)
If you're just looking to know who's at your door, get alerted when a window is opened, or prove you have trespassers with video footage, DIY-ing your own system with a handful of devices that fit the needs you're looking for is a fine solution. Personally, I worry most about my front door, while someone else might worry about trespassers in their backyard. Buying accessories à la carte allows you to get exactly what you want without paying extra.
Best Subscription-Free Security Devices to Build Your Own System
Smart locks are my most-used smart-home item by far. Having a smart lock makes it so easy for my entire family to access our home, including my 4-year-old, who has memorized the code. Smart locks make it easy to confirm your door is locked when it should be, and you can see the access history to know who's opening it and when. These are two of my favorite options that don't require any sort of subscription to get event history in an app, but you will need to buy a separate Wi-Fi hub or bridge for both if you want remote access. However, that's a one-time purchase instead of a forever one.
Most video doorbells have a no-subscription option, but you'll usually lose out on video storage, so you can't scroll back and see what happened when an alert went off. You'll also miss out on some notification types and features like package detection. I think doorbells and video cameras are impacted the most by the loss of features without a subscription, since so many then lose the ability to show you what happened that day or who rang the bell. These video doorbells below get around that with local storage options, so your footage is saved to a microSD card rather than the cloud. However, if you don't properly secure the camera, you could lose the footage and camera both, since all data is stored in the device.
Similar to video doorbells, you'll often run into subscription fees for security cameras in order to store footage in the cloud and review it. Instead, choose one of these cameras for the inside or outside of your home that allows local storage, so you can live subscription-free. We've got a whole guide to subscription-free security cameras if you want more options. Again, make sure the camera is secured so you don't lose the camera and footage in one go.
Motion sensors are a primary feature of most smart home security kits, but they usually don't need a subscription fee to work—when a sensor is triggered, the base station will sound an alarm. The subscription really just allows for an agent to call your local authorities if the alarm sounds; otherwise, you'll just get a notification on your phone to find out if someone's where they shouldn't be.
If you're looking for motion sensors that will activate smart-home features like turning on a switch when you walk by, these aren't it. These are designed to set off an immediate alarm when any motion is detected. Check out our guide to the Best Motion Sensors for more ideas there.
This is another popular feature of smart home security kits. It's great for getting an alert on a door that doesn't have a smart lock, or wouldn't be regularly locked. Even better for windows or sliding doors that have no other way to alert you if they're opened.
I haven't tested these yet, but I've tested other products from these brands and have liked the experience, and share more about both below. They're next on my testing list for this story.

Tenth body found in South Africa amid hunt for culprit
A tenth woman’s body has been found dead in South Africa’s Gauteng province amid a series of suspected serial killings, local media reported on Monday, citing police.
The corpse of the unidentified woman, believed to be in her 20s, was discovered in a dam in Moroka, Soweto, at around 5 PM on September 20. Her body had been wrapped in a duvet, according to a police statement aired by SABC.
South African Deputy National Police Commissioner Tebello Mosikili confirmed the discovery of the tenth body on Monday as authorities continue to investigate the deaths of nine women found in neighboring Ekurhuleni since July. Police have not established whether the latest case is connected to the previous ones.
“Behind every one of these women is a human being, a family and a life that mattered. We owe it to them to find the truth. We owe it to their families to pursue justice,” South African Police Service (SAPS) said in a statement.
The series of killings has raised concerns that a serial killer could be operating in the area. Police, however, have cautioned against drawing conclusions while investigations are ongoing.
A multidisciplinary team of detectives, forensic experts and criminal profilers has been assigned to the cases. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has directed that the investigation must receive the “highest level of attention” from the government and law enforcement agencies.
The nine women in Ekurhuleni were found between July 15 and September 17 in areas including Kempton Park, Olifantsfontein, Kwa-Thema and Dawn Park. The government said eight of the nine had been identified as of September 20. The first body was discovered near the R21 highway in Kempton Park. The 37-year-old victim was found naked and restrained with cable ties.
The ninth victim, Jabulile Ntimba, was found in Dawn Park on September 17. Police arrested two women and a man in connection with her killing over the weekend.

Tato Architects completes charred timber-clad home in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:30:46 UTC
19:30:46 KST

Tato Architects completes charred timber-clad home in Japan
Charred-timber cladding is contrasted with warm plywood-lined interiors at House in Mibu, a home in Tochigi Prefecture, Japan, completed by local studio Tato Architects.
The 108-square-metre home was designed for a couple and their three children in the backyard of the client's parental home, tucked off a residential street in the town of Mibu.
As the site needed to accommodate access to an existing garage and workshop, Kobe-based Tato Architects aimed to balance "enclosure and openness" in its design.
According to the studio, this is reflected in the final layout where the first floor overhangs on one side, and the ground floor is sunk 500 millimetres below ground and partially topped with a sloped green roof.
"The core concept is what Dutch architect Aldo van Eyck called the 'in-between' – a realm where enclosure and openness are experienced at once," studio founder Yo Shimada told Dezeen.
"The challenge was to add a whole house without making the yard feel crowded or cutting off the life already flowing through it. Rather than treating these as constraints, we let them shape the building," Shimada continued.
"We sank the living room into the ground and planted its roof with grass: sinking into the earth encloses, touching the earth opens, and the two appear as faces of a single operation."
House in Mibu is entered beneath the overhang of the first floor, where a welcome area with a cloakroom and bathroom steps down into a sunken living, dining and kitchen area.
Full-height windows wrap this lower space to the west, aiming to emphasise its close relationship to the ground while offering views into the neighbouring workshop.
A pair of timber and green-painted steel staircases lead up through a rectilinear void to the home's first floor, where the bedrooms are organised on either side of a raised, loft-like space that can serve as a study or guest room.
The lines of sight created by these stepped levels define the home's interiors, along with walls and ceilings lined entirely in lauan plywood, which Shimada chose for its ability to "record use and age gracefully".
"Sitting in the living room, the ground of the garden spreads out almost at eye level, so family members working in the yard and those inside exchange glances across a slight shift in height," Shimada explained.
"The first floor is the counterpart: a nest-like composition of small rooms – three children's rooms and a bedroom – linked by two staircases, with a loft raised 690 millimetres above the floor that connects the rooms and doubles as a desk or a place to sleep."
Outside, the home is clad in planks of charred cedar and finished with a corrugated metal roof, chosen to nod to the character of the workshop building.
Other homes in Japan recently completed by Tato Architects include a dwelling with similarly open interiors and silver-painted ceilings that help maximise daylight on a compact plot, and a skinny home that is combined with a ceramics studio.
The photography is courtesy of Tato Architects.

Why United Nations says US boat strikes may be ‘crimes against humanity’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:30:42 UTC
19:30:42 KST

Why United Nations says US boat strikes may be ‘crimes against humanity’
Washington justifies the attacks as necessary to halt the flow of lethal drugs into the US.
A United Nations report has concluded that US strikes on alleged drug-trafficking boats in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific are illegal and could constitute “crimes against humanity”.
In a report published on Monday, UN Special Rapporteur Ben Saul said attacks on 68 vessels from September last year to August killed at least 223 people and entailed the “illegal use” of disproportionate force.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US strikes on alleged drug boats may be ‘crimes against humanity’, UN says
- list 2 of 4‘Handcuffed and blindfolded’: Is the US targeting Ecuadorian fishermen?
- list 3 of 4Ecuador defends US sinking of vessels as joint anti-drug operation
- list 4 of 4US announces $45m in security funding, additional naval vessels for Ecuador
The findings were released just days after the US military announced its latest attack on another boat, which killed four people. US President Donald Trump’s administration, which frames the operations against the boats as part of a military conflict, said they are necessary to prevent the flow of lethal drugs into the United States. It has described the drug shipments as an “armed attack” on US territory.
Here’s what we know about why the US has been attacking the boats and whether these strikes are legal:
What does the UN report say?
The report found that the strikes by US forces are unjustified under national and international law and thus amount to “serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life”.
They “plausibly constitute crimes against humanity”, it said.
Even if those attacked were found to be members of organised criminal or “terrorist” groups as the US has claimed, there is no evidence that they had launched an armed attack on the US or were being used as proxies by other countries, which would warrant a US military attack, the report noted.
Saul, the UN special rapporteur on counterterrorism and human rights, added that drug trafficking “is not equivalent to a military attack”.
Furthermore, observers have noted, the Trump administration has never provided any evidence that any of the boats it has struck were trafficking drugs.
The UN report also cast doubt over the legality of the US abduction of former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January, during which 75 people were killed, as well as collaborations with other Latin American countries under the Trump administration-initiated “Shield of the Americas”. The initiative seeks to extend US antidrug operations to land across the region.
The UN report called for internal investigations and for commanders involved in the operations to be held accountable.
It concluded that the strikes have failed to prevent the arrival of cocaine in the US on container ships. which are not adequately checked.
Why has the US launched strikes on boats?
Washington first began striking boats it claimed were trafficking drugs from Venezuela to the US across the Eastern Pacific and Caribbean in September last year.
The US military has routinely released videos on social media showing the moments the vessels are hit but has disclosed little about those killed and has not provided evidence tying them to drug trafficking.
Furthermore, experts said most drugs come into the US via Mexico by land through its southern border and do not originate in Venezuela. Families of those killed have often said they were fishermen and not drug smugglers.
The UN report listed 223 casualties from 68 strikes carried out through August.
Two additional attacks this month have raised the number of those killed to 234 in 70 strikes.
In the first set of attacks on September 2, 2025, the US military allegedly used a “double tap” tactic, launching a second attack to finish off the survivors of an initial strike. The first attacks killed 11 people.
The move drew intense criticism from the US Congress, which called for the Pentagon to release full videos of the strikes.
There were also allegations that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had given the order to “kill them all” in the double-tap strike. However, senior military commanders later testified in Congress that he did not.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Michael Vigil, former chief of international operations at the US Drug Enforcement Administration, said: “That is murder. No matter how you spell it out, it’s murder, … and it shocks the moral conscience.”
How does the US justify the strikes?
The most recent attack on Saturday killed four people, according to the US military. It alleged that the boat was travelling “along established narco-trafficking routes” and “confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel’s active involvement in narco-trafficking”.
Trump has claimed the US is in an “armed conflict” with drug cartels and has repeatedly justified the boat attacks as necessary to halt the flow of drugs into the country.
Senior officials have also claimed the US is abiding by due process. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a Senate hearing in July that “every strike has a legal officer on the deck that has to make a determination about whether the call is legal or not”.
Rights organisations, however, have challenged the killings. In January, the families of two Trinidadian men – Chad Joseph, 26, and Rishi Samaroo, 41 – brought the first case against the US government over the boat attacks to a federal court in Massachusetts. The suit, aided by US legal groups, argued the victims were fishermen.
Separately in December, the family of Colombian Alejandro Carranza Medina filed a human rights complaint with the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, which is part of the Organization of American States.
Can any action be taken against US officials?
The term “crimes against humanity” implies that killings have been carried out systematically in accordance with a plan by a state or an organised group and are an especially serious crime.
Perpetrators accused of such crimes can be tried and convicted only before the International Criminal Court (ICC), which examines whether those carrying out attacks were aware that their actions targeted a civilian population and whether their actions resulted in the killing of multiple people.
US courts cannot try such cases because no specific federal laws criminalise crimes against humanity.
The US is not a member of the ICC, and no American has been tried before the court in The Hague.
The Trump administration has been hostile to the ICC because of arrest warrants issued for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza. The US has complained the court is targeting officials from non-ICC countries.
Washington has sanctioned more than a dozen ICC judges and prosecutors since February last year and is reportedly preparing more sanctions against the court itself.

Can China’s grain reserves protect food security against El Nino?

However, the main accused in Jamui molestation incident Nandan Yadav was injured in a police encounter, while he was being taken to the crime scene.Tejashwi alleged that the incident was another indication of what he described as the collapse of law and order in Bihar, saying the state was witnessing "gundaraaj".
Abhishek Mishra is a Digital Content Producer at The Times of India, working with the news desk. He writes with a keen eye on foreign policy, defence developments, and the shifting currents of geopolitics-and yes, Indian politics always finds a way onto his radar too.

The UK Government Faces a Reckoning Over Palantir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

When Andy Burnham sat in his office in Manchester as the regional mayor, building an unrivaled power base on Britain’s left that ultimately catapulted him into the prime minister’s office, he did so in the only region of England that refused Palantir access to its data.
Now, as Burnham enters his first parliamentary session as British leader, Palantir could prove to be his first major test in office, as sources in Westminster tell WIRED the prime minister is under significant pressure from his new colleagues to break the company’s contentious contract with the National Health Service. The dispute could become the first major crisis of Burnham’s premiership, with those sources saying pressure is mounting on him to decide the future of Palantir’s growing role across the British state in the coming weeks.
Palantir currently holds contracts worth around £670m in the public sector, including major deals in health, defence, and policing. The largest—a £330m contract to manage healthcare data on the NHS Federated Data Platform—is the one Palantir opponents have opted to focus on. Reports circulated during Labour’s leadership election that Burnham would block Palantir, but they were swiftly cut down in follow-up reporting. Campaigners are now pushing for Burnham to use a break clause in Palantir’s contract with the NHS, which would see the deal end in 2027.
Burnham’s government and the Labour Party he leads are fractiously split on the issue. On one side, leading officials and parliamentary veterans argue cautiously in favor of the provider. On the other, Labour’s left-leaning grassroots and influential backbench MPs are pressuring the government to end the relationship, and in the process begin a huge schism with the company.
The government has so far obfuscated in response to an official petition asking for people to be able to opt out of Palantir’s FDP, after it got 10,000 signatures, saying only that the government would consider it in future policy making. A similar, non-official petition calls for Palantir to be removed from the NHS entirely and has already reached 177,000 signatures.
Growing public opposition to the company has put the government under real pressure to reduce Palantir’s role in the British state. WIRED spoke to three Whitehall sources who believe that, if the deal is to be broken, a decision to do so would need to be made in the next few weeks.
“Given the need to hire an alternate provider or make a decision to move the contract in house, any decision to tear up the contract would need to be done by the Autumn,” one Whitehall source tells WIRED. “Otherwise the government would risk botching any changeover.”
Many of the supporters who secured Burnham’s position in Downing Street are natural Palantir skeptics who come from the soft left. Intrinsically wary of privatisation, they want to see the firm’s role reduced or removed entirely from British politics.
Beyond the inner circle, opposition to Palantir is organised and loud, including many members of the Socialist Campaign Group, a faction within the Labour Party, who are on the whole more experienced MPs. Burnham supporters like Rachael Maskell have vocally opposed Palantir.
Maskell has highlighted her own work as an NHS clinician to justify her opposition to the company in a parliamentary debate in April. During a debate on Palantir’s FDP in February, she said: “This US spytech company is now deep into the data of our NHS and of course patients across the country. I know as a former clinician in the NHS, trust is key. If you do not have the confidence and trust of your patients, that results in people having worse health outcomes. So in the interest of our constituents' health, I urge the government to end this contract.”
Another MP known to oppose the company is Clive Lewis, a vocal supporter of Burnham’s ascension to Downing Street. “By taking on contracts across the NHS, policing, defense, and other public services, Palantir followed a coordinated strategy to embed themselves deeper and deeper into the British state,” he tells WIRED. “This leaves us dangerously exposed to the whims of a shady spy tech company that operates under the laws of the US, not our own.”
But on the other side, there are plenty of politicians and advisers close to Burnham who quietly advocate for the firm’s work in the UK. One of those is Varun Chandra, the man chiefly in charge of maintaining the relationship between Westminster and Big Tech, who has been kept in position by Andy Burnham.
Chandra made his name working for a corporate intelligence turned venture capital firm called Hakluyt When Chandra rose to managing partner of the company at only 34, he became the first person to do so who had not worked for the UK’s Secret Intelligence Service. Shortly after taking the helm, he launched Hakluyt Capital, a venture capital investment fund fronted by the company with numerous investments in and around AI.
Chandra plays a critical role for the British government in dealing with the US and MAGA. During Sir Keir Starmer’s visit to Washington in 2025, Michael Ellam, a senior civil servant in the Cabinet Office, told the UK’s then-ambassador to the US that Chandra was better “stylistically” than a career diplomat like himself when dealing with the decision-makers in Trump’s circle.
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick singled Chandra out for praise upon his promotion, saying the adviser played an “essential” role in the US trade deal reached in 2025. Meanwhile, the New Statesman has reported that Chandra holds a particularly strong rapport with Stephen Miller, the White House’s controversial homeland security adviser.
Chandra also appears to be a point man in managing Palantir.
Joe Lonsdale, a Palantir cofounder who has remained close to those in charge of the firm, dined with Chandra in December 2024. Shortly after, Lonsdale told The Shawn Ryan Show podcast that his friends working for Keir Starmer were fully bought into the DOGE-adjacent viewpoints that Palantir has thrived off in the US.
“I was with someone [in] Keir Starmer’s government, which I have some issues with over in the UK, they’re really hard left. Even people out there [are] like, they know they have to cut their bureaucracies. Bureaucracies are like these cancers, man.”
Elsewhere, the Financial Times have revealed a number of conflict of interests involving civil servants and Palantir, including that the Department for Health’s permanent secretary worked for Carnall Farrar, a consortium partner of Palantir’s, while it bid on the NHS data platform contract, forcing her to recuse herself.
Palantir’s UK CEO Louis Mosley (the grandson of Britain’s most prominent fascist, Sir Oswald Mosley) has vocally criticized Palantir’s opponents, accusing them of putting politics before performance. He was quoted as saying “If NATO went to war, it would go to war using Palantir.”
Influential Labour voices have begun to defend the company, including Lord Spellar, a former defense minister under Tony Blair, who said Starmer’s government was “quite right to resist attempts to … demonize individual companies,” in respect to Palantir.
Outside campaigners are also putting pressure on Burnham. Campaigning journalists at Democracy for Sale have revealed little use of Palantir’s software within the NHS, aiding a concerted effort by activists to focus the campaign against Palantir on competence rather than ethics.
“The initial campaign was focused around the company’s ethical issues, but we found that it didn’t have the success we were hoping for,” one campaigner tells WIRED. “By focusing on competence we’ve found a lot more success, and by targeting the contract break.”
Donald Campbell, director of advocacy at Foxglove, tells WIRED that the decision over the NHS contract would be pivotal to the future path of the new government.
“Andy Burnham needs to make a clean break with Keir Starmer by putting an end to Trump backing Big Tech’s influence over the British government,” says Campbell.
“Palantir’s lavishly funded lobbying and influence operation has led to a catalog of apparent conflicts of interest among government personnel. Story after story has emerged where senior civil servants or politicians, who are meant to hold Palantir to account, have instead held alarmingly cozy relationships with the company.”
A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson told WIRED: “As per standard practice, this contract will be reviewed ahead of the February 2027 break clause, but it is clear that thousands more patients are benefitting from the NHS Federated Data Platform every month, including through the reduction in the number of unnecessary days spent in hospital after treatment.” Palantir did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
As of today, Burnham has still stayed quiet about Britain’s future relationship with Palantir. Very soon, silence won’t be an option. A ticking clock begins when Parliament resumes in September, MPs will continue pressure on the new Prime Minister to break the contract, and coordinated opposition at Labour’s upcoming party conference in Liverpool, where Burnham will speak to members for the first time as party leader, and Mosley is expected to make his case at fringe events and parties with Labour’s great and good.
No matter what, an overall ban on Palantir appears highly unlikely. While British law does allow it, the move would be unprecedented and could have major implications for Britain’s military, which has an active relationship with the company—and a reckoning in the country’s relationship with the US, too.
