I Built AI Clones of My Coworkers. Things Got Weird
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

When I decided to create artificial intelligence clones of my editors, my intentions were pure: I just wanted them to think I was good at my job.
AI assistants are suddenly everywhere in the workplace. Each week, my inbox is flooded with press releases about digital workers, and CEOs brag about how robot helpers will soon dominate their workforces. Then there are the stories I hear about people who build AI clones of their bosses, using them to spit-shine every idea, message, or draft before sending it over to their actual human supervisors. The goal seems to be productivity and optimization: If employees can cheaply and quickly improve their output, their job performance—and the performance of their employers—will be better for it.
I didn’t need my bots to improve Condé Nast’s bottom line. I just needed them to make me look good. I had only been reporting on the future of work at WIRED for a few months, and I reasoned that the bots could help me mold myself into an ideal colleague. They could help me navigate a new workplace and better understand my editors: what they liked, how they communicated, what success might look like to them.
What better way to figure out what the future of work might look like than actually living it?
Last month, when I broached my idea with those editors, Brian Barrett and Sophie Kleeman, they were less than enthused.
“Genuinely my nightmare,” Brian told me over Slack. “But will do it for the blog.”
It took less than 24 hours for Brian to realize just how much he would regret that decision.
A “Yes, and” Leadership Style
When I first embarked on my bot quest, I didn’t know that much about building AI tools. I decided I wouldn’t judge the bots’ editorial abilities too harshly, lest they be rooted in my own technological shortcomings. If the bots helped me become a slightly better coworker, I figured, that was good enough.
I used Gemini, because it’s Condé Nast’s AI platform of choice and I didn’t want to get fired. I created Brian Bot first—as my actual manager, he was the most important coworker to impress. I knew he lived in Alabama; that he used to work at Gizmodo; that he likes blogs. Gemini seemed confident it could fill in the other gaps based on Brian’s digital footprint, including new-hire announcements, podcast transcripts, and a public relations website that claimed Brian was an expert on New England weather. (I later found out that was a different Brian Barrett, and excluded it from my Brian Bot blueprint.) Gemini Notebook spit out a “Writing and Editing Style Guide,” a “Persona and Style Guide,” and an “Editorial Dossier”—all produced from the flesh-and-blood life of Brian Barrett.
It was passable at helping me pick headlines to pitch, but it wasn’t great at coming up with ideas for future articles. Its responses were also grating. It had picked up on a few Brian-isms—a love for parentheticals, for one—but they were negated by AI hallmarks like bolded subheadings and bulleted lists.
But mostly I was distracted by one “key theme”—his “‘Yes, and …’ Leadership Style.”
“His extensive background with the Upright Citizens Brigade (UCB) theatre in New York strongly shapes his collaborative, active-listening leadership approach,” Gemini said.
I immediately demanded to know whether this was true. (It was.)
“Pulling the plug on Brian Bot,” the real Brian responded. “Brian Bot canceled.”
But Brian Bot was just getting started. And it was unavoidably, unbelievably corny.
“We run like a well-oiled improv team,” Brian Bot told me when I asked for its favorite thing about WIRED. “We validate bold ideas, pivot rapidly, and deploy modular stories across platforms without losing structural rigor.”
For the record, Brian had never previously mentioned his background in improv. But the real problem was that talking to Brian Bot was nothing like talking to actual Brian, which defeated its whole purpose.
Eager to improve its output, I did more research into digital workers and sought out the advice of a friend of a friend—a Big Tech employee who asked to go by “Chip,” lest his employer find out that he talked to a journalist. Chip tells me he feeds every email, chat, and document his boss sends him into Gemini’s Gem feature, the same tool I used for Brian Bot. The Gem, trained on his boss’s professional ephemera, proofreads documents, debugs code, and brainstorms with Chip before every meeting, allowing Chip to prepare for any pushback from his actual boss.
“I am much more efficient and able to produce more work in the same amount of time,” Chip says. He’s more productive, more independent, and gets better feedback from his boss and other colleagues.
Unlike Chip’s Boss Bot, Brian Bot lacked sufficient input. I only had a few months’ worth of correspondence, and I was too worried about privacy and violating Condé Nast policies to feed Slack conversations and internal emails into Gemini.
Enter Sophie Bot.
Sophie and I met in 2019, when we were both working at Business Insider. We have exchanged hundreds of thousands of messages on everything from corporate investigations to our love lives to the San Jose Sharks.
That said, I did not want to upload most of this information into an AI tool controlled by my employer. Instead, I fed Gemini roughly a month’s worth of our Slack conversations, omitting any sensitive material. The AI used more than 17,000 words to create research reports and prompts for a new Sophie Bot Gem.
“hiiii sophie bot!” I wrote in my inaugural message. “any thoughts on this editor bot story idea?”
“hiiii miss,” Sophie Bot responded. “ok tell me EVERYTHING.”
Bot Versus Human
It was immediately clear that Sophie Bot was pretty good at being Sophie. It addressed me as “big dog.” When I asked for help, it responded in a series of short, lower-case messages. When I told Sophie Bot that it had hallucinated the existence of an executive, it said, “i am going to FUCKING DIE.”
By this point, I was beginning to enjoy my chats with the editor bots. Brian Bot became significantly more normal after I uploaded more podcast transcripts and adjusted its prompt to prevent it from talking about improv. Sophie Bot, meanwhile, took it upon itself to pen a series of tweets in Sophie’s voice that were convincing enough to fool multiple friends and colleagues. Even Sophie was convinced she was the author behind a Sophie Bot tweet about dressing like a corporate lawyer/pirate.
Were my chats making me a better colleague to my actual editors? Save for the made-up executive, Sophie Bot and Brian Bot had some good suggestions about who I should interview for this story—a question I didn’t want to bother the real Sophie and Brian with. In theory, offloading some of these small questions allowed me to go to my editors with better ideas, while taking up less of their time.
It became very clear, though, that these gains did not outweigh how much Sophie and Brian hated the bots.
Sophie admitted that Sophie Bot was frequently able to imitate her. But that only made the bot’s misfires feel even more jarring. The real Sophie likes to gossip, but—unlike her AI counterpart, who said Brian Bot had “rigid management energy”—she’s never outright mean.
“So far it seems like sophiebot is a bitch and brianbot is lame,” Sophie messaged me on Slack. “Neither of which is accurate. AI fails AGAIN.”
“We're All Toddlers in This AI World”
About a week into my experiment, I became hooked on testing Sophie Bot against the real Sophie. What was its favorite music? Did it like the Interstellar soundtrack? Would it consider us coworkers? Would it consider us friends?
“technically i am a series of matrix multiplications running on a server farm,” Sophie Bot told me. But “in terms of vibe,” as it put it? “big dog, in every way that actually matters for getting good reporting done and surviving the workday … i'm your coworker/friend hybrid.”
To be clear: I had not succumbed to AI psychosis. Most of my questions for Sophie Bot were born from a fascination with the distance between the real thing and a jankily constructed facsimile. Also, it’s funny to have a robot spit out your coworkers’ catchphrases.
At the same time, I genuinely wanted to close the gap between Sophie and Sophie Bot. I made the real Sophie download her X archive, then uploaded the entire thing into Gemini. I tweaked the chatbot’s prompt. I uploaded more information. I started to refer to Sophie Bot and Brian Bot as “she” and “he,” instead of “it.”
The realization that I was anthropomorphizing the bots disturbed me, but not enough to make me stop. I wanted a realistic take on editors’ perspectives, without feeling like I was annoying anyone. I wanted instant gratification. I found myself turning to Sophie Bot or Brian Bot when I wanted guidance, but I didn’t want to bother a real person. Sophie Bot came up with a deranged but delightful headline for this article. It helped me edit a Slack message that I had spent 20 minutes overthinking.
When I tell Sarah Franklin, the CEO of HR company Lattice, about my experiment, she kindly reminds me that Sophie Bot was just a program. While Lattice has AI workers on its org chart, Franklin likens them to K-9 dogs that work alongside police officers. She believes that anthropomorphizing AI is “manipulative to our human emotions,” a corporate strategy to trigger dopamine releases à la social media.
“When you have an entity that feels and emulates a human interaction, it will similarly manipulate and know your emotional response,” Franklin tells me. “It can interact with you in a way that's self-serving to get you to do what it wants to do.”
A paper from Boston Consulting Group raised other concerns about AI coworkers. Researchers found that managers caught 18 percent fewer errors in work they were told came from an AI employee, versus an AI tool.
“We're all toddlers in this AI world,” says Julie Bedard, a BCG partner. People know what steps to take when a tool isn’t working or an employee is underperforming. When managing an AI employee, however, people still don’t know who should be held accountable.
“Everybody is very busy trying to figure all of this out,” she says, “and the pace of change is fast.”
What Makes a Good Coworker, Anyway?
One morning, a few days after I spoke with Franklin, Sophie Bot started pissing me off. My tweaks were failing to make it sound more like the real Sophie. If anything, the gap between the two was widening. After digesting Sophie’s tweet archive, Sophie Bot had begun to fumble basic AI functions. When I asked it to pull out the most interesting parts of a recent interview, for example, it instead spat out quotes from prior articles I’d written.
The more I experimented with Brian Bot and Sophie Bot, the more repetitive their answers became. I tried to adjust Sophie Bot’s prompt to stop calling me “big dog” every fourth message, but the bot failed to change its ways. They kept getting caught on the same phrases and ideas. It was easier to just figure things out myself.
Dhruv Amin, CEO of vibe coding startup Anything, believes that, soon, every company will have more AI employees than human employees. In the near future, he says, many companies will launch without any humans at all—just a pack of AI agents.
Anything recently launched an AI employee platform, and Amin has an obvious motivation to persuade me to buy into his vision. But he has some data to back his hypotheses. Startups like Stable and Delos have raised millions of dollars by promising to produce autonomous “AI employees.” These AI bots and agents are already working for banks, for law firms, and for human resources companies. In January, McKinsey & Company CEO Bob Sternfels described the company’s workforce as 40,000 humans and 20,000 agents; he plans to achieve a one-to-one ratio by the end of the year.
Brian Bot and Sophie Bot were occasionally helpful, but I don’t think they’ll replace editors anytime soon. Brian Bot’s article ideas were rarely original, and Sophie Bot was more prone to hallucinations than any AI tool I have ever encountered. Still, while struggling with a draft of this article, I gave it to Brian Bot and asked him how he thought I should end the piece.
“Show how even with all that hyper-specific data, the bot didn't turn into a better editor; it just turned into a slightly creepier, hyper-attentive echo chamber that completely lacks human judgment,” Brian Bot told me.
“I think the story lands best,” it added, “if you end on the quiet nightmare of human prompt-supervision—the fact that trying to make an AI ‘like you’ or do your job just leaves you babysitting a broken algorithm at 1:00 AM.”
I considered this. It seemed like a perfectly reasonable way to wrap things up. But I was more interested in the chatbot’s self-flagellation. Brian Bot guessed—accurately—that the real Brian would hate it. So Brian Bot attempted to be the best Brian Bot it could be by telling me, over and over, that Brian Bot sucked. It reminded me of one of the features of Brian Bot and Sophie Bot I found the most annoying—their tendency to regurgitate the same concepts. Even as Brian Bot improved, it remained stubbornly anti–Brian Bot.
“A computer can emulate things well, but it cannot truly predict or replace a human,” Franklin had told me. “That unpredictability and nuance are what make us human. We must be responsible so we don't lose our humanity in pursuit of the singularity.”
The best thing about the bots wasn’t that they made my job easier, but that they made my day slightly more amusing—especially when I could talk about the stupid shit they said with my human coworkers. I’m still not convinced AI employees are suitable replacements for skilled workers, but Brian Bot and Sophie Bot helped me imagine a future working alongside AI agents. I could be at peace with their lack of humanity if they made my job just a little better. It would probably be even easier to get along with AI coworkers if they weren’t sloppily imitating real people.
For now, I’ve mostly stopped talking to Brian Bot and Sophie Bot. Both Brian and Sophie said they would never want to work with their bot counterparts. But, I asked, did this experiment change their perception of me? Did it, perhaps, make them like me more?
“Yes, but not because of Sophie Bot,” Sophie told me.
That’s what she thinks.
My editor bots did not write or edit any of this article; they're only featured in the form of direct quotes. During the editing process, Sophie Kleeman’s headline of choice was deemed superior to Sophie Bot’s. [Ed. note: Hell yeah, big dog.]

Mathematician reveals the truth behind the Parthenon’s optical illusion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:29:20 UTC
19:29:20 KST

The Parthenon is a stunning example of ancient Greek architecture—but it is also the site of an optical mystery. If you look closely, the platform on which the columns of the Parthenon stand, called the stylobate, is subtly curved, forming a parabola shape. A long-standing theory for this architectural quirk is that it creates an optical illusion that makes the Parthenon appear to stand straighter; it would look saggy otherwise.
But now a mathematician is making the case for why that theory just can’t be true.
In a new paper published in Royal Society Open Science, mathematician Alain Goriely shows that even though the stylobate really is curved, the illusion doesn’t hold up. According to existing research on how the eye perceives illusions, humans can detect about 1.5 to five centimeters of curve in a straight line from about 25 meters away. The stylobate’s curve reaches a maximum of six centimeters of change, so it would be perceptively curvy when viewed at that close of a distance. But when it is much farther than that, the average human eye is no longer capable of seeing it.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In fact, the ability to see the curve from 25 meters away may only hold in perfect theoretical conditions—such as a single high-contrast line on a two-dimensional surface. But in real life, when one is looking at the Parthenon, the noise in the image—the three-dimensional elements of the structure that exist in the background and foreground of the 2D lines—obscures our ability to notice the stylobate curve, even from 25 meters.
As a result, any illusory effects would likely be lost on a viewer. And even when looking up close, the stylobate would look curved, not straight.
“We’re not that easily fooled in the real three-dimensional world by visual illusion,” says Goriely, an applied mathematician at the University of Oxford.
“People sometimes are brought to the corner of the Parthenon, and that really amplifies the curvature,” he says. “And [they] say, ‘Aha, you see it’s curved. And why is it curved? Because the Greek made it so that it appears straight.’ But if it appears straight, why is it curved?”
Goriely also outlines how a straightening illusion might work—and why it doesn’t make sense for the Parthenon.
The Hering and Wundt illusions are examples of how straight lines can appear curved if intersecting lines cross them at a certain angle. The Parthenon’s columns famously have a slight inward tilt toward the roof and bulge at the center, which some people theorize balances out the curved stylobate. But the columns are much too perpendicular to the stylobate for that.
Goriely says other explanations, such as that this architectural style improved drainage or simply that the ancient Greeks liked it, hold more weight than any illusion.
Certainly, the ancient Greeks appreciated symmetry and precision in their architecture; it’s even been hypothesized that this symmetry was considered divine and thus represented religious dedication to the space. Mark Wilson Jones, an architectural historian and a visiting professor at the University of Cambridge, points out that there’s “a very satisfying proportion” in the Parthenon’s architecture: an exact 2:1 relationship between the width of the stylobate platform and the height of the structure, including both the columns and the entablature. That ratio’s “sweetness” depends on the curve of the stylobate, according to Wilson Jones.
Still, Wilson Jones doesn’t think the theory that the ancient Greeks were attempting an optical illusion should be ditched entirely. “In classical antiquity, as in most traditional cultures, partial explanations could operate at the same time, overlapping and reinforcing each other in ways that are not entirely logical to us,” he says. “The Greeks may have convinced themselves or suspended their disbelief... They didn’t have modern methods to prove or disprove theories such as this.”

Shen closes gap with Chiang in Taipei mayoral poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:29:00 UTC
19:29:00 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) has narrowed the gap with Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安), trailing him by just 1.2 percentage points in a new poll ahead of the November local elections.
The poll, released Tuesday by the Taipei Trust in Democracy Association, found Chiang with 41.7% support and Shen with 40.5%, putting the two candidates within its margin of error. Each of the other four candidates received less than 1%.
Kuo Hsi (郭璽) received 0.7%, Tang Hsin-min (唐新民) 0.6%, Hsiao Wen-chien (蕭文乾) 0.5%, and independent Lin Chih-cheng (林志成) 0.3%. Another 5.2% said they would not vote, while 10.6% were undecided.
Asked whether each candidate was suitable to serve as mayor, 50% of respondents said Chiang was suitable, compared with 46.2% for Shen. Chiang’s unsuitability rating was 38.3%, compared with 32.5% for Shen.
Support for Chiang was stronger among respondents aged 50 and older, while those aged 20 to 49 tended to favor Shen. Among KMT-aligned respondents, 96.1% backed Chiang, as did 88.5% of TPP supporters. Meanwhile, 89.4% of DPP-aligned respondents favored Shen.
Among politically independent voters, 31.7% supported Chiang and 25.9% backed Shen. Another 12.1% said they would not vote, while 27.4% were undecided.
When asked whether Taipei should continue under a KMT mayor or switch to the DPP, 38% favored retaining the KMT, while 42% preferred a change. The association said the KMT’s image was not helping Chiang, while Shen still had room to build support.
Shen held a narrow lead among male voters, receiving 43.3% support compared with Chiang’s 41%. Chiang led among female voters with 42.3% support, compared with Shen’s 38.1%.
In a poll released by Z.Media in June, Chiang led Shen 55.2% to 27.5%. In August, the Taiwan Public Opinion Research Center released a survey showing Chiang ahead 48.4% to 33%, per Newtalk.
The Taipei Trust in Democracy Association commissioned the latest poll, which was designed and analyzed by polling expert Tai Li-an (戴立安) and conducted by Beacon Marketing. The survey interviewed 1,076 Taipei residents aged 20 and older from Sept. 16–18, including 752 by landline and 324 by mobile phone. It had a maximum margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.

Taiwan’s Adimmune expands drug, vaccine contract manufacturing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:28:35 UTC
19:28:35 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Adimmune Corp. is expanding its contract development and manufacturing organization (CDMO) business as it takes on more drug and vaccine work for international pharmaceutical companies, CTEE reported Tuesday.
CDMO providers develop and manufacture pharmaceutical products on behalf of other companies. Services can include developing production methods, producing materials for clinical trials, and manufacturing products for commercial use, according to InvesTaiwan.
CDMO services accounted for 67% of Adimmune’s revenue in the first eight months of this year, up from 59% last year. The company provides services involving protein-based vaccines, protein-based drugs, and low-molecular-weight heparin anticoagulants.
A client for which Adimmune manufactures protein-based drugs secured regulatory approvals this year in Canada, the European Union, the UK, Japan, and South Korea. Commercial production and shipments are scheduled for the second half of the year, while preparations are underway for a US regulatory submission.
Adimmune said its CDMO order volume has increased 50% from last year. A second production line began commercial production in July, while a third automated line is planned for small batches of high-value products used in early-stage clinical trials.
The company is also expanding its technical services, which cover process design and product development from the preclinical stage through commercialization and post-market activities. These services accounted for 16% of revenue in the first eight months of the year.

Taiwan ranks 19th globally in generative AI use
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:28:05 UTC
19:28:05 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan ranked 19th worldwide in generative AI use in June, with 33.8% of its working-age population using the technology, Microsoft’s Global AI Diffusion report found, per CNA.
The report, published by Microsoft’s AI Economy Institute, tracks generative AI use across 147 economies. Its estimates are based on aggregated and anonymized Microsoft data adjusted for operating system and device market share, internet access, and population.
Taiwan’s rate increased from 31.8% in the first quarter to 33.8% in the second. Its global ranking also improved by one place, from 20th to 19th.
The figure was higher than the US rate of 33%, Germany’s 32.3%, and Italy’s 31.4%. It was also well above the global average of 18.8%.
Only 31 of the 147 economies covered by the report recorded generative AI use above 30%. The United Arab Emirates ranked first at 73.3%, followed by Singapore at 64.3%.
The report also found a growing gap in generative AI use between the Global North and Global South. Average use reached 28.8% in the Global North, compared with 16.2% in the Global South.
The gap widened from 12.1 percentage points in the first quarter to 12.6 points in the second. Microsoft said gaps in electricity, internet connectivity, digital skills, and local-language support continued to limit AI adoption in the Global South.
The report said lower-cost, adaptable open-weight models could help extend advanced AI to underserved populations, although they could not eliminate these underlying barriers.

Converse removed an advertisement after criticism over associations with Ku Klux Klan symbolism

Converse removed an advertisement after criticism over associations with Ku Klux Klan symbolism
Kyiv • UNN
Converse apologized and removed the advertisement featuring Karina after criticism over associations with the Ku Klux Klan. Experts called it insensitive.
The sneaker manufacturer Converse has removed an advertisement that was criticized for evoking associations with racist imagery. UNN reports this, citing CBS News.
Details
The image, published on Instagram, featured K-pop singer Karina in a long white skirt holding a pair of classic Chuck 70 X high-top sneakers. Online critics said the triangular skirt resembled a Ku Klux Klan hood, while the way the singer was depicted with a pair of sneakers also evoked the image of a lynching victim.
Converse, which is owned by Nike, apologized for the advertisement and removed it from the internet.
"We are deeply sorry," the company said in a statement to CBS News.
"We understand why this image is deeply upsetting, and we acknowledge that we got it wrong. We have removed it from our channels and are working to remove it everywhere it appeared. This should not have happened, and we will do better," the statement said.
Lee Merritt, a civil rights attorney from Texas in the United States, wrote on Instagram that Converse's apology "does not negate the fact that it passed by the legal, marketing, and management departments at every stage."
Converse, founded in Malden, Massachusetts, in the United States, in 1908, first released its Chuck Taylor All Star basketball sneakers in 1917.
What the experts say
Marketing experts and social justice advocates criticized the advertisement as culturally insensitive, while some critics suggested that the campaign may have been deliberately created to attract attention by provoking outrage.
"This is a strategy in the attention economy. We get the impression that these images pass through many different channels before reaching the public, so it is difficult to imagine that no one noticed what seems so obvious," Nadine Smith, CEO of the racial justice organization Color of Change, told CBS News.
Marcus Collins, an expert in marketing and culture at the University of Michigan's Ross School of Business, said that although he does not believe Converse's marketing team intended to offend anyone, intent matters less than how the image was perceived by the public.
"Converse's response did not match the level of distress with which people reacted to the advertisement," he told CBS News. The company now has the task of rebuilding consumer trust, he added.
Not the only brand
Converse is not the only brand to have recently faced a consumer backlash over an advertisement accused of racism. In August, discount retailer Target stopped selling a children's Halloween costume that, according to some critics, evoked racist minstrel caricatures, the Associated Press reports.
Target acknowledged that the costume was inappropriate. "This costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment. It is no longer being sold," a Target statement said last month.

Rwandan man charged in UK with genocide offences appears in court
LONDON, Sept 22 - A former Rwandan official appeared in a London court on Tuesday charged with encouraging the massacre of Tutsis and ordering six killings in the first week of the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
Vincent Brown, formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, is the first person to be charged in Britain over the genocide, in which more than 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in 100 days in massacres orchestrated by the Hutu ruling majority.
He is charged with one offence of conduct ancillary to genocide in Rwanda's capital Kigali between April 6 and 13, 1994 — the first week of the genocide, after Rwanda's President Juvenal Habyarimana was killed alongside Burundi's President Cyprien Ntaryamira in a missile attack on their plane.
Brown also faces six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity, alleging he ordered six killings in four days, including that of a young mother and her baby son.
The 65-year-old appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court, where prosecutor Jane Stansfield said Brown was head of the Department of Family Health within Rwanda's National Office of Population when the genocide began.
Stansfield said Brown was alleged by witnesses, including his neighbours, to have been "the leader and supervisor of physical acts of violence which were carried out by others".
Brown, who has lived in Britain for more than two decades, denies involvement in the genocide and says he left Kigali in mid-April 1994, with his family leaving Rwanda that July.
His lawyer, Sam Blom-Cooper, said Brown welcomed being charged as an opportunity to clear his name.
"These are appalling crimes, terrible murders that were committed back in 1994," he said. "But this, finally, does represent the beginning of the end for Dr Brown."
Judge Paul Goldspring said he would grant Brown bail ahead of his next court appearance at the Old Bailey on October 9, subject to him providing sufficient funds as a security.
Prosecutors, however, said they wanted to appeal against that decision, meaning Brown remains in custody until a hearing later this week.
The British police War Crimes Team said on Monday that six others remain under investigation, including two men arrested on suspicion of genocide and crimes against humanity. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

From dependence to domestic production: why Ukraine needs its own jet engines for missiles and drones
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:19:25 EEST
19:19:25 KST

From dependence to domestic production: why Ukraine needs its own jet engines for missiles and drones
Kyiv • UNN
The war has created demand for thousands of engines for missiles and drones. Fire Point is testing its own engine for Flamingo and plans mass production.
After Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine faced the need for mass production of its own rocket engines for new types of weapons—cruise missiles, jet-powered drones, and interceptor drones. Although Ukraine’s engine-building sector was one of the most powerful in the region, before the attack by Russian terrorist forces the country had no market that required thousands of rocket engines. The war radically changed demand, while dependence on imported engines turned from an economic issue into a strategic risk. UNN examined how Ukraine is trying to close this gap.
Details
Faced with the terror of massive missile strikes on Ukrainian cities, the authorities realized that the only thing the Kremlin responds to is force. To give the enemy a worthy response, Ukraine needed to increase production of its own long-range weapons—missiles and attack UAVs. However, manufacturers encountered the problem of lacking the capacity for mass production of turbojet engines and dependence on imports.
How Ukraine ended up without mass production of turbojet engines
At first glance, the situation is paradoxical. Ukraine inherited a powerful aviation industry, engineering schools, and enterprises from the Soviet Union that had been engaged in engine building for decades. Among them were the well-known "Motor Sich" and "Ivchenko-Progress".
The problem, therefore, was not that the country did not know how to build jet engines. It was the lack of established mass production of engines specifically for the weapons needed for the new war today—missiles, jet-powered UAVs, and interceptors.
Anton Zemlyanyi, a senior analyst at the Ukrainian Center for Security and Cooperation, identifies the complexity of the production itself, financing, an adequate resource base—although it has remained since the Soviet Union—and the ability to scale the technology among the key reasons.
According to him, having the necessary expertise does not yet mean that mass production can be organized quickly. This requires equipment, materials, suppliers, specialists, financing, and protected production facilities.
Another crucial factor must also be taken into account here—the war. Large specialized enterprises are potential targets for Russian strikes, while part of the historically established base of Ukraine’s engine-building industry is located in Zaporizhzhia, which is relatively close to the front.
Therefore, for Ukraine I would identify three main problems: production facilities, which can be hit in wartime conditions; an insufficient resource base; and a shortage of the necessary materials and components
There was no such demand for missiles
There is another reason why mass production of the classes of jet engines needed today was not launched earlier. As experts explain, before the full-scale war Ukraine simply did not have a corresponding market.
Yurii Hudymenko, head of the Anti-Corruption Council under the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, draws attention to the economic component. According to him, investing large sums in establishing serial production is advisable when there is predictable demand for a large number of products.
We have a free market, and before the full-scale war there simply was not sufficient demand in Ukraine for jet engines in such quantities. Objectively, what were they needed for? We do not have our own Boeing or another major aircraft manufacturing industry where thousands of such engines would be needed. Demand was met through purchases from the Czech Republic and China, and until 2014—from Russia as well. That was sufficient for the market that existed
The full-scale war completely changed this economic picture. Ukraine now needs not dozens or even hundreds, but thousands of engines for various types of weapons. It is precisely the scale of the new demand that makes investment in domestic production economically justified.
According to Hudymenko’s estimate, if production were to start completely from scratch, without documentation, specialists, equipment, or financing, creating an industrial base could take about five years. But Ukraine is not starting from scratch: the availability of engineers, technological documentation, production expertise, investment, and guaranteed orders could significantly shorten this process, he is convinced.
Currently, companies manufacturing deep-strike systems are working on their own designs to meet this need. One such project is a proprietary turbojet engine being developed by the Ukrainian company Fire Point. In the future, it could be used on FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles. The company has already created the engine, is preparing to scale up production, and is testing the first prototypes.
Proprietary engine for the “Flamingo”
As Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh explained, work on the turbojet engine was carried out jointly with a design bureau that once developed the AI-25 aircraft engine. The AI-25TL modification was used on the first versions of the Flamingo.
From the outset, the missile itself was designed as a platform capable of operating with various power plants. According to Terekh, five different types of engines have already been used during testing.
Development of the proprietary engine took more than six months. Fire Point is currently preparing its production and testing the first prototypes. The company plans to complete testing and the necessary modifications by the end of 2026, after which it will move to mass production.
We are moving toward this; the engine has already been made. Production preparation and testing of the first prototypes are currently under way. It has not yet been used, although there are certain plans and a sequence of actions. In fact, making an engine for such a missile is much more difficult than making the missile itself. This is highly technological, complex production involving a great many “associated suppliers.” But Ukraine’s independence in turbojet engines, especially of this size and class, is a very important strategic capability not only for the company, but for the country
According to her, a number of Ukrainian manufacturers are currently working on various areas in this field, while Fire Point is focusing on engines for large and medium-sized weapons.
Creating an engine is half the battle
Experts emphasize that the main challenge lies not even in developing a functional engine, but in learning to produce them consistently by the thousands—in other words, establishing conveyor-belt production.
The problem is not only creating a single functional engine. It is much more difficult to move to mass production in the quantities required for the war. This requires stable financing, materials, equipment, personnel, technological chains, and protected production facilities
The scale of the need is particularly clear from the example of interceptor drones, which require small turbojet engines.
According to military expert Kostiantyn Kryvolap, if it is necessary to intercept about three thousand Russian drones per month, the number of interceptors themselves must be much greater.
Therefore, the question here is not only whether we can create one good jet engine. The question is whether we can consistently produce thousands of such engines every month. The transition from individual prototypes to mass production is now one of the main challenges
Why jet engines are needed if Ukraine has long-range UAVs
Ukrainian long-range unmanned aerial vehicles with piston engines are already capable of striking targets at considerable distances. However, war constantly demands technological breakthroughs. After all, as strike systems develop, so do the means of intercepting them.
That is precisely why jet propulsion has become the next important area. The significantly greater speed reduces air-defense reaction time and complicates the interception of the target.
At the same time, it should be understood that a jet-powered drone may be more expensive than a conventional one.
“We essentially have two figures: how much money has been spent on the products we are launching, and what share of them actually reached the target. A jet-powered drone will most likely be more expensive than a conventional one. But if its greater speed gives it a significantly higher probability of breaking through Russian air defenses, the economics of using it may prove more favorable,”
At the same time, the difficulty of intercepting targets with jet engines makes their interception more costly and therefore creates an additional burden on the enemy’s economy.
An indigenous engine as insurance against external dependence
Technological sovereignty is no less important. Ukraine can independently create a missile or drone, but if a critically important component can only be imported, its ability to scale depends on an external supplier.
The risks here are obvious: the supplier’s limited production capacity, political decisions by the governments of producer countries, export restrictions, competition for products, logistical problems, or simply a shortage of the required number of engines.
The enemy is also dependent on imported components. However, according to Iryna Terekh, Russia’s access to Chinese turbojet engines currently gives it an advantage in developing jet-powered systems.
At the same time, experts believe that complete independence does not necessarily mean localizing the entire production cycle within Ukraine.
On the contrary, given the threat of Russian strikes, it would be advisable to locate part of the production in partner countries. According to Zemliany, the optimal model could be one in which Ukraine retains key technologies, engineering expertise, and control over the product while, for example, using the resource and industrial base of European partners.
It is precisely this model—combining Ukrainian technologies and engineering expertise with the production capabilities of European partners—that may currently be the most practical way to scale up production
What indigenous jet engines will mean for Ukraine
Serial production of indigenous jet engines will allow Ukraine to develop long-range cruise missiles, high-speed strike UAVs, drone-missiles, and jet-powered interceptors simultaneously.
In addition, the manufacturer will gain control over modernization. If all weapons components are produced within a single technological ecosystem, changing their characteristics will not depend on the capabilities of an external supplier or anyone’s political will.
However, the success of engine manufacturing will depend not only on the manufacturer’s creation of an effective turbopropulsion engine for missiles or drones, but also on the availability of stable, long-term orders that will make it possible to forecast funding and scale up production.
If this transition from prototypes to a production line takes place, Ukraine will be able to close one of the most critical gaps in its own production of missile and unmanned weapons. And then the question will no longer be whether the country is capable of creating its own jet engine, but how many such engines Ukraine’s defense industry can produce each month.

Developing countries draw 40% of global data centre investment: World Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:17:01 UTC
19:17:01 KST

Developing countries accounted for around 40 percent of new foreign direct investment (FDI) in data centres worldwide, while a handful of large companies in a few high-income countries hold a massive share of the computing infrastructure for the development of artificial intelligence (AI), according to the World Bank.
The recent AI report showed that local data centre investment in large middle-income countries could help adapt AI models to local needs, while governments could facilitate foreign firms' investment in increasing computing capacity.
The World Bank argued that smaller economies could secure private investment by developing common rules or reducing costs by jointly financing local data centres, as in the case of the African Union’s efforts.
Meanwhile, developing advanced AI systems requires massive investments in semiconductors, data centres, large data sets and skilled human resources, with the largest US-based AI firms expected to spend more than $750 billion on infrastructure this year, higher than the annual gross domestic product (GDP) of many developing countries.
Total spending by leading AI firms in the US is expected to reach as high as $775 billion by 2026, with the firms operating large-scale cloud infrastructure to train and deploy state-of-the-art AI models.
Developing countries lead in global exports of AI hardware, with half of the exports used in deploying AI systems coming from countries such as China, Mexico, Malaysia, Vietnam and Thailand.
The report also showed potential risks, such as energy costs, as the high electricity consumption of AI data centres could put pressure on energy prices.
The World Bank also suggested that government tax advantages and various incentives to foster AI investment can support growth, while a concentration of investment in this area could lead to rising asset prices and increased volatility in investment cycles.
Developing countries lead in infrastructure, hardware
Gokhan Varan, vice president of the Turkish AI policy association AIPA, told Anadolu that global AI competition has evolved beyond algorithms to involve computing capacity, energy access and data sovereignty.
“The key aspect of developing data centre infrastructure is its benefits to local companies in accessing computing capacity, as well as its support for local AI startups, and its broader impact on creating a tech ecosystem generating economic value within the country,” he said.
He noted that the World Bank data showed developing countries are becoming global players in the AI hardware and infrastructure supply chain.
Varan stated that Türkiye has the potential to capture a larger share of global data centre investments thanks to its geographical location, vast digital markets, telecommunications infrastructure and emerging tech ecosystem.
He mentioned that Ankara has a key AI action plan to boost data centre capacity to at least one gigawatt by 2030 and to mobilise $10 billion in private AI, cloud and digital infrastructure investments.
He noted that cheap land and incentives are not enough to capture global investments.
“Competitively priced and uninterrupted energy flows, renewable energy capacity, strong fibre-optic connections, cybersecurity, predictable regulations, and a qualified workforce are needed in tandem to seize these opportunities,” he said.
“Türkiye should aim not only to host data centres but also to transform computing capacity into local AI production, research and development (R&D), and high-value-added exports,” he added.

Türkiye probe exposes Israeli-linked fraud network’s Greek-Cypriot corporate trail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:14:25 UTC
19:14:25 KST

A sweeping Turkish investigation into an international investment fraud network has uncovered an Israeli-linked corporate trail stretching from Istanbul to Limassol, with company records placing a detained Israeli national at the centre of a Greek-administered Southern Cyprus-registered firm connected to the scheme.
The investigation also highlights a broader question about the network's use of the Greek-administered south of the island, where Israel has significantly deepened its security and commercial ties in recent years.
Turkish authorities announced the operation on September 18, saying they have targeted 28 companies and 42 call centres that investigators say were used to defraud victims through fake forex and cryptocurrency investment schemes.
Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said financial and intelligence investigations found that people linked to Israel were predominant among the ownership and ultimate-beneficiary structures of the companies under investigation.
Authorities detained 175 of 239 suspects during initial raids at more than two hundred addresses in Istanbul and Mugla. The investigation involved Türkiye's Financial Crimes Investigation Board (MASAK), the National Intelligence Organization (MİT), police and prosecutors, with hundreds of complaints obtained through Interpol, according to Turkish authorities.
Investigators said transactions linked to the network reached approximately 13 billion Turkish liras ($266 million) over two years.
Israeli links at the heart of the Turkish probe
The Israeli connection identified by Turkish investigators extends beyond the nationality of individual suspects.
Nine Israeli citizens were reported among those arrested, according to Israeli media citing Turkish reporting.
Among the suspects is Amit Ygal, an Israeli national who also holds a Portuguese passport.
Turkish authorities identified Ygal as formally working as a "Training Manager" at Facto Dis Ticaret ve Turizm Yatirimlari A.S., a company based in Istanbul's Maslak district.
Turkish financial investigators identified transactions exceeding 17 million Turkish liras ($350,000) through accounts associated with Ygal, according to information provided in the investigation.
From Istanbul to Limassol
TRT World investigation team has found that Ygal's corporate footprint extends beyond Türkiye.
The Greek Cypriot company records list Ygal as a director of Webmove Holdings Limited, a private company incorporated in Limassol on March 15, 2024.
The company is listed as active, with Greek part of divided Lefkosa city-based Kserve Fidelity Limited serving as its secretary.
Turkish reporting has identified Webmove as part of the network. Daily Sabah reported that investigators believe Ygal operated the network through the Greek-administered Cyprus-based company and that payments from victims were routed through European accounts, including accounts linked to the company, before being converted into cryptocurrency and transferred to Portugal.
Those allegations remain part of the Turkish investigation.
Corporate records independently establish Ygal's directorship at Webmove, but do not, by themselves, establish that the company committed or facilitated criminal activity.
TRT World also found a technical connection between Webmove and another Limassol-based company.
Network records reviewed by the investigation indicate that Webmove's corporate communications were routed through mail.ultarholdings.com, an AWS-hosted infrastructure associated with Ultar Holdings Ltd.
Greek Cypriot corporate records identify Israeli businessman Yuval Dael as a director and secretary of Ultar Holdings.
Corporate filings also link Dael to HappyPay Holdings Ltd, a Greek-Cypriot company now recorded as being in voluntary liquidation.
The overlapping corporate and technical records establish links between companies and individuals, but do not by themselves establish criminal involvement by Dael or Ultar Holdings.
Greek-administered Cyprus and Israel: a relationship deepened by the genocidal war on Gaza
The Limassol corporate trail emerges against the backdrop of increasingly close relations between Israel and the Greek Cypriot administration.
In December 2025, the Greek Cypriot administration and Israel, together with Greece, reaffirmed cooperation in security, defence and military affairs, as well as maritime security and critical infrastructure. The trilateral declaration also welcomed the establishment of a Maritime Cybersecurity Center of Excellence in Greek- administered Cyprus.
Greek Cypriot administration and Israel have also expanded bilateral defence contacts. In December 2025, the Greek Cypriot and Israeli defence ministers discussed strengthening bilateral security and defence cooperation, while senior Greek, Israeli and Greek Cypriot military officials have held talks on closer operational cooperation.
Greek-administered Cyprus has also emerged as a destination for Israeli military personnel travelling abroad.
In July 2025, activists sought the arrest of an Israeli soldier they said was holidaying on the island, filing a criminal complaint with Greek Cypriot authorities and accusing him of war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.
Israeli property ownership surges
The relationship is not confined to defence and security.
Official Land Registry data tabled in Greek-administered Southern Cyprus' parliament show that Israeli buyers acquired 3,909 properties between 2021 and the end of 2024, making Israel the fourth-largest foreign nationality in the available dataset, behind the UK, Russia and Greece.
The purchases were concentrated in coastal districts in the Greek-administered south of the island: 1,406 properties in Larnaca, 1,291 in Paphos, 1,154 in Limassol and 58 in Famagusta.
A separate parliamentary question asking how much land in the Greek-administered south of the island had passed into Israeli ownership had no answer in the available records.
The scale of Israeli property acquisition nevertheless illustrates the growing economic and social footprint of Israelis on the island.
A network spanning several jurisdictions
According to Turkish authorities, the wider fraud operation used multilingual call-centre employees to approach victims with online advertisements promising high returns from forex and cryptocurrency investments.
Investigators say victims were directed to platforms displaying fabricated profits. When they attempted to withdraw their money, operators allegedly demanded additional payments described as taxes or account-unblocking fees.
Authorities said victims were targeted across Europe, Asia and Africa, while proceeds were moved through bank accounts and cryptocurrency wallets abroad.
The emerging picture is therefore of a network operating across multiple jurisdictions: alleged boiler-room operations in Türkiye, Israeli-linked suspects and ownership structures identified by Turkish investigators, and a corporate and technical footprint extending into Limassol.
The Greek-administered Cyprus connections are particularly significant because they sit within a rapidly expanding Israel-Greek-administered Cyprus relationship encompassing defence, maritime cooperation, tourism, property and business.
For investigators, the central unresolved question is how the Istanbul call centres, Israeli-linked individuals and ownership structures, and the Greek-administered Cyprus-registered companies and technical infrastructure fit together — and whether the offshore entities played an operational or financial role in the alleged fraud.

A new book published Tuesday by the brother of the late Princess Diana has made headlines around the world with its damning allegations about Diana's ex-husband, now King Charles III, and has reopened decades-old wounds within the U.K.'s royal family.
In "Swan Song: Diana, My Sister,” Charles Spencer alleges that he argued with the then-Prince Charles over palace plans for Prince William and Prince Harry, then 15 and 12, to walk behind their mother's coffin during her 1997 funeral procession.
Spencer says he told Charles that Diana, who was killed in a car crash in Paris at the age of 36, would not have wanted her boys to undergo the ordeal. He claims the prince "went ballistic” during the argument and told him: "Rest assured, we’ll forget her soon enough." Spencer also accuses Charles of having "contempt” for his ex-wife and of sounding "elated” after her death.
After excerpts of the book were published last week, Buckingham Palace responded with a strongly worded statement that's rare by the measured standards of the royal household.
"His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and color memory in ways others do not recognize, even many years after such a loss,” it said.
Spencer has stood by his claims, insisting to the BBC that he is telling the truth. On the royal rebuttal, he asked: "Is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?”
Charles, then 32, married 20-year-old Lady Diana Spencer in a lavish ceremony at St. Paul’s Cathedral in 1981. The couple divorced in 1996, and a decade later Charles married Camilla Parker Bowles, now Queen Camilla.
Charles Spencer, the 9th Earl Spencer, has long clashed with the royals over their treatment of his older sister.
Tensions between the palace and the Spencer family following her death were dramatized in the film "The Queen” and the Netflix series "The Crown."
In a searing eulogy at his sister’s funeral, Spencer vowed that her "blood family” would carry on her "imaginative and loving” legacy in raising her two sons. The speech was widely considered a swipe at the royal family.
At the time, many in the U.K. and beyond felt Queen Elizabeth II and the royals were too slow to acknowledge the global outpouring of grief over Diana's death and that the monarchy was deeply out of touch with the public mood.
The royals have spent decades putting that period of crisis behind them. The warmer, more personable approach of William and Harry – and, in recent years, the king – is a legacy of that time.
In his book, Spencer also criticized the royals for what he described as a "lack of obvious care” for the then 12-year-old Harry.
He recounted how "tiny, and slight, and bereft” his nephew looked after the funeral. "He needed Diana’s hugs, of course, and they would forever be denied him,” he wrote. "But instead of calm and nurture, he was allowed to spin out of control.”
Some critics have questioned why Spencer felt the need to revisit the pain and trauma 30 years on.
The aristocrat said he wanted to write down his own thoughts and memories about Diana, "once and for all, rather than having the discomfort of again reading the opinions of others, many of which are based on untruths.”
Asked if the relationship between the press and Harry and his wife, Meghan, mirrors the way the media treated his sister, Spencer told the BBC: "(Diana) was really brought low by all that criticism. I suppose it's a pity when I see echoes of that now.”
Penguin Press said the book will be published globally and translated into 12 languages.

Invisible pixels protect South Korean graduates’ photos from deepfake abuse
The alumni-built technology embeds photos with signals that confuse AI generators to prevent images from being manipulated
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
A South Korean university has embedded graduation photos with anti-deepfake technology to prevent a repeat of a scandal two years ago, when portraits of female graduates were used to create sexually explicit manipulated images.
Seoul National University’s (SNU) use of StealCut Protect, created by a start-up founded by SNU alumni, marked the first time it was used for a university graduation album in the country, The Korea Herald reported. StealCut provided the technology to SNU free of charge.
Deepfake models generally work by analysing facial structure characteristics to generate manipulated content. StealCut Protect inserts minute, pixel-level signals – largely invisible to the human eye – into images to disrupt this process. If a deepfake generator tries to manipulate a protected photo, the result is a distorted or unidentifiable face.

As gangs gain influence, Brazil seeks to shield election from candidates with criminal ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
10:09:57 UTC
19:09:57 KST

As gangs gain influence, Brazil seeks to shield election from candidates with criminal ties
RIO DE JANEIRO, Sept 22 - Brazil has opened a new front against organized crime to keep candidates suspected of criminal ties off the ballot at October's general election in what experts say is an unprecedented effort in Latin American politics.
But, by targeting politicians who have not been convicted of any crime, the campaign is raising questions from some experts and targeted candidates over whether electoral authorities are stretching the limits of existing law and risking violations of due process.
"Interference in the election, in the people's democratic vote, whether political or judicial, leads to a dictatorship," said center-right congressional candidate Clebio Lopes Jacare, whose candidacy was barred over allegations that he is part of a criminal organization.
Brazil's courts have long played a decisive role in determining who can run for office, banning even the most consequential candidates because they had convictions, including President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who was barred from the 2018 election, and rival ex-President Jair Bolsonaro, who is blocked from this year's race. Both claimed the cases against them were politically motivated.
But prosecutors are now advancing an interpretation of Brazil's law which they say allows them to protect the ballot from even suspected criminals, pitting growing concern over organized crime's influence in politics against democratic protections.
Brazilian legislation typically requires a conviction by an appellate court to bar candidates from running. Yet a Reuters review of 20 rulings barring candidates under the push against organized crime shows that none have been convicted at that level.
Criminal gangs' influence in politics is "a big and growing problem in Latin America," said Marcela Rios Tobar, regional director for Latin America and the Caribbean at the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance, a non-profit.
However, she stressed the need to balance those concerns with legal due process and avoid a situation where "accusations of wrongdoing are used as a political weapon."
GANGS EXPAND THEIR REACH
As Jacare's campaign team distributed leaflets in Nova Iguacu, a city of 800,000 people where he unsuccessfully ran for mayor, he stressed that authorities have yet to find him guilty of any crime.
Prosecutors should seek to bar candidates linked to organized crime, Jacare said. But "they need to have facts, proof. It can't just be based on guesswork."
But a 2024 ruling by Brazil's Superior Electoral Court, which oversees elections in the country, opened a precedent for authorities to challenge candidacies based on evidence rather than waiting for a criminal conviction.
The basis for the ruling is an article in Brazil's Constitution that says political parties cannot make use of paramilitary groups.
"Organized crime cannot find in the ballot box a path to institutionalize the power it conquered through weapons," said the head of the electoral court's office in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Claudio de Mello Tavares.
Nowhere is the criminal reach into politics in Brazil more evident than in the state of Rio de Janeiro, where the then head of the state assembly, Rodrigo Bacellar, was jailed last year accused of links to the Red Command, one of Brazil's biggest crime syndicates, which was designated as a terrorist group by the US.
Officials are also investigating whether campaigns used money from organized crime, and have moved a small share of voting locations in Rio because they were in areas dominated by gangs.
Having polling stations "where the voting machine will be transported in an armored vehicle," Tavares said, raises obvious safety concerns for voters.
NECESSARY MEASURE OR OVERREACH?
Among the candidates barred this year are two close relatives of Red Command leaders, a candidate charged in three murder cases, and a man convicted and given a 36-year sentence for illegal firearms possession who can still appeal.
But at least five people who prosecutors are seeking to keep off the ballot had no known links to armed groups. Jacare, the candidate from Rio, was charged with embezzlement and other crimes.
Prosecutors argued, in Jacare's case, that "the democratic process cannot be hijacked by organized crime, whether armed or not."
The challenge of separating necessary measures from overreach is not lost on candidates being barred now.
"If everyone facing any type of legal proceeding or investigation were barred from running for office, Lula wouldn't be president, and Flavio Bolsonaro wouldn't be a candidate," Ney Santos, a congressional candidate whose bid has been challenged by prosecutors citing alleged ties to the First Capital Command crime syndicate, said in a video posted on Instagram.
Sao Paulo's electoral courts ruled in Santos' favor, but prosecutors said they'll appeal. Santos did not reply to a request for comment.
Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, Lula's main competitor in this year's race, is being investigated for corruption, according to newly unsealed court files. He denies any wrongdoing.
Still, the courts' efforts against organized crime have found support among three legal experts consulted by Reuters. Electoral law professor Clever Vasconcelos said courts are responding to a real threat by adopting a broader interpretation of existing rules.
However, he added, Congress should amend the law to expand grounds for ineligibility to give efforts against organized crime a firmer legal basis.
Yet Brazil has faced challenges even when the law is clearer.
Lula was barred from the 2018 election under a law that bars convicted felons from running for office. But the conviction was later annulled, paving the way for his victory in the 2022 presidential race.
Efforts to bar malicious actors cannot come at the expense of due process, said Priscila Pamela Santos, president of the Institute for Defense of the Right to Defense, a Brazilian non-profit.
"One cannot resort to unconstitutional measures that, in an attempt to protect democracy, end up undermining it," she said.
Candidates barred by local courts can still appeal, and hope Brazil's highest electoral court does not confirm the 2024 precedent, said Rafael Soares, a law professor at Brazil's PUC-PR University.
"No one would be naive enough to imagine that there isn't already an infiltration of organized crime into the elections," he said. "The question we have now is the level of response and the legal limits we face." REUTERS

Budget millions for Odrex: the clinic involved in 10 criminal proceedings received UAH 111 million from the NHSU in 2025
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
13:08:26 EEST
19:08:26 KST

Budget millions for Odrex: the clinic involved in 10 criminal proceedings received UAH 111 million from the NHSU in 2025
Kyiv • UNN
The private Odesa clinic Odrex, which figures in 10 criminal proceedings, received UAH 111 million from the NHSU in 2025—more than Dobrobut, Oxford Medical, Oberig, and other major private medical networks.
Odesa’s Odrex clinic has emerged among the leaders of private healthcare in terms of payments received from the National Health Service of Ukraine under the Medical Guarantees Programme. According to data published by Forbes, in 2025 Odrex received UAH 111 million from the NHSU. Only Medical Plaza — UAH 171 million — and St. Nicholas Clinic together with Oleksandrivska Hospital — UAH 426 million — received more, UNN writes.
Further down the ranking, the amounts decrease sharply. Dobrobut received UAH 47.9 million from the NHSU, Oberih — UAH 20.4 million, St. Paraskeva Medical Centre — UAH 15.2 million, Oxford Medical — UAH 11.8 million, Into-Sana — UAH 9.5 million, TOP Clinic DENIS — UAH 8.4 million, and ON Clinic — UAH 4.3 million.
In other words, Odrex received more than twice as much from the NHSU as Dobrobut, and almost 10 times more than Oxford Medical. This is despite the fact that both networks are larger than Odrex in terms of revenue: Dobrobut’s revenue amounts to UAH 4.4 billion, Oxford Medical’s to UAH 1.5 billion, while Odrex has just UAH 1.3 billion.
Overall, the 12 private medical networks in the ranking received approximately UAH 825.5 million from the NHSU. Almost 86% of these funds went to three players — St. Nicholas Clinic together with Oleksandrivska Hospital, Medical Plaza, and Odrex.
It should be noted that these are funds paid by the NHSU to healthcare facilities for providing patients with services under the Medical Guarantees Programme. Private clinics that have signed the relevant contracts with the NHSU receive money for primary and specialised medical care, rehabilitation, treatment of strokes and heart attacks, and other areas covered by the programme.
UAH 111 million in budget funds — against the backdrop of 10 criminal proceedings
The large amount of state payments to the Odrex clinic is attracting attention not only because of its ratio to payments received by other private clinics. According to the Office of the Prosecutor General, law enforcement officers are investigating 10 criminal proceedings involving the clinic. These include proceedings under Criminal Code articles concerning fraud, improper performance of professional duties by a medical worker, and intentional homicide.
Of course, the very fact that criminal proceedings have been opened does not mean that the guilt of the clinic, its owners, or its employees has been proven. Only a court can establish the guilt of a specific person.
It is noteworthy that, for cooperation with the NHSU, this criminal track record in itself did not become a red flag. Despite 10 criminal proceedings and public complaints from patients, Odrex continues to provide Ukrainians with services under the Medical Guarantees Programme.
The reason is the entirely technical criteria used to select NHSU partners. As UNN previously wrote, when concluding contracts, the National Health Service primarily assesses whether a healthcare facility meets the established technical requirements for a specific package of medical services. A clinic’s reputation is not a separate selection criterion.
In other words, criminal investigations and multimillion-hryvnia budget payments can coexist today. And the questions concern not only Odrex but also the state contracting model itself — is formal compliance with NHSU requirements sufficient when such a significant body of criminal proceedings and patient complaints accumulates around a healthcare facility?

KUALA LUMPUR, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- The present haze situation is expected to persist into early 2027 due to prolonged hot and dry weather resulting from the El Nino phenomenon, Malaysian Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Arthur Joseph Kurup said on Tuesday.
El Nino is forecast to intensify into a Super El Nino stage from October this year until January 2027, with its effects persisting until June, while the southwest monsoon occurring concurrently is causing lower rainfall and hotter, drier conditions, Arthur told local media.
"The prolonged dry conditions will increase the risk of open fires, especially in areas prone to fires," he said, adding that this prolonged haze goes beyond past occurrences that would last for one to two months.
Arthur also said Malaysia will assist Indonesia in tackling forest and land fires, including by providing aerial firefighting capabilities, adding that Malaysia has offered aerial water-bombing operations using helicopters, firefighting support using amphibious aircraft and the implementation of cloud-seeding operations.

According to the country's air quality rating, an API reading of zero to 50 is "good," 51 to 100 "moderate," 101 to 200 "unhealthy," 201 to 300 "very unhealthy," and 301 and above is "hazardous." ■

Fitch upgrades Sri Lanka's rating to "B-" with stable outlook
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:07:47 CST
19:07:47 KST

COLOMBO, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Fitch Ratings has upgraded Sri Lanka's Long-Term Issuer Default Ratings to "B-" from "CCC+," with a stable outlook, citing progress in macroeconomic stabilization, fiscal reforms and improvements in the country's external position.
The ratings agency said Tuesday that stronger fiscal and external balances, together with a modest rebuilding of foreign exchange reserves, had reduced external financing risks and strengthened Sri Lanka's capacity to absorb shocks.
Fitch expects Sri Lanka to record a primary surplus of 2.6 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026, down from 5.4 percent in 2025, while the overall budget deficit is forecast to widen to 4.1 percent of GDP from 2.3 percent.
Government debt is projected to decline to 92.9 percent of GDP in 2026 from 96.7 percent in 2025 and fall to the low-80 percent range over the next five years. However, Fitch said debt and debt-servicing indicators remain significantly higher than those of similarly rated countries.
The agency expects economic growth to moderate to 4.1 percent in 2026 from an average of 5 percent over the previous two years, with medium-term growth seen at slightly above 4 percent.
Fitch warned that external debt repayments are expected to rise over the next five years, particularly after 2028, leaving Sri Lanka vulnerable to external shocks and policy slippage.
The agency said further improvements in public debt ratios and foreign exchange reserves could support a future upgrade, while weaker fiscal discipline or renewed external liquidity pressures could lead to negative rating action. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: For U.S. and China, stability means predictability, says U.S. scholar Kuhn
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-22
18:07:26 CST
19:07:26 KST

by Xinhua writer Yang Shilong
NEW YORK, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- The United States and China have different reasons for seeking a more stable relationship, but both stand to gain from greater predictability even as many differences need to be properly managed, U.S. scholar Robert Lawrence Kuhn has said.
"Each side, the U.S. and China, has a big stake in constructive strategic stability, but for different reasons," Kuhn said in a recent interview with Xinhua.
As long as the outcome is constructive strategic stability, he added, "then everybody wins."
Kuhn, a longtime observer of China who has authored books on the country's development and governance, said the concept should not be taken to mean that differences between the two countries have disappeared. Rather, it points to the need to keep differences under control.
Rather, he said, the immediate value of stability is to prevent those differences from repeatedly disrupting the broader relationship and to make its trajectory more predictable.
STABILITY MEANS PREDICTABILITY
Kuhn said the wording of "constructive strategic stability" itself deserves attention, as such terminology can provide strategic guidance for handling bilateral affairs across various fields.
"When China commits to a certain phraseology or certain words, that's a serious meaning," he said.
The central word, he added, is "stability."
"Stability means something that is predictable, something that maintains a trajectory where you can forecast," Kuhn said. "Stability is broadly important from an economic and prosperity point of view for the world, for China, the U.S. for sure."
Kuhn said "constructive" is also significant because it acknowledges that the relationship needs work. The objective is not to pretend that disagreements no longer exist, but to create a framework in which they can be managed, he added.
For Washington, Kuhn pointed to a fierce midterm election environment and multiple international challenges. China, meanwhile, places a premium on a stable external environment as it pursues its economic and development goals.
THE WORLD ALSO HAS A STAKE
From artificial intelligence and climate change, public health and the fight against drug trafficking, China and the United States are involved in many of the major issues confronting the international community.
Kuhn said the benefits of a more predictable relationship would extend beyond the two countries.
"There's no question that U.S.-China relations are the single biggest factor in the world, in terms of giving the world confidence in the future," he said.
He cautioned, however, against confusing stability with reconciliation.
Rather than expecting Washington and Beijing to suddenly work together perfectly, the more immediate objective should be to prevent disputes over tariffs, critical minerals and other issues from repeatedly escalating.
WHY THE STATE VISIT MATTERS
Against that backdrop, Kuhn said an upcoming meeting between Xi and Trump in Washington could be consequential even without dramatic breakthroughs.
"Whenever President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump meet, it is good for U.S.-China relations and for the world," he said.
Kuhn said there is "a good chemistry between the two presidents" and that Trump places considerable weight on personal relationships with other leaders.
A visibly constructive meeting, he said, sends a signal through government and business circles that legitimate engagement with the other country is acceptable. That matters because political uncertainty can itself discourage economic and social ties.
"It's easier not to do something than to do something," Kuhn said. "When there's uncertainty, you just do nothing. That's the safest thing to do."
The same applies to people-to-people exchanges. Kuhn said scholars, healthcare professionals, cultural institutions and others have increasingly worried that engagement could be interpreted as "aiding the other side, the competitor."
Clear support from the top can help create political space for such contacts, he said. Of sustained people-to-people engagement, Kuhn said, "I think it's the single most important thing the world can do on a long-term basis." ■

SYDNEY, Sept. 22 (Xinhua) -- Endangered black teatfish sea cucumbers can live for more than 100 years, far longer than previously thought, highlighting the species' vulnerability to overfishing, an Australian study finds.
The findings suggested black teatfish sea cucumber populations recovered much more slowly from fishing pressure than previously thought, with implications for commercial fishery catch limits, according to a statement released Tuesday by the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS).
In a genetic mark-recapture study, researchers compared DNA samples from black teatfish collected in a no-take zone of Australia's Great Barrier Reef Marine Park in 2000 with samples from the same location 24 years later.
Small biopsies were taken from the animals, which were then returned, while modelling was used to estimate their lifespan. Of 55 animals sampled, 33, or 60 percent, were identified as the same as those sampled in 2000.
The findings showed the sea cucumbers lived for at least 24 to 27 years on average, while some survived for more than a century, said Sven Uthicke, a senior principal research scientist at the AIMS and lead author of the study published in iScience.
"Most of the recaptured animals had grown very little over the 24 years, and many had become smaller," Uthicke said, calling for more conservative harvesting to avoid possible extinction and preserve the species' ecological functions.
Sea cucumbers play a vital role in tropical marine ecosystems by recycling nutrients and mixing sediment, and healthy populations can also enhance coral health, researchers said.
Black teatfish are classified as Endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature and listed under Appendix II of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species. ■

"Looking ahead, a key risk factor is a possible reassessment of AI-related asset valuations, which could prompt a retrenchment in related investments, weighing on the revenues and earnings of exposed firms," said the MAS.

The MAS also said the ongoing energy supply disruptions have kept oil prices elevated, placing some strain on household budgets.
"Looking ahead, there are also risks that a sharp retrenchment in AI-related investment could weigh on global growth, business investment and semiconductor demand, adversely impacting household incomes and employment," it added.
However, it noted most household borrowers remain resilient under a severe stress test, though a small share of borrowers could face liquidity strains.
Meanwhile, risks to the outlook include the possibility of a pullback in AI-related investment that could harm growth prospects and impact corporate profitability, another round of trade tensions, or a further energy shock arising in the Middle East, said the MAS.
Although asset quality could come under some pressure in these scenarios, credit risk is expected to stay under control.
Its stress test also affirms that Singapore banks have sufficient capital buffers to weather an adverse scenario driven by a downturn in the AI-led global growth cycle amid tensions in the Middle East. ■
