Mooncakes made at the Keelung Detention Center have proven a surprise hit ahead of this year’s Mid-Autumn Festival, with a pair of inmate-bakers preparing to ship out about 10,000 of the traditional pastries over the holiday period.
During a visit to the prison yesterday, the Central News Agency toured the cramped 3 ping (9.92m²) kitchen, where two inmates, using three ovens, have been churning out trays of egg yolk pastry — a Taiwanese-style mooncake also known as danhuangs.
The work is labor-intensive, with each batch of cakes needing to be flipped twice during their 25-to-30-minute baking time in order to evenly cook the flaky, layered pastry skin that holds the red bean paste and salted duck egg filling.
Photo: CNA
The two inmates running the kitchen — one with previous experience as a baker and one without — each received training from a professional baker hired by the detention center, officials said.
Wan Shih-chiang (萬世強), the prison’s secretary, said that orders for the pastries were currently fully booked, as the scale of production was constrained by the kitchen’s small size.
The prison initially planned to sell the cakes on a limited-time basis, Wan said, but if demand continues after the holiday, it would evaluate whether to continue production.
Wan said he hoped the work experience, including the positive feedback from customers, would give the inmates confidence in their ability to reintegrate into society after their release.
According to the Keelung Detention Center, its egg yolk pastries are sold under the name Hou Chiang Bakery (鱟江烘焙坊), and are available in boxes of 12 for NT$480 or six for NT$250.

EDITORIAL: Central bank bucks the trend
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:09 UTC
01:46:09 KST

The central bank on Thursday kept interest rates unchanged for a 10th consecutive quarter, while further easing housing credit controls by raising the loan-to-value ratio cap on loans for a second home to 70 percent from 60 percent. The bank also raised its GDP growth forecast for this year to 11.48 percent, up from 9.45 percent estimated in June, and revised its full-year inflation forecasts upward to 2.03 percent for the consumer price index (CPI) and 2.16 percent for core CPI (excluding vegetables, fruit and energy items) from 1.91 percent and 1.9 percent respectively.
The move surprised market observers who had expected the bank to follow the global tightening trend after the US Federal Reserve raised rates by 0.25 percentage points last week. The Bank of Japan also raised its rates on Friday. The European Central Bank and the Bank of Korea have lifted rates twice since June. Taiwan’s central bank has held its policy rates unchanged since March 2024. Before the board meeting, it faced considerable pressure over whether to raise rates, as CPI had remained above its 2 percent alert threshold for four consecutive months. Last week’s decision was not unanimous, with two board members voting for a rate hike.
After the meeting, central bank Governor Yang Chin-long (楊金龍) reiterated that the bank had adopted a more hawkish stance since March 2024, which included several rounds of selective credit controls on the housing market. He cited three reasons the bank was bucking the global tightening trend. First, consumer inflation remains relatively moderate, and the forecast points to downward pressure on inflation next year. Second, the bank is using quantitative tools and monetary operations rather than interest rates to manage money supply conditions and contain liquidity expansion. Third, and perhaps most important, the economic recovery remains uneven. The artificial intelligence (AI)-driven export boom has boosted the high-tech industry, but traditional industries and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) are still struggling, while domestic consumption and wage growth remain moderate. A rate hike would increase mortgage burdens for first-time homebuyers and harm traditional industries and SMEs, Yang said.
Keeping rates unchanged demonstrated the central bank’s belief that imported inflation remains under control. However, economists at DBS Bank Ltd and Capital Economics Ltd said that the central bank’s inflation outlook seemed a bit sanguine. DBS cited elevated international energy and commodity prices and persistent domestic inflation expectations. The central bank itself said services inflation showed downward rigidity.
Compared with its June meeting, the bank last week devoted significantly more time to the importance of the M2 money supply. The bank said that as the M2 annual growth rate is still lower than the economic growth rate plus the inflation rate, its monetary-policy stance remains relatively high. That shows that the bank’s policy framework relies not only on interest rates but also on open market operations. Even without rate hikes, the bank has effectively guided market rates upward and contained monetary expansion through quantitative adjustments.
Overall, the bank remains cautious about conveying its slightly hawkish bias in monetary policy and points to a clear K-shaped divergence in the economy. The bank’s latest changes to certain housing credit rules reflect its observation of a decline in real-estate loan concentration, continued weakness in property transactions and softer expectations for housing price increases. The market’s attention has shifted to December. Can Taiwan firmly chart its own course if the Fed continues to raise rates, or if the US-Iran conflict escalates and inflationary pressures persist?
Moreover, uneven economic growth has challenged the bank’s monetary policy. While keeping rates steady helps safeguard traditional industries and SMEs, the AI-driven economic boom has led local lenders to prioritize funding for tech companies, putting traditional industries and SMEs under pressure, Yang said. This uneven capital allocation is a structural issue the central bank cannot solve through monetary policy alone.
Yang called for interagency coordination to address this problem. For example, state-owned banks could use their influence to improve funding access for companies in need; the Financial Supervisory Commission could encourage local lenders to support traditional industries and SMEs; the Small and Medium Enterprise Credit Guarantee Fund could bolster credit guarantees to reduce lenders’ concerns about extending loans; and Chunghwa Post, with its large deposit base, could assist in market fund allocation. As funding demand from tech companies and stock market transactions has risen, even though liquidity in the overall banking system remains ample, the current structural problems require broader action from government agencies, not just interest rate adjustments by the central bank.
Taiwan’s democracy and high-tech economy play a crucial role in global affairs and are central to the world’s embrace of a raft of next-generation technologies, including AI. It is underpinned by a security relationship with the United States that’s existed in several iterations since 1949 and the Chinese Nationalist Party’s (KMT) retreat from China. A central pillar of that security relationship is the American willingness to sell arms to Taiwan. Indeed, since 1979 it has been embedded in US law, with the Taiwan Relations Act (TRA) charging the US with helping to improve the island’s ability to deter an attack from
Academia Historica director Chen Tsui-lien (陳翠蓮), speaking at the handover ceremony for her new role on Monday, said that when she accepted the position, she knew that her peaceful life as a history professor was a thing of the past, and that from now on she would have to “wear a helmet.” A specialist in Taiwan’s post-World War II history and the 228 Incident, she has been accused of being politically divisive. The US’ Taiwan policy will not change, official says

With US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) expected to meet in Washington this week, Mainland Affairs Council Deputy Minister Shen Yu-chung (沈有忠) yesterday said he believes the US would not change its policy toward Taiwan.
Shen made the remarks at a seminar held by the Cross-Strait Policy Association and Tamkang University’s Center for Cross-Strait Relations Studies in Taipei, adding that he believes there would be “three no changes” in the relations among the US, Taiwan and China after the meeting.
First, the fundamental nature and structure of US-China competition would not change; second, US policy toward Taiwan would not fundamentally change; and third, the government’s determination to maintain the “status quo” of peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait will not change, he said.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
Trade and economic issues, including artificial intelligence (AI) competition, tariffs and rare earth export controls, remain the top priority for the US and China in the upcoming summit, he said.
Purchases of US goods, such as soybeans and beef, by China might see further progress during this summit, he said, adding that while they might make some progress on procurement lists, structural competition would persist in areas such as AI and tariffs.
Shen said Xi might continue to exert pressure on Trump on Taiwan and Indo-Pacific, and conduct personal cognitive warfare against him.
The Chinese president might accuse Japan and Taiwan as the real “troublemakers” destroying the “status quo” in the region, and falsely reframe the meaning of maintaining the “status quo,” to pressure the US to compromise to China, he said.
Since the Trump-Xi summit in May, cross-agency and bipartisan US political figures, including US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and House of Representatives Speaker Mike Johnson, have repeatedly stated that US policy toward Taiwan will remain unchanged, Shen said.
The council believes the US would not change its long-established policy toward Taiwan and would sustain deterrent capabilities across the First Island Chain, and Taiwan would continue to deepen cooperation with the US on this basis, he said.
The government will also continue to closely monitor the manipulation of “US skepticism,” “Taiwan skepticism” and “Taiwan abandonment” narratives before and after the summit, he said.
China might leverage this summit to spread defeatist and pessimistic narratives in Taiwan, to drive a wedge between Taiwan and the US, undermine Taiwanese society’s morale and extend those efforts to November’s local elections, he added.
Tamkang University cross-strait relations expert Chang Wu-ueh (張五岳) said the upcoming meeting should not be viewed as a major turning point in US-China relations, but rather managing differences and paving the way for future interactions, with
Chang said he believes Beijing would reiterate its position, but it is unlikely that the US and China would make major new declarations or reach significant deals.
Another Tamkang University cross-strait relations expert, Chen Chien-fu (陳建甫), said observers should not only focus on how many times Taiwan is mentioned in the meeting or if Taiwan would be “sold out,” but instead observe the “boundaries” of any US-China deal and Taiwan’s position within them.
Taiwan must bolster its defense and societal resilience, solidify ties with the US Congress and the First Island Chain allies such as Japan, and reinforce the semiconductor industry as a “silicon shield,” he said.

Taiwan-built sub could reach navy next month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:46:06 UTC
01:46:06 KST

Taiwan’s first domestically built submarine, the Hai Kun (Narwhal, 海鯤), could be delivered to the navy as early as next month, military expert and Taiwan Association for Security and Development chairman Chi Tung-yun (紀東昀) said yesterday.
The submarine was yesterday morning observed departing for its 21st sea trial and its 15th submerged test.
The vessel missed the initial delivery deadline of November last year due to “testing delays,” its primary contractor, shipbuilder CSBC Corp, Taiwan, said in June.
Photo: CNA
The contractor also cited “political pressure from China” in procuring critical equipment.
All testing operations are in the final stages, with the vessel likely to depart on a further round of sea trials this week, based on its prior testing schedule, Chi said.
The submarine has spent about a month in dry dock undergoing adjustments, as many of its systems and equipment are supplied from overseas and require optimization, often needing assistance from the original manufacturer, he said.
Photo: Lee Hui-chou, Taipei Times
Moreover, when equipment inside the vessel requires adjustment, the submarine has to return to dry dock, making the process more time-consuming, he said.
Provided the navy and CSBC Corp, Taiwan continue prioritizing safety, there is a high likelihood of delivery by next month, which would signal the next round of preparations, he said.
The vessel would still need to undergo combined systems testing and crew training for navy personnel before it is ready for mission, which would take an additional several months or even more than a year, he added.

Did OpenAI solve the wrong Navier-Stokes problem?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:40:10 UTC
01:40:10 KST

Two weeks ago OpenAI claimed a solution to one of the biggest open problems in math—the Navier-Stokes problem—an achievement worth a $1-million prize from the Clay Mathematics Institute. The proof ignited a powder keg of concern over artificial intelligence companies’ race to disrupt the subject.
But with the dust still far from settled, a different controversy is emerging: Did OpenAI even solve the right Navier-Stokes problem?
Generated by an internal large language model (LLM), OpenAI’s proof relies on an approach that many experts find unnatural. It solves a variant of the problem that mathematicians say is disconnected from reality and thus less interesting. In a sense, the LLM found and exploited a loophole in the framing of the question.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“The most important problem is unsolved,” says Luis Silvestre, a mathematician at the University of Chicago. “The Clay problem is settled, but the main problem for the Navier-Stokes equations is not.”
Furthermore, last Thursday, three mathematicians posted a proof of their own that showed that OpenAI’s method can never be extended to solve the full problem. In other words, the loophole will never be closed, barring some completely new idea.
The Navier-Stokes equations are supposed to describe how fluids flow, but mathematicians doubt whether they can always be trusted. The million-dollar problem is about whether the equations ever “blow up,” which would mean they’d allow the flow to be infinitely fast at points—something that can’t happen in the real world.
But there’s one piece of the equations that’s optional—sometimes it’s there; sometimes it isn’t. The “it” here is an external force such as gravity that affects how a fluid moves. “All fluids we know of are under some kind of external force,” says mathematician Diego Córdoba. “So to have the force makes complete sense.”
When most experts think about the Navier-Stokes problem, though, it’s without this force. They want to find a purer, more fundamental way for the equations to blow up by using only the intrinsic forces within any fluid—not by applying some specific, precisely contrived external force. “Most of the other groups, it’s true, were specifically considering the scenario without a force,” says mathematician Luis Martínez-Zoroa.
In the past few years, though, Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa put all their focus on this niche piece of the equations and laid out a method to build a very specific external force to trigger a blowup. On September 7 two other mathematicians used their program (and AI) to produce a blowup for a frictionless fluid—considered a major step toward blowing up Navier-Stokes. OpenAI finished the job less than a day later—timing that has led to a heated dispute between the latter two mathematicians and the company.
But the new work released last Thursday shows unequivocally that if the force is removed, the blowup will disappear. OpenAI’s method can never work, in fact, without using a very contrived equation for the force that is unlike anything that could occur in the real world. “They essentially prove that the formulation with an external force was different from the problem we really wanted to solve,” Silvestre says.
In other words, the LLM’s result does not—and will never—answer the Navier-Stokes problem that mathematicians really care about.
It did, however, unambiguously solve the problem according to the Clay Institute’s original formulation. The official problem statement, penned in 2000 by mathematician Charles Fefferman, offers an option called “C,” in which solutions are allowed to use an external force like OpenAI’s.
Now fluid dynamicists are grappling with a possibility few had considered before: the idea that the Navier-Stokes equations can blow up but only with an external force. In this scenario, you can mathematically place a fluid in a specific, unrealistic situation to break the equations, yet the blowup can never come from the fluid itself.
“It’s really uncertain at this moment,” says mathematician Gonzalo Cao-Labora. “Depending on the answer to this, I think the contribution of OpenAI will be regarded differently.” If it turns out to be true, he adds, “people would probably think about the Clay problem and say, ‘We shouldn’t have put the external force in the statement.’”
This might even be good news for “team humanity.” LLMs are great at finding blowups that exist—at searching the infinite landscape of fluid scenarios and plucking out the precise situation that breaks the equations. But proving that blow-up is impossible is a kind of math AI still struggles with. “We may be at less of a disadvantage, or maybe an advantage, compared to LLMs,” says Cao-Labora. “LLMs are especially good at constructing things that are very explicit and not as good—for now—in making new theory.”
But regardless of whether the path to solving the full Navier-Stokes problem requires a clever new blowup or a whole new mathematical discipline, everyone is becoming more hesitant to bet against the machines.
“We are really amazed with how [the technology] has evolved in the last year—so we don't know how it will look in one year,” says Cao-Labora. “It’s really a wake-up call to the community.”

International Day of Peace: Where are conflicts still raging?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:39:34 UTC
01:39:34 KST

Breadcrumb
International Day of Peace: What does the global war map look like?
The world is marking the International Day of Peace on Monday as wars and conflict rage across five continents, with hundreds of thousands of people killed by military violence over the past year.
This year's United Nations observance of the occasion is being held under the theme "Invest in Peace - For Everyone, Everywhere, Every Day", emphasising that peace means more than simply the absence of war and requires security, dignity, opportunity and cooperation.
The day comes as conflicts grow in number and complexity, from Gaza and Sudan to Yemen, Ukraine and Myanmar, alongside armed violence across large parts of Africa and Latin America.
So where are the world's major conflicts, and what does the global picture look like on the International Day of Peace?
How many conflicts are there around the world?
The scale of global conflict has risen sharply in recent years. According to the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO), using data from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, 65 armed conflicts involving a state were recorded across 35 countries in 2025.
That marked the highest number recorded since 1946.
More than 255,000 people were killed in battle-related and other direct violence, with the Russia-Ukraine war, Gaza and Sudan among the biggest contributors to the death toll.
But conventional wars between states or organised armed forces represent only part of the picture. Insurgencies, civil wars and violence involving armed groups continue across Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean.
What is happening in Gaza and the occupied Palestinian territories?
Gaza remains one of the starkest examples of the gulf between the International Day of Peace's message and realities on the ground.
Despite a so-called ceasefire agreement reached last year, Israeli attacks have continued to kill Palestinians in the enclave, with more than 1,000 killed since the agreement was signed and the overall death toll since 7 October 2023 surpassing 73,000.
Most of Gaza's population also remains displaced, with more than two million Palestinians living in the midst of widespread destruction and severe shortages of essential services.
Reconstruction has not taken place amid a continuing Israeli siege and disputes over the next phase of the agreement.
In the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, Israeli military raids, arrests and settler attacks have also continued, alongside Palestinian attacks.
What about Lebanon and Syria?
Lebanon is another front where Israel has continued attacks despite a ceasefire agreement, while occupying areas of the south.
Since 2 March, 4,386 people have been killed and 12,407 wounded, according to Lebanon's Health Ministry, bringing the toll since October 2023 to more than 8,950 killed and at least 30,643 wounded.
Israeli officials have also said troops will not withdraw from the areas they occupy until Hezbollah is "disarmed".
In neighbouring Syria, Israeli forces have also carried out raids and arrests in occupied southern areas while expanding their military presence.
A UN inquiry said this month that some Israeli actions may amount to war crimes, amid Israeli rhetoric indicating no intention to withdraw from areas its forces occupy and plans to maintain a long-term military presence there.
Why does Sudan remain one of the world's worst conflicts?
Sudan's war between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces has entered its fourth year with no political settlement in sight.
Fighting continues across several parts of the country, while civilians face one of the world's largest displacement crises.
Around 14 million people have been forced from their homes during the conflict, according to the UN, with many displaced more than once.
Millions more face acute food insecurity.
External support for the warring sides has also helped prolong the conflict and reduced the prospects for a settlement, according to the UN's expert on Sudan.
Why has Yemen returned to the spotlight?
Yemen has witnessed a major escalation this month after several years of comparatively reduced fighting.
Clashes between the Houthis and government forces have intensified along the country's western coast and elsewhere, triggering another wave of displacement.
More than 112,000 people have been internally displaced during the latest escalation, according to the International Organization for Migration, while more than 3,000 have fled across the Red Sea to Djibouti.
The fighting comes after more than a decade of conflict that has already left Yemen facing a prolonged humanitarian crisis.
Where else are conflicts raging?
Across Africa, several conflicts and insurgencies remain unresolved.
In eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, diplomatic efforts have struggled to translate ceasefire initiatives into lasting calm, while armed groups continue to operate across the region.
Ethiopia has also seen renewed clashes in Tigray this year, raising fears over the durability of the Pretoria agreement that ended the region's previous large-scale war.
Armed groups remain active across the Sahel, Somalia, the Lake Chad Basin and Mozambique.
The Africa Center for Strategic Studies recorded 23,872 deaths linked to militant violence during the 12 months ending in mid-2026, marking the fourth consecutive year in which the toll exceeded 20,000.
Elsewhere, Russia's war in Ukraine is entering its fifth year, while Myanmar remains engulfed in civil war.
What about Latin America and the Caribbean?
Violence in Latin America and the Caribbean often looks different from conventional warfare, but several countries continue to experience armed conflicts involving organised groups.
In Colombia, armed factions linked to the country's decades-long conflict continue to fight each other and government forces.
Haiti faces an even more acute crisis, with armed groups controlling large parts of the capital and expanding attacks into other areas. The UN recorded 1,408 people killed and another 656 injured by violence between April and June this year alone.
Ecuador is also confronting violence linked to organised crime and competition over drug-trafficking routes, which authorities have designated an "internal armed conflict".

How hospitals will operate during the "yellow" and "red" levels of an air raid threat — the government has provided an answer
Kyiv • UNN
At the red level, patients and medical personnel are transferred to shelters, but emergency care does not stop. Emergency medical services operate continuously.
The government has approved new rules for the operation of medical facilities depending on the level of the aerial threat. Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi reported this, according to UNN.
At the yellow level, medical facilities continue to operate. Full access to shelters must be ensured for employees, patients, and visitors. At the red level, patients and medical workers must move to shelters. At the same time, assistance that would be dangerous to interrupt does not stop, including during operations, resuscitation, intensive care, and so on. Patients who cannot be moved continue to receive treatment in the safest available premises. Medical assistance may be provided, medicines dispensed, and patients accommodated in shelters and such premises
According to the prime minister, emergency medical services operate continuously. Patients with urgent conditions are admitted regardless of the threat level. Dispatch services take calls, and ambulance crews go to patients.
The government also instructed that protection be strengthened for operating rooms, intensive care units, maternity and emergency departments, premises with backup power sources, and critically important medical equipment. Special attention should be paid to places where patients who cannot be moved promptly are staying, Koretskyi concluded.

The AI system will offer business matching, multilingual support, exhibition navigation, meeting management and post-event engagement.

'Germany's Mamdani': Who is Berlin mayor hopeful Elif Eralp?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:32:19 UTC
01:32:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Who is Elif Eralp, the leftist leader with Turkish roots dubbed 'Germany's Mamdani'
Born into a Turkish family that fled the 1980 military coup, Elif Eralp is now within reach of governing Berlin after leading the left-wing Die Linke party to a historic election victory in the German capital.
The 45-year-old lawyer emerged as one of the biggest winners of Sunday's Berlin state election, with Die Linke finishing first and putting her in contention to become the city's next governing mayor.
Eralp has presented herself as a politician from a migrant background who puts housing, social justice and combating racism at the heart of local politics.
She has also spoken out against Germany's crackdown on pro-Palestinian activism, saying that "Germany must end its repression of those who stand in solidarity with Palestine and hold the Israeli government accountable".
Eralp's parents were socialists and trade unionists who were forced to leave Turkey after the 1980 coup for fear of persecution.
Her mother was pregnant with her when the family arrived in Germany, where Eralp was born in Munich in 1981. The family later moved to Dortmund and then Hamburg, where she grew up and studied law. She is married and has two children.
Early political activism
Eralp became politically active at an early age. As a child, she founded an environmental club before becoming involved in the anti-nuclear movement in Hamburg and Gorleben.
After studying law, she moved to Berlin in 2010 and worked as a legal adviser to Die Linke's federal parliamentary group alongside her trade union activities.
She officially joined the party in 2017 after years of working within its parliamentary groups.
She has linked her decision to join to the need for a political force that would offer an alternative to liberal economic policies and confront the rise of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).
In 2018, she joined Die Linke's Berlin leadership and entered the state parliament in 2021. She later became deputy parliamentary group leader and has served as a deputy party leader in Berlin since last year.
Housing fuels Eralp's political rise
Eralp has built much of her political profile around Berlin's housing crisis, advocating rent controls, more public housing and bringing some properties owned by major housing companies into public ownership.
She has also called for curbs on the influence of major property companies and stronger protections against tenants being forced out by rising rents, advocating for Berlin to become a "city of solidarity".
Her focus on housing has allowed her to campaign heavily on everyday concerns such as rents, living costs and public services.
She has reportedly drawn inspiration from progressive US politician Zohran Mamdani in New York, particularly his focus on affordability as an issue capable of mobilising voters.
Palestine and Israel
Eralp's victory took on added significance as the far-right AfD won a separate state election in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern on the same day.
Confronting the far right and combating racism have been central to Eralp's political message, alongside calls for greater political and social participation among people from migrant backgrounds.
But her rise has also brought renewed attention to one of the most sensitive issues within Germany's left: Israel and Palestine.
During the campaign, Eralp stressed that antisemitism must be confronted and that she takes the concerns of Berlin's Jewish community seriously.
At the same time, she has expressed solidarity with Palestinians and stressed her desire to protect Jewish, Muslim and Palestinian communities in Berlin.
The position reflects a broader challenge for Die Linke as it seeks to maintain its focus on migration, anti-racism and Palestinian rights while addressing concerns over antisemitism and appealing to Berlin's diverse electorate.
Elif Eralp's path to governing Berlin
Eralp's rise was far from assured at the start of the campaign, but she put the housing crisis, cost of living, social justice and confronting the far right at the centre of her message.
Sunday's result transformed her political standing.
Die Linke won 25.7% of the vote, the party’s best result in Berlin since reunification, and more than double its 12.2% share in 2023.
Meanwhile, the governing coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Social Democratic Party (SPD) lost its majority.
Eralp has said she wants to negotiate with the Greens and SPD over forming a new state government.
But finishing first does not automatically make her governing mayor. Taking the post will depend on coalition negotiations and whether the parties can agree on a governing programme.
Housing is likely to be among the most difficult issues in those talks, given Eralp's support for bringing major housing companies into public ownership and implementing the result of Berlin's 2021 housing referendum.
Any new government will also face significant financial constraints, potentially putting ambitious campaign promises up against competing spending priorities.
Die Linke's positions on Israel and Gaza could prove another point of contention as Eralp attempts to move the party from opposition into government in one of Europe's most diverse capitals.
Her rise is therefore no longer simply the story of the daughter of Turkish refugees who reached parliament. It now raises the question of whether she can turn a campaign built around housing, social justice and combating racism into a governing programme while navigating the demands of potential coalition partners.

How Washington left Saudi Arabia’s plea for help unanswered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:31:34 UTC
01:31:34 KST

Breadcrumb
How Trump failed to answer Saudi plea for help against Houthis when Riyadh needed it most
Saudi Arabia has spent decades building its security partnership with Washington, buying billions of dollars in US weapons and cultivating close ties with successive American administrations.
But when Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman made a direct plea to US President Donald Trump for military help against Yemen's Houthis, Washington ultimately stepped away.
For two weeks, Trump had wrestled with whether to order US strikes on Houthi targets as the Iran-backed group intensified attacks on Saudi Arabia and made territorial gains in Yemen.
The issue came to a head on Thursday when Mohammed bin Salman called Trump and urged him to intervene against the rapidly advancing Iran-backed group, according to the New York Times.
Trump had told advisers a day earlier that he opposed strikes. After the call, however, he changed course and ordered the Pentagon to prepare for an attack.
By Sunday, US commanders had reportedly approved target lists and troops were loading bombs onto warplanes. Then Trump reversed course again, calling off the strikes, at least for now.
So why did Trump stop short when one of Washington's closest Middle Eastern partners was asking for help?
Why is Saudi Arabia asking for US help?
Riyadh's plea comes at one of its most vulnerable moments in years, as the Houthis renewed attacks on Saudi cities, oil infrastructure and shipping while making significant advances in western Yemen, taking the whole of Yemen's Red Sea coast including the area around the strategically important Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
The threat has been compounded by the wider war with Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and increased Saudi Arabia's reliance on alternative export routes through the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline, a crucial route for bypassing Hormuz, has also been largely shut following an attack Riyadh blamed on Iran-backed Iraqi militias.
That has left the kingdom facing pressure on its oil export routes from multiple directions.
Former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia Michael Ratney said Riyadh had spent decades investing in its US security partnership precisely for such a crisis.
"The reason a country like Saudi Arabia invests so heavily in developing a security partnership with the United States is for just this sort of eventuality," Ratney told the NYT.
Saudi officials have also made clear that they do not want to confront the Houthis alone after the kingdom's previous military campaign in Yemen became a costly, years-long conflict.
Why did Trump hesitate?
For Trump, intervening would mean opening another front while the US is already at war with Iran.
Most of his inner circle were either deeply sceptical of or opposed to joining Saudi Arabia's fight, amid concerns over pressure on the US military and its weapons stockpiles.
There were also doubts that another bombing campaign would work. The US struck more than 1,000 Houthi targets during a campaign lasting more than 50 days in 2025, but the group survived and has since rebuilt much of its military capability.
Trump has also stressed that the Houthis are currently targeting Saudi Arabia rather than the United States.
He said on Sunday that Washington had remained in communication with the group and that the Houthis had so far agreed not to fight the US. Houthi officials have disputed Trump's claim that they contacted Washington.
That gives Trump little incentive to restart a direct confrontation that could bring American ships back into the Houthis' sights and further threaten shipping through Bab al-Mandeb.
What does this mean for the US-Saudi relationship?
The Trump administration last week asked Congress to approve the sale of 48 F-35 fighter jets to Saudi Arabia in a deal estimated at $24.3 billion, saying it would strengthen the security of a "major non-NATO ally", can be an indication that Washington has not abandoned Riyadh altogether.
But advanced weapons sales are different from direct US military intervention, and the latest crisis has exposed the limits of what Riyadh can expect from Washington when their immediate interests diverge.
Saudi Arabia has already been looking to broaden its security partnerships. Last month, it signed the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement (MJDA) with Turkey and Pakistan, under which an armed attack on one of the three countries is considered an attack on all.
Turkey has since said it is prepared to help meet Saudi military needs as Houthi attacks intensify.
For Riyadh, it is a reminder that even close ties with Washington offer no guarantee of US support when American interests lie elsewhere.

Ground-based beam could keep British solar drone flying
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
17:30:56 BST
01:30:56 KST

PHASA-35, the solar-powered stratospheric aircraft developed by BAE Systems’ Prismatic, has been selected as the flight demonstration platform for a power beaming technology intended to keep high-altitude aircraft flying through the night and the winter, under a £15.7 million contract linked to the Advanced Research and Invention Agency, the company stated.
The work forms part of ARIA’s Enduring Atmospheric Platforms programme, which aims to develop low-cost, long-endurance platforms for high-altitude communications. It runs in three stages over three and a half years and concludes with an integrated flight demonstration aboard PHASA-35.
The problem it addresses is the one every solar-powered high-altitude aircraft faces. Flight depends on the sun, and the company describes that as a significant challenge in places like Britain, where winter daylight is limited and the nights are long. According to BAE Systems, power beaming removes that dependency by supplying constant power regardless of season, making it easier to fly continuously for up to several months at a time.
The system uses what the company describes as a highly controlled ground-based energy beam directed at a dedicated receiver built into the aircraft’s wing, which converts it back into electricity to power the aircraft and charge its batteries. The release notes that similar microwave frequencies are already widely used in aviation, satellite communications and radar.
Bob Davidson, chief executive of Prismatic, said: “PHASA-35 has already proven its worth in the stratosphere as a low-cost alternative to satellites and now this exciting project will explore whether we can make it even more capable. This is a strong example of British organisations working together to advance an emerging technology.”
Rico Chandra, programme director for Enduring Atmospheric Platforms at ARIA, said: “This research expands the UK’s leadership in high-altitude platforms to become the place where this industry is designed, built and scaled. Getting there means backing bold ideas, from fixed-wing solar aircraft to designs nobody predicted, including aircraft that fly on spinning wings instead of propellers.”
PHASA-35 has a 35-metre wingspan and weighs 150kg, and according to the company has the potential to operate above 66,000ft for months at a time, delivering persistent communications, Earth observation and surveillance at a fraction of the cost of traditional satellites and with greater flexibility to deploy and upgrade.
According to the company the benefit may extend beyond endurance, since reducing the weight of onboard battery arrays could free capacity on an aircraft that already carries a payload of up to 15kg, which the company says can be used for sensors across intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, communications, Earth observation and defence applications.
Batteries are a large share of the weight on any solar aircraft of this kind, since they have to carry the aircraft through every hour of darkness, and the longer the night the more of them are needed. An aircraft able to draw power from the ground overnight could, in principle, carry fewer batteries and more equipment.
ARIA was established in 2023 as an independent body funding high-risk research, modelled in part on the American Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, with the freedom to back programmes that conventional funding routes would not.
Prismatic became part of BAE Systems in 2019, and PHASA-35 has flown a series of stratospheric trials in recent years.

A Government programme intended to raise public awareness of threats to the UK and strengthen national resilience is already under way and will continue through 2027, according to a parliamentary answer.
The timetable was set out in response to a written question from Conservative MP Ben Obese-Jecty, who asked when the national conversation on defence and security promised in the Defence Investment Plan would be delivered. Armed Forces Minister Louise Sandher-Jones said the work is being led by the Cabinet Office through the Home Defence Programme.
She said: “The National Conversation is a programme of public engagement led by the Cabinet Office as part of the Home Defence Programme. Delivery is already underway and will continue through 2027.”
Defence will support the programme through public engagement and communications intended to explain the threats facing the UK, the role played by the Armed Forces in deterrence and resilience, and how individuals, communities and employers can contribute.
Sandher-Jones said: “Defence is supporting this work through planned public engagement activities and a coherent programme of communications. These have been designed to improve understanding of the threats facing the UK, explain the role of Defence in deterrence and national resilience, and encourage practical participation by individuals, communities and employers.”
The work also links into the National Risk Register, which was updated in July 2026, and the internal National Security Risk Assessment used by government to assess the likelihood and potential impact of risks affecting the UK and its interests. According to Sandher-Jones, the public-facing register is intended to show how the Government is preparing for those risks while improving public awareness and supporting a broader approach to national resilience.
Defence is also contributing to a separate Cabinet Office-led national resilience public awareness campaign announced in the Annual Statement on National Resilience on 14 July. The Government intends to judge the wider programme against levels of public preparedness, participation and resilience.
Sandher-Jones said: “Success will be measured by increased public preparedness, participation and resilience.”
Government communications on defence and security are expected to increase ahead of ALBISTON SHADOW, described in the answer as a major UK Home Defence exercise, and NATO’s Crisis Management Exercise in spring 2027.

The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland, and Slovenia did not participate in the competition, while Spain, Ireland, and Slovenia also declined to broadcast the contest.
Lithuania remained in the 2026 competition. Its representative, Lion Ceccah, finished 22nd in the final in Vienna in May with the song “Solo quiero mas.”

Israel prevented Palestinian patients and wounded people in the Gaza Strip from traveling abroad for treatment Monday for the second consecutive day because of Jewish holidays, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
“For the second consecutive day, no patients or wounded people have been evacuated through the Rafah and Kerem Shalom crossings because of holidays observed by the occupation,” the ministry said in a brief statement.
According to Yoram Halevi, Israel’s coordinator of government activities in the Palestinian territories, the Rafah and Kerem Shalom crossings in southern Gaza were closed Sunday and Monday because of Jewish holidays.
The closures came after Israel on Thursday reduced the number of patients, wounded people, and their companions scheduled to leave Gaza for treatment in Egypt from 136 to 61 Palestinians, according to an earlier ministry statement.
The ministry described the move as “a blatant violation of the right to treatment,” warning that it puts hundreds of patients at risk of death by preventing them from reaching specialized hospitals in time.
It called on the World Health Organization, the UN humanitarian chief, and other international organizations to “intervene immediately and exert direct pressure” on Israeli authorities to end what it described as “arbitrary conditions.”
In late August, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said thousands of patients in Gaza were still awaiting medical evacuation for urgent treatment.
Some 13,237 patients, including 6,276 children, along with 16,406 companions, had been evacuated from Gaza since October 2023, he said.
According to an earlier Health Ministry statement, 20,719 patients and wounded people remained on the waiting list to leave Gaza for treatment.
On Feb. 2, Israel partially reopened the Rafah crossing, which it has controlled since May 2024, under strict restrictions to allow limited departures of patients, wounded people, and their companions, as well as the return of Palestinians from abroad.
Months later, Israel also began allowing patients and wounded people to leave through the Kerem Shalom commercial crossing.

The closures come as Gaza’s health sector continues to suffer the consequences of the Israeli war, during which 445 attacks have targeted health facilities and damaged 155 facilities, according to official figures.
Since Oct. 8, 2023, Israel has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians and injured over 174,000 others in its genocide in Gaza, while destroying around 90% of the enclave’s civilian infrastructure.

UK charges man over alleged Rwanda genocide offences
LONDON, Sept 21 - A 65-year-old Rwandan man has been charged with genocide-related offences allegedly committed during the 1994 Rwanda Tutsi killings, British prosecutors said on Monday.
Vincent Brown, formerly known as Vincent Bajinya, was charged with one offence of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity.
Britain's Counter Terrorism Policing War Crimes Team said Brown was accused of encouraging others to kill Tutsis in Kigali in April 1994. The investigation began in 2019 following a request from the Rwandan government and involved years of international cooperation, it added.
Brown was accused of having "directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others", the Crown Prosecution Service said.
The charges against Brown were the first brought in the United Kingdom relating to the Rwandan genocide, the CPS added.
Brown, who is remanded in custody, is due to appear at London's Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.
Police said investigations into six other individuals remain ongoing, including two men arrested in 2024 and 2026 on suspicion of genocide and crimes against humanity who remain on bail.
More than 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed in 100 days in the 1994 genocide, orchestrated by the Hutu ruling majority and meticulously executed by local officials and ordinary citizens. REUTERS

After 9 women murdered, police link 1 death to possible love triangle

Police investigating murders of 9 women in South Africa neighborhood link 1 death to possible love triangle
South African police said Monday they had arrested three people over the killing of one of nine women found dead in a neighborhood east of Johannesburg in a series of murders that have alarmed the nation.
The discovery of the nine bodies in Kempton Park over two months has fueled fear and anger, as authorities investigate whether a serial killer or killers were responsible.
A man and two women were arrested over the weekend over the killing of Jabulile Ntimba, whose body was found on Sept. 17 and was the ninth victim, police said.
As in most of the cases, her body was found on the side of the road, partly clothed.
"There does appear to be an indication that her murder may have stemmed from a relationship-related matter, including what has been described as a possible love triangle," deputy police chief Tebello Mosikili said.
Gender-based violence is endemic in South Africa, despite years of government pledges to tackle the problem and even declaring it a national disaster.
The South African Police Service has issued a public warning for women to be cautious when doing activities like jogging in the area.
President Cyril Ramaphosa on Monday echoed the police pledge that those responsible for the killings would be held accountable.
"We will be pulling out all stops to find these perpetrators," he told journalists, vowing additional measures to tackle violence against women.
"We are going to be deploying more money, more resources, more technology, to ensure that we deal with the fear that women are now subjected to," he said.
The latest arrests bring to four the number of people held by police in connection with the Kempton Park killings.
"While the investigation must establish whether these cases are linked, the possibility that a perpetrator or perpetrators may be targeting women demands our urgent and determined attention," acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia said in a statement. "A multidisciplinary investigation has been established to examine possible links between the cases, identify those responsible and bring them to justice."
A man arrested over the murder of a woman whose body was found in July remains in custody and is due back in court on Oct. 28, police said.
"We are not going to rush these investigations simply to make arrests. We owe it to the victims, we owe it to their families, and we owe it to justice to get this right," Mosikili said.
Separately, police said another woman was found dead on Sunday in Soweto, south of Johannesburg, her body wrapped in a duvet and dumped near a dam.
Police also said two alleged serial rapists were due in court in the eastern province of KwaZulu-Natal. A 46-year-old man has been linked by DNA to 16 rape cases in the province's largest city, Durban, while a 36-year-old man has been linked to at least 14 cases across two provinces.
Violence continues to plague South Africa
South Africa suffers from a murder rate of more than 60 a day on average, one of the highest globally.
The country recorded 5,427 murders between April and July — an average of 45 a day — according to the latest crime statistics.
Femicide rates in South Africa are among the highest in the world, according to the U.N.'s agency for gender equality. Last year, the government declared gender-based violence and femicide a national disaster, according to the U.N.
A 2024 study in South Africa revealed that three women were killed every day by an intimate partner from 2020 to 2021. A study in 2022 found that more than 35% of South African adult women had experienced physical or sexual violence at some point.
Amnesty International South Africa previously said the recent discovery of the bodies was "just another horrific reminder that women in South Africa are not safe."
The Commission for Gender Equality has called for urgent preventive action, including a safety audit of the affected areas involving police, municipal officials, transport authorities and community safety structures.
It said the audit should assess lighting, surveillance, pedestrian and public transport routes, neglected spaces, police visibility and access to emergency assistance.
"Women should not have to be killed before an area receives heightened attention," commission spokesperson Javu Baloyi said.

The United States wants to buy cheaper potash from Belarus; Trump announced preparations for a major deal
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
19:11:59 EEST
01:11:59 KST

The United States wants to buy cheaper potash from Belarus; Trump announced preparations for a major deal
Kyiv • UNN
The United States is negotiating the purchase of Belarusian potash fertilizers at a price lower than Canada's. The volume and timing of the deal have not been determined.
US President Donald Trump said that Washington is working on a large-scale deal to purchase potash fertilizers from Belarus. The specific parameters of the prospective deal have not yet been announced, UNN reports, citing a post by the American leader.
According to Trump, the US side expects to receive Belarusian potash at a price significantly lower than what the United States currently pays for supplies from Canada.
"The United States is working on a large-scale deal to purchase potash fertilizers from Belarus. The price will be significantly lower than what we are currently paying Canada, which is very good news for our farmers and ranchers," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Details
As of September 21, the White House had not released information about the possible volume of purchases, the value of the contract, or the timeline for its conclusion or the start of supplies. At present, the matter concerns negotiations on a prospective deal, not an already signed contract.
Trump's statement came amid the gradual restoration of economic contacts between Washington and Minsk. In March 2026, the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) removed Belaruskali and the Belarusian Potash Company from the US sanctions list. The decision was made after negotiations between the United States and the Belarusian authorities and the release of 250 prisoners, thus removing one of the main legal obstacles for US companies that might purchase Belarusian potash.
However, European restrictions remain in effect. Until 2022, a significant portion of Belarusian potash fertilizers was exported through the Lithuanian port of Klaipėda, but this route was closed after sanctions were imposed.
In May, Reuters reported that the United States had raised with Lithuania the issue of restoring the transit of Belarusian potash through Klaipėda. Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said at the time that Vilnius had no intention of discussing the resumption of supplies while EU sanctions remained in effect. European restrictions on Belarusian potash remain in force at least until February 2027. Therefore, even if the US-Belarusian deal is concluded, the route for delivering the fertilizers to the United States would remain a separate issue.
Why the US critically depends on potash imports
Washington's interest in a new supplier is explained by the significant dependence of US agriculture on imported potash fertilizers.
According to the US Geological Survey, in 2025, the United States' net import reliance on potash amounted to about 92% of domestic consumption. In 2021–2024, approximately 79% of US potash imports came from Canada. Russia supplied about 12% more, Israel 3%, and other suppliers accounted for about 6%. That is why the possible entry of Belarusian producers into the US market could provide the United States with an alternative source of fertilizers and intensify competition among suppliers.
How international markets reacted to the prospect of a deal between Washington and Minsk
The stock market has already reacted to Trump's statement. Shares of several major fertilizer producers, including Canada's Nutrien and the US-based Mosaic, declined after reports of a potential deal with Belarus. Investors view the prospect of cheaper Belarusian supplies as a possible factor putting pressure on potash fertilizer prices.
Context
The possible potash deal is being discussed amid intensified negotiations between Washington and Minsk. On September 15, US presidential special envoy John Coale met with Alexander Lukashenko. The parties discussed, among other issues, the release of prisoners and the unblocking of Belarusian assets in the United States. Coale said Washington was ready to facilitate the return of tens of millions of dollars in Belarusian funds blocked in US banks.
The following day, another 25 prisoners were released in Belarus. At the same time, the United States eased sanctions on two Belarusian enterprises. The American representative said he expected to continue negotiations on the release of hundreds more people in the near future.
Reminder
Trump's special envoy established contact with Lukashenko with the help of jokes and vodka.

Far-left leader pushing to lead Berlin says city has voted for change
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:09:24 UTC
01:09:24 KST

Far-left leader pushing to lead Berlin says city has voted for change
BERLIN, Sept 21 - The far-left leader pushing to take over as mayor of Berlin promised on Monday to tackle unaffordable rents in the German capital, but faced early pressure to take action over accusations of antisemitism in parts of the local party.
Elif Eralp led the Left Party to their best result in Berlin where they displaced Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative party in the mayor's office and look set to head a coalition governing the city for the first time.
"Berlin has clearly voted in favour of a change in policy, for an affordable Berlin where everyone can live with dignity, regardless of income or background, and for the rent crisis to be tackled consistently at long last," she said on Monday.
PLAN TARGETS CORPORATE LANDLORDS
Famously described by former mayor Klaus Wowereit as "poor but sexy", Berlin has become increasingly expensive and its once famously cheap rents are now a thing of the past.
Eralp has pledged to expropriate more than 200,000 housing units from corporate landlords in a campaign which saw the party, whose roots lie in the former East German communist party, make gains in central and western areas of the city as well as its traditional strongholds in the east.
"I still stand by that," she said on Monday, despite questions about how to finance a move the centre-left Social Democrats estimated would cost some €20 billion ($22.94 billion).
She said she aimed to reduce the influence of corporate landlords such as Deutsche Wohnen and Vonovia. Vonovia Chief Executive Luka Mucic said the group was ready to discuss solutions to Berlin's housing shortage but that "socialisation doesn't create any new housing".
Merz, who said the policy would have "devastating effects" on foreign investment if it were ever implemented, said he expected swift legislation to prevent expropriations.
MAMDANI AN EXAMPLE
Compared by some to New York mayor Zohran Mamdani, whose campaign to make the city more affordable saw him win an unexpected victory last year, the 45-year-old Eralp is the child of left-wing Turkish parents who sought asylum in Germany after a military coup in 1980.
Like Mamdani, her campaign focused heavily on personal campaigning and social media and she scored particularly strongly among the young, while winning support from thousands of Berliners who previously did not vote.
"As a woman, I'm reluctant to compare myself to a man. But naturally Mamdani's success was a big example for us," she said. "And we were very happy about it, because that election victory sent a very clear signal — not just to New York, but to the entire world."
Little known outside left-wing circles before the campaign, she now stands poised to lead the German capital at a time when the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made increasing gains across the country and posted its best-ever result in liberal Berlin.
Potential coalition partners in the centre-left Social Democrats and the environmental Greens have indicated they are ready to talk about forming a government.
But both have demanded Eralp address the longstanding accusations over antisemitism that have been levelled against some local branches of the Berlin party, often in connection with criticism of Israel.
The issue has been extremely sensitive in Germany, which has seen a surge in antisemitic incidents since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by the militant group Hamas and the Israeli campaign that has laid waste to Gaza and killed tens of thousands.
Merz said the rise in antisemitism was a "disgrace for Germany" and pledged action to combat incidents in Berlin that he said had caused concern to European partners.
Eralp said it was her "absolute priority" to ensure that Jewish people in Berlin along with Muslims and all other groups "feel safe and can lead a good life here".
"It is absolutely clear to me that the glorification of violence and terrorism is completely unacceptable," Eralp told a news conference. REUTERS

China expels 2 top generals from ruling party, military over discipline, law violations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:08:15 UTC
01:08:15 KST

Faisal Mahmud
21 September 2026•Update: 21 September 2026
- With latest purge, China’s top military decision-making body left with only 2 members, including President Xi Jinping
China on Monday expelled two of its most senior generals from the ruling Communist Party and military service over "serious discipline and law violations," state media reported.
The Communist Party of China’s (CPC) Political Bureau approved the expulsions of Zhang Youxia and Liu Zhenli after reviewing reports submitted by the Central Military Commission (CMC), according to state-run Xinhua News Agency.
Zhang, 75, served as a CPC Politburo member and CMC vice chairman, while Liu was a CMC member and chief of staff of its Joint Staff Department.
China’s top legislature removed both generals from the CMC last month after authorities opened investigations against them.
The Defense Ministry announced on Jan. 24 that Zhang and Liu were being investigated for suspected “serious discipline and law violations.”
The CMC, headed by President Xi Jinping, exercises overall command over the People’s Liberation Army.
Zhang had been China’s highest-ranking uniformed military officer.
The PLA Daily earlier accused the two generals of undermining Xi’s authority and Communist Party leadership over the armed forces and damaging military combat effectiveness.
Their removal follows investigations and expulsions involving several senior military officials, including former Defense Minister Li Shangfu and former CMC members He Weidong and Miao Hua, amid Beijing’s continuing anti-corruption campaign in the armed forces.
Who remains on CMC?
The latest expulsions leave the seven-member CMC formed at the Communist Party’s 20th National Congress in October 2022 with only two of its original members: Xi, who chairs the commission, and Gen. Zhang Shengmin, secretary of the CMC’s discipline inspection commission.
The other five original members — Zhang Youxia, He Weidong, Li Shangfu, Miao Hua and Liu Zhenli — have all been removed following investigations.
Zhang and Liu had been under investigation since Jan. 24 and were formally removed from the state CMC by China’s top legislature in August before Monday’s expulsions from the party and military.
The US-based Wall Street Journal reported in January, citing people familiar with a high-level briefing, that Zhang was accused of passing information about China’s nuclear weapons program to the US and accepting bribes linked to official decisions, including the promotion of an officer.
Beijing has not publicly confirmed the nuclear-related allegation.

22 countries back call to keep AI ‘under human control’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:06:51 UTC
01:06:51 KST

The motto "The future is human," used by The Be Human Company, is seen during the ALL IN 2026 conference in Montreal, Canada, on Sept. 17, 2026. | Andrek Ivanov/AFP via Getty Images
NEW YORK — Several European countries were among a group of 22 nations that adopted a declaration Monday saying that artificial intelligence “must remain under human direction, oversight and control” and suggesting to create a global supervisory regime.
The declaration, adopted on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week, acknowledged AI’s “potential to improve lives, advance science and strengthen our economies” but warned that “the rapid development of frontier AI models poses serious risks to safety and security if not appropriately managed.”
The push comes ahead of the meeting of U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the leaders of the world’s leading AI-developing nations, in Washington Thursday.
Advertisement
Neither the U.S. nor China are part of the new declaration. But Finnish President Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board: “I think it will be in the interest of both China and the United States to have some kind of guardrails. And our message here is that we need human intervention, so humans need to be in charge,” he said in an interview.
Referring to the recent cyberattack by rogue AI agents on the Hugging Face platform, the declaration urges to “address these risks” by obliging AI companies “to develop transparent safety protocols, including mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation, with qualified evaluators granted sufficient access to assess risks.”
Yet the document falls short of calling for slowing down or pausing AI development, with organizers saying they want to focus on managing risks instead.
Alexander Stubb, one of the main organizers of the document, told POLITICO that he hopes to create “momentum” and get more actors on board. | Alessandro Rampazzo/AFP via Getty Images
To do that, countries should “further develop and coordinate common standards” and strengthen transparency, “including shared reporting of serious safety incidents.” Moreover, UN member countries should “build on existing international mechanisms and explore creating an international institution” to oversee AI.
Stubb, who spoke to POLITICO at Finland’s consular office in New York, said that “our preference personally” would be to create a new institution similar to the International Atomic Energy Agency “within the U.N. framework.” Yet he added, with a nod to Trump’s skepticism of the United Nations, “we have to leave it open-ended so that people don’t reject it just because it would be within the U.N. framework.”
Norway’s Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who initiated the declaration together with Stubb and who joined the interview via video, said that, “we would be very encouraged to see both G7 and the upcoming G20 presidency of the United Kingdom take on this ... The U.N. is big, but the G7, G20 is a bit more focused.”
Advertisement
However, the U.K. has not signed up to the declaration yet. Among the big European countries, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz supports the initiative, while signatures from France, Italy and Poland are notably absent.
Stubb added that neither he nor Støre were “doomsdayers” about artificial intelligence but named three reasons why the lack of effective oversight is threatening: AI-created bioweapons, cyberattacks by AI agents and killer robots using AI for lethal attacks.
Stubb stressed that the upside of AI can be “much higher” — if the tech is used correctly — ranging from “the eradication of diseases, productivity, information and many other things.”

How to align AI development with global climate goals - Türkiye proposed an important agreement ahead of the COP31 summit
Kyiv • UNN
Türkiye initiated an agreement to align AI development with climate goals. It also proposed increasing the share of electricity\r\nto 35% by 2035.
Turkey, which will host the COP31 climate summit in Antalya in November, initiated the process of drafting a political agreement on Monday on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Its goal is to address the rapid growth in energy demand from artificial intelligence (AI) by committing countries to align the development of AI infrastructure with global climate goals, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
A new "Antalya Declaration on Artificial Intelligence" is being developed jointly with the UN International Telecommunication Union; its draft will be published ahead of the COP31 summit, the Turkish side, which will chair the conference, said.
"We must openly discuss the increase in energy consumption by AI systems, and it is time for governments to begin establishing appropriate rules. We expect companies to ensure transparency regarding energy consumption data and to use clean energy for their operations," said Murat Kurum, Turkey's Minister of Environment and Urbanization, who has been appointed president of COP31.
Ahead of the UN's annual climate summit, Turkey also officially presented its key initiative — a call for a global agreement to increase the share of electricity in final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. The initiative includes measures to electrify buildings, transport and industry.
The "35x35" initiative aims to encourage countries to use clean energy and energy storage systems, modernize power grids, and support developing countries in the process of moving away from fossil fuels.
Trump said that concerns about AI are being stoked by "negative forces"13.09.26, 18:01 • 4926 views
Electricity currently accounts for around 20% of global energy demand. The remainder is covered primarily by fossil fuels, as well as biofuels and waste, which account for around 10%.
The voluntary agreement also provides for the creation of a global mechanism to track joint progress in electrification.
Turkey said that one day of the COP summit would be dedicated to technology and artificial intelligence. An initiative will also be launched to create a "portfolio of AI-based clean technology pilot projects" that will bring together technology developers, industrial partners and investors, particularly in the automotive and heat pump manufacturing sectors.

How France’s 2027 election could reshape Palestine solidarity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-21
16:00:36 UTC
01:00:36 KST

Breadcrumb
How France’s 2027 election could reshape Palestine solidarity
France’s 2027 presidential election is, in many ways, a referendum on whether the country wants the far-right in power or a progressive left-wing future. The outcome will certainly shape how pro-Palestinian voices in France will be treated. Will they face more intense repression in the form of arrests, fines, dissolved organisations, and academic exile, or will they be able to organise, protest and speak out without fear of being criminalised?
The results of the race will also have a detrimental impact on Paris continuing to push for Palestinian statehood, a ceasefire and accountability for what happens in Gaza and the West Bank or whether it will instead fall fully behind Israel.
Whilst some might mistake the question of Palestine as a niche issue, in reality it is a test of how far a democracy will go in policing conscience and what role France chooses to play in the world beyond it.
Already a hostile climate
To understand what's at stake, it helps to remember that France did not wait for a far-right government to start restricting Palestine solidarity. Indeed, since October 2023, authorities have taken an increasingly restrictive approach towards Palestine activism. Police have used tear gas and water cannons against demonstrators, and the Interior Ministry even banned protests.
Under Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau, authorities have also sought to dissolve Urgence Palestine, one of France’s largest Palestine solidarity groups, accusing it of promoting and glorifying terrorism.
University students have also faced disciplinary and legal action over their involvement in Palestine solidarity protests. Some have even been accused of antisemitism linked to their anti-Zionist views. In May 2024, 88 Sorbonne University students were held in police custody after they took over a lecture hall in solidarity with Gaza.
Dozens of others have been handed criminal records and fined for “entering a school with the intent to disturb the peace or good order of the institution".
Concerns were also raised over the proposed Yadan bill that was introduced under the guise of strengthening the fight against antisemitism. However, it soon became clear that it was being used to repress criticism of Israel. One of its most controversial proposals would have made “incitement to the destruction of a state” a criminal offence, punishable by up to five years in prison and a €75,000 fine.
Critics warned that the broad wording used would restrict legitimate political speech or expressions of solidarity with Palestinians. Nevertheless, after significant pressure, the legislation was withdrawn.
What a far-right victory would likely mean
If the National Rally (NR) wins the presidency, the measures already available to the state could take on greater significance. NR leader Marine Le Pen, previously barred from standing after her fraud conviction, is now proving popular in early polling after her ban was lifted. Worryingly, this means she has a good chance of taking power, and would therefore inherit an extensive set of legal and administrative tools to restrict protests, prosecute certain forms of speech, and shut down solidarity groups.
We know this is highly likely under Le Pen because she has worked to present the RN as a defender of French Jews and a strong supporter of Israel, which marked a significant shift in the public image of a party that had a long history of antisemitism.
This repositioning has allowed the party to incorporate the fight against antisemitism into its broader emphasis on security, immigration and national identity. This has particular negative implications for Palestine and other forms of activism, young people, French Muslims and people of North African and Middle Eastern backgrounds who will likely face increased racism, Islamophobia, anti-migrant policies and a curtailment of civil liberties.
Given the party’s positions on public order, protest bans could also become more frequent through the weaponisation of counter-terrorism, as we’ve seen implemented across Europe and the US.
Online speech will also likely remain an important battleground. If legislation like the Yadan bill becomes law, one of the central questions will be where authorities draw the line between antisemitism, anti-Zionism and legitimate criticism of the Israeli government. After all, under a far-right administration, these boundaries are likely to widen rather than be clearly defined.
On the international stage, a far-right government would almost certainly pull France closer to Israel's positions, making it harder to advocate for aid to Gaza, a real ceasefire or accountability for Israeli crimes without that advocacy being cast as disloyalty or extremism.
It seems impossible to imagine that France will remain a country that recognises a Palestinian state under an RN presidency.
A different direction
On the other side of the political spectrum is Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise (LFI), a party that has made support for Palestinian rights a prominent part of its platform and has attracted significant support among younger and more diverse voters. This position stands in sharp contrast to the RN’s increasingly pro-Israel stance and reflects a wider political divide over how France should approach both the genocide and Palestine activism at home.
When the left-wing New Popular Front emerged as the largest bloc in the 2024 legislative elections, Mélenchon declared that recognising a Palestinian state should be among the priorities of a left-led government. LFI has also consistently criticised restrictions on Palestine demonstrations, as well as the use of terrorism allegations against activists and political figures who express solidarity.
A government led by LFI or the broader left would more likely resist legislation that blurs the distinction between antisemitism and criticism of Israel.
On the foreign policy front, such a government would also likely impose an arms embargo on Israel over its continued crimes in Gaza, while pushing more overtly for an independent Palestinian state and humanitarian assistance, as well as apply greater diplomatic pressure on the occupation.
Next year’s election will show the world whether France will vote to defend its democratic rights, like dissent, or fall for the divisive rhetoric of the far-right that will likely weaken people’s liberties.
Palestine activists and the Palestinian diaspora are understandably worried, given they are already in fear of the legal and professional repercussions that come with expressing their solidarity. A country led by the far-right will likely worsen their ability to exercise free speech, and criminalise them for daring to.
Ultimately, a democracy is tested not only by its willingness to protect speech it agrees with, but by how it responds to speech that challenges, unsettles and divides it.
Oman Alyahyai is a writer and journalist based in Paris.
